questions.stem: BULKING of sand is the phenomenon in which:
options: The VOLUME of sand INCREASES when it contains a small amount of MOISTURE
Sand becomes heavier when stored in bulk
Fine particles rise to the surface of a stockpile
Sand shrinks permanently after being wetted and dried
questions.solution:
**The volume of sand INCREASES when a small amount of moisture is present**, reaching a maximum at about 4 to 6 per cent moisture content.

**The mechanism:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Bone dry sand** | **Particles pack closely; no bulking** ← |
| **A little moisture added** | **A thin film of water forms on each grain, and SURFACE TENSION holds the grains apart** ← |
| **The grains are pushed apart** | **The same mass now occupies a greater VOLUME** ← |
| **Maximum bulking, at about 4 to 6 % moisture** | **Volume increase of 20 to 30 % for fine sand** ← |
| **More water still** | **The films merge, the water no longer holds the grains apart, and the sand SETTLES back** ← |
| **Fully SATURATED (flooded) sand** | **Volume returns essentially to that of dry sand** ← |

> **THE SHAPE OF THE CURVE IS WHAT MAKES BULKING DANGEROUS: it rises steeply, peaks, and comes back down.**

> **So sand that is merely DAMP occupies far more space than either dry sand or saturated sand, and a stockpile that has been rained on and then partly dried is at its worst.**

**Why it matters — VOLUME BATCHING of concrete:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A box of damp sand contains 20 to 30 % LESS sand by mass than the same box of dry sand** ← | **Which is the whole problem** ← |
| **A 1 : 2 : 4 mix batched by volume therefore becomes SAND-DEFICIENT** | **The actual mix might be 1 : 1.5 : 4** ← |
| **The concrete becomes HARSH, difficult to place and prone to honeycombing** | **Too little fine aggregate to fill the voids between the coarse** ← |
| **Strength and durability both suffer** | ← |

> **THE REMEDIES, in order of preference:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **Batch by MASS, not by volume** ← | **Mass is unaffected by bulking — the definitive answer, and the reason weigh-batching is specified for all structural concrete** ← |
| **Measure the bulking and increase the sand volume accordingly** | **By the field test below** ← |
| **FLOOD the measuring box** | **Saturated sand does not bulk, so a box filled and flooded gives the true volume — crude but effective** ← |

**The FIELD TEST for bulking, which is simple enough to do on any site:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Fill a measuring jar to a marked level, say 200 mm, with the damp sand, loosely** | ← |
| **Fill the jar with water and stir thoroughly, so the sand settles fully** | ← |
| **Read the new level of the sand, say 160 mm** | **This is the true, unbulked volume** ← |
| **Percentage bulking = (200 − 160) / 160 × 100 = 25 %** ← | **Note the denominator: the SETTLED volume, not the bulked one** ← |

> **THE DENOMINATOR IN THE LAST ROW IS THE DETAIL THAT IS MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG: bulking is expressed as a percentage of the TRUE (settled) volume, because that is the quantity of sand you actually have.**

> **Dividing by the bulked volume gives 20 per cent instead of 25, and it understates the correction needed.**

**And the grading effect, which is worth knowing:**

| Sand | Maximum bulking |
|---|---|
| **FINE sand** | **25 to 40 % — the most affected** ← |
| **Medium sand** | **About 20 to 25 %** |
| **COARSE sand** | **15 to 20 %** |
| **Gravel and coarse aggregate** | **NEGLIGIBLE — the grains are too heavy for surface tension to lift them apart** ← |

> **The trend follows directly from the mechanism: surface tension is a force acting on the grain SURFACE, and gravity acts on its VOLUME.**

> **The smaller the grain, the larger its surface area relative to its weight, and the more easily the water film can hold it apart from its neighbours.**

> **That is the same surface-area-to-volume argument that explains why fine particles need more water in a mix, why they dominate the fineness modulus, and why clay behaves so differently from sand — one idea doing a great deal of work across the subject.**

examTip.trick: **Damp sand bulks by 20-30 %, peaking at 4-6 % moisture; SATURATED sand does not bulk at all.** The curve rises, peaks and falls back.
examTip.trap: **Percentage bulking is divided by the SETTLED volume, not the bulked one** — (200−160)/160 = 25 %, not (200−160)/200 = 20 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **Weigh-batching is immune to bulking — that is why it is specified for structural concrete.** And fine sand bulks most because surface tension acts on AREA while gravity acts on VOLUME.

questions.stem: A RETARDING admixture is added to concrete principally to:
options: Increase the ultimate compressive strength
Reduce the quantity of cement required
DELAY the setting of the concrete
Entrain air for frost resistance
questions.solution:
**To DELAY the setting**, keeping the concrete workable for longer — in hot weather, over a long transport haul, or during a large continuous pour.

**When a retarder is needed:**

| Situation | Why |
|---|---|
| **HOT weather concreting** | **High temperature accelerates hydration; the concrete may stiffen before it can be placed and compacted** ← |
| **A long HAUL from the batching plant** | **Ready-mixed concrete travelling an hour or more in traffic** ← |
| **A large CONTINUOUS pour — a raft, a mat foundation, a bridge deck** ← | **Each layer must still be plastic when the next is placed, or a COLD JOINT forms** ← |
| **Slip-forming and complicated placing** | **Where the sequence takes time** ← |
| **To reduce the peak temperature rise in mass concrete** | **By spreading the heat of hydration over a longer period** ← |

> **THE COLD JOINT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE SPECIFIC DEFECT A RETARDER PREVENTS, and it is worth naming:**

> **If the lower layer of a large pour has already set when the next layer arrives, the two do not knit together. The result is a plane of weakness running through the member — no bond, no aggregate interlock, and a direct path for water.**

> **On a raft or a bridge deck the pour may take many hours, and the concrete placed first must still respond to the vibrator when the concrete above it is placed.**

> **A retarder buys exactly that time, and it is why large pours are planned around the initial setting time rather than around the concrete's strength.**

**The admixture families, so the retarder is placed among them:**

| Admixture | Effect | Common basis |
|---|---|---|
| **PLASTICISER (water reducer)** | **Same workability with 5 to 12 % LESS water — hence higher strength; or more workability at the same water** ← | Lignosulphonates |
| **SUPERPLASTICISER (high range)** | **A 15 to 30 % water reduction — makes high-strength and self-compacting concrete possible** ← | **Polycarboxylate ethers** ← |
| **RETARDER** | **Delays setting** ← | **Sugars, gypsum, lignosulphonates** ← |
| **ACCELERATOR** | **Speeds setting and early strength gain — cold weather, urgent formwork striking, repairs** ← | **Calcium chloride — but NEVER in reinforced or prestressed concrete** ← |
| **AIR ENTRAINING** | **Introduces microscopic bubbles for FROST resistance** ← (option d) | Vinsol resin |
| **Waterproofing / permeability reducing** | Reduces water penetration | ← |

> **THE CALCIUM CHLORIDE WARNING IN THE ACCELERATOR ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SINGLE FACT ABOUT ADMIXTURES, and it is worth repeating firmly: chloride ions destroy the passive film that protects steel reinforcement, and they cause corrosion that cannot be arrested.**

> **A cheap accelerator used to strike formwork a day earlier can destroy the structure over twenty years, and the damage is invisible until the concrete spalls.**

> **Chloride-free accelerators exist and cost more; the extra cost is trivial against the consequence, and codes now limit the total chloride content of the mix from all sources — cement, aggregate, water and admixture together.**

**Two cautions about retarders themselves, which the question's distractors point at:**

| Caution | Note |
|---|---|
| **A retarder does NOT reduce the ultimate strength** ← | **Indeed retarded concrete often gains slightly HIGHER ultimate strength, because slower hydration produces a denser gel — but the EARLY strength is lower, which is what matters for formwork** ← (option a is wrong for the wrong reason) |
| **OVERDOSING is a real risk** | **A large excess can prevent the concrete setting at all, and the remedy is demolition** ← |
| **The dosage is temperature-sensitive** | **A dose that works in October may be excessive in January** ← |
| **It is not a cement reducer** | **Option (b) describes what a water-reducing plasticiser can achieve indirectly, not a retarder** ← |

> **The overdosing hazard is why admixtures are dispensed by calibrated equipment rather than poured from a bucket, and why the dosage is expressed as a percentage of the CEMENT mass rather than of the batch — a detail that has caused failures when the person mixing did not know which.**

It remains workable for longer in hot weather or during a long haul or a large continuous pour.

examTip.trick: **A retarder DELAYS setting** — for hot weather, long hauls and large continuous pours. Option (d) is the air-entraining agent; option (b) is closer to a water reducer.
examTip.trap: **Retarding lowers EARLY strength but not the ultimate strength** — slower hydration often gives a slightly denser gel and marginally higher final strength.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never use CALCIUM CHLORIDE accelerator in reinforced or prestressed concrete** — chlorides destroy the steel's passive film and the corrosion cannot be stopped. A day saved on formwork costs the structure.

questions.stem: For ordinary Portland cement, the INITIAL setting time and the FINAL setting time specified by the standard are, respectively:
options: Not less than 10 minutes and not more than 90 minutes
Not less than 30 MINUTES and not more than 600 MINUTES (10 hours)
Not less than 60 minutes and not more than 24 hours
Not less than 2 hours and not more than 48 hours
questions.solution:
**Initial setting time NOT LESS than 30 minutes; final setting time NOT MORE than 600 minutes (10 hours).**

**The two limits, and why each is set where it is:**

| Limit | Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **INITIAL setting time** | **MINIMUM 30 minutes** ← | **The concrete must remain workable long enough to be MIXED, TRANSPORTED, PLACED and COMPACTED** ← |
| **FINAL setting time** | **MAXIMUM 600 minutes = 10 hours** ← | **The concrete must harden within a reasonable time, so that curing can start and the works can proceed** ← |

> **NOTE THE DIRECTION OF EACH LIMIT, WHICH IS THE CRUX OF THE QUESTION: the initial time has a MINIMUM (it must not set too fast) and the final time has a MAXIMUM (it must not take too long).**

> **They are not a range within which the setting must fall — they are two separate one-sided requirements at the two ends of the process.**

**What each term means physically:**

| Term | Definition | Measured by |
|---|---|---|
| **INITIAL SET** | **The paste begins to lose its plasticity — the point beyond which it must not be disturbed** ← | **The Vicat needle (1 mm square) fails to penetrate to within 5 to 7 mm of the bottom of the mould** ← |
| **FINAL SET** | **The paste has completely lost plasticity and has acquired sufficient firmness to resist a defined pressure** ← | **The Vicat needle with an annular attachment makes an impression, but the attachment does not** ← |

> **BOTH ARE MEASURED ON A PASTE OF STANDARD CONSISTENCY, using the same Vicat apparatus that determines the consistency itself — with a different attachment for each test, which is the detail examinations like to check.**

**Setting against HARDENING, which are constantly confused:**

| Process | What it is |
|---|---|
| **SETTING** | **The transition from a fluid paste to a rigid solid — a change of STATE, occurring in hours** ← |
| **HARDENING** | **The gain of STRENGTH after setting — continuing for months and years** ← |

> **A cement paste that has set has almost no strength; it is merely no longer plastic. The strength comes afterwards, from continued hydration, which is why CURING matters so much and for so long.**

**Setting times for the other cements, since they differ usefully:**

| Cement | Setting behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary Portland (OPC 33, 43, 53)** | **30 min / 600 min as above** ← |
| **RAPID HARDENING cement** | **Same setting times — it HARDENS faster, it does not SET faster** ← |
| **Portland POZZOLANA (PPC)** | **Setting times similar; slower early strength gain, higher long-term strength** ← |
| **QUICK SETTING cement** | **Initial set as low as 5 minutes, final set within 30 minutes — for underwater work and grouting** ← |
| **Low heat cement** | **Slower setting and hardening; for mass concrete** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE DISTINCTION THAT CATCHES PEOPLE OUT AND IT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM THE SETTING-VERSUS-HARDENING POINT: rapid hardening cement is not quick setting cement.**

> **Rapid hardening cement sets at the normal rate, giving the usual time to place and compact it, and then gains strength much faster — it reaches in three days what OPC reaches in seven.**

> **Quick setting cement is a genuinely different product with almost no working time, used where the concrete must set before flowing water can wash it away.**

> **Confusing them on site is consequential in both directions: quick setting cement in a normal pour is unplaceable, and rapid hardening cement will not stay put underwater.**

**And a note on what makes setting go wrong in practice:**

| Cause | Effect |
|---|---|
| **FALSE SET** | **The paste stiffens within minutes but recovers its plasticity on further mixing, with no heat evolved — caused by dehydrated gypsum in the cement** ← |
| **FLASH SET** | **Rapid, irreversible stiffening with considerable heat — caused by INSUFFICIENT gypsum, so the C₃A hydrates uncontrolled** ← |
| **Aged or badly stored cement** | **Absorbs moisture and carbon dioxide; lumps form and strength falls** ← |

> **The distinction in the first two rows is worth carrying: FALSE set is recoverable by continued mixing and does no harm; FLASH set is not recoverable and the batch must be discarded.**

> **It is also the practical justification for the gypsum added at the grinding stage — a few per cent of gypsum standing between usable cement and a material that would set in the mixer.**

examTip.trick: **Initial set NOT LESS than 30 minutes; final set NOT MORE than 600 minutes.** Two one-sided limits at opposite ends, not a range.
examTip.trap: **RAPID HARDENING cement is not QUICK SETTING cement** — rapid hardening sets at the normal rate and gains strength faster; quick setting has an initial set of about 5 minutes and is for underwater work.
examTip.mnemonic: **FALSE set recovers on further mixing (dehydrated gypsum, no heat); FLASH set does not (too little gypsum, much heat).** The few per cent of gypsum in cement stands between usable material and setting in the mixer.

questions.stem: In the EFFLORESCENCE test on burnt clay bricks, the brick is stood in water in a shallow dish until the water is absorbed and evaporated. The white deposit that may then appear on the brick surface indicates the presence of:
options: Excess clay in the brick
Under-burning of the brick
Free lime in the mortar used
SOLUBLE SALTS in the brick
questions.solution:
**SOLUBLE SALTS in the brick** — sulphates and chlorides of sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium — carried to the surface in solution and deposited there as the water evaporates.

**The mechanism, which is the same wherever efflorescence appears:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Soluble salts are present in the brick, from the clay or from the fuel used in firing** ← | **Or in the mortar, the sand or the ground water** ← |
| **Water enters the masonry — rain, rising damp, or the test's dish** ← | **And DISSOLVES the salts** ← |
| **The water migrates to the surface and EVAPORATES** ← | ← |
| **The salt is left behind as a white crystalline deposit** | **Efflorescence** ← |

> **THREE THINGS MUST BE PRESENT TOGETHER, and removing any one of them stops it: SALTS, WATER, and a path for EVAPORATION.**

> **That is the key to both diagnosis and cure — and since the salts are usually already in the material, the practical remedy is nearly always to stop the WATER.**

**The test and its rating:**

| Rating | Deposit |
|---|---|
| **NIL** | **No perceptible deposit** ← |
| **SLIGHT** | **Up to 10 % of the exposed area covered** ← |
| **MODERATE** | **10 to 50 %, but no powdering or flaking** ← |
| **HEAVY** | **More than 50 %, but no powdering or flaking** ← |
| **SERIOUS** | **A thick deposit, WITH powdering or flaking of the surface** ← |

> **Standards typically require the efflorescence to be NOT MORE THAN "slight" for first class bricks, and not more than "moderate" for lower classes.**

**Why it matters, and why it is more than a cosmetic defect:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Unsightly white staining, especially on fair-faced brickwork** | **The obvious one** |
| **The salts CRYSTALLISE within the pores just below the surface** ← | **CRYPTO-florescence, which is far more damaging** ← |
| **Crystal growth exerts pressure and SPALLS the brick face** ← | **The "serious" rating's powdering and flaking** ← |
| **Paint and plaster applied over it FAIL** | **The deposit prevents adhesion and lifts the finish off** ← |
| **Repeated wetting and drying makes it worse over years** | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS DESCRIBE THE REAL DAMAGE, and the distinction is worth knowing:**

> **When the salt crystallises ON the surface, the result is ugly but harmless — it can be brushed off dry.**

> **When evaporation happens just BELOW the surface, the crystals grow inside the pores, and the pressure they generate is enough to break the brick face away.**

> **Which of the two happens depends on the rate of evaporation and the brick's pore structure — a dense, slow-drying brick is more likely to suffer the damaging form, which is a counter-intuitive result worth remembering.**

**Prevention and treatment:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Use bricks tested and found low in soluble salts** | **The test exists for exactly this purpose** ← |
| **Keep bricks off the ground and covered before use** | **Ground water is a common salt source** ← |
| **An effective DAMP PROOF COURSE** ← | **Stops rising damp, which is the commonest water path** ← |
| **Good rainwater disposal, copings, sills and drips** | **Stops water entering from above** ← |
| **Brush off DRY with a stiff brush** | **The correct treatment for a fresh deposit** ← |
| **Do NOT wash it off with water** ← | **Washing dissolves the salt and carries it straight back INTO the brick, to reappear next time it dries** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL POINT THAT IS ALMOST ALWAYS GOT WRONG ON SITE, and it deserves the emphasis: the instinctive response to a white stain is to wash it off, and washing makes it worse.**

> **The salt has come out of the brick and is sitting on the surface where it can be removed permanently with a dry brush. Wetting it puts it back in solution, and it soaks back in to emerge again.**

> **Efflorescence also tends to diminish of its own accord over the first year or two as the finite supply of salts is exhausted — provided the water is stopped. If it keeps recurring after several years, there is a continuing source of water, and that, not the staining, is the problem to solve.**

Carried to the surface by water and left there as the water evaporates.

examTip.trick: **Soluble salts dissolved by water, carried to the surface, left as the water evaporates.** Ratings: nil, slight, moderate, heavy, serious — first class bricks must not exceed SLIGHT.
examTip.trap: **Crystallisation just BELOW the surface (crypto-florescence) spalls the brick face** — far worse than the visible deposit, and more likely in a dense, slow-drying brick.
examTip.mnemonic: **Brush it off DRY — never wash it.** Washing redissolves the salt and carries it back into the brick to reappear. And recurrence after a year or two means a continuing WATER source, which is the real problem.

questions.stem: UNDERPINNING in building construction is the operation of:
options: STRENGTHENING or DEEPENING the foundation of an EXISTING structure, by transferring its load to a lower or firmer stratum
Supporting a wall temporarily with inclined props while it is repaired
Providing a horizontal member over an opening
Filling voids beneath a floor slab with lean concrete
questions.solution:
**Strengthening or deepening the foundation of an EXISTING structure**, transferring its load to a lower or firmer stratum.

**When underpinning is needed:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The existing foundation has SETTLED, or is settling** ← | **Because it was inadequate, or the soil has deteriorated** ← |
| **An ADJACENT excavation goes deeper than the existing foundation** ← | **A new basement next door removes the lateral support of the old footing — the commonest cause in urban work** ← |
| **Additional STOREYS are to be added** | **The existing foundation cannot carry the increased load** ← |
| **The use of the building changes to a heavier one** | ← |
| **The soil has been weakened** | **By a leaking drain, a rising or falling water table, or nearby tunnelling** ← |
| **A basement is to be added beneath an existing building** | ← |

> **Options (b), (c) and (d) describe SHORING, a LINTEL and grouting respectively — the first of these being the one most often confused with underpinning, and the distinction is clear once stated:**

> **SHORING is TEMPORARY support given from the side or above while other work proceeds. UNDERPINNING is a PERMANENT reconstruction of the foundation from below.**

> **Shoring holds the building up while you work; underpinning is the work.**

**The methods:**

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **PIT (traditional) method** | **The wall is underpinned in short SECTIONS — "legs" or "bays" — each excavated, the new foundation built beneath, and dry-packed up to the old work before the next is started** ← |
| **PILE method** | **Piles are driven or bored on both sides of the wall and connected by needle beams beneath it** ← |
| **NEEDLE and pile / cantilever needle** | **Where access is available on one side only** ← |
| **JACK PILE** | **Segmental piles jacked down against the existing structure's own weight — useful in restricted headroom** ← |
| **Chemical / grout injection** | **Strengthening the soil rather than replacing the foundation** ← |
| **MINI-PILING** | **Small-diameter piles for restricted access — the common modern solution** ← |

> **THE PIT METHOD'S "SHORT SECTIONS" RULE IS THE GOVERNING PRINCIPLE OF ALL UNDERPINNING, and it is the thing to state if asked how it is done safely:**

> **You never excavate under the whole wall at once. You work in short lengths — typically 1.0 to 1.5 m, and not more than about a quarter of the wall's length open at any one time — with each section completed before the next adjacent one is begun.**

> **The masonry above spans, arch-like, across the short gap while it is open, and the intact lengths on either side carry the load.**

> **The sequence in which the bays are taken is planned so that no two adjacent bays are ever open together, and it is a genuine piece of structural reasoning rather than a rule of thumb — get the sequence wrong and the wall has no support over a length it cannot span.**

**The other essential precautions:**

| Precaution | Note |
|---|---|
| **A thorough survey of the existing structure FIRST** ← | **Existing cracks recorded and marked, with tell-tales or gauges, BEFORE work begins** ← |
| **The building may need SHORING while underpinning proceeds** | **The two operations often go together** ← |
| **DRY PACKING the gap between new and old work** ← | **A very dry, rammed mortar — because ordinary mortar SHRINKS, leaving a gap, and the load is then never actually transferred** ← |
| **Continuous MONITORING of levels and cracks throughout** | ← |
| **The adjoining owner notified, and their property surveyed too** | **A legal requirement in many jurisdictions, and prudent everywhere** ← |

> **THE DRY PACKING IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE DETAIL ON WHICH THE WHOLE OPERATION SUCCEEDS OR FAILS, and it is easily underestimated: you may build a perfect new foundation beneath the wall, but if the joint between it and the old work shrinks by a few millimetres, the old foundation is still carrying the load and nothing has been achieved.**

> **Hence the very dry mix rammed hard into the gap, and hence also the practice of leaving the final packing until the new concrete has taken up most of its own shrinkage.**

> **THE TELL-TALES IN THE FIRST ROW SERVE A PURPOSE THAT IS AS MUCH LEGAL AS TECHNICAL: recording the existing cracks before starting establishes what was already there, and an adjoining owner's claim that the work caused damage is answered by the survey rather than by argument.**

examTip.trick: **Underpinning = PERMANENT reconstruction of an existing foundation from below. SHORING = TEMPORARY support from the side or above.** Shoring holds the building up while you work; underpinning is the work.
examTip.trap: **Never open more than short bays (1.0-1.5 m), and never two adjacent bays together** — the wall arches across the gap while it is open, so the sequence is structural reasoning, not a rule of thumb.
examTip.mnemonic: **DRY PACK the joint** — ordinary mortar shrinks, leaves a gap, and the load is never transferred, so a perfect new foundation achieves nothing. And record existing cracks with tell-tales BEFORE starting.

questions.stem: Comparing ENGLISH BOND and FLEMISH BOND in brick masonry:
options: Flemish bond is stronger and English bond gives a better appearance
Both are identical in strength and appearance
ENGLISH bond is STRONGER, while FLEMISH bond gives a better APPEARANCE and uses more brickbats
Neither can be used for walls thicker than one brick
questions.solution:
**ENGLISH bond is the STRONGER; FLEMISH bond gives the better APPEARANCE but requires more brickbats (cut bricks).**

**The two bonds:**

| Feature | ENGLISH BOND | FLEMISH BOND |
|---|---|---|
| **Arrangement** | **ALTERNATE COURSES of headers and stretchers** ← | **Headers and stretchers ALTERNATING within EVERY course** ← |
| **Strength** | **STRONGER — the preferred bond for structural walls** ← | **Somewhat weaker** ← |
| **Appearance** | **Plainer, more utilitarian** | **BETTER — the regular chequer pattern of headers is more attractive** ← |
| **Brickbats (cut bricks)** | **Fewer — a queen closer next to each quoin header** ← | **MORE — a large number of cut bricks is unavoidable** ← |
| **Economy** | **More economical** ← | **Less — more cutting, more labour, more waste** ← |
| **Longitudinal joints** | **Fewer continuous vertical joints through the thickness** ← | **More — which is the source of the weakness** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW EXPLAINS THE STRENGTH DIFFERENCE, and it is the answer to give if asked WHY English bond is stronger:**

> **A wall's strength through its thickness depends on the courses being properly tied front to back. English bond's full course of headers ties the whole thickness together at every second course.**

> **Flemish bond ties it with individual headers scattered along each course, which leaves more continuous vertical joints running through the wall's thickness — and a continuous joint is a plane on which the wall can split.**

> **The difference is not enormous, which is why Flemish bond is perfectly acceptable for ordinary walls; but for heavily loaded work, and for any wall where strength governs, English bond is specified.**

**Where each is used:**

| Bond | Typical use |
|---|---|
| **ENGLISH** | **Structural load-bearing walls, retaining walls, foundations, engineering work** ← |
| **FLEMISH — double** | **Fair-faced work seen on both sides — garden walls, boundary walls, exposed piers** ← |
| **FLEMISH — single** | **Flemish appearance on the face, English bond behind — the best of both, for a wall seen from one side only** ← |
| **STRETCHER (running) bond** | **HALF-BRICK walls only — partitions, and the outer leaf of a cavity wall** ← |
| **HEADER bond** | **Curved walls and footings, where the short face suits the curve** ← |

> **THE SINGLE FLEMISH ROW IN THE MIDDLE IS THE PRACTICAL COMPROMISE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: the facing course is laid in Flemish bond for appearance, and the backing in English bond for strength.**

> **It gets the attractive face where it can be seen and the stronger arrangement where it cannot, at the cost of a little more skill from the bricklayer — which is a good example of how masonry practice resolves competing requirements by putting each in the place where it matters.**

**The rules that ALL bonds obey, since these are the examinable fundamentals:**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Vertical joints in consecutive courses must NOT coincide** ← | **A continuous vertical joint is a crack waiting to happen — the load cannot distribute across it** ← |
| **The LAP is a quarter brick minimum** ← | **Achieved with a QUEEN CLOSER — a brick cut lengthwise in half, placed next to the quoin header** ← |
| **Courses must be horizontal and of uniform thickness** | ← |
| **The face and the backing must be BONDED to each other** | **Not two independent leaves standing side by side** ← |
| **Bricks must be soaked before laying** | **A dry brick sucks the water from the mortar and the mortar never gains strength** ← |

> **THE QUEEN CLOSER'S JOB IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISSTATED: it is not a decorative or filling brick, it is the device that DISPLACES the course by a quarter brick so that the lap is achieved at the quoin.**

> **Omit it and the vertical joints line up straight down the corner of the wall — which is precisely the weakest place to have them, since a corner is where two walls must act together.**

> **THE SOAKING RULE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN IGNORED ON SITE and it has a direct effect on strength: a dry brick draws water out of the mortar within seconds, and mortar that loses its water cannot hydrate. The joint then has a fraction of its intended strength, and no inspection afterwards will reveal it.**

examTip.trick: **ENGLISH = alternate courses of headers and stretchers, STRONGER, fewer brickbats. FLEMISH = headers and stretchers alternating in EVERY course, better looking, more cut bricks.**
examTip.trap: **English bond is stronger because a full header course ties the thickness front-to-back at every second course**, leaving fewer continuous vertical joints through the wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **SINGLE Flemish is the compromise: Flemish face, English backing.** And a QUEEN CLOSER is not decoration — it displaces the course by a quarter brick so the lap is achieved at the quoin.

questions.stem: A rectangular section is 200 mm wide and 300 mm deep. Its SECTION MODULUS about the centroidal axis parallel to the width is:
options: 2.0 × 10⁶ mm³
3.0 × 10⁶ mm³
4.5 × 10⁶ mm³
9.0 × 10⁶ mm³
questions.solution:
**3.0 × 10⁶ mm³.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Section modulus** | **Z = I / y_max** ← |
| **For a rectangle about the centroidal axis** | **I = b d³ / 12, and y_max = d / 2** ← |
| **So** | **Z = (b d³ / 12) ÷ (d / 2) = b d² / 6** ← |
| **Substituting b = 200 mm, d = 300 mm** | **Z = 200 × 300² / 6 = 200 × 90,000 / 6** |
| **Z** | **= 18,000,000 / 6 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³** ← |

> **Option (a) 2.0 × 10⁶ is the value with b and d INTERCHANGED — that is, bending about the other axis, which is a different and much weaker section.**

> **Options (c) and (d) use bd²/4 and bd²/2, wrong divisors.**

**Why Z is worth having as a separate quantity:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bending stress σ = M y / I** | **The general form** |
| **At the extreme fibre, y = y_max** | **Which is where the stress is greatest and where the check is made** ← |
| **So σ_max = M / Z** ← | **A single division, with no need to carry I and y separately** ← |
| **And the design form: Z_required = M / σ_permissible** ← | **The section is chosen directly** ← |

> **THAT LAST LINE IS THE WHOLE VALUE OF THE SECTION MODULUS: it converts a strength requirement straight into a geometric requirement.**

> **Given the moment and the permissible stress you obtain a required Z, and then look for a section whose Z equals or exceeds it — which is exactly how a steel section is selected from a table, and why steel section tables list Z prominently alongside I.**

**The d² TERM AND ITS CONSEQUENCE, which is the most useful thing here:**

| Change | Effect on Z |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLE the width b** | **Z DOUBLES — proportional** ← |
| **DOUBLE the depth d** | **Z QUADRUPLES — it goes as d²** ← |

> **DEPTH IS WORTH FAR MORE THAN WIDTH IN BENDING, and that single fact explains an enormous amount of structural form:**

> **It is why beams are deep and narrow rather than square; why a plank laid on edge carries several times what it carries laid flat; why joists are turned on edge; why an I-section puts nearly all its material in the flanges as far from the neutral axis as possible.**

> **The present section illustrates it directly: 200 × 300 gives Z = 3.0 × 10⁶, and the same rectangle turned on its side gives only 2.0 × 10⁶ — a third less capacity from exactly the same quantity of material, differing only in orientation.**

**And a caution about pushing depth too far:**

| Limit | Note |
|---|---|
| **A very deep, thin section buckles LATERALLY** ← | **Lateral torsional buckling — it twists and deflects sideways before the bending stress is reached** ← |
| **The web may buckle in SHEAR** | **Hence web stiffeners in plate girders** ← |
| **Headroom and floor depth limit it in practice** | ← |
| **Deflection and vibration must also be checked** | **A slender deep beam may satisfy stress and still be unserviceable** ← |

> **So the depth is increased until one of those constraints bites, and structural design in bending is largely the business of getting the material as far from the neutral axis as the buckling and the headroom will allow.**

> **The I-section is the mature answer to that problem: flanges out at the extremes where the d² term rewards them, a web just thick enough to carry the shear and to hold the flanges apart, and stiffeners where the web would otherwise buckle.**

examTip.trick: **Z = I/y_max = (bd³/12)/(d/2) = bd²/6 = 200 × 300²/6 = 3.0 × 10⁶ mm³.** Option (a) has b and d swapped — the weaker axis.
examTip.trap: **Z goes as d² but only as b¹** — double the depth and Z quadruples; double the width and it merely doubles. The same rectangle on its side gives a third less capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Z_required = M / σ_permissible** turns a strength requirement straight into a geometric one — which is how a steel section is picked from a table. Depth is limited by lateral buckling, not by the algebra.

questions.stem: The PARALLEL AXIS theorem for the moment of inertia of a plane area states that:
options: I about any axis = I about the PARALLEL CENTROIDAL axis + A h², where A is the area and h the distance between the two axes
I about any axis = I about the parallel centroidal axis − A h²
The moment of inertia about a polar axis equals the sum of the moments of inertia about two perpendicular axes in the plane
The moment of inertia is independent of the axis chosen
questions.solution:
**I = I_G + A h²** — the moment of inertia about any axis equals that about the PARALLEL CENTROIDAL axis plus the area times the square of the distance between them.

**The statement:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **I** | **Moment of inertia about the axis in question** |
| **I_G** | **Moment of inertia about the PARALLEL axis through the CENTROID** ← |
| **A** | **The area of the section** |
| **h** | **The perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes** ← |

> **THE TERM A h² IS ALWAYS POSITIVE, since h is squared — which yields the most useful corollary of the theorem:**

> **The moment of inertia about the CENTROIDAL axis is the MINIMUM of all parallel axes. Move away from the centroid in either direction and I increases.**

> **Option (b) reverses the sign and would make the centroidal value the maximum, which is impossible.**

> **Option (c) states the PERPENDICULAR axis theorem — I_zz = I_xx + I_yy — a different and equally important result, which is what makes it a good distractor.**

**Using it — the standard procedure for a composite section:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Divide the section into simple rectangles, triangles and circles** | ← |
| **2. Find the CENTROID of the whole section** | **Take moments of area about a convenient reference line: ȳ = Σ(A y) / ΣA** ← |
| **3. For each part, compute I about ITS OWN centroid** | **bd³/12 for a rectangle, and so on** ← |
| **4. TRANSFER each part's I to the composite centroidal axis** | **Adding A h², with h the distance from that part's centroid to the whole section's centroid** ← |
| **5. SUM them** | **I_total = Σ(I_own + A h²)** ← |

> **THE ORDER OF STEPS 2 AND 4 IS WHERE MOST ERRORS OCCUR, and the rule is simple: you must find the composite centroid BEFORE transferring anything, because h is measured to that centroid.**

> **Transferring to some other convenient line and then hoping to correct later works, but only if the final correction is made with the TOTAL area and the distance from that line to the true centroid — and it is easy to omit.**

**Why the A h² term is so often DOMINANT, which is the practical insight:**

| Case | Note |
|---|---|
| **The flange of an I-section** | **A thin plate has a tiny I of its own (bd³/12 with d small), but sits at a large h from the neutral axis** ← |
| **So A h² is many times the flange's own I** ← | **Frequently 50 or 100 times** ← |
| **The consequence** | **Nearly all an I-section's stiffness comes from the TRANSFER term, not from the flanges' own bending stiffness** ← |

> **THIS IS THE ANALYTICAL EXPRESSION OF WHY MATERIAL IS PUT AT THE EXTREMES, and it connects the theorem directly to structural form:**

> **A flange plate lying flat has almost no bending stiffness on its own. Placed 300 mm from the neutral axis, it contributes A × 300² — an enormous quantity — simply because of where it is.**

> **So the designer's lever is POSITION rather than the shape of the individual parts, and the whole logic of I-sections, box girders, trusses and hollow tubes follows from that one term.**

> **A truss is the extreme case: two chords with essentially no bending stiffness of their own, separated by a large depth, connected by a web of members whose only job is to hold them apart and carry the shear. Almost 100 per cent of its stiffness is A h².**

**And a common trap worth flagging:**

> **The theorem transfers between PARALLEL axes only, and one of the two must pass through the CENTROID.**

> **It cannot be used to jump directly between two arbitrary non-centroidal axes in one step — you must transfer down to the centroidal axis first and then out again, which changes the sign of the first operation.**

> **Attempting a single-step transfer between two off-centre axes is a standard examination error, and it gives an answer that is wrong by 2 A h₁ h₂ rather than obviously absurd, so it survives a sanity check.**

examTip.trick: **I = I_G + A h².** Option (c) is the PERPENDICULAR axis theorem (I_zz = I_xx + I_yy) — a different result, and a well-made distractor.
examTip.trap: **A h² is always positive, so the CENTROIDAL axis gives the MINIMUM I** of all parallel axes. Option (b)'s minus sign would make it the maximum, which is impossible.
examTip.mnemonic: **The transfer term dominates**: an I-section flange contributes 50-100 times more through A h² than through its own bd³/12. Position, not shape, is the designer's lever — and a truss is the extreme case.

questions.stem: A tacheometer with a multiplying constant of 100 and an additive constant of zero is sighted on a vertically held staff, the line of sight being horizontal. The stadia hair readings are 1.150 m and 2.400 m. The horizontal distance to the staff is:
questions.solution:
**125 m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Staff INTERCEPT** | **S = upper reading − lower reading = 2.400 − 1.150 = 1.250 m** ← |
| **Stadia formula, horizontal sight** | **D = K S + C** ← |
| **With K = 100 and C = 0** | **D = 100 × 1.250 + 0** |
| **Horizontal distance** | **= 125 m** ← |

> **The wrong options are the right figure with the decimal point in the wrong place, which is exactly the error the arithmetic invites — so it is worth pausing on the magnitude: an intercept of 1.25 m with a multiplier of 100 must give something of the order of a hundred metres, and 12.5 m or 1,250 m are both implausible for a staff sight.**

**The constants and where they come from:**

| Constant | Meaning | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **K — the MULTIPLYING constant** | **f / i, the focal length divided by the stadia hair spacing** ← | **Almost universally 100, by design** ← |
| **C — the ADDITIVE constant** | **f + d, the focal length plus the distance from the objective to the instrument's vertical axis** ← | **Zero for an ANALLATIC telescope; about 0.3 m for older external-focusing instruments** ← |

> **THE ANALLATIC LENS IS WORTH KNOWING ABOUT because it explains why C is almost always zero in practice: an additional lens is fitted inside the telescope which brings the apparent origin of the sighting rays to the instrument's vertical axis.**

> **With that done, C vanishes and the formula reduces to the very convenient D = 100 S — the distance in metres is simply a hundred times the intercept in metres, which can be read off mentally at the instrument.**

> **That convenience is the whole reason K is set to exactly 100 rather than to whatever the optics happen to give.**

**The INCLINED sight, since a horizontal line of sight is the exception in hilly ground:**

| Quantity | Formula (staff held VERTICAL, angle of elevation θ) |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal distance** | **D = K S cos²θ + C cos θ** ← |
| **Vertical component** | **V = K S (sin 2θ)/2 + C sin θ** ← |
| **Reduced level of the staff station** | **RL = instrument RL + h_i + V − middle hair reading** ← |

> **THE cos²θ IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE PART TO REMEMBER, and it has a satisfying explanation: one cosine projects the SLOPE distance onto the horizontal, exactly as expected — and the SECOND cosine appears because the staff is held VERTICAL rather than perpendicular to the line of sight, so the intercept the instrument reads is longer than the true perpendicular intercept by a further factor of cos θ.**

> **If the staff were held NORMAL to the line of sight, the second cosine would disappear. It is held vertical because that is what a staff-holder can actually do reliably on a hillside, and the arithmetic absorbs the consequence.**

**Where tacheometry is used, and why it survives:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Rapid topographic and contour surveying** ← | **Distance and height from a single observation, with no chaining** ← |
| **Broken, steep or inaccessible ground** ← | **Where taping is difficult, slow or impossible — the Himalayan case** ← |
| **Across obstacles — rivers, ravines, standing crops** | ← |
| **Preliminary surveys where speed matters more than millimetre accuracy** | **Accuracy is about 1 in 400 to 1 in 1,000** ← |

> **Its accuracy is modest by modern standards, and total stations with EDM have displaced it for new work — measuring the same distance to a few millimetres in a second.**

> **But the method retains real value: it needs no power, no prism, no reflector and no electronics, and a theodolite and a levelling staff will work in a place where a total station's battery has died or where the instrument cannot be risked.**

> **It is also the clearest way to understand what an EDM instrument is doing, which is why it stays on the syllabus long after it left most field parties.**

examTip.trick: **S = 2.400 − 1.150 = 1.250 m; D = KS + C = 100 × 1.250 + 0 = 125 m.** All the wrong options are decimal-point slips — sanity-check the magnitude.
examTip.trap: **K = 100 and C = 0 are by DESIGN, not by accident** — the anallatic lens moves the apparent ray origin to the vertical axis so that C vanishes and D = 100 S can be read mentally.
examTip.mnemonic: **Inclined sight, vertical staff: D = KS cos²θ.** One cosine projects the slope onto the horizontal; the SECOND appears only because the staff is held vertical instead of normal to the sight.

questions.stem: In the detailed estimate of a building, the CENTRE LINE method of computing quantities differs from the LONG WALL–SHORT WALL method in that the centre line method:
options: Can only be used for circular buildings
Uses the TOTAL LENGTH of the centre line of all the walls, with a deduction at each junction
Measures each wall separately from outside face to outside face
Is used only for estimating the cost of finishes
questions.solution:
**It uses the TOTAL LENGTH of the centre line of all the walls — one length, with a deduction at each junction — so the same length serves for excavation, for every step of the footing, and for the superstructure.**

**The two methods:**

| Method | How the length is obtained |
|---|---|
| **LONG WALL – SHORT WALL** | **The long walls are measured OUT to OUT and the short walls IN to IN, SEPARATELY for each layer — and because each layer has a different width, both lengths change from layer to layer** ← |
| **CENTRE LINE** | **The total centre line length of all walls is computed ONCE. It is the SAME for every layer, since the centre line does not move as the width changes** ← |

> **THAT LAST SENTENCE IS THE WHOLE ADVANTAGE OF THE METHOD: the footing is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so the out-to-out and in-to-in lengths change at every step — but the CENTRE LINE stays exactly where it is.**

> **One length, computed once, multiplied by each layer's own width and depth. The arithmetic collapses from a table of changing lengths to a single constant, and the commonest source of error in a detailed estimate disappears with it.**

**The JUNCTION DEDUCTION, which is the one thing the method requires care with:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **At every junction of walls, deduct HALF the layer's WIDTH for EACH side of the junction** ← | **Because the centre lines cross, and the corner would otherwise be counted twice** ← |
| **For a simple rectangular building** | **Four corners, each a right-angle junction: total deduction = 4 × 2 × (W/2) = 4 W** ← |
| **For a T-junction (a cross wall meeting a main wall)** | **Deduct W/2 × 2 = W for that junction** ← |
| **The deduction DEPENDS on the layer's width W** ← | **So it changes from layer to layer even though the gross centre line length does not** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN, and forgetting it is the method's characteristic error: people are so pleased that the centre line length is constant that they apply the same DEDUCTION to every layer too.**

> **The gross centre line length is constant; the deduction is not, because it is a function of the layer's width. A 900 mm wide footing course loses more at the corners than a 300 mm wide wall does.**

> **Get that wrong and the estimate is consistently short at the bottom and long at the top, which is exactly the sort of error that does not look wrong on the page.**

**When to prefer each:**

| Situation | Method |
|---|---|
| **A building with walls of UNIFORM thickness throughout** | **CENTRE LINE — much quicker, and less error-prone** ← |
| **Walls of DIFFERENT thicknesses meeting at a junction** | **LONG WALL – SHORT WALL, or the centre line method applied SEPARATELY to each thickness group** ← |
| **Complicated plan with many offsets and re-entrants** | **Long wall – short wall is safer, since each length is explicit** ← |
| **Circular, curved or irregular plans** | **Centre line, using the mean circumference** ← |

> **The second row is the real limitation and it is worth being clear about: where a 230 mm wall meets a 350 mm wall, their centre lines do not intersect at a single convenient point, and the deduction rule becomes awkward.**

> **The remedy is to break the building into groups of equal-thickness walls and apply the method within each group — which preserves most of its speed while keeping the arithmetic honest.**

**And the wider point about estimating method, since this is the subject's recurring theme:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **BOTH methods must give the SAME answer** ← | **They are two routes to one quantity, and if they disagree, one of them is wrong** ← |
| **Which is why checking a doubtful quantity by the OTHER method is standard practice** ← | **An independent route, not a re-reading of the same arithmetic** ← |
| **Quantities should be taken in a fixed, documented ORDER** | **So that nothing is missed and another person can follow the take-off** ← |
| **Show the dimensions, not just the result** | **A quantity without its dimensions cannot be checked or corrected** ← |

> **The second row is the most valuable habit in the whole subject: re-adding your own column finds arithmetic slips but never finds a wrong method or an omitted item, whereas an independent route finds all three.**

> **It is the same principle as checking a structural calculation by an approximate hand method rather than by re-running the same analysis — the value lies in the independence, not in the precision.**

A single length serves for every layer of the footing.

examTip.trick: **Centre line length is the SAME for every layer of the footing, because the centre line does not move as the width changes.** One length, multiplied by each layer's own width and depth.
examTip.trap: **The DEDUCTION is not constant even though the length is** — deduct W/2 per side at each junction, and W changes layer by layer. A 900 mm footing loses more at the corners than a 300 mm wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Both methods must give the same answer**, so check a doubtful quantity by the OTHER one — an independent route finds wrong methods and omitted items, which re-adding your own column never will.

questions.stem: The ACTIVITY of a clay is defined as the ratio of:
options: Liquid limit to plastic limit
PLASTICITY INDEX to the percentage of clay-size particles (finer than 2 micrometres)
Natural water content to liquid limit
Plastic limit to the percentage of clay-size particles
questions.solution:
**Activity = PLASTICITY INDEX ÷ (percentage of particles finer than 2 μm).**

**Why the definition takes this form:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **The plasticity index measures how much water a soil can absorb while remaining plastic** ← | **A property of the whole soil** |
| **But that depends on TWO things: how much clay there is, and what KIND of clay it is** ← | ← |
| **Dividing PI by the clay FRACTION removes the first** ← | **Leaving a measure of the clay MINERAL's own character** ← |
| **So activity isolates the mineralogy from the quantity** | **Which is exactly what makes it useful** ← |

> **Two soils can have the same plasticity index — one being a large quantity of an inactive clay, the other a small quantity of a very active one — and they will behave quite differently. Activity separates them.**

**The classification and the minerals:**

| Activity | Class | Typical mineral |
|---|---|---|
| **Below 0.75** | **INACTIVE** ← | **KAOLINITE — activity about 0.4 to 0.5** ← |
| **0.75 to 1.25** | **NORMAL** | **ILLITE — about 0.9** ← |
| **Above 1.25** | **ACTIVE** ← | **MONTMORILLONITE — 1.5 to 7, and higher for sodium montmorillonite** ← |

> **THE MINERAL COLUMN IS THE PRACTICAL POINT OF THE WHOLE CONCEPT, and it explains the behaviour that matters on site:**

> **MONTMORILLONITE has a lattice that admits water BETWEEN its layers, so the mineral itself swells. Kaolinite's layers are hydrogen-bonded together and water cannot get between them, so it does not.**

> **A high activity is therefore a direct warning of SWELLING and SHRINKAGE — the black cotton soils and expansive clays that lift light structures in the wet season and crack them in the dry.**

> **And it is a warning obtainable from two simple index tests, without any mineralogical analysis at all, which is why activity has survived as a working parameter.**

**What high activity implies for design:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Large volume change with water content** | **Heave and shrinkage of light structures, floors, pavements, canal linings** ← |
| **Low permeability, slow consolidation** | **Settlements take years** ← |
| **Low shear strength when wet, and sensitivity to remoulding** | ← |
| **Poor as a fill, and troublesome as a subgrade** | **Hence the lime stabilisation of plastic clay subgrades** ← |
| **BUT: excellent as a barrier** ← | **Bentonite (sodium montmorillonite) is used exactly because it swells — in drilling mud, cut-off walls, and landfill liners** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WORTH KEEPING IN MIND BECAUSE IT REVERSES THE SIGN: the property that makes montmorillonite the worst possible foundation soil makes it the best possible sealant.**

> **Bentonite swells on contact with water, closing every void it can reach, which is precisely the behaviour wanted in a diaphragm wall slurry or a landfill liner — and precisely the behaviour not wanted under a house.**

> **A soil property is rarely good or bad in itself; it is good or bad for a purpose, and recognising which purpose is at hand is most of geotechnical judgement.**

**The related index properties, gathered:**

| Index | Definition | Tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **PLASTICITY INDEX** | **PI = LL − PL** ← | **The range of water content over which the soil is plastic** ← |
| **LIQUIDITY INDEX** | **LI = (w − PL) / PI** ← | **Where the NATURAL water content sits in that range — LI near 1 means the soil is close to its liquid limit and is weak** ← |
| **CONSISTENCY INDEX** | **CI = (LL − w) / PI** ← | **The complement: CI + LI = 1** ← |
| **ACTIVITY** | **PI / (% < 2 μm)** ← | **The clay MINERAL's character** ← |
| **SHRINKAGE INDEX** | **PL − shrinkage limit** | The shrinkage range |

> **The LIQUIDITY INDEX in the second row is the one that carries the most immediate warning about a natural deposit, and it deserves the emphasis: a soft clay with LI close to or above 1 is at or beyond its liquid limit in the ground, held together only by its structure.**

> **Disturb it — by driving a pile, by excavating beside it, by an earthquake — and it can lose most of its strength, which is the phenomenon of SENSITIVITY and, at the extreme, of quick clays.**

examTip.trick: **Activity = PI ÷ (% finer than 2 μm)** — dividing out the QUANTITY of clay leaves a measure of the clay MINERAL's character.
examTip.trap: **Below 0.75 inactive (kaolinite ~0.4); 0.75-1.25 normal (illite ~0.9); above 1.25 active (montmorillonite 1.5-7).** High activity is a direct warning of swelling and shrinkage.
examTip.mnemonic: **The property that makes montmorillonite the worst foundation soil makes bentonite the best sealant** — swelling closes every void, which is wanted in a liner and not under a house.

questions.stem: A soil has a water content of 20 per cent, a void ratio of 0.70 and a specific gravity of solids of 2.70. Its DEGREE OF SATURATION is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 77 per cent.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The fundamental phase relation** | **S e = w G** ← |
| **Rearranged** | **S = w G / e** ← |
| **Substituting** | **S = 0.20 × 2.70 / 0.70** |
| **Numerator** | **= 0.540** |
| **S** | **= 0.540 / 0.70 = 0.771 = 77.1 %** ← |

> **Option (b) 54 % is w G with the division by e omitted; option (c) 71 % uses G = 2.50; option (a) 28.6 % is w/e, omitting G altogether.**

**Where S e = w G comes from, since deriving it once makes it unforgettable:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Take the volume of SOLIDS as 1 unit** | **Then the volume of VOIDS is e, by the definition of void ratio** ← |
| **Volume of WATER = S × e** | **By the definition of degree of saturation** ← |
| **Mass of water = S e × ρ_w** | ← |
| **Mass of solids = 1 × G ρ_w** | **By the definition of specific gravity** ← |
| **Water content w = mass of water / mass of solids** | **= S e ρ_w / (G ρ_w) = S e / G** ← |
| **Hence** | **w G = S e** ← |

> **THE TRICK IS THE FIRST LINE — setting the volume of solids to unity — and it is worth adopting as a habit, because every phase relation falls out of it in two or three lines.**

> **There is no need to memorise a table of formulae for dry density, bulk density, saturated density and submerged density: draw the three-phase diagram with V_s = 1, fill in e, S and G, and read off whatever is wanted.**

**The phase relations that follow immediately:**

| Quantity | In terms of e, S, G |
|---|---|
| **Bulk (moist) unit weight** | **γ = (G + S e) γ_w / (1 + e)** ← |
| **Dry unit weight** | **γ_d = G γ_w / (1 + e)** ← |
| **Saturated unit weight (S = 1)** | **γ_sat = (G + e) γ_w / (1 + e)** ← |
| **Submerged (buoyant) unit weight** | **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = (G − 1) γ_w / (1 + e)** ← |
| **Porosity from void ratio** | **n = e / (1 + e), and e = n / (1 − n)** ← |
| **Dry unit weight from bulk** | **γ_d = γ / (1 + w)** ← |

> **EVERY ONE OF THOSE HAS (1 + e) IN THE DENOMINATOR, which is simply the TOTAL volume when the solids are taken as 1 — so the pattern is a consequence of the derivation rather than a coincidence to be memorised.**

> **The numerator is whatever mass is being counted: G for solids alone (dry), G + Se for solids plus water (bulk), G + e when saturated, and G − 1 when buoyancy removes the weight of the displaced water.**

**A sanity check on this answer, which is worth performing on every phase problem:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **S must lie between 0 and 1** | **0.771 does** ← |
| **If S came out above 1, the data are inconsistent** | **Either the water content is too high for that void ratio, or e is wrong** ← |
| **The water content at FULL saturation here would be** | **w_sat = e/G = 0.70/2.70 = 25.9 % — and 20 % is comfortably below it, consistent with S = 77 %** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL CHECK AVAILABLE IN THIS TOPIC and takes five seconds: compute the saturated water content e/G, and confirm that the given water content is less than it.**

> **If the given w exceeds e/G, then S would exceed 1 and the problem as stated is impossible — which does occur in badly set questions and, more importantly, in real laboratory data where it signals an error in the measurements.**

examTip.trick: **S e = w G, so S = wG/e = 0.20 × 2.70 / 0.70 = 77 %.** Option (b) omits the division by e; option (a) omits G.
examTip.trap: **Derive it by setting the volume of SOLIDS to 1** — then voids = e, water = Se, and every phase relation follows in two lines with (1+e) in the denominator. No table to memorise.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check with w_sat = e/G = 25.9 %** — the given 20 % is below it, so S < 1 as it must be. If w exceeds e/G the data are impossible.

questions.stem: A sand has a specific gravity of solids of 2.65 and a void ratio of 0.65. The CRITICAL HYDRAULIC GRADIENT at which a quick condition (boiling) occurs under upward seepage is:
questions.solution:
**1.00.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Critical hydraulic gradient** | **i_c = (G − 1) / (1 + e)** ← |
| **Substituting** | **i_c = (2.65 − 1) / (1 + 0.65)** |
| **= 1.65 / 1.65** | **= 1.00** ← |

> **Option (d) 1.65 forgets the denominator; option (a) 0.62 divides by G rather than by (1 + e).**

> **The values chosen here are close to the commonest natural case, and the result of almost exactly 1.0 is not a coincidence worth ignoring: for most sands, G is near 2.65 and e near 0.65 to 0.70, so the critical gradient is generally CLOSE TO UNITY.**

> **That is a genuinely useful thing to carry: if the head loss across a soil roughly equals the thickness of soil it is flowing through, the soil is on the point of boiling.**

**The derivation, which explains why the answer has the form it does:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **The soil grains are held down by their SUBMERGED weight** | **γ′ = (G − 1) γ_w / (1 + e) per unit volume** ← |
| **Upward seepage exerts a SEEPAGE FORCE per unit volume** | **j = i γ_w** ← |
| **A quick condition occurs when the seepage force EQUALS the submerged weight** ← | **i_c γ_w = (G − 1) γ_w / (1 + e)** ← |
| **Cancelling γ_w** | **i_c = (G − 1) / (1 + e)** ← |

> **THE PHYSICAL PICTURE IS THE THING TO REMEMBER: at the critical gradient the upward drag of the water exactly cancels the grains' submerged weight, so the EFFECTIVE STRESS falls to ZERO.**

> **The soil then has no shear strength at all — since for a cohesionless soil τ = σ′ tan φ, and σ′ = 0 gives τ = 0 whatever the value of φ.**

> **The sand behaves as a heavy fluid. It will not support anything, and objects denser than the mixture sink into it.**

**What this looks like in practice:**

| Manifestation | Note |
|---|---|
| **BOILING or piping at the downstream toe of a dam or sheet pile wall** ← | **Where the flow lines emerge and the exit gradient is highest** ← |
| **Heave of the base of a deep excavation** | **When dewatering is inadequate and water flows up into the excavation** ← |
| **"Running sand" in a trench** | ← |
| **SAND BOILS during earthquakes** | **A related phenomenon — there the excess pore pressure is generated by cyclic shearing rather than by seepage, but the end state is the same: σ′ = 0** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW LINKS THIS DIRECTLY TO LIQUEFACTION, and the link is worth making explicitly because the two topics are usually taught apart:**

> **A quick condition and liquefaction are the SAME END STATE — zero effective stress — reached by two different routes.**

> **In a quick condition, water flowing upward carries the pore pressure up to the total stress. In liquefaction, cyclic shaking makes a loose saturated sand try to contract, and because the water cannot escape quickly the pore pressure rises to the same point.**

> **Either way σ′ = 0 and the soil has no strength, which is why the ground fails in exactly the same manner in both — buildings settle and tilt, buried tanks float, and sand and water erupt at the surface.**

> **In the Kathmandu valley, with its deep lacustrine deposits and shallow water table, liquefaction is a recognised hazard and it was observed in 2015 — which makes this piece of theory a local design concern rather than a textbook curiosity.**

**And the design response:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **A FACTOR OF SAFETY of 4 to 5 against the critical gradient** ← | **High, because the failure is sudden and total, and the gradient is not precisely known** ← |
| **Lengthen the seepage path** | **Cut-offs, sheet piles, upstream blankets — reducing i by increasing the path length** ← |
| **A loaded INVERTED FILTER at the exit** ← | **Adds weight (raising the resisting term) while allowing water out freely, so it does not raise the pressure** ← |
| **Relief wells** | **Reduce the uplift beneath a downstream blanket** ← |

> **The inverted filter in the third row is the classic and elegant answer: it must be permeable enough that water escapes without building pressure, and graded finely enough that the sand beneath cannot wash through it — the two filter criteria that govern every drainage layer in geotechnical work.**

examTip.trick: **i_c = (G−1)/(1+e) = 1.65/1.65 = 1.00.** For most sands G ≈ 2.65 and e ≈ 0.65-0.70, so the critical gradient is generally CLOSE TO UNITY — a useful rule of thumb.
examTip.trap: **At i_c the effective stress is ZERO, so τ = σ′ tan φ = 0 whatever φ is** — the sand has no strength at all and behaves as a heavy fluid.
examTip.mnemonic: **Quick condition and LIQUEFACTION are the same end state (σ′ = 0) by two routes** — upward seepage, or cyclic shaking of a loose saturated sand. Use FoS 4-5, because the failure is sudden and total.

questions.stem: If the water table in a sand deposit RISES from a great depth to the ground surface, the EFFECTIVE stress at a given depth below the surface will:
options: Remain unchanged, since the total stress also rises
DECREASE
Increase, because the soil becomes heavier
Fall to zero at every depth
questions.solution:
**It DECREASES** — the pore water pressure rises by the full γ_w z, while the total stress rises only by the small difference between the moist and saturated unit weights.

**The arithmetic at a depth z, worked both ways:**

| Condition | Total stress σ | Pore pressure u | Effective stress σ′ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water table DEEP (soil moist above z)** | **γ_moist × z** ← | **ZERO (or negative)** ← | **γ_moist × z** ← |
| **Water table at the SURFACE** | **γ_sat × z** ← | **γ_w × z** ← | **(γ_sat − γ_w) z = γ′ z** ← |

> **With typical values — γ_moist ≈ 18, γ_sat ≈ 20, γ_w = 9.81 kN/m³ — at z = 5 m:**

| Case | σ′ |
|---|---|
| **Water table deep** | **18 × 5 = 90 kPa** ← |
| **Water table at the surface** | **(20 − 9.81) × 5 = 10.19 × 5 = 51 kPa** ← |

> **THE EFFECTIVE STRESS HAS FALLEN BY ALMOST HALF, and that is the size of effect the question is asking about.**

> **Option (c) reflects the intuitive but wrong reasoning — the soil IS heavier when saturated, but the buoyancy the water provides more than offsets the extra weight.**

> **Option (a) is wrong because the two do not rise equally: total stress gains only (γ_sat − γ_moist) ≈ 2 kN/m³ per metre, while pore pressure gains 9.81.**

**Why this matters, since it is one of the most consequential facts in geotechnics:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **BEARING CAPACITY falls** ← | **Both the surcharge term and the γ term use the submerged unit weight — the capacity of a footing on sand can drop by nearly HALF when the water table rises to founding level** ← |
| **Shear strength falls throughout the deposit** | **τ = σ′ tan φ, and σ′ has halved** ← |
| **SLOPES become less stable** | **Which is why slope failures happen in the monsoon and not in the dry season** ← |
| **Retaining walls carry more pressure** | **Submerged soil pressure PLUS full water pressure exceeds dry soil pressure substantially** ← |
| **Liquefaction becomes possible** | **It requires saturation** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL PRACTICAL COROLLARY IN NEPAL, and it explains the seasonal pattern of landslides completely:**

> **A slope that has stood for decades fails in July not because anything about the soil changed, but because the water table rose. The driving weight barely altered; the resisting shear strength collapsed with the effective stress.**

> **Which is why DRAINAGE is the first and cheapest slope stabilisation measure, ahead of any retaining structure: lowering the water table restores the effective stress, and restoring the effective stress restores the strength.**

> **A horizontal drain costing a few thousand rupees can do what a wall costing lakhs cannot, because it attacks the cause rather than resisting the effect.**

**And the retaining wall case in the fourth row deserves its own arithmetic, because designers underestimate it:**

| Case behind a wall, 5 m of backfill, φ = 30°, K_a = 1/3 | Lateral force |
|---|---|
| **DRY backfill, γ = 18** | **½ × (1/3 × 18) × 5² = 75 kN/m** ← |
| **SUBMERGED backfill, γ′ = 10, PLUS full water pressure** | **½ × (1/3 × 10) × 5² + ½ × 9.81 × 5² = 41.7 + 122.6 = 164 kN/m** ← |

> **The force has MORE THAN DOUBLED, and the reason is that the water pushes with K = 1 while the soil pushes with K_a = 1/3.**

> **Water does not have an angle of friction; it transmits its full pressure sideways.**

> **That is why WEEP HOLES and a granular drainage layer behind a retaining wall are not a refinement but a structural necessity, and why blocked weep holes are among the commonest causes of retaining wall failure.**

The pore water pressure increases while the total stress rises only from moist to saturated unit weight.

examTip.trick: **Pore pressure gains 9.81 kN/m³ per metre; total stress gains only (γ_sat − γ_moist) ≈ 2.** So effective stress FALLS — at 5 m depth, from about 90 kPa to 51 kPa.
examTip.trap: **"The soil is heavier when saturated" is true but misleading** — buoyancy more than offsets the extra weight. Bearing capacity on sand can drop by nearly half.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slopes fail in the monsoon because the water table rose, not because the soil changed** — hence DRAINAGE first, before any wall. And behind a wall, water pushes with K = 1 while soil pushes with K_a = 1/3.

questions.stem: For an EMBANKMENT built rapidly on a soft saturated clay foundation, the CRITICAL condition for stability occurs:
options: Many years after construction, when the clay has fully consolidated
Only during an earthquake
At no particular time — the factor of safety does not change with time
IMMEDIATELY at the END OF CONSTRUCTION, and it is analysed in TOTAL stress terms using the undrained strength
questions.solution:
**Immediately at the END OF CONSTRUCTION** — analysed in TOTAL stress terms (a φ = 0 analysis) using the undrained shear strength c_u.

**Why the end of construction is the worst moment:**

| Stage | What is happening |
|---|---|
| **During rapid construction** | **The load is applied faster than water can drain out of the clay** ← |
| **So the load is carried by EXCESS PORE PRESSURE** ← | **The effective stress in the clay has barely increased** ← |
| **End of construction** | **The full embankment load is on, and the pore pressures are at their HIGHEST — so the effective stress, and hence the strength, is at its LOWEST relative to the load** ← |
| **Afterwards, the excess pore pressure DISSIPATES** ← | **Effective stress rises, the clay CONSOLIDATES and GAINS strength** ← |
| **Long term** | **The factor of safety is HIGHER than it was at the end of construction** ← |

> **SO THE EMBANKMENT ON CLAY GETS SAFER WITH TIME, and if it survives the end of construction it will survive.**

**The contrasting case, which is where the mirror-image mistake is made:**

| Situation | Critical condition | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **EMBANKMENT (loading) on clay** | **END OF CONSTRUCTION — short term** ← | **Pore pressures are POSITIVE and dissipate, so strength INCREASES with time** ← |
| **EXCAVATION or CUTTING (unloading) in clay** | **LONG TERM** ← | **Pore pressures are NEGATIVE (suction) and dissipate upward toward equilibrium, so the effective stress FALLS and strength DECREASES with time** ← |

> **THAT PAIR IS THE HEART OF THE TOPIC AND IS WORTH LEARNING AS A PAIR RATHER THAN SEPARATELY:**

> **LOADING generates positive excess pore pressure; unloading generates negative. Both dissipate toward the long-term equilibrium value.**

> **So loading gets SAFER with time and unloading gets more DANGEROUS with time.**

> **The practical consequence is disquieting and well documented: a cutting in stiff clay may stand perfectly for years and then fail — the delayed failures observed in railway cuttings decades after construction — because the negative pore pressures set up by the excavation are still slowly equalising.**

> **An embankment that has stood for a year is safe; a cutting that has stood for a year is not necessarily safe.**

**The two analyses, and which parameters go with which:**

| Analysis | Parameters | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| **TOTAL stress (undrained, φ = 0)** | **c_u from an unconsolidated undrained triaxial, unconfined compression or vane test** ← | **SHORT-TERM stability of saturated clay: end of construction, rapid loading, a trench just excavated** ← |
| **EFFECTIVE stress (drained)** | **c′ and φ′ from a consolidated drained test, or a CU test with pore pressure measured** ← | **LONG-TERM stability; sands and gravels always; any case where pore pressures are known** ← |

> **THE φ = 0 ANALYSIS IS A GENUINE SIMPLIFICATION AND NOT A CRUDE ONE: a saturated clay loaded without drainage has the same undrained strength whatever the confining pressure, because any increase in cell pressure simply goes into the pore water and leaves the effective stress unchanged.**

> **The Mohr circles for a UU test on a saturated clay therefore all have the same diameter, and the failure envelope is a horizontal line — φ_u = 0 and c_u = half the deviator stress.**

> **That is not an approximation made for convenience; it follows directly from the principle of effective stress, and it is one of the most satisfying results in the subject.**

**And the practical technique the whole idea makes possible:**

> **STAGED CONSTRUCTION: since the clay gains strength as it consolidates, an embankment too high to be built at once can be built in LIFTS.**

> **Each lift is placed, the pore pressures are allowed to dissipate — monitored with piezometers — and the next lift is placed on the now-stronger foundation.**

> **VERTICAL DRAINS (sand drains or prefabricated band drains) accelerate the process enormously by shortening the drainage path, turning years into months.**

> **This is one of the clearest cases in civil engineering where understanding a mechanism makes possible something that would otherwise be impossible — the embankment cannot be built in one operation at any cost, and can be built in three lifts quite economically.**

examTip.trick: **Embankment on clay: critical at the END OF CONSTRUCTION, analysed with c_u in total stress (φ = 0).** Pore pressures then dissipate, the clay consolidates, and the factor of safety rises.
examTip.trap: **LOADING gets safer with time; UNLOADING (a cutting) gets more DANGEROUS** — negative pore pressures equalise, effective stress falls, and cuttings have failed decades after construction.
examTip.mnemonic: **φ_u = 0 is exact, not a fudge** — in a saturated clay any cell pressure increase goes into the pore water, so every UU Mohr circle has the same diameter. Hence staged construction with piezometers and vertical drains.

questions.stem: The VANE SHEAR test is used principally to determine:
options: The UNDRAINED shear strength of a soft to medium saturated CLAY, in situ or in the laboratory
The angle of internal friction of a dense sand
The permeability of a silt
The compaction characteristics of a fill material
questions.solution:
**The UNDRAINED shear strength (c_u) of a soft to medium saturated CLAY**, either in the borehole or on a laboratory specimen.

**How it works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A four-bladed cross-shaped VANE is pushed into the undisturbed clay** ← | **At the bottom of a borehole, or from the surface in soft ground** ← |
| **It is rotated slowly at a standard rate** | **Typically 0.1° per second — slow enough to remain undrained but not so slow that drainage occurs** ← |
| **The TORQUE is measured** | **Rising to a peak as the clay fails** ← |
| **Failure occurs on a CYLINDRICAL surface** ← | **The circumscribing cylinder swept by the blades, plus its two circular ends** ← |
| **c_u is computed from the torque and the vane's geometry** | **T = c_u × π D² (H/2 + D/6) for a vane failing on the sides and both ends** ← |

> **THE FORMULA'S TWO TERMS CORRESPOND TO THE TWO SURFACES — the cylindrical side (H/2) and the two circular ends (D/6) — which is why the vane's height-to-diameter ratio is standardised at 2:1 and why using a non-standard vane requires the formula to be adjusted.**

**Its advantages, which explain why it is used at all:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Tests the soil IN PLACE, without sampling** ← | **Soft clay is almost impossible to sample without disturbing it — and disturbance destroys exactly the strength being measured** ← |
| **Quick, simple and cheap** | ← |
| **Gives strength at any chosen depth** | **A continuous profile can be built up** ← |
| **Measures the REMOULDED strength too** ← | **Rotate the vane rapidly through several complete turns and test again — the ratio of the two gives the SENSITIVITY** ← |

> **THE SENSITIVITY MEASUREMENT IN THE LAST ROW IS A REAL BONUS OF THE TEST and costs nothing extra: sensitivity = undisturbed strength ÷ remoulded strength.**

| Sensitivity | Description |
|---|---|
| **1 to 2** | Insensitive |
| **2 to 4** | **Moderately sensitive — most clays** ← |
| **4 to 8** | Sensitive |
| **8 to 16** | Extra sensitive |
| **Above 16** | **QUICK clay — loses nearly all its strength on remoulding and can flow like a liquid** ← |

> **A high sensitivity is a serious warning: it means the clay's strength depends on a structure that driving a pile, excavating beside it, or an earthquake will destroy.**

**The limitations, stated fairly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Suitable only for SOFT to MEDIUM clays** ← | **A stiff clay will not let the vane in, and the torque required damages the equipment** ← |
| **Useless in sand, gravel or fissured clay** ← | **Drainage occurs, so the test is not undrained; and a fissured clay fails on its fissures rather than on the vane's cylinder** ← |
| **Stones or roots wreck the result** | **A single gravel particle on the failure surface gives a spuriously high torque** ← |
| **It over-estimates c_u in HIGHLY PLASTIC clays** ← | **Which is why Bjerrum's correction factor μ, reducing with plasticity index, is applied for embankment design** ← |
| **It measures strength on a mainly VERTICAL failure surface** | **Whereas most field problems fail on a mainly horizontal one, and clays are anisotropic** ← |

> **BJERRUM'S CORRECTION IN THE FOURTH ROW HAS AN INSTRUCTIVE ORIGIN and is worth knowing about: it was derived not from theory but from BACK-ANALYSIS of embankment failures.**

> **Engineers observed that embankments designed with the vane strength were failing at factors of safety that should have been adequate, gathered the case histories, and found the discrepancy correlated with plasticity index.**

> **The correction factor is therefore an empirical adjustment calibrated against actual failures — reducing c_u by up to about 30 per cent for very plastic clays.**

> **That is a common and honourable pattern in geotechnical engineering: the theory gives the form of the answer, and the observed behaviour of real structures calibrates it. It is also a reminder that a test result is not a soil property but a measurement made in a particular way, and using it well requires knowing how the two differ.**

examTip.trick: **Undrained strength c_u of SOFT to MEDIUM saturated clay, in situ.** Failure on a cylindrical surface: T = c_u π D² (H/2 + D/6) — sides plus two ends.
examTip.trap: **Useless in sand, gravel or FISSURED clay** — drainage occurs, or the clay fails on its fissures instead of the vane's cylinder. A single gravel particle gives a spuriously high torque.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rotate rapidly through several turns and retest: undisturbed ÷ remoulded = SENSITIVITY** (above 16 is quick clay). And apply BJERRUM's correction, derived by back-analysing embankments that failed.

questions.stem: For a cohesionless soil with an angle of internal friction of 30°, the RANKINE coefficient of PASSIVE earth pressure is:
questions.solution:
**3.00.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Rankine passive coefficient** | **K_p = (1 + sin φ) / (1 − sin φ)** ← |
| **Equivalently** | **K_p = tan²(45° + φ/2)** ← |
| **With φ = 30°, sin 30° = 0.5** | **K_p = 1.5 / 0.5** |
| **K_p** | **= 3.00** ← |
| **Check by the other form** | **tan²(45 + 15) = tan²60° = (1.732)² = 3.00** ✓ ← |

> **Option (a) 0.33 is the ACTIVE coefficient K_a — and note that K_a and K_p are exact RECIPROCALS: 1/3 and 3.**
