> **That reciprocal relation, K_p = 1/K_a, is the fastest check available and holds for the Rankine case with a horizontal surface and a smooth vertical wall.**

**Active against passive, which is the substance of the topic:**

| Aspect | ACTIVE | PASSIVE |
|---|---|---|
| **Wall movement** | **AWAY from the soil** ← | **INTO the soil** ← |
| **The soil is** | **Allowed to expand and mobilise its strength to hold itself up** ← | **COMPRESSED, and resists** ← |
| **Coefficient at φ = 30°** | **0.33** | **3.00** ← |
| **Magnitude** | **The MINIMUM possible lateral pressure** ← | **The MAXIMUM possible lateral resistance** ← |
| **Movement needed to mobilise it** | **SMALL — about 0.1 to 0.5 % of the wall height** ← | **LARGE — 2 to 5 % of the height, sometimes more** ← |
| **At rest (no movement), K₀ = 1 − sin φ** | **0.5 at φ = 30° — between the two** ← | ← |

> **THE MOVEMENT ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT AND THE ONE MOST OFTEN NEGLECTED IN DESIGN, so it is worth stating plainly:**

> **The active state is reached almost immediately — a wall need only move a few millimetres for the soil behind it to relax to the active pressure, and virtually any real wall moves that much.**

> **The PASSIVE state requires movement an order of magnitude larger. A 5 m wall might need 100 to 250 mm of movement INTO the soil before the full passive resistance develops.**

> **So designing to the full K_p assumes a displacement that would itself be a serviceability failure — the structure the wall supports would have cracked long before.**

> **For that reason passive resistance is routinely reduced by a factor of two or more, or the design is checked against the movement that can actually be tolerated, rather than against the theoretical maximum.**

**The other cautions about relying on passive resistance:**

| Caution | Note |
|---|---|
| **Passive pressure is very SENSITIVE to φ** ← | **K_p at φ = 35° is 3.69, and at 25° it is 2.46 — a 10° error changes it by 50 per cent, whereas the same error changes K_a by far less** ← |
| **The soil in front may be REMOVED** | **A service trench, scour, or future excavation in front of a wall destroys the resistance the design relied on** ← |
| **Rankine's theory IGNORES wall friction** | **Which makes it CONSERVATIVE for active and UNCONSERVATIVE for passive** ← |
| **The passive failure surface is CURVED, not planar** | **Rankine and Coulomb both assume a plane, which overestimates K_p at high φ** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE THAT CAUSES ACTUAL FAILURES AND IS PURELY A MATTER OF FORESIGHT: the passive resistance in front of a sheet pile or a retaining wall toe is provided by soil that somebody may dig up.**

> **A trench cut in front of an embedded wall for a drain or a cable can remove the toe restraint entirely, and walls have failed in exactly that way — not during construction, but years later during unrelated works by people who had no idea the soil was structural.**

> **The defence is partly design (do not rely on the top metre or two of passive soil) and partly record-keeping, which is a weaker defence than it should be.**

examTip.trick: **K_p = (1+sin φ)/(1−sin φ) = 1.5/0.5 = 3.00 = tan²(45+φ/2) = tan²60°.** And K_p = 1/K_a exactly, so 0.33 and 3.00 pair up — the fastest check there is.
examTip.trap: **Active needs 0.1-0.5 % of wall height to mobilise; PASSIVE needs 2-5 %** — a 5 m wall might need 100-250 mm of movement, which would itself be a serviceability failure. Reduce K_p accordingly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Somebody may dig up your passive soil** — a service trench in front of an embedded wall removes the toe restraint entirely, and walls have failed years later that way. Never rely on the top metre or two.

questions.stem: The field N-value obtained from a Standard Penetration Test must be corrected before use principally for:
options: Temperature and humidity at the time of testing
OVERBURDEN PRESSURE and, in fine saturated sands and silts, DILATANCY
The colour and odour of the recovered sample
The age of the drilling rig
questions.solution:
**Overburden pressure and dilatancy**, together with corrections for hammer energy, rod length, borehole diameter and sampler type.

**The corrections and why each is needed:**

| Correction | Reason |
|---|---|
| **OVERBURDEN pressure** ← | **The same sand gives a HIGHER N at depth simply because it is more confined — so N must be normalised to a standard overburden of about 100 kPa before densities at different depths can be compared** ← |
| **DILATANCY (water table) correction** ← | **In fine saturated sand or silt below the water table, driving the sampler generates NEGATIVE pore pressure, which temporarily strengthens the soil and inflates N** ← |
| **ENERGY ratio** | **Different hammer and release systems deliver different fractions of the theoretical energy — 45 to 80 per cent. N is normalised to 60 per cent (N₆₀)** ← |
| **ROD LENGTH** | **Short rods reflect energy back and reduce what reaches the sampler; the correction applies below about 10 m of rod** ← |
| **BOREHOLE diameter** | **A large borehole relieves confinement** |
| **SAMPLER type** | **Whether a liner is used** |

> **The two named in the answer are the ones examinations ask for, and they are also the two largest.**

**The DILATANCY correction, since it is the one with the counter-intuitive form:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Applied only in FINE saturated sand and silt below the water table** ← | **Not in gravel, not in clay, not above the water table** ← |
| **Applied only when the corrected N exceeds 15** ← | ← |
| **N_corrected = 15 + 0.5 (N − 15)** ← | **So an N of 35 becomes 15 + 0.5(20) = 25** ← |
| **It always REDUCES N** ← | **Because the observed value was inflated by the negative pore pressure** ← |

> **THE ORDER OF THE TWO CORRECTIONS MATTERS AND IS OFTEN GOT WRONG: the OVERBURDEN correction is applied FIRST, and the dilatancy correction is applied to the result.**

> **Applying them the other way round gives a different answer, and the standard sequence exists precisely because the dilatancy rule's threshold of 15 refers to the overburden-corrected value.**

**Why N is so widely used despite being crude:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Simple, cheap, and possible with basic equipment** ← | **Which matters enormously where sophisticated testing is unavailable** ← |
| **A sample is RECOVERED, so the soil can be identified** ← | **A cone penetration test gives better numbers but no sample** ← |
| **An enormous body of empirical CORRELATIONS exists** ← | **To relative density, φ, bearing capacity, settlement, and liquefaction resistance** ← |
| **It works in soils where other tests cannot be performed** | **Gravelly and stony ground defeats a CPT** ← |

> **THE CORRELATIONS IN THE THIRD ROW ARE BOTH THE TEST'S GREAT STRENGTH AND ITS GREAT WEAKNESS, and it is worth being clear-eyed about it:**

> **The SPT is not a fundamental measurement of anything. It counts the blows to drive a tube, which depends on the equipment, the operator, the borehole condition and the soil together.**

> **Its value lies entirely in decades of accumulated correlation with observed behaviour — which is genuine and useful knowledge, but it means an N-value obtained with non-standard equipment or careless practice is correlated with nothing at all.**

> **So the corrections are not academic refinements; they are what makes one rig's numbers comparable with the case histories the correlations were built from.**

**And the practical rules that make the raw number reliable in the first place:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **N is the blows for the LAST 300 mm of a 450 mm drive** ← | **The first 150 mm is a SEATING drive and is discarded, because the material at the bottom of a borehole is disturbed** ← |
| **Standard hammer: 63.5 kg falling 750 mm** ← | ← |
| **REFUSAL at 50 blows for 300 mm, or 100 blows total** | **Reported as refusal rather than extrapolated** ← |
| **The borehole must be kept FULL of water or mud below the water table** ← | **Or the base heaves upward, loosening the sand and giving a low, meaningless N** ← |

> **The last row is the commonest and most damaging field error in the whole procedure: allowing the water level in the borehole to fall below the ground water level creates an upward gradient at the base, the sand boils, and the test is then performed on soil the drilling itself has destroyed.**

> **It gives dangerously LOW values, and unlike most errors that direction is not conservative — it leads to over-design, wasted money, and a loss of confidence in the investigation that may cause the next set of results to be discounted when they should not be.**

Together with corrections for energy, rod length, borehole diameter and sampler type.

examTip.trick: **Overburden and dilatancy are the two big ones**, plus energy (N₆₀), rod length, borehole diameter and sampler type.
examTip.trap: **Dilatancy: only in fine SATURATED sand/silt, only when N > 15, and N_c = 15 + 0.5(N − 15) — always a REDUCTION.** Apply the OVERBURDEN correction first; the threshold of 15 refers to that corrected value.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep the borehole FULL of water below the water table** — let it drop and the base boils, giving dangerously LOW N values on soil the drilling destroyed. N is the last 300 mm of a 450 mm drive.

questions.stem: The GROUP EFFICIENCY of a pile group is defined as the ratio of:
options: The ULTIMATE CAPACITY OF THE GROUP to the sum of the ultimate capacities of the individual piles acting alone
The load on the group to the load on the heaviest pile
The settlement of the group to the settlement of a single pile
The number of piles in the group to the number theoretically required
questions.solution:
**The ultimate capacity of the GROUP divided by the SUM of the ultimate capacities of the individual piles acting alone.**

**Written out:**

> **η = Q_ultimate(group) ÷ (n × Q_ultimate(single pile))**

> **Where n is the number of piles. If η = 1 the piles behave independently; below 1 they interfere with one another.**

**Why the group is generally NOT the sum of its parts:**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **The stress BULBS of adjacent piles OVERLAP** ← | **Each pile is working the same soil as its neighbours, so the soil is stressed more than a single-pile analysis assumes** ← |
| **In CLAY, the group may fail as a single BLOCK** ← | **Shearing around the perimeter of the whole group plus bearing on its base, rather than around each pile** ← |
| **In loose SAND, driving DENSIFIES the soil between the piles** ← | **Which can make the efficiency GREATER than 1** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE EXCEPTION WORTH KNOWING, and it surprises people: in loose sand, driving a group of piles compacts the soil between them, and the group can be STRONGER than the sum of its individual piles — efficiency above 1, sometimes 1.3 or more.**

> **In clay, no such densification occurs; the driving remoulds the clay instead, and the efficiency is generally BELOW 1.**

> **So the sign of the group effect depends on the soil, which is why a single blanket rule cannot be applied.**

**How it is assessed:**

| Approach | Note |
|---|---|
| **For piles in CLAY, take the LESSER of: the sum of individual capacities, and the BLOCK failure capacity** ← | **The block is treated as one large pier — perimeter shear plus base bearing** ← |
| **CONVERSE-LABARRE and similar empirical formulae** | **Give η from the spacing, diameter and the numbers of rows and columns — widely quoted, of limited real authority** ← |
| **For piles in SAND at normal spacing** | **η is usually taken as 1.0, and no reduction is applied** ← |
| **In every case, SETTLEMENT of the group must be checked separately** ← | **Efficiency addresses capacity, not settlement** ← |

> **THE BLOCK FAILURE CHECK IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE ONE THAT GOVERNS CLOSELY SPACED GROUPS IN CLAY, and the reason is geometric: as the spacing reduces, the perimeter of the block grows much more slowly than the number of piles does.**

> **Doubling the number of piles in a compact group barely changes the block's perimeter, so beyond a point additional piles add almost nothing to the block capacity — and the block capacity is what governs.**

> **This is why pile spacing has a MINIMUM (2.5 to 3 diameters for friction piles) rather than being packed as tightly as the pile cap allows: closer spacing costs money and adds no capacity.**

**THE SETTLEMENT POINT IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES ITS OWN EMPHASIS, because it is the one most often missed and is frequently what actually governs the design:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A single pile's stress bulb extends about 1 to 2 diameters below its base** ← | **A shallow zone** |
| **A GROUP's combined stress bulb extends to a depth comparable with the GROUP's WIDTH** ← | **Which may be ten or twenty times deeper** ← |
| **So the group stresses soil that no single-pile test ever loaded** ← | **Including compressible layers well below the pile toes** ← |
| **Group settlement can therefore be MANY TIMES a single pile's settlement at the same load per pile** ← | **A factor of five or ten is unremarkable** ← |

> **THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT IDEA IN PILE GROUP BEHAVIOUR AND IT HAS CAUSED REAL FAILURES: a pile load test on a single pile can show a perfectly satisfactory settlement, and the completed group can settle unacceptably.**

> **The test loaded a small bulb of soil near the toe; the group loads a great volume of ground far deeper, and a soft clay layer sitting well below the pile bases — invisible to the single pile test — is compressed by the group and consolidates for years.**

> **Which is why the site investigation must extend well below the anticipated pile toes, to a depth related to the GROUP's width rather than to the pile's diameter, and why a satisfactory single-pile test is not evidence that the foundation will perform.**

examTip.trick: **η = group capacity ÷ (n × single pile capacity).** Below 1 means the piles interfere; in clay take the LESSER of the pile sum and the BLOCK failure capacity.
examTip.trap: **In loose SAND, driving densifies the soil between piles and η can EXCEED 1.** The sign of the group effect depends on the soil — no blanket rule.
examTip.mnemonic: **A single pile's bulb reaches 1-2 diameters below the toe; the GROUP's reaches its own WIDTH.** So a satisfactory single-pile test proves nothing about group settlement, and the investigation must go far deeper.

questions.stem: In foundation design, DIFFERENTIAL settlement is generally more critical than total settlement because:
options: It is easier to measure
It always occurs first
It causes DISTORTION of the structure
It is not covered by the codes
questions.solution:
**Because differential settlement DISTORTS the structure**, inducing additional stresses and cracking, whereas uniform settlement simply lowers the whole building without straining it.

**The distinction:**

| Type | What happens | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **UNIFORM (total) settlement** | **Every part of the structure descends by the SAME amount** ← | **No distortion, no additional stress in the frame; connections to drains, services and adjoining structures are the only problem** ← |
| **DIFFERENTIAL settlement** | **Different parts settle by DIFFERENT amounts** ← | **The structure is FORCED OUT OF SHAPE — members are bent, joints rotate, and stresses appear that the design never allowed for** ← |
| **ANGULAR DISTORTION (δ/L)** | **The differential settlement divided by the distance between the two points** ← | **The parameter that actually governs the damage** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS, and it is why total settlement figures alone are misleading: 50 mm of differential settlement over 3 m is severe; the same 50 mm over 30 m is barely noticeable.**

> **It is the ROTATION, not the displacement, that cracks a building.**

**The limits commonly quoted:**

| Criterion | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Angular distortion for CRACKING of load-bearing brick walls** | **1 in 500 to 1 in 1,000 — masonry is very intolerant** ← |
| **Angular distortion for structural damage to a frame** | **About 1 in 150** ← |
| **Angular distortion where visible cracking in panel walls begins** | **About 1 in 300** ← |
| **Angular distortion for machinery and crane rails** | **1 in 500 or tighter — the machine, not the structure, governs** ← |
| **Maximum TOTAL settlement, isolated footing on SAND** | **25 mm** ← |
| **Maximum total settlement, RAFT on sand** | **40 to 65 mm** ← |
| **Maximum total settlement, isolated footing on CLAY** | **65 mm** ← |
| **Maximum total settlement, raft on clay** | **65 to 100 mm** ← |

> **THE RAFT VALUES ARE HIGHER THAN THE ISOLATED FOOTING VALUES IN BOTH SOILS, and the reason is the whole argument for using a raft: a raft is a single stiff element, so it settles largely as a unit.**

> **The differential settlement across a raft is therefore a small fraction of its total settlement, whereas separate footings can settle by quite different amounts with nothing tying them together.**

> **A raft is permitted more total settlement because it delivers less differential settlement — which is the point of the whole comparison, and it also explains why rafts are the natural answer on variable or weak ground.**

**The causes of differential settlement, since prevention is better than allowance:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **VARIABLE soil conditions across the site** ← | **The commonest cause — and the one adequate site investigation reveals** ← |
| **Unequal LOADING — a tower beside a low wing** | **Different pressures, different settlements** ← |
| **Different foundation TYPES or DEPTHS in one structure** ← | **Part on piles and part on footings is a classic error — they settle by quite different amounts and on quite different timescales** ← |
| **A structure of differing stiffness in different parts** | ← |
| **Localised causes** | **A leaking drain, a tree removed or planted, an adjacent excavation, or a lowered water table** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A MISTAKE MADE OFTEN ENOUGH TO BE WORTH NAMING FIRMLY: mixing foundation types within one structure invites differential settlement, because piled and shallow foundations settle by different amounts AND at different rates.**

> **Where it is unavoidable — an extension to an existing building, for instance — the correct response is a MOVEMENT JOINT that separates the two parts completely, so that each may settle independently without distorting the other.**

> **Trying to tie them together stiff enough to prevent relative movement is almost always the wrong answer: the forces required are enormous, and the joint cracks anyway, in a less controlled place than a designed joint would have.**

> **That is the general principle for handling movement in structures — provide for it where you choose, or the structure will provide for it where it chooses.**

Uniform settlement moves the whole structure together without distorting it.

Inducing additional stresses, cracking and loss of serviceability.

examTip.trick: **Uniform settlement lowers the building without straining it; DIFFERENTIAL settlement distorts it.** The governing parameter is ANGULAR DISTORTION δ/L, not the displacement itself.
examTip.trap: **Rafts are allowed MORE total settlement (40-100 mm) than isolated footings (25 mm sand, 65 mm clay)** — precisely because a stiff raft settles as a unit and delivers less DIFFERENTIAL movement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never mix foundation types in one structure** — piles and footings settle by different amounts at different rates. If unavoidable, provide a MOVEMENT JOINT: provide for movement where you choose, or the structure chooses for you.

questions.stem: For a soap BUBBLE of diameter d in air, with surface tension σ, the excess pressure inside is:
options: 2σ / d
4σ / d
6σ / d
8σ / d
questions.solution:
**8σ / d** — twice that of a liquid droplet of the same diameter.

**The three standard cases, which must be kept apart:**

| Case | Excess pressure | Number of surfaces |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid DROPLET** | **4σ / d** ← | **ONE — the outer surface only** ← |
| **Soap BUBBLE** | **8σ / d** ← | **TWO — an inner and an outer surface, both in contact with air** ← |
| **Liquid JET (cylinder)** | **2σ / d** ← | **One, but the geometry is cylindrical, not spherical** ← |

> **THE FACTOR OF TWO BETWEEN THE DROPLET AND THE BUBBLE IS THE WHOLE QUESTION, and the reason is purely geometric:**

> **A droplet is solid liquid throughout, with a single surface separating liquid from air.**

> **A soap bubble is a THIN FILM with air inside and air outside — so it has TWO surfaces, each exerting surface tension, and the resisting force doubles.**

**The derivation for the droplet, which makes both results obvious:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Imagine the droplet cut in half** | ← |
| **Pressure force pushing the halves apart** | **Δp × (π d² / 4) — the pressure acting on the projected circular area** ← |
| **Surface tension holding them together** | **σ × (π d) — acting around the circumference of the cut** ← |
| **Equating** | **Δp × π d² / 4 = σ π d** |
| **Hence** | **Δp = 4σ / d** ← |
| **For a bubble, the tension acts on TWO circumferences** | **Δp × π d²/4 = 2 σ π d, giving Δp = 8σ / d** ← |

> **The cylindrical JET case follows the same way: cut a length L of the jet lengthwise, and the pressure acts on d × L while the tension acts on 2 × L — giving Δp = 2σ/d.**

**The 1/d DEPENDENCE, which is the physically interesting part:**

| Observation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **The excess pressure is INVERSELY proportional to diameter** ← | **A SMALL bubble has a HIGHER internal pressure than a large one** ← |
| **So if two bubbles of different size are connected** | **The SMALL one deflates INTO the large one — the opposite of most people's expectation** ← |
| **This is why foam coarsens over time** | **Small bubbles feed large ones, and the average size grows** ← |

> **THE CONNECTED-BUBBLES RESULT IN THE SECOND ROW IS A GENUINELY COUNTER-INTUITIVE ONE and is worth remembering, because the same 1/r law governs several important engineering phenomena:**

> **CAVITATION nucleation depends on it — a very small vapour bubble needs an enormous pressure difference to survive, which is why cavitation requires nucleation sites rather than starting spontaneously.**

> **CAPILLARY rise depends on it — a narrow tube gives a small radius of curvature and hence a large pressure difference, so water climbs higher in a fine tube.**

> **And SOIL SUCTION above the water table depends on it — fine-grained soils hold water at much greater negative pressures than coarse ones, purely because their pore radii are smaller, which is why a clay stays damp when a sand beside it has drained.**

> **One geometric relation, appearing in three quite separate parts of the syllabus, and it is worth noticing the connection rather than learning each case independently.**

examTip.trick: **Droplet 4σ/d (ONE surface), soap bubble 8σ/d (TWO surfaces), cylindrical jet 2σ/d.** The bubble's factor of two is purely because a film has an inside and an outside.
examTip.trap: **Excess pressure goes as 1/d**, so a SMALL bubble is at HIGHER pressure — connect two bubbles and the small one deflates into the large one.
examTip.mnemonic: **The same 1/r law drives capillary rise, cavitation nucleation and soil suction** — fine pores hold water at greater negative pressure, which is why a clay stays damp when the sand beside it has drained.

questions.stem: Water boils at a temperature BELOW 100 °C at high altitude because:
options: The ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE is lower
The surface tension of water decreases with altitude
Water is less dense at altitude
The specific heat of water falls with altitude
questions.solution:
**Because the atmospheric pressure is lower**, so the water's vapour pressure reaches the ambient pressure — the condition for boiling — at a lower temperature.

**The principle:**

| Statement | Note |
|---|---|
| **BOILING occurs when a liquid's VAPOUR PRESSURE equals the pressure of its surroundings** ← | **That is the definition of boiling, and the whole answer** ← |
| **Vapour pressure RISES with temperature** | **For water: 2.34 kPa at 20 °C, 101.3 kPa at 100 °C** ← |
| **At sea level the ambient pressure is 101.3 kPa** | **So water boils at 100 °C — by construction, since that is how the scale was defined** ← |
| **At altitude the ambient pressure is LOWER** | **So a lower vapour pressure suffices, and hence a lower temperature** ← |

**The figures, which matter in Nepal:**

| Altitude | Approximate pressure | Boiling point of water |
|---|---|---|
| **Sea level** | **101.3 kPa** | **100 °C** |
| **1,400 m (Kathmandu)** | **About 86 kPa** ← | **About 95 °C** ← |
| **3,000 m** | **About 70 kPa** | **About 90 °C** ← |
| **5,000 m** | **About 54 kPa** | **About 83 °C** ← |
| **8,848 m (Everest)** | **About 34 kPa** | **About 71 °C** ← |

> **THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE IS FAMILIAR TO EVERYONE WHO HAS COOKED IN THE HILLS: rice and dal take much longer, and above about 3,500 m they may not cook properly at all in an open pot.**

> **The water is boiling vigorously — but at only 90 °C, and cooking depends on TEMPERATURE, not on the visible boiling.**

> **A pressure cooker solves it directly by raising the pressure inside, which raises the boiling point back above 100 °C, and it is why pressure cookers are near-universal in the Nepali hills rather than a convenience.**

**The same principle, running the other way — CAVITATION:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cavitation is BOILING caused by a fall in PRESSURE rather than a rise in temperature** ← | **The same physical event reached from the other direction** ← |
| **Water at 20 °C boils if the local pressure falls to 2.34 kPa absolute** ← | **Which happens on the suction side of a pump, at a turbine runner, or in a venturi throat** ← |
| **The vapour bubbles collapse on reaching higher pressure** | **Eroding the metal** ← |

> **SO BOILING AT ALTITUDE AND CAVITATION IN A PUMP ARE THE SAME PHENOMENON, and recognising that makes both easier to remember: a liquid boils whenever its vapour pressure meets the ambient pressure, whether because the vapour pressure was raised or the ambient pressure was lowered.**

**And the engineering consequence for pumps at altitude, which follows directly:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The available NPSH depends on ATMOSPHERIC pressure at the pump** ← | **NPSH_available = (p_atm − p_vapour)/ρg − suction lift − friction losses** ← |
| **At Kathmandu's altitude the atmospheric head is about 8.8 m, not 10.3 m** ← | **A metre and a half less to work with** ← |
| **So the permissible SUCTION LIFT is reduced correspondingly** | ← |
| **A pump installation copied from a sea-level design may CAVITATE at altitude** ← | **The same trap met in turbine setting** ← |

> **This is a real and recurring error in water supply schemes in the hills: a pump specified from a manufacturer's catalogue, with the suction lift the catalogue permits, cavitates on installation because the catalogue assumed sea level.**

> **The correction is a single subtraction and takes a minute; the failure damages the impeller within weeks and is often misdiagnosed as a manufacturing defect.**

> **Which is a good general lesson about standard data: every table is written for some assumed condition, and the engineer's job includes knowing what that condition was.**

The water's vapour pressure equals the ambient pressure at a lower temperature.

examTip.trick: **Boiling occurs when VAPOUR pressure equals AMBIENT pressure.** At altitude the ambient pressure is lower, so a lower temperature suffices — about 95 °C at Kathmandu, 71 °C on Everest.
examTip.trap: **Cavitation is the SAME event from the other direction** — the ambient pressure falls to the vapour pressure instead of the vapour pressure rising to the ambient.
examTip.mnemonic: **Atmospheric head is 8.8 m at Kathmandu, not 10.3 m** — so the permissible pump SUCTION LIFT shrinks, and a catalogue design copied from sea level cavitates. Every table assumes a condition; know which.

questions.stem: For a submerged CURVED surface, the HORIZONTAL component of the total hydrostatic force is equal to:
options: The weight of the liquid vertically above the surface
Zero, since the surface is curved
The total force divided by two
The force on the VERTICAL PROJECTION of the curved surface onto a vertical plane
questions.solution:
**The force on the VERTICAL PROJECTION of the curved surface** onto a vertical plane — computed exactly as for a plane surface, and acting through the centre of pressure of that projection.

**The two components:**

| Component | Equal to | Acting through |
|---|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL, F_H** | **The force on the VERTICAL PROJECTION of the curved surface** ← | **The centre of pressure of that projected area** ← |
| **VERTICAL, F_V** | **The WEIGHT of the liquid contained in the volume vertically above the surface, up to the free surface (real or imaginary)** ← (option a) | **The centroid of that volume** ← |
| **RESULTANT** | **F = √(F_H² + F_V²), inclined at θ = tan⁻¹(F_V / F_H) to the horizontal** ← | ← |

> **Option (a) is the VERTICAL component, which makes it the well-made distractor — the two components are exactly the pair being distinguished.**

**Why the horizontal component takes this form:**

> **Pressure always acts NORMAL to a surface. On a curved surface the normals point in different directions, so the elemental forces cannot simply be added.**

> **Resolve each elemental force horizontally, and the horizontal component of the pressure on an element depends only on the element's VERTICAL PROJECTION — the horizontal area it presents.**

> **Summing, the total horizontal force equals the force on the whole surface's vertical projection: a plane problem, which is already solved.**

> **The same reasoning gives the vertical component from the horizontal projections, and it comes out as the weight of the liquid column above.**

**The IMAGINARY liquid case, which is the standard trap:**

| Situation | Vertical component |
|---|---|
| **Liquid lies ABOVE the curved surface** | **F_V = weight of that liquid, acting DOWNWARD** ← |
| **Liquid lies BELOW the curved surface** ← | **F_V = weight of the liquid that WOULD occupy the volume above the surface up to the free surface — acting UPWARD** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHERE MARKS ARE LOST, and the rule is worth stating carefully: when the water is underneath the curved surface — a radial gate holding water on its convex side, the underside of a submerged dome, a Tainter gate — there is no real liquid above it.**

> **You nevertheless compute the weight of the IMAGINARY liquid that would fill the space between the surface and the free surface level, and that force acts UPWARD.**

> **The result is exact, not an approximation: it follows from the fact that the pressure distribution on the surface does not know whether the liquid above it is present.**

**A useful special case, which is worth knowing for its elegance:**

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| **A CIRCULAR arc gate (Tainter or radial gate) pivoted at the centre of its arc** ← | **Every elemental pressure force is NORMAL to the arc and therefore passes through the CENTRE** ← |
| **Consequence** | **The RESULTANT also passes through the pivot, so it exerts NO MOMENT about it** ← |
| **Practical benefit** | **The gate can be raised against the full water load with very little force — only friction and the gate's own weight need be overcome** ← |

> **THAT IS THE ENGINEERING REASON RADIAL GATES ARE USED ON LARGE BARRAGES AND SPILLWAYS, and it is a beautiful piece of design: the geometry is chosen so that the enormous water thrust produces no turning moment at all on the operating mechanism.**

> **A vertical lift gate of the same size must be dragged up against the full friction generated by the water load pressing it into its guides, needing much larger hoists.**

> **The radial gate's thrust goes straight into the trunnion bearings in the piers, where it is easily carried, and the hoist has almost nothing to do — which is why a single small motor can operate a barrage gate several metres across.**

examTip.trick: **F_H = force on the VERTICAL PROJECTION; F_V = weight of the liquid above.** Option (a) is the vertical component — the exact pair being distinguished.
examTip.trap: **Liquid BELOW the surface: use the IMAGINARY liquid above it, and F_V acts UPWARD.** The result is exact, because the pressure does not know whether that liquid is really there.
examTip.mnemonic: **A radial (Tainter) gate pivoted at its arc centre has every pressure force passing through the pivot — so ZERO moment.** That is why a small motor can lift a barrage gate against the full river.

questions.stem: The VELOCITY POTENTIAL function φ can be defined for a flow only if the flow is:
options: Compressible
IRROTATIONAL
Unsteady
Turbulent
questions.solution:
**IRROTATIONAL** — a velocity potential exists only for irrotational flow.

**The two functions compared, since they are always examined together:**

| Function | Defined for | Definition | Lines of constant value |
|---|---|---|---|
| **STREAM FUNCTION ψ** | **Any TWO-DIMENSIONAL flow satisfying CONTINUITY — rotational or not** ← | **u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x** ← | **STREAMLINES** ← |
| **VELOCITY POTENTIAL φ** | **IRROTATIONAL flow only — of any dimension** ← | **u = −∂φ/∂x, v = −∂φ/∂y** ← | **EQUIPOTENTIAL lines** ← |

> **THE CONDITIONS ARE DIFFERENT AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION: ψ requires continuity and two-dimensionality; φ requires irrotationality.**

> **A flow may have a stream function and no velocity potential (any rotational 2-D flow), and it may have a velocity potential and no stream function (irrotational 3-D flow).**

> **When BOTH exist — a two-dimensional irrotational flow — the flow is called POTENTIAL FLOW, and it is the case for which the whole apparatus of flow nets was developed.**

**Why irrotationality is the requirement:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **If φ exists, then u = −∂φ/∂x and v = −∂φ/∂y** | ← |
| **Rotation about z is ω_z = ½ (∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y)** | ← |
| **Substituting: ω_z = ½ (−∂²φ/∂x∂y + ∂²φ/∂y∂x)** | ← |
| **The mixed partial derivatives are EQUAL for a well-behaved function** ← | **So ω_z = 0 automatically** ← |
| **Hence the mere EXISTENCE of φ forces the flow to be irrotational** ← | **It is not an extra assumption but a mathematical consequence** ← |

> **That is a satisfying result: irrotationality is not a restriction imposed on the potential function from outside — it is built into what a potential function IS.**

**The properties that follow, and their practical use:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Streamlines and equipotential lines are ORTHOGONAL** ← | **They cross at right angles everywhere except at stagnation points** ← |
| **Both ψ and φ satisfy the LAPLACE equation, ∇²ψ = 0 and ∇²φ = 0** ← | **For 2-D irrotational incompressible flow** ← |
| **The difference in ψ between two streamlines equals the DISCHARGE between them** ← | **Which is what makes flow nets quantitative** ← |
| **Solutions can be SUPERPOSED, since Laplace's equation is linear** ← | **A source plus a uniform stream gives flow past a half-body, and so on** ← |

> **THE ORTHOGONALITY AND THE LAPLACE EQUATION TOGETHER ARE WHY THE FLOW NET METHOD WORKS AT ALL, and the connection is worth making explicit because the same net appears in an apparently unrelated topic:**

> **SEEPAGE through soil is governed by exactly the same Laplace equation, with hydraulic head in place of velocity potential.**

> **So the flow net sketched beneath a sheet pile wall in soil mechanics and the flow net around an aerofoil in fluid mechanics are solutions to the same mathematics, obtained by the same graphical rules of orthogonal curvilinear squares.**

> **That is why one technique, learned once, serves both — and why the number of flow channels and equipotential drops gives the discharge in the seepage case by precisely the analogous argument.**

**And a caution about real flows:**

> **Potential flow theory ignores VISCOSITY, so it cannot predict drag — the famous d'Alembert paradox, which says a body in ideal flow experiences no drag at all.**

> **The resolution is that viscosity matters only in a thin BOUNDARY LAYER next to the surface, and the potential flow solution remains an excellent description of the flow OUTSIDE that layer.**

> **So the theory is not wrong, merely incomplete: it describes the bulk flow very well and says nothing about the thin region where the drag is actually generated — which is exactly the division of labour that boundary layer theory formalised.**

examTip.trick: **ψ needs CONTINUITY and 2-D; φ needs IRROTATIONALITY.** Different conditions — a rotational 2-D flow has ψ but no φ; an irrotational 3-D flow has φ but no ψ.
examTip.trap: **Irrotationality is not an extra assumption** — if φ exists, the mixed partial derivatives cancel and ω_z = 0 automatically. It is built into what a potential function is.
examTip.mnemonic: **Seepage obeys the SAME Laplace equation with head in place of φ** — so the flow net under a sheet pile and the flow net round an aerofoil are the same mathematics, drawn by the same curvilinear-square rules.

questions.stem: A jet of water 50 mm in diameter, moving at 20 m/s, strikes a fixed flat plate held NORMAL to the jet. Taking the density of water as 1,000 kg/m³, the force on the plate is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 785 N.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Impulse-momentum: F = mass flow rate × change in velocity in the direction of the force** | **F = ρ A V × (V − 0)** ← |
| **So** | **F = ρ A V²** ← |
| **Area of the jet** | **A = π/4 × 0.05² = 1.9635 × 10⁻³ m²** |
| **Substituting** | **F = 1,000 × 1.9635 × 10⁻³ × 20²** |
| **= 1,000 × 1.9635 × 10⁻³ × 400** | **= 785.4 N** ← |

> **Option (b) 393 N is ½ρAV², which is the dynamic PRESSURE times the area — a different quantity, and the commonest error here.**

> **Option (d) 1,571 N is 2ρAV², the correct answer for a CURVED vane that turns the jet through 180°.**

**Why the momentum equation and not Bernoulli:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The jet strikes the plate and is deflected sideways, losing energy in turbulence** ← | **So Bernoulli, which assumes no losses, cannot be applied across the impact** ← |
| **The MOMENTUM equation does not care about losses** ← | **It is a statement of Newton's second law, valid whether energy is dissipated or not** ← |
| **Which is why momentum is used for jets, bends, sudden enlargements and hydraulic jumps** ← | **Precisely the situations where energy is lost by an unknown amount** ← |

> **THAT IS THE GENERAL RULE WORTH CARRYING: use ENERGY (Bernoulli) when you know the losses are small and want to relate pressure to velocity; use MOMENTUM when a FORCE is wanted, or when losses are significant and unknown.**

**The standard jet impact cases, which differ only in the momentum change:**

| Case | Force |
|---|---|
| **Fixed FLAT plate, normal to the jet** | **F = ρ A V²** ← (this question) |
| **Fixed flat plate, INCLINED at θ to the jet** | **F_normal = ρ A V² sin θ** ← |
| **Fixed CURVED vane, jet turned through 180°** | **F = 2 ρ A V² — DOUBLE, because the momentum is reversed rather than merely stopped** ← |
| **MOVING flat plate at velocity u** | **F = ρ A (V − u)² — the relative velocity governs, and the mass striking the plate per second falls too** ← |
| **Moving curved vane (a turbine bucket)** | **F = 2 ρ A (V − u)(1 + k cos θ)** ← |

> **THE FACTOR OF TWO IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT ENTRY AND IT IS THE BASIS OF THE PELTON WHEEL: turning the jet right round changes its momentum by 2mV rather than mV, so the force doubles for the same jet.**

> **That is why a Pelton bucket is shaped as a double hemispherical cup that turns the water back on itself, rather than as a flat paddle.**

> **In practice the deflection is about 165° rather than a full 180°, so that the returning water clears the following bucket instead of striking it — a small compromise costing a few per cent of the force and preventing a serious interference problem.**

**And the MOVING plate case, since it leads somewhere important:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Work done per second = F × u = ρ A (V − u)² u** | **For a flat plate** ← |
| **This is ZERO at u = 0 (no movement) and ZERO at u = V (the plate runs away from the jet)** ← | **So there is a maximum in between** ← |
| **Differentiating gives maximum power at u = V/3 for a flat plate** | ← |
| **And at u = V/2 for a hemispherical vane** ← | **Which is why a Pelton wheel's bucket speed is designed at about HALF the jet velocity** ← |

> **That result — bucket speed equals half the jet speed for maximum efficiency — is one of the most useful single facts in hydropower machinery, and it drops straight out of this elementary jet analysis.**

examTip.trick: **F = ρAV² = 1000 × 1.9635×10⁻³ × 400 = 785 N.** Option (b) 393 N is ½ρAV², the dynamic pressure times area — a different quantity.
examTip.trap: **Use MOMENTUM, not Bernoulli** — the jet loses energy in turbulence on impact, and momentum does not care about losses. Energy for pressure-velocity, momentum for forces.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 180° curved vane gives 2ρAV² — DOUBLE — because momentum is reversed, not merely stopped.** Hence the Pelton bucket's double cup, and maximum power at bucket speed = V/2.

questions.stem: Water of kinematic viscosity 1 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s flows at 2 m/s through a pipe of 100 mm diameter. The REYNOLDS NUMBER of the flow is:
questions.solution:
**2 × 10⁵.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Reynolds number for pipe flow** | **Re = V D / ν** ← |
| **Substituting** | **Re = 2 × 0.100 / (1 × 10⁻⁶)** |
| **Numerator** | **= 0.200** |
| **Re** | **= 0.200 / 10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁵** ← |

> **Note that Re is DIMENSIONLESS — m/s × m ÷ m²/s cancels completely, which is the quickest check that the formula has been assembled correctly.**

> **A common slip is to use the radius rather than the diameter, giving 1 × 10⁵. For pipe flow the characteristic length is always the DIAMETER.**

**What the number means physically:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Re = INERTIA forces ÷ VISCOUS forces** ← | **The ratio of the two competing influences on the flow** ← |
| **LOW Re** | **Viscosity dominates; disturbances are damped out; the flow is LAMINAR** ← |
| **HIGH Re** | **Inertia dominates; disturbances grow; the flow is TURBULENT** ← |

> **So the transition from laminar to turbulent is not a property of the fluid or of the pipe but of the BALANCE between the two — which is why one dimensionless number captures it for every fluid, every pipe size and every velocity.**

**The ranges for pipe flow:**

| Re | Regime |
|---|---|
| **Below 2,000** | **LAMINAR** ← |
| **2,000 to 4,000** | **TRANSITIONAL — unpredictable** ← |
| **Above 4,000** | **TURBULENT** ← |
| **This flow, at 2 × 10⁵** | **Firmly TURBULENT — as almost all practical water pipe flows are** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL POINT WORTH TAKING FROM THE NUMBER: laminar flow in a water pipe is a laboratory curiosity.**

> **To get Re below 2,000 in a 100 mm pipe carrying water you would need a velocity of about 0.02 m/s — a trickle. Every real water main, sewer and penstock is turbulent.**

> **Laminar flow matters where the viscosity is high or the passage is tiny: oil pipelines, lubrication films, groundwater seepage through soil, and the flow of blood in small vessels.**

> **Which is why Darcy's law for soil is linear (laminar) while pipe flow head loss goes as roughly V² (turbulent) — the same distinction, appearing in a different chapter.**

**Why the ranges differ for other geometries:**

| Geometry | Characteristic length | Transition around |
|---|---|---|
| **PIPE (full)** | **Diameter D** | **Re = 2,000** ← |
| **OPEN CHANNEL** | **HYDRAULIC RADIUS R = A/P** ← | **Re = 500** ← |
| **Flow past a flat plate** | **Distance x from the leading edge** | **Re = 5 × 10⁵** ← |
| **Flow around a sphere** | **Diameter** | **Re ≈ 1 for creeping flow to cease** |

> **THE SECOND ROW EXPLAINS AN APPARENT INCONSISTENCY THAT PUZZLES STUDENTS: why is the critical Reynolds number 2,000 for a pipe and 500 for a channel?**

> **Because a different LENGTH is used. For a circular pipe running full, R = D/4, so a channel Re of 500 corresponds to a pipe Re of 2,000 — they are the same criterion expressed with different characteristic lengths.**

> **The lesson generalises: a dimensionless number has no meaning without its definition, and quoting a critical value without saying which length was used is an invitation to error.**

> **The same caution applies to the Froude number, to specific speed, and to every other dimensionless group in the subject.**

examTip.trick: **Re = VD/ν = 2 × 0.1 / 10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁵.** Use the DIAMETER, not the radius — using the radius gives 1 × 10⁵.
examTip.trap: **Re = inertia ÷ viscous forces**, so the transition depends on the balance, not on the fluid alone. Below 2,000 laminar, above 4,000 turbulent — and virtually every real water pipe is turbulent.
examTip.mnemonic: **Channels transition at Re = 500, pipes at 2,000, only because channels use R = A/P and D = 4R.** Same criterion, different characteristic length — never quote a critical value without saying which.

questions.stem: The EQUIVALENT LENGTH method of allowing for MINOR LOSSES in a pipeline expresses each fitting as:
options: The LENGTH of straight pipe of the same diameter that would produce the same head loss as the fitting
The diameter of pipe that would eliminate the loss
The pressure drop across the fitting in metres of mercury
The time taken for water to pass through the fitting
questions.solution:
**The LENGTH of straight pipe, of the same diameter, that would produce the SAME head loss as the fitting.**

**How the method works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A fitting's loss is normally written h = K V²/2g** ← | **With K a coefficient for that fitting** |
| **A length of pipe's loss is h = f L V² / (2 g D)** ← | **Darcy-Weisbach** |
| **Equating the two** | **K V²/2g = f L_e V² / (2 g D)** ← |
| **Hence** | **L_e = K D / f** ← |
| **All the equivalent lengths are ADDED to the actual pipe length** | **And one Darcy calculation gives the total loss** ← |

> **THE CONVENIENCE IS THE WHOLE POINT: instead of computing the friction loss and then a dozen separate fitting losses, you add the equivalent lengths to the real length and do ONE calculation on the total.**

**Typical values, for both K and L_e/D:**

| Fitting | K | Equivalent length L_e/D |
|---|---|---|
| **Sharp-edged ENTRANCE from a reservoir** | **0.5** ← | About 20 |
| **Bell-mouthed entrance** | **0.05** ← | 2 |
| **EXIT into a reservoir** | **1.0 — the entire velocity head is lost** ← | 40 |
| **90° elbow, standard** | **0.9** | **30 to 40** ← |
| **90° bend, long radius** | **0.3** ← | 15 |
| **GATE valve, fully open** | **0.15 to 0.2** ← | **8** ← |
| **GLOBE valve, fully open** | **6 to 10** ← | **300 or more** ← |
| **Sudden enlargement** | **(1 − A₁/A₂)²** | — |
| **Tee, flow through branch** | **1.8** | 60 |

> **THE COMPARISON BETWEEN THE TWO VALVES IS THE MOST USEFUL LINE IN THE TABLE and it has a real cost attached:**

> **A fully open GATE valve is equivalent to about 8 diameters of pipe; a fully open GLOBE valve to 300 or more — nearly forty times as much.**

> **A globe valve makes the water turn through two right angles and pass through a restricted seat even when fully open, whereas a gate valve withdraws entirely from the bore and leaves a clear passage.**

> **So a globe valve used as an isolating valve on a long main imposes a permanent, pointless pumping cost for the life of the installation.**

> **The rule that follows is worth knowing: GATE valves for isolation (open or shut, minimal loss); GLOBE valves for THROTTLING, where the loss is the point and the valve's fine control is wanted.**

**When minor losses can be neglected, and when they cannot:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A LONG pipeline — length more than about 1,000 diameters** ← | **Minor losses are typically a few per cent; often neglected** ← |
| **A SHORT pipe with many fittings — a pump house, a treatment plant's pipework, house plumbing** ← | **The "minor" losses may EXCEED the friction loss entirely** ← |
| **A suction pipe to a pump** | **NEVER neglect them — they reduce the available NPSH directly and cause cavitation** ← |

> **THE NAME IS THEREFORE MISLEADING, and it is worth saying so plainly: "minor" losses are minor only in long pipelines.**

> **In the pipework inside a pumping station, with its bends, valves, strainers, expansions and contractions in a few metres of pipe, they are the dominant loss, and treating them as an afterthought produces a pump that cannot deliver its duty.**

> **The third row is the case with real consequences: a strainer and two bends on a suction line can consume enough head to push the pump into cavitation, and the loss is entirely of the "minor" kind.**

> **A name given for the usual case has misled generations of designers dealing with the unusual one, which is a reasonable argument for preferring the alternative term LOCAL losses.**

examTip.trick: **L_e = K D / f** — equating K V²/2g to the Darcy loss. Add every fitting's equivalent length to the real pipe length and do ONE calculation.
examTip.trap: **Gate valve fully open ≈ 8 diameters; GLOBE valve ≈ 300+.** A globe valve used for isolation imposes a permanent pumping cost. Gate for isolating, globe for throttling.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Minor" losses are minor only in LONG pipelines** — in a pump house they dominate, and on a suction line they eat the NPSH and cause cavitation. Prefer the term LOCAL losses.

questions.stem: Water flows in a wide rectangular channel at a depth of 0.5 m with a mean velocity of 3 m/s. The FROUDE NUMBER and the flow regime are:
options: 0.74, subcritical
1.00, critical
1.35, SUPERCRITICAL
1.83, supercritical
questions.solution:
**Fr = 1.35, and the flow is SUPERCRITICAL.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Froude number for a rectangular channel** | **Fr = V / √(g y)** ← |
| **Substituting** | **Fr = 3 / √(9.81 × 0.5)** |
| **Denominator** | **√4.905 = 2.215 m/s — this is the CELERITY of a small surface wave** ← |
| **Fr** | **= 3 / 2.215 = 1.355 ≈ 1.35** ← |
| **Since Fr > 1** | **SUPERCRITICAL** ← |

> **Option (a) 0.74 is the reciprocal, √(gy)/V.**

**What the Froude number means:**

| Interpretation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Fr = INERTIA forces ÷ GRAVITY forces** ← | **The formal definition** |
| **Fr = flow VELOCITY ÷ the speed of a small SURFACE WAVE** ← | **The interpretation that is actually useful** ← |

> **THE SECOND READING IS THE ONE TO CARRY, because it makes every consequence obvious:**

| Regime | Fr | Meaning | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SUBCRITICAL (tranquil)** | **< 1** | **The flow is SLOWER than a wave, so a disturbance CAN travel UPSTREAM** ← | **Deep, slow; controlled from DOWNSTREAM** ← |
| **CRITICAL** | **= 1** | **Wave speed equals flow speed** | **Specific energy is a MINIMUM for the given discharge** ← |
| **SUPERCRITICAL (rapid, shooting)** | **> 1** | **The flow OUTRUNS its own waves, so nothing can travel upstream** ← | **Shallow, fast; controlled from UPSTREAM** ← |

> **THE CONTROL DIRECTION IN THE LAST COLUMN IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE AND IT GOVERNS HOW A WATER SURFACE PROFILE IS COMPUTED:**

> **In SUBCRITICAL flow, information travels upstream, so a downstream obstruction — a weir, a gate, a lake — is felt for a long distance upstream. The backwater profile is therefore computed starting at the DOWNSTREAM control and working UPSTREAM.**

> **In SUPERCRITICAL flow, nothing travels upstream at all. The flow is determined entirely by conditions at the UPSTREAM end, and the computation proceeds DOWNSTREAM.**

> **Get the direction of computation wrong and the profile diverges rather than converging, which is a numerical symptom of a physical error.**

**A test anyone can perform, which makes the concept concrete:**

> **Drop a stone into a flowing stream and watch the ripples.**

> **If the ripples spread UPSTREAM as well as downstream, the flow is SUBCRITICAL.**

> **If every ripple is swept downstream and none can move against the current, the flow is SUPERCRITICAL.**

> **That is the Froude number made visible, and it is exactly what the formula says.**

**And what supercritical flow implies for design:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **It cannot persist over a mild slope** | **It will return to subcritical through a HYDRAULIC JUMP** ← |
| **The jump dissipates ENERGY, sometimes a great deal** ← | **Which is why stilling basins are placed exactly where the jump will occur** ← |
| **Supercritical flow is EROSIVE** | **High velocity, high shear — an unlined channel will scour** ← |
| **Cross-waves and standing waves form at bends and transitions** | **They do not damp out as they would in subcritical flow, so transitions must be gentle and long** ← |
| **Air entrainment (bulking) increases the depth** | **Freeboard must allow for it on a spillway chute** ← |

> **The fourth row is the design point most often underestimated: a bend in a supercritical channel throws a standing wave across to the opposite wall, which reflects, and the pattern persists far downstream with the water surface much higher than the calculated depth on alternate sides.**

> **Chutes and spillway channels are therefore kept straight wherever possible, and where a bend is unavoidable it is given a very large radius and sometimes a banked invert — the same reasoning as superelevation on a road, and for the same reason.**

examTip.trick: **Fr = V/√(gy) = 3/√(9.81 × 0.5) = 3/2.215 = 1.35 > 1, so SUPERCRITICAL.** Option (a) is the reciprocal.
examTip.trap: **Fr is the flow speed divided by the WAVE speed** — subcritical flow lets disturbances travel upstream, so it is controlled from DOWNSTREAM; supercritical is controlled from UPSTREAM, and the profile is computed in that direction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Drop a stone: if ripples spread upstream it is subcritical; if all are swept away it is supercritical.** And supercritical flow at a bend throws standing cross-waves that never damp out — keep chutes straight.

questions.stem: The φ-INDEX used in hydrology is:
options: The ratio of runoff to rainfall for a catchment
A CONSTANT rate of rainfall LOSS (in mm/h) such that the rainfall in excess of it equals the volume of direct runoff
The maximum rate at which a soil can absorb water
The time from the centroid of rainfall excess to the peak of the hydrograph
questions.solution:
**A CONSTANT rate of loss, in mm per hour, such that the rainfall in excess of it exactly equals the observed volume of DIRECT RUNOFF.**

**How it is used:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A storm hyetograph (rainfall intensity against time) and the resulting hydrograph are available** ← | ← |
| **The direct runoff volume is obtained by separating the BASE FLOW from the hydrograph** ← | **And expressed as a DEPTH over the catchment** ← |
| **A horizontal line is drawn across the hyetograph at height φ** | ← |
| **φ is adjusted until the rainfall ABOVE the line — the rainfall excess — equals that depth** ← | **Usually by trial** ← |
| **The area below the line is the total LOSS** | **Infiltration, interception, depression storage and evaporation, lumped together** ← |

> **Option (c) describes INFILTRATION CAPACITY, a related but different quantity; option (d) is the BASIN LAG; option (a) is the runoff coefficient.**

**Why a constant is used, when losses are obviously not constant:**

| Reality | The φ-index's treatment |
|---|---|
| **Infiltration starts high and DECLINES as the soil wets — Horton's curve** ← | **Replaced by a single average value** ← |
| **Interception and depression storage occur mainly at the START of the storm** | **Absorbed into the same average** ← |
| **Losses vary across the catchment** | **Lumped** ← |

> **SO THE φ-INDEX IS AVOWEDLY CRUDE, AND THAT IS ITS VIRTUE RATHER THAN ITS DEFECT: it requires only the rainfall record and the hydrograph, both of which exist, and it produces a single number that can be applied to a design storm.**

> **A physically realistic infiltration model needs soil parameters that are rarely measured, varies across the catchment, and depends on the antecedent moisture — so its apparent precision is illusory in most practical cases.**

> **The φ-index is honest about being an average, and for estimating the runoff from a design storm on an ungauged or lightly gauged catchment it is often as good as anything more elaborate.**

**A worked illustration, since the trial process is what examinations test:**

| Hour | Rainfall (mm) |
|---|---|
| 1 | **10** |
| 2 | **25** |
| 3 | **30** |
| 4 | **8** |

> **Suppose the direct runoff depth is 32 mm. Total rainfall is 73 mm, so the total loss is 41 mm over 4 hours — suggesting φ = 10.25 mm/h.**

> **BUT hour 4 received only 8 mm, less than 10.25, so that hour contributes NO excess and its loss is only 8 mm, not 10.25.**

> **Recompute over the remaining 3 hours: excess needed 32 mm from 10 + 25 + 30 = 65 mm, so the loss is 33 mm over 3 hours, φ = 11 mm/h.**

> **Check: hour 1 gives 10 − 11 → 0 (no excess), so hour 1 also drops out. Excess from hours 2 and 3 only: (25 + 30) − 2φ = 32 gives φ = 11.5 mm/h. Check hour 1: 10 < 11.5 ✓ and hour 4: 8 < 11.5 ✓. Consistent.**

> **THE ITERATION IS THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY OF THESE PROBLEMS: any interval whose rainfall is LESS than φ contributes no excess and must be EXCLUDED from the averaging, and excluding it changes φ, which may exclude another interval.**

> **Work through until the set of contributing intervals is stable, and always check every excluded interval against the final φ.**

**The related indices, for completeness:**

| Index | Definition |
|---|---|
| **φ-index** | **Constant loss rate; excess = direct runoff** ← |
| **W-index** | **The average INFILTRATION rate alone — the φ-index refined by subtracting interception and depression storage first, so it is more physically meaningful and always ≤ φ** ← |
| **W_min** | **The W-index for a very wet catchment, approaching the constant final infiltration rate** ← |
| **Runoff COEFFICIENT** | **A ratio, not a rate — used in the rational method** ← (option a) |

> **The relation W ≤ φ in the second row follows directly from the definitions and is worth stating: φ lumps everything into a rate, while W removes the initial abstractions first, so what remains is smaller.**

examTip.trick: **A constant loss RATE (mm/h) such that the rainfall above it equals the direct runoff depth.** Option (c) is infiltration capacity, (d) is basin lag, (a) is the runoff coefficient.
examTip.trap: **Any interval with rainfall LESS than φ contributes no excess and must be EXCLUDED from the averaging** — and excluding it changes φ, which may exclude another. Iterate until stable, then check every excluded interval.
examTip.mnemonic: **W-index ≤ φ-index always** — W removes interception and depression storage first and leaves infiltration alone, so what remains is smaller.

questions.stem: The DOUBLE MASS CURVE technique is used in hydrology to:
options: Estimate the peak discharge of a flood
Compute the mean areal rainfall over a catchment
Determine the infiltration capacity of a soil
CHECK and ADJUST the CONSISTENCY of a rainfall record at a station
questions.solution:
**To check and adjust the CONSISTENCY of a rainfall record**, by plotting the station's cumulative rainfall against the cumulative mean of a group of surrounding stations.

**How it works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Select a GROUP of nearby stations known or assumed to be consistent** ← | **Usually 5 to 10, in the same climatic region** ← |
| **Compute the cumulative annual rainfall for the suspect station** | **Working BACKWARD from the most recent year** ← |
| **Compute the cumulative MEAN annual rainfall of the group over the same years** | ← |
| **PLOT one against the other** | **Suspect station on the y-axis, group mean on the x-axis** ← |
| **A consistent record gives a STRAIGHT LINE** ← | **Because the station's rainfall bears a constant proportion to the region's** ← |
| **A CHANGE OF SLOPE indicates an INCONSISTENCY** ← | **Something changed at that station at that date** ← |

> **THE LOGIC IS THAT REGIONAL RAINFALL VARIES TOGETHER: a wet year is wet at every station and a dry year dry at all of them.**

> **So the RATIO between one station and its neighbours should be stable, even though the rainfall itself varies enormously. A change in that ratio cannot be meteorological — the neighbours would have changed too — so it must be caused by something at the station.**

**What causes an inconsistency:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **The gauge was MOVED** ← | **Even a short distance, or a change of elevation** ← |
| **The gauge's EXPOSURE changed** | **A building erected nearby, or trees grown up around it — both reduce the catch** ← |
| **The instrument was replaced or the observation practice changed** | **A different observer, a different reading time** ← |
| **The gauge was damaged or poorly maintained** | ← |

> **THE EXPOSURE ROW IN THE SECOND POSITION IS THE COMMONEST AND THE MOST INSIDIOUS, and it deserves emphasis because it happens without anybody noticing:**

> **A rain gauge installed in an open field twenty years ago may now be surrounded by trees that have grown up, or shielded by a new building.**

> **Nobody moved the gauge and nobody changed the procedure — but the catch has fallen, gradually, and the record now understates the rainfall.**

> **The change appears in the double mass curve as a slope change, and it is often the only way such a drift is ever detected, since the individual annual figures look perfectly plausible in isolation.**

**How the record is CORRECTED:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The RECENT portion of the record is taken as correct** ← | **Which is why the cumulation is done backward from the present** ← |
| **The earlier records are ADJUSTED to the recent slope** | **P_corrected = P_recorded × (slope of recent segment ÷ slope of earlier segment)** ← |
| **The whole earlier period is scaled by that constant ratio** | ← |

> **THE CHOICE OF THE RECENT PERIOD AS THE STANDARD IS DELIBERATE AND WORTH UNDERSTANDING: the object is usually to produce a record consistent with the CURRENT gauge conditions, since future observations will continue under those conditions.**

> **Adjusting the recent data to match the old would produce a record that is internally consistent but disconnected from everything measured from now on.**

> **Where the purpose is different — reconstructing a historical series, say — the choice may be reversed, and the point is that it is a CHOICE, made for a reason, rather than a rule.**

**The cautions, since the technique is easy to over-apply:**

| Caution | Note |
|---|---|
| **A slope change must be sustained over SEVERAL YEARS to be real** ← | **A one-year deviation is noise, not an inconsistency** ← |
| **The base stations must themselves be consistent** ← | **If a common cause affected them all, the method finds nothing** ← |
| **Use enough base stations** | **A single neighbour's own inconsistency would be mistaken for the suspect station's** ← |
| **It cannot detect an error common to the whole region** | **Such as a change of national observation practice** ← |

> **The last two rows describe the method's fundamental limitation, and it is inherent rather than a matter of technique: the double mass curve is a RELATIVE test.**

> **It can only find a station that has drifted away from its neighbours, and is blind to anything that moved all of them together — which is a reasonable trade, since regional consistency is what most hydrological analysis actually requires.**

By plotting its cumulative rainfall against the cumulative mean of surrounding stations.

examTip.trick: **Cumulative rainfall of the suspect station against the cumulative mean of surrounding stations.** A straight line means consistent; a CHANGE OF SLOPE means something changed at that station.
examTip.trap: **Cumulate BACKWARD from the present, and adjust the OLDER data to the recent slope** — so the record is consistent with the gauge's current conditions, under which future readings will be taken.
examTip.mnemonic: **Trees growing up around a gauge is the classic undetectable drift** — nobody moved anything, but the catch fell. The method is RELATIVE, so it is blind to anything that changed all the stations together.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 10 m carries two equal point loads of 30 kN each, placed 3 m from each support. The MAXIMUM bending moment in the beam is:
options: 90 kNm
150 kNm
180 kNm
210 kNm
questions.solution:
**90 kNm.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Reactions, by symmetry** | **R_A = R_B = (30 + 30) / 2 = 30 kN** ← |
| **Bending moment at the left load, 3 m from A** | **M = R_A × 3 = 30 × 3 = 90 kNm** ← |
| **Bending moment at midspan, 5 m from A** | **M = R_A × 5 − 30 × 2 = 150 − 60 = 90 kNm** ← |
| **The two are EQUAL** | **The bending moment is CONSTANT between the loads** ← |
| **Maximum bending moment** | **= 90 kNm** ← |

> **Option (b) 150 kNm is R_A × 5, forgetting to deduct the near load's relieving moment — the commonest error.**

**Why the moment is CONSTANT between the loads, which is the point of the question:**

| Region | Shear force | Bending moment |
|---|---|---|
| **A to the first load (0 to 3 m)** | **+30 kN, constant** | **Rising linearly, 0 → 90 kNm** ← |
| **BETWEEN the loads (3 to 7 m)** | **30 − 30 = ZERO** ← | **CONSTANT at 90 kNm** ← |
| **Second load to B (7 to 10 m)** | **−30 kN, constant** | **Falling linearly, 90 → 0** ← |

> **SINCE dM/dx = V, A ZERO SHEAR FORCE MEANS A CONSTANT BENDING MOMENT — which is exactly what happens in the middle 4 m.**

> **That region is in PURE BENDING: it carries a bending moment with no shear at all.**

**Why pure bending matters — this is the basis of a standard laboratory test:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The FOUR-POINT BENDING test uses precisely this arrangement** ← | **Two symmetric loads on a simply supported beam** ← |
| **The central region has constant moment and zero shear** | **So the material there is in a pure, uniform bending state** ← |
| **Failure in that region is a genuine FLEXURAL failure** ← | **Uncontaminated by shear effects** ← |
| **Contrast with the THREE-point test (a single central load)** | **There the maximum moment occurs at the one section where the shear also changes sign — a stress concentration under the load** ← |

> **THAT IS WHY THE FLEXURAL STRENGTH (MODULUS OF RUPTURE) OF CONCRETE IS MEASURED IN FOUR-POINT BENDING, with two loads at the third points of the span.**

> **The middle third is in pure bending, so the beam fails at its genuinely weakest section within that region — which gives a more reliable measure of the material than a three-point test, where failure is forced to occur at the loading point whether or not that is the weakest place.**

> **The standard even distinguishes the two cases in its reporting: if a four-point test specimen fails OUTSIDE the middle third, the result is treated differently or discarded, because the failure was then influenced by shear.**

**And the general rules for sketching diagrams, which this example illustrates:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **dV/dx = −w** | **The slope of the shear diagram is the load intensity** ← |
| **dM/dx = V** | **The slope of the moment diagram is the shear** ← |
| **Maximum moment occurs where the SHEAR CROSSES ZERO** ← | **Or over a whole region where the shear IS zero, as here** ← |
| **A point load causes a JUMP in shear and a KINK in moment** | ← |
| **An applied couple causes a JUMP in moment and NO change in shear** | ← |
| **No load → shear constant, moment linear; UDL → shear linear, moment parabolic** | **Each integration raises the degree by one** ← |

> **The third row is the one that answers most examination questions in a single step: find where the shear is zero, and evaluate the moment there.**

examTip.trick: **R = 30 kN, M = 30 × 3 = 90 kNm, and it is CONSTANT between the loads** because the shear there is zero. Option (b) forgets to deduct the near load's relieving moment.
examTip.trap: **Zero shear between the loads means constant moment — a region of PURE BENDING.** Maximum moment always occurs where the shear crosses zero, or throughout a region where it is zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **This is the FOUR-POINT bending test** — the middle third is in pure bending, so concrete fails at its genuinely weakest section there, not at a loading point as in a three-point test.

questions.stem: When an external COUPLE (a concentrated moment) is applied at a section of a beam, the diagrams show:
options: A jump in the shear force and no change in the bending moment
A jump in both the shear force and the bending moment
No change in either diagram
NO change in the SHEAR FORCE at that section, and a sudden JUMP in the BENDING MOMENT equal to the applied couple
questions.solution:
**No change in the SHEAR FORCE, and a sudden JUMP in the BENDING MOMENT equal to the magnitude of the applied couple.**

**Why:**

| Consideration | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **A couple applies NO net FORCE to the beam** ← | **It is two equal and opposite forces; their resultant is zero** ← |
| **So vertical equilibrium of an element at that section is unaffected** | **The shear force is therefore CONTINUOUS across it** ← |
| **But the couple DOES apply a moment** ← | **So moment equilibrium of the element requires the bending moment to change abruptly** ← |
| **The jump equals the applied couple, M₀** | **Its SENSE determines whether the diagram steps up or down** ← |

> **Note that the SUPPORT REACTIONS do change when a couple is applied — a couple on a simply supported beam produces equal and opposite reactions M₀/L — so the shear force in the beam as a whole is altered.**

> **What does NOT change is the shear AT the section where the couple acts: there is no discontinuity there.**

**The contrast with a point LOAD, which is the pair to remember:**

| Applied at a section | Shear force | Bending moment |
|---|---|---|
| **Point LOAD (a force)** | **JUMPS by the load** ← | **CONTINUOUS, but with a KINK (a sudden change of slope)** ← |
| **Couple (a moment)** | **CONTINUOUS — no change** ← | **JUMPS by the couple** ← |

> **THE SYMMETRY IS EXACT AND MAKES BOTH EASY TO REMEMBER: a FORCE discontinuity appears in the SHEAR diagram, and a MOMENT discontinuity appears in the MOMENT diagram.**

> **Each applied action produces a jump in its own diagram and, at most, a change of slope in the other — which follows directly from dM/dx = V.**

**Where applied couples arise in practice, since they can seem artificial:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **An ECCENTRIC axial load on a column or beam** ← | **Statically equivalent to an axial force plus a couple P × e** ← |
| **A bracket or corbel attached to a beam's side** | **The load's eccentricity from the beam's axis becomes a couple** ← |
| **A beam-to-column connection carrying moment** | ← |
| **A cantilevered balcony framing into a spandrel beam** ← | **Which twists the beam — this is where the couple becomes a TORSION, not a bending moment** ← |
| **Prestressing applied eccentrically at an anchorage** | **The classic case: force plus couple at the end block** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW POINTS AT A DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS AND IS OFTEN BLURRED: whether an applied couple produces BENDING or TORSION in the member depends on the AXIS about which it acts.**

> **A couple about an axis PERPENDICULAR to the beam's length bends it and produces the jump described here.**

> **A couple about the beam's LONGITUDINAL axis TWISTS it, and appears in a torsion diagram rather than the bending moment diagram — and it is the case that catches designers out, because a balcony or a cantilevered slab framing into the side of a beam loads that beam in torsion continuously along its length.**

> **Reinforced concrete spandrel beams have failed from exactly that, designed for bending and shear alone while carrying a substantial distributed torsion — which is why torsion reinforcement (closed stirrups and longitudinal bars in every corner) is specified for such members.**

**And the diagram-sketching consequence:**

> **When a couple acts at an INTERNAL section, the bending moment diagram has a vertical step there, and the beam has TWO different moments at the same point — one just to the left, one just to the right.**

> **When a couple acts at a free END of a cantilever, the moment diagram starts at that value rather than at zero, which is the simplest case and a useful check on the sign convention.**

examTip.trick: **A couple applies no net FORCE, so shear is continuous; it applies a moment, so the bending moment JUMPS by M₀.**
examTip.trap: **Exact symmetry with a point load: a FORCE jumps the SHEAR diagram and kinks the moment; a COUPLE jumps the MOMENT diagram and leaves the shear alone.** Both follow from dM/dx = V.
examTip.mnemonic: **A couple about the beam's LONGITUDINAL axis is TORSION, not bending** — a balcony framing into a spandrel beam's side loads it in distributed torsion, and beams designed for bending alone have failed from it.

questions.stem: For a material with a modulus of elasticity of 200 GPa and a Poisson's ratio of 0.30, the BULK MODULUS is:
options: 76.9 GPa
250 GPa
500 GPa
questions.solution:
**166.7 GPa.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The elastic constant relation** | **E = 3 K (1 − 2ν)** ← |
| **Rearranged** | **K = E / [3 (1 − 2ν)]** ← |
| **Substituting** | **K = 200 / [3 × (1 − 0.60)]** |
| **Denominator** | **= 3 × 0.40 = 1.20** |
| **K** | **= 200 / 1.20 = 166.7 GPa** ← |

> **Option (a) 76.9 GPa is the SHEAR modulus G = E/[2(1+ν)] = 200/2.6 — the other relation, and the most likely confusion.**

> **Option (d) 500 GPa omits the factor 3.**

**The four elastic constants and the relations between them:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **E = 2 G (1 + ν)** ← | **Links E, G and ν** |
| **E = 3 K (1 − 2ν)** ← | **Links E, K and ν** |
| **E = 9 K G / (3K + G)** ← | **Links E, K and G, eliminating ν** |
| **ν = (3K − 2G) / (6K + 2G)** | ← |

> **FOR AN ISOTROPIC MATERIAL ONLY TWO CONSTANTS ARE INDEPENDENT — know any two and the rest follow, which is why these relations exist at all.**

**The LIMITS ON POISSON'S RATIO, which fall straight out of the second relation:**

| Requirement | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **K must be POSITIVE** | **A material that expanded under hydrostatic compression would be unstable** ← |
| **So (1 − 2ν) > 0** | **Hence ν < 0.5** ← |
| **At ν = 0.5 exactly, K → INFINITY** ← | **The material is perfectly INCOMPRESSIBLE — rubber approaches this, and so does saturated clay under undrained loading** ← |
| **G must also be positive, so ν > −1** | **The theoretical lower limit** ← |

> **THE ν = 0.5 CASE IN THE THIRD ROW IS NOT A MATHEMATICAL CURIOSITY BUT A WORKING ASSUMPTION IN GEOTECHNICS: a saturated clay loaded rapidly cannot change volume, because the water has nowhere to go.**

> **It therefore behaves as an incompressible material, and undrained analysis uses ν_u = 0.5 exactly.**

> **That single value carries a great deal: it is why the immediate settlement of a footing on saturated clay is a pure DISTORTION with no volume change, and why the consolidation settlement that follows — which does involve volume change — is a separate calculation performed with drained parameters.**

**Typical values, for a sense of scale:**

| Material | E (GPa) | ν | K (GPa) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Steel** | **200** | **0.30** | **167** ← |
| **Concrete** | **25 to 35** | **0.15 to 0.20** | **About 15** |
| **Aluminium** | **70** | **0.33** | **69** |
| **Cork** | **Low** | **Near ZERO** ← | **Which is why a cork can be pushed into a bottle neck without bulging sideways** ← |
| **Rubber** | **Low** | **≈ 0.4999** ← | **Very high — nearly incompressible** ← |

> **THE CORK AND RUBBER ENTRIES TOGETHER MAKE POISSON'S RATIO INTUITIVE, and the contrast is worth keeping:**

> **Cork has ν ≈ 0, so squeezing it lengthwise does not make it expand sideways — which is precisely why it works as a bottle stopper and why no other common material would.**

> **Rubber has ν ≈ 0.5, so it conserves its volume exactly: squeeze it in one direction and it bulges in the others by just enough to keep the volume constant.**

> **A rubber block confined in a steel box cannot be compressed at all, because it has nowhere to bulge to — which is the same reason a saturated clay behaves as it does, and why rubber bearings for bridges are made of thin layers bonded between steel plates: the steel restrains the bulging, and the confined rubber becomes very stiff vertically while remaining flexible in shear.**

examTip.trick: **K = E/[3(1−2ν)] = 200/(3 × 0.4) = 166.7 GPa.** Option (a) 76.9 is G = E/[2(1+ν)] — the other relation.
examTip.trap: **Only TWO elastic constants are independent for an isotropic material.** And K > 0 forces ν < 0.5, with K → ∞ at exactly 0.5.
examTip.mnemonic: **ν = 0.5 means incompressible — used exactly for undrained saturated clay.** Cork has ν ≈ 0, which is why it goes into a bottle neck; rubber has ν ≈ 0.5, which is why a confined rubber bearing is stiff vertically and soft in shear.

questions.stem: In a tensile test on mild steel, the engineering (nominal) stress-strain curve shows the stress FALLING after the ultimate point, even though the material is still being stretched further, because:
options: NECKING reduces the actual cross-sectional area
The material becomes weaker with strain
The testing machine loses power
The modulus of elasticity decreases
questions.solution:
**Because NECKING reduces the true cross-sectional area, while the nominal stress continues to be computed on the ORIGINAL area.**

**What actually happens after the ultimate point:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Up to the ultimate point, deformation is UNIFORM along the bar** ← | **The area reduces evenly** |
| **At the ultimate point, deformation LOCALISES at one section** ← | **A NECK forms** ← |
| **The area at the neck falls rapidly** | **Much faster than elsewhere** ← |
| **The LOAD the specimen can carry therefore falls** | **Even though the material at the neck is still hardening** ← |
| **Nominal stress = LOAD ÷ ORIGINAL area** ← | **So it falls with the load** ← |
| **TRUE stress = load ÷ ACTUAL (reduced) area** ← | **Which continues to RISE right up to fracture** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS RESOLVE THE APPARENT PARADOX COMPLETELY: the material never weakens.**

> **The true stress-strain curve rises monotonically to fracture. The apparent drop is entirely an artefact of dividing by an area that no longer exists.**

> **Option (b) states the intuitive but wrong reading, and it is worth rejecting explicitly: strain HARDENING continues throughout, which is precisely why the neck does not run away instantly — the material at the neck gets stronger as it thins, which is what allows the deformation to spread at all.**

**The full mild steel curve, with the standard points:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **LIMIT OF PROPORTIONALITY** | **Up to here stress ∝ strain, and Hooke's law holds** ← |
| **ELASTIC LIMIT** | **Beyond here, some deformation is PERMANENT — slightly above the proportional limit** ← |
