| **UPPER and LOWER YIELD POINTS** | **The distinct yield plateau is characteristic of MILD STEEL and largely absent in high-strength and cold-worked steels** ← |
| **Yield plateau** | **Large strain at almost constant stress — the source of steel's DUCTILITY** ← |
| **STRAIN HARDENING region** | **Stress rises again as the material work-hardens** ← |
| **ULTIMATE stress** | **The maximum NOMINAL stress; necking begins here** ← |
| **BREAKING (fracture) stress** | **Lower in nominal terms, HIGHER in true stress** ← |

> **THE YIELD PLATEAU IS THE SINGLE MOST VALUABLE PROPERTY OF MILD STEEL FOR STRUCTURAL PURPOSES, and it is worth saying why:**

> **It means the material can absorb very large deformation without losing strength — so a member that is overloaded deforms visibly and dramatically before it fails.**

> **It gives WARNING. It also allows a structure to redistribute load: an overstressed section yields, stops taking more, and passes the excess to less stressed parts, which is the whole basis of plastic design and of the ductility requirements in seismic codes.**

> **A brittle material — cast iron, or a high-strength steel with no plateau — fails suddenly and without warning, and a structure made of it cannot redistribute.**

> **This is why reinforced concrete is designed to be UNDER-reinforced: it forces the ductile steel to yield before the brittle concrete crushes, so the beam sags, cracks widely and warns before it collapses.**

**And the two measures of ductility, since both are quoted in steel specifications:**

| Measure | Definition | Typical for mild steel |
|---|---|---|
| **PERCENTAGE ELONGATION** | **(final gauge length − original) ÷ original × 100** ← | **20 to 25 %** ← |
| **PERCENTAGE REDUCTION IN AREA** | **(original area − area at the neck) ÷ original × 100** ← | **60 to 70 %** ← |

> **The reduction in area is much the larger figure because it measures deformation AT THE NECK, where it is concentrated, while the elongation averages it over the whole gauge length.**

> **This is also why the GAUGE LENGTH must always be stated with an elongation figure: the same specimen tested over a longer gauge length reports a SMALLER percentage elongation, since the localised necking extension is divided by a greater length.**

> **An elongation quoted without its gauge length is therefore not a material property at all, which is why standards specify it as a multiple of the diameter — commonly 5.65√A₀ — rather than as an absolute length.**

The nominal stress is still computed on the ORIGINAL area.

examTip.trick: **Nominal stress divides by the ORIGINAL area; the actual area has necked down.** True stress rises monotonically to fracture — the material never weakens.
examTip.trap: **Strain HARDENING continues throughout necking** — that is what stops the neck running away instantly. Option (b) states the intuitive but wrong reading.
examTip.mnemonic: **The yield plateau is why steel warns before it fails and can redistribute load** — the basis of plastic design and of under-reinforcing concrete. And an elongation figure means nothing without its GAUGE LENGTH.

questions.stem: The SLENDERNESS RATIO of a column is defined as:
options: The ratio of the column's length to its least lateral dimension, in all cases
The ratio of the applied load to the crippling load
The ratio of the column's EFFECTIVE LENGTH to the LEAST RADIUS OF GYRATION of its cross-section
The ratio of the cross-sectional area to the perimeter
questions.solution:
**The ratio of the EFFECTIVE LENGTH to the LEAST RADIUS OF GYRATION** — λ = L_e / r_min.

**Why each part of the definition is as it is:**

| Element | Reason |
|---|---|
| **EFFECTIVE length, not actual length** ← | **Because the end conditions change the buckling behaviour entirely — a fixed-ended column buckles as though it were half its length** ← |
| **LEAST radius of gyration** ← | **A column buckles about the axis of LEAST resistance, and will find it whether the designer looks for it or not** ← |
| **Radius of gyration, not a lateral dimension** ← | **r = √(I/A) measures how the material is DISTRIBUTED, which is what governs buckling — a hollow tube and a solid bar of the same area behave quite differently** ← |

> **Option (a) is the definition sometimes used loosely for a rectangular masonry or concrete column, and it is not the general definition — it fails immediately for an I-section or a tube.**

**The effective lengths:**

| End conditions | L_e | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Both ends HINGED (pinned)** | **L** ← | **The reference case for Euler's formula** |
| **Both ends FIXED** | **0.5 L** ← | **The strongest — four times the Euler load** ← |
| **One end FIXED, other HINGED** | **0.7 L** ← | **Approximately; exactly L/√2** |
| **One end FIXED, other FREE (a flagpole)** | **2 L** ← | **The weakest — a QUARTER of the hinged case's load** ← |

> **THE RANGE FROM 0.5 L TO 2 L IS A FACTOR OF FOUR IN LENGTH AND THEREFORE SIXTEEN IN BUCKLING LOAD, which is why end restraint is the single most valuable thing a designer can obtain for a column, and why it is worth real effort in the connection detailing.**

**The classification by slenderness:**

| λ | Type | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| **Below about 32 (or L/d < 12 for concrete)** | **SHORT column** ← | **CRUSHING — the material fails in compression** ← |
| **32 to about 120** | **INTERMEDIATE** | **Combined crushing and buckling — the practical majority** ← |
| **Above about 120** | **LONG (slender)** ← | **Elastic BUCKLING — Euler's formula applies** ← |
| **Codes cap λ at 180 for compression members, 250 for tension members carrying reversal** ← | **Not a strength requirement** | **A limit to prevent excessive flexibility, handling damage and vibration** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WORTH NOTING BECAUSE IT IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF LIMIT: a very slender member may satisfy every stress check and still be unacceptable, because it sags visibly under its own weight, is bent during transport, and rattles in the wind.**

> **A limit imposed for robustness and workmanship rather than for calculated strength is common in codes and is sometimes dismissed as arbitrary — it is not: it encodes accumulated experience of what actually goes wrong.**

**Why EULER'S formula fails for short columns, which is the practical consequence:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Euler: P_cr = π² E I / L_e², so the critical STRESS is π² E / λ²** ← | **As λ falls, the predicted stress rises without limit** ← |
| **At λ = 20 in steel it predicts about 4,900 MPa** ← | **Which is absurd — the material would have crushed at about 250 MPa** ← |
| **So Euler's formula is valid only ABOVE a limiting slenderness** ← | **The value at which the Euler stress equals the yield stress — about 90 to 100 for mild steel** ← |
| **Below that, RANKINE's formula or an empirical code curve is used** ← | **Which blends the crushing and buckling limits smoothly** ← |

> **Rankine's formula, 1/P = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler, is the elegant expression of the idea: it automatically tends to the crushing load for a short column and to the Euler load for a long one, with a smooth transition between.**

> **Real code curves go further and allow for INITIAL CROOKEDNESS and RESIDUAL STRESSES, both of which reduce the real capacity below the theoretical value — which is why a design curve always sits below the Euler hyperbola, and by the largest margin at intermediate slenderness where imperfections matter most.**

examTip.trick: **λ = L_e / r_min** — EFFECTIVE length (end conditions matter) over the LEAST radius of gyration (the column finds its weakest axis).
examTip.trap: **Effective length runs from 0.5 L (both fixed) to 2 L (fixed-free)** — a factor of 4 in length and 16 in buckling load, which is why end restraint is worth detailing effort.
examTip.mnemonic: **Euler predicts 4,900 MPa at λ = 20, which is absurd** — it is valid only above λ ≈ 90-100 for mild steel. Below that, Rankine (1/P = 1/P_c + 1/P_E) blends crushing into buckling.

questions.stem: In an I-section beam subjected to transverse shear, the shear stress distribution over the depth is such that:
options: The shear stress is uniform over the whole section
The flanges carry almost all the shear
The shear stress is greatest at the extreme fibres
The WEB carries the great majority of the shear
questions.solution:
**The WEB carries the great majority of the shear** — commonly 90 to 95 per cent — and the shear stress drops ABRUPTLY at the flange-web junction.

**The distribution, following the shear stress formula:**

| Location | Shear stress τ = V A ȳ / (I b) |
|---|---|
| **At the extreme fibres (top and bottom of the flange)** | **ZERO — there is no area beyond, so A ȳ = 0** ← (which disposes of option c) |
| **Through the flange** | **Rises parabolically, but stays SMALL because b is the full flange width** ← |
| **At the junction, on the FLANGE side** | **A modest value, computed with b = flange width** ← |
| **At the junction, on the WEB side** | **JUMPS UP sharply — the same A ȳ divided by the much smaller web thickness** ← |
| **At the NEUTRAL AXIS** | **MAXIMUM** ← |

> **THE ABRUPT JUMP AT THE JUNCTION IS PURELY AN EFFECT OF THE WIDTH b IN THE DENOMINATOR: the quantity A ȳ is continuous across the junction, but b changes suddenly from the flange width to the web thickness — often by a factor of ten or more.**

> **So the shear stress is multiplied by that factor at a stroke, and the diagram shows a step.**

> **The step is a consequence of the formula's ASSUMPTION of uniform shear stress across the width, which is poor near the junction; the real distribution is smoother, but the overall picture — nearly all the shear in the web — is correct.**

**The practical consequence, which governs steel design:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The WEB is designed for shear; the FLANGES for bending** ← | **A clean division of labour** ← |
| **Codes permit the average web shear stress, V ÷ (web depth × web thickness), to be used** ← | **A simplification justified by the near-uniformity of the web stress** ← |
| **A thin web may BUCKLE in shear before it yields** | **Hence intermediate and bearing STIFFENERS in plate girders** ← |
| **Web crippling and bearing must be checked at concentrated loads and supports** ← | **Where a large force is delivered into a thin web** ← |
| **Holes cut in a web for services reduce shear capacity directly** ← | **And are placed near midspan, where shear is low, never near supports** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS ON SITE AND IS ROUTINELY GOT WRONG: services need to pass through beams, and the hole gets cut wherever the duct happens to run.**

> **A hole near the SUPPORT, where the shear is at its maximum, removes exactly the material carrying it. A hole at MIDSPAN, where shear is near zero, removes material that was doing very little.**

> **The rule is therefore simple and worth stating firmly: web penetrations belong in the middle of the span, they must be approved by the designer, and they are never cut on site without that approval.**

**The complementary picture for bending, which completes the I-section's logic:**

| Stress | Where it is greatest | Which part carries it |
|---|---|---|
| **BENDING** | **At the EXTREME fibres, furthest from the neutral axis** ← | **The FLANGES** ← |
| **SHEAR** | **At the NEUTRAL AXIS** ← | **The WEB** ← |

> **THE TWO ARE EXACTLY COMPLEMENTARY, AND THAT IS WHY THE I-SECTION IS THE SHAPE IT IS.**

> **Bending wants material far from the neutral axis, so the flanges go there. Shear wants material at the neutral axis, so the web is there. Neither wants material where the other does not, so nothing is wasted.**

> **The section is the direct geometric expression of the two stress distributions, which is a rare and satisfying case of a structural form being derivable almost entirely from first principles — and it explains why the same shape appears independently in rolled steel, plate girders, precast concrete beams and even in the cross-section of a bird's bone.**

examTip.trick: **The web carries 90-95 % of the shear; the stress jumps at the flange-web junction because b drops from flange width to web thickness.** Maximum at the neutral axis, zero at the extreme fibres.
examTip.trap: **Codes let you use the AVERAGE web shear stress** — V ÷ (web depth × thickness) — justified by how nearly uniform the web stress is.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bending wants material FAR from the neutral axis (flanges); shear wants it AT the neutral axis (web).** That is the I-section, derived from first principles. And web holes belong at MIDSPAN, never near supports.

questions.stem: At an UNLOADED joint of a pin-jointed truss where THREE members meet, and TWO of those members are COLLINEAR, the force in the third member is:
options: ZERO, and the two collinear members carry equal forces
Equal to the sum of the forces in the other two
Equal to half the force in each collinear member
Indeterminate without further analysis
questions.solution:
**ZERO** — and the two collinear members carry equal and opposite forces (that is, the same force passes straight through the joint).

**The proof, which takes one line:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **Resolve forces PERPENDICULAR to the two collinear members** ← | **The two collinear members have NO component in that direction** ← |
| **So the only force with a perpendicular component is the third member's** | ← |
| **Equilibrium in that direction therefore requires it to be ZERO** ← | ← |
| **Resolving ALONG the collinear direction then gives** | **The two collinear members carry equal forces** ← |

> **The whole result comes from choosing the right direction to resolve in — perpendicular to the collinear pair — which is a good general habit in joint analysis.**

**The two zero-force rules, which should be learned as a pair:**

| Rule | Condition | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **TWO-member rule** | **An unloaded joint with exactly TWO non-collinear members** ← | **BOTH forces are zero** ← |
| **THREE-member rule** | **An unloaded joint with THREE members, two of them collinear** ← | **The THIRD (non-collinear) member is zero; the collinear pair carries equal force** ← (this question) |

> **In both cases the joint must carry NO external load and no support reaction — a load or a reaction at the joint destroys the argument immediately, and that is the condition most often overlooked.**

**Why zero-force members are provided at all, since a member carrying nothing looks wasteful:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **They carry force under a DIFFERENT load case** ← | **A member with zero force under dead load may be heavily loaded under wind from one side, or under a moving load in one position** ← |
| **They REDUCE the buckling length of a long compression chord** ← | **By bracing it laterally at intermediate points — which is often their whole purpose** ← |
| **They maintain the truss's geometric STABILITY** | **Preventing it from becoming a mechanism** ← |
| **They resist load REVERSAL** | ← |
| **They support the structure during ERECTION** | **When the load path is quite different from the finished condition** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST COMMON REASON IN PRACTICE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING PROPERLY: a long compression chord in a roof truss would buckle at a low load if unrestrained over its full length.**

> **A member framing into it at midlength carries no axial force at all under the design loading, yet it is essential — it halves the chord's effective length and therefore quadruples its buckling capacity.**

> **So the member is not carrying LOAD, it is providing RESTRAINT, and the two are quite different functions. An analysis that reports zero force says nothing about whether the member is needed.**

> **Removing zero-force members from a truss because "the analysis says they carry nothing" is a real and recurring error, and it has caused collapses — most often during erection, when the temporary condition differs from the analysed one.**

**The practical value of the rules in analysis:**

> **Identifying the zero-force members FIRST, before any calculation, can eliminate a third of the members from a large truss and turn an intimidating problem into a short one.**

> **Better still, it often cascades: setting one member to zero makes an adjacent joint qualify under one of the rules, which sets another to zero, and so on around the truss.**

> **Scanning for these joints before starting is therefore the single most efficient first step in truss analysis, and in an examination it is frequently the intended route rather than a shortcut.**

examTip.trick: **Resolve PERPENDICULAR to the collinear pair** — they have no component there, so the third member must be zero. Learn it with the two-member rule as a pair.
examTip.trap: **Both rules require the joint to be UNLOADED** — no external load and no support reaction. That condition is the one most often overlooked.
examTip.mnemonic: **A zero-force member may exist to RESTRAIN, not to carry load** — halving a compression chord's buckling length quadruples its capacity. Never delete one because the analysis reports zero.

questions.stem: In a flexible cable suspended between two supports at the same level and carrying a load uniformly distributed over the horizontal span, the tension in the cable is:
options: Uniform throughout its length
MAXIMUM at the SUPPORTS and MINIMUM at the lowest point
Maximum at the lowest point
Zero at the supports
questions.solution:
**Maximum at the SUPPORTS and minimum at the LOWEST POINT**, where it equals the horizontal thrust H.

**The reasoning:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A flexible cable can carry only TENSION along its own length** ← | **No bending, no shear — that is what "flexible" means** ← |
| **The HORIZONTAL component of the tension is CONSTANT everywhere** ← | **Because no horizontal load is applied along the cable** ← |
| **The VERTICAL component varies** | **It equals the vertical load carried between that point and the lowest point** ← |
| **At the LOWEST point the cable is horizontal** | **So the vertical component is zero and T = H — the MINIMUM** ← |
| **At the SUPPORTS the slope is steepest** | **So the vertical component is greatest, and T = √(H² + V²) is the MAXIMUM** ← |

> **THE CONSTANT HORIZONTAL COMPONENT IS THE KEY IDEA AND IT MAKES EVERYTHING ELSE FOLLOW: since H is fixed, the tension varies only because the SLOPE varies, and the tension is greatest where the cable is steepest.**

**The standard results:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Shape (load uniform over the HORIZONTAL span)** | **A PARABOLA** ← |
| **Shape (load uniform along the CABLE's own length, i.e. self-weight)** | **A CATENARY** ← |
| **Horizontal thrust** | **H = w L² / (8 h), with h the central dip** ← |
| **Maximum tension at the support** | **T_max = √(H² + (wL/2)²)** ← |
| **Minimum tension** | **T_min = H, at the lowest point** ← |

> **THE PARABOLA-VERSUS-CATENARY DISTINCTION IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS OFTEN ASKED AND IS EASILY REMEMBERED BY ITS CAUSE: the load's distribution determines the shape.**

> **A suspension bridge's cable carries a deck hung at uniform horizontal intervals, so the load is uniform per horizontal metre and the cable is a PARABOLA.**

> **A free-hanging chain or power line carries only its own weight, which is uniform per metre OF CABLE — more weight per horizontal metre where the cable is steep — so it is a CATENARY.**

> **For a shallow cable the two curves are almost indistinguishable, which is why the parabolic approximation is used for design even where the loading is strictly catenary.**

**The H = wL²/(8h) relation and what it implies for design:**

| Change | Effect on H |
|---|---|
| **Increase the DIP h** | **H falls, INVERSELY** ← |
| **HALVE the dip** | **H DOUBLES** ← |
| **A very flat cable** | **Enormous tension, and very large anchorage forces** ← |

> **THIS IS THE CENTRAL DESIGN TRADE FOR EVERY CABLE STRUCTURE, and it is worth appreciating:**

> **A deep sag gives low cable tension, small cables and modest anchorages — but tall towers and a lot of headroom consumed.**

> **A shallow sag looks elegant and needs short towers, and it multiplies the tension, the cable size and the anchorage cost.**

> **Suspension bridges settle at a sag-to-span ratio of about 1 in 8 to 1 in 12 as the economic compromise, and it is a genuine optimum rather than a convention.**

> **The same relation explains why a tightrope walker's rope is under such enormous tension: the walker insists on a nearly horizontal rope, h is tiny, and H is correspondingly vast — which is why the rope must be anchored so heavily and why a rope pulled perfectly straight can never be achieved at all.**

> **And it is the reason a SUSPENSION FOOTBRIDGE in the hills — of which Nepal has thousands — is built with a generous sag: it keeps the cable size, the anchorage blocks and the tower heights all within what can be carried to a remote site and built by hand.**

examTip.trick: **H is constant along the cable, so tension varies only with SLOPE** — maximum at the steep supports, minimum (= H) at the horizontal lowest point.
examTip.trap: **Load uniform over the HORIZONTAL span → parabola; load uniform along the CABLE (self-weight) → catenary.** For shallow cables the two are nearly identical.
examTip.mnemonic: **H = wL²/(8h): halve the dip and DOUBLE the tension.** Suspension bridges settle at a sag/span of 1:8 to 1:12 as a genuine economic optimum — and Nepal's hill footbridges are given generous sag so the anchorages can be built by hand.

questions.stem: In the UNIT LOAD (virtual work) method for finding the deflection of a pin-jointed truss, the deflection at a joint is computed as:
options: The sum of the member forces divided by the number of members
The largest member elongation in the truss
Σ (P k L / A E), where P is the member force under the REAL loading and k is the member force under a UNIT LOAD applied at the point and in the direction of the required deflection
The area of the bending moment diagram divided by EI
questions.solution:
**δ = Σ (P k L / A E)** — summed over all members, with P the force under the REAL loading and k the force under a UNIT load applied at the point and in the direction of the deflection sought.

**The method in steps:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Analyse the truss for the REAL loads** | **Giving the force P in every member** ← |
| **2. Remove the real loads and apply a UNIT LOAD** ← | **At the joint where the deflection is wanted, in the direction it is wanted** ← |
| **3. Analyse again** | **Giving the force k in every member** ← |
| **4. For each member compute P k L / (A E)** | **L its length, A its area, E its modulus** ← |
| **5. SUM over all members** | **The result is the deflection δ** ← |
| **A negative result** | **Means the deflection is OPPOSITE to the assumed unit load's direction** ← |

> **Option (d) describes the moment-area or conjugate beam approach for a flexural member — a different method for a different kind of structure.**

**The principle behind it:**

| Statement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The method is an application of VIRTUAL WORK** ← | **External virtual work = internal virtual work** ← |
| **The unit load is the VIRTUAL force system** | **It need not be real, only in equilibrium** ← |
| **P L / (A E) is the REAL elongation of each member** ← | **The deformation the actual loads produce** ← |
| **k × (that elongation) is the internal virtual work in that member** | ← |
| **1 × δ is the external virtual work of the unit load** ← | **Which is why the answer comes out directly as δ, with no scaling** ← |

> **THE ELEGANCE IS IN THE LAST ROW: because the virtual load is exactly ONE unit, the external virtual work is 1 × δ, and δ falls out of the equation with no division at any stage.**

> **That is the whole reason a UNIT load is used rather than any other value.**

**Its great advantages:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **It gives the deflection at ONE chosen point, in ONE chosen direction** ← | **Efficient when only one answer is needed** ← |
| **It handles ANY truss geometry, however irregular** | ← |
| **It works for TEMPERATURE changes and FABRICATION errors** ← | **Replace P L / A E with the actual member length change, α L ΔT or the lack of fit — the rest is unchanged** ← |
| **It extends directly to beams and frames** | **δ = ∫ (M m / EI) dx, with m the moment under the unit load** ← |
| **It gives ROTATION if a unit COUPLE is applied instead of a unit force** ← | **Which is a neat and often forgotten extension** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A GENUINELY VALUABLE PROPERTY AND IT IS WHY THE METHOD SURVIVES: the P L/AE term is simply "how much this member changed length".**

> **It does not matter WHY it changed. A temperature rise, a member fabricated 5 mm too short, a support settlement — substitute the actual change and the same summation gives the deflection.**

> **A method that separates the cause of the deformation from the calculation of its effect is far more general than one that assumes the cause, and it is why virtual work handles lack-of-fit and thermal problems that defeat more specialised techniques.**

**And its relation to the neighbouring theorems:**

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **UNIT LOAD method** | **δ = Σ P k L / AE — this question** ← |
| **CASTIGLIANO's second theorem** | **δ = ∂U/∂P — the partial derivative of the strain energy with respect to the load at that point** ← |
| **MAXWELL's reciprocal theorem** | **The deflection at A due to a load at B equals the deflection at B due to the same load at A** ← |
| **BETTI's law** | **The general form of Maxwell's, for two whole load systems** ← |

> **CASTIGLIANO'S SECOND THEOREM GIVES THE SAME ANSWER BY A DIFFERENT ROUTE — and indeed ∂P/∂W plays exactly the role that k does in the unit load method, which is not a coincidence but the same mathematics in different clothing.**

> **Where the two differ is in convenience: Castigliano needs a load actually present at the point of interest (or a fictitious one introduced and later set to zero), while the unit load method simply applies its unit load wherever the answer is wanted — which is usually the easier route.**

examTip.trick: **δ = Σ P k L / AE** — P from the real loads, k from a UNIT load at the point and direction wanted. A negative answer means the deflection is opposite to the assumed direction.
examTip.trap: **The load is UNITY so that the external virtual work is 1 × δ** — that is why δ falls out with no scaling at any stage.
examTip.mnemonic: **P L/AE just means "how much the member changed length"** — swap in α L ΔT for temperature, or the lack of fit, and the same summation works. Apply a unit COUPLE instead and you get a ROTATION.

questions.stem: The KINEMATIC indeterminacy (degree of freedom) of a structure is:
options: The number of independent equations of static equilibrium available
The number of members meeting at the most heavily loaded joint
The number of redundant forces that must be released to make it statically determinate
The number of independent JOINT DISPLACEMENTS (translations and rotations) needed to define the deformed shape completely
questions.solution:
**The number of independent JOINT DISPLACEMENTS — translations and rotations — required to describe the deformed shape completely.**

**The two indeterminacies, which must be kept apart:**

| Indeterminacy | Counts | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| **STATIC (D_s)** | **The number of unknown FORCES in excess of the equilibrium equations** ← | **The FORCE (flexibility) methods — consistent deformation, three-moment equation, column analogy** ← (option c) |
| **KINEMATIC (D_k)** | **The number of unknown DISPLACEMENTS at the joints** ← | **The DISPLACEMENT (stiffness) methods — slope-deflection, moment distribution, matrix stiffness** ← |

> **THE CHOICE OF METHOD FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM WHICH NUMBER IS SMALLER, and that is the practical reason for computing both:**

> **A structure with D_s = 2 and D_k = 12 is far easier by a force method; one with D_s = 15 and D_k = 3 is far easier by a displacement method.**

> **The two are NOT complementary and do not sum to anything meaningful — a highly statically indeterminate structure may have few degrees of freedom, and vice versa.**

**How D_k is counted:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Each free joint in a PLANE FRAME has 3 degrees of freedom** ← | **Two translations and one rotation** ← |
| **Subtract those restrained by SUPPORTS** | **A fixed support removes 3, a hinge 2, a roller 1** ← |
| **If members are assumed AXIALLY RIGID (inextensible)** ← | **Each such assumption removes one further degree of freedom, and this is standard in hand methods** ← |
| **For a plane TRUSS (pin joints, no moments)** | **Each joint has only 2 degrees of freedom** ← |
| **A hinge at a joint ADDS a degree of freedom** | **The members either side can rotate independently** ← |

> **THE AXIAL RIGIDITY ASSUMPTION IN THE THIRD ROW IS WHAT MAKES HAND ANALYSIS POSSIBLE AT ALL, and its justification is sound: in a normal building frame, axial shortening of columns and beams is a tiny fraction of the flexural deflections.**

> **Neglecting it removes most of the translational freedoms and leaves mainly the joint ROTATIONS, which is why the slope-deflection and moment distribution methods deal with rotations and only a small number of "sway" translations.**

> **A continuous beam on unyielding supports, with axial deformation neglected, has D_k equal simply to the number of joints free to rotate — which is why moment distribution is so quick for continuous beams even when they are highly statically indeterminate.**

**A worked comparison, which shows why both numbers matter:**

| Structure | D_s | D_k (axially rigid) | Better method |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A 4-span continuous beam on simple supports** | **3** ← | **3 joint rotations (plus end rotations)** | Either |
| **A single-bay portal frame with FIXED bases** | **3** ← | **3: two joint rotations plus one SWAY** ← | Either |
| **A single-bay portal frame with HINGED bases** | **1** ← | **4: three rotations plus sway** | **FORCE method — one unknown** ← |
| **A multi-storey rigid frame** | **Large** | **Moderate** | **DISPLACEMENT method** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CLEAREST ILLUSTRATION: hinging the bases makes the frame LESS statically indeterminate (1 instead of 3) while making it MORE kinematically indeterminate (4 instead of 3).**

> **The two numbers move in opposite directions, because a release removes a force unknown and adds a displacement unknown — which is the general relationship between them, and the reason neither alone tells you how hard the analysis will be.**

> **THE LAST ROW EXPLAINS WHY ALL MODERN COMPUTER ANALYSIS USES THE STIFFNESS (DISPLACEMENT) METHOD despite hand methods historically favouring forces:**

> **The displacement method can be made entirely SYSTEMATIC — assemble each member's stiffness matrix, add them into a global matrix by joint number, apply the boundary conditions, and solve.**

> **There is no judgement required about which redundants to release, which is the step in a force method that cannot be automated well.**

> **So the method that is often harder by hand is the one that is trivially programmable, and that single property decided the matter once computers existed.**

examTip.trick: **D_k counts unknown DISPLACEMENTS; D_s counts unknown FORCES.** Option (c) defines static indeterminacy. Pick the method matching the SMALLER number.
examTip.trap: **They are not complementary** — hinging a portal frame's bases lowers D_s from 3 to 1 while raising D_k from 3 to 4. A release removes a force unknown and adds a displacement unknown.
examTip.mnemonic: **Assuming members axially rigid is what makes hand methods work** — it strips out most translations and leaves joint rotations plus a little sway. And the stiffness method won because it is systematic enough to program.

questions.stem: In the limit state load combination 0.9 DL + 1.5 WL (or EL), the partial safety factor on dead load is REDUCED to 0.9 because:
options: The dead load RESISTS the overturning or uplift caused by the wind or earthquake
Dead loads are always overestimated by designers
Wind and dead load never act together
The code requires all factors to sum to 2.4
questions.solution:
**Because in that combination the dead load is RESISTING rather than causing the effect** — so the unsafe assumption is to have too MUCH of it, and the factor is reduced accordingly.

**The principle behind partial safety factors:**

| Situation | Factor on dead load | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Dead load ADDS to the effect being checked** ← | **1.5 (or 1.2 in combination with three loads)** ← | **Increase it — more dead load is worse** ← |
| **Dead load RESISTS the effect being checked** ← | **0.9** ← | **Reduce it — LESS dead load is worse** ← |

> **THE FACTOR ALWAYS MOVES THE LOAD IN THE DIRECTION THAT MAKES THE SITUATION WORSE, and that is the whole logic of partial safety factors.**

> **It is not a statement about how accurately dead load can be estimated; it is a statement about which way an error hurts.**

> **Option (b) inverts the reasoning: the point is not that designers overestimate dead load, but that if the real dead load turns out to be LESS than assumed — a lighter finish, a partition never built, a roof screed omitted — the structure is less able to resist uplift.**

**Where the 0.9 factor governs:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **OVERTURNING of a whole building or a wall under wind** ← | **The weight is the only thing holding it down** ← |
| **UPLIFT on a light roof under wind suction** ← | **A light steel truss roof can be lifted bodily off its supports** ← |
| **Uplift on the windward footings of a frame** | **Requiring tension anchorage into the foundation** ← |
| **SLIDING of a retaining wall** | **Friction depends on the vertical load** ← |
| **Flotation of a basement or a buried tank** ← | **Where the resisting weight is all that opposes buoyancy** ← |

> **THE ROOF UPLIFT CASE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMONEST FAILURE OF THIS KIND IN PRACTICE, and it is worth being explicit about:**

> **A light CGI roof on a steel or timber truss weighs very little. Wind blowing over it generates SUCTION on the leeward slope and often on the windward slope too, and internal pressure through an open door or a broken window adds to it.**

> **The net uplift can easily exceed the roof's own weight, and the roof departs — usually as a single sheet, taking the purlins with it.**

> **The remedy is not more strength but ANCHORAGE: holding-down bolts or straps tying the truss to the wall, and the wall to the foundation, forming a continuous load path from the roof sheet to the ground.**

> **A roof that is strong but not tied down is exactly the case the 0.9 factor exists to catch, and it is the reason storm damage so often takes roofs off buildings whose walls are undamaged.**

**The main IS 456 combinations, for reference:**

| Combination | Ultimate limit state | Serviceability limit state |
|---|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.5 (DL + LL)** ← | **1.0 DL + 1.0 LL** ← |
| **DL + WL (or EL)** | **1.5 (DL + WL) and 0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** ← | **1.0 DL + 1.0 WL** ← |
| **DL + LL + WL** | **1.2 (DL + LL + WL)** ← | **1.0 DL + 0.8 LL + 0.8 WL** ← |

> **THE 1.2 IN THE THIRD ROW IS LOWER THAN 1.5 AND THE REASON IS PROBABILISTIC: it is unlikely that the full imposed load and the design wind will occur at their maximum values simultaneously.**

> **Requiring both at 1.5 together would be excessively conservative, so the factor is reduced when three loads are combined.**

> **The serviceability factors are all 1.0 or less, because serviceability is checked against the loads actually EXPECTED in service rather than against extreme values — the consequence of exceeding a deflection limit is discomfort and cracking, not collapse, so the margin required is much smaller.**

> **That distinction — different consequences deserving different margins — is the whole reason limit state design separates the two states rather than applying one global factor of safety, and it is the central advance of limit state over working stress design.**

UNDERESTIMATING it is the unsafe assumption.

examTip.trick: **The factor always moves the load in the direction that makes things WORSE.** Dead load resisting uplift or overturning is factored DOWN to 0.9, not up.
examTip.trap: **It is not about estimating accuracy** — it is about which way an error hurts. If the real dead load is less than assumed, the uplift resistance is less.
examTip.mnemonic: **A light CGI roof departs in a storm while the walls stand** — the answer is ANCHORAGE, a continuous load path from sheet to foundation. And 1.2 for DL+LL+WL because all three rarely peak together.

questions.stem: In designing the COLUMNS and FOUNDATIONS of a multi-storey building, codes permit the total imposed (live) load from the floors above to be REDUCED as the number of floors increases, because:
options: Imposed loads decrease with height in all buildings
The columns become stronger lower down
It is IMPROBABLE that every floor will carry its full design imposed load at the same moment
Dead load dominates at lower levels
questions.solution:
**Because it is statistically improbable that EVERY floor will simultaneously carry its full design imposed load.**

**The principle:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A floor's design imposed load is a rare MAXIMUM, not an everyday value** ← | **It represents a crowded, heavily furnished condition** ← |
| **One floor may reach it occasionally** | **A meeting, a party, a store room filled** ← |
| **TEN floors reaching it at the same instant is vanishingly unlikely** ← | **The probabilities multiply** ← |
| **So summing ten full floor loads onto one column is unrealistically severe** ← | **And the code permits a reduction** ← |

> **The reduction is therefore a probabilistic correction, not a relaxation of safety — the target reliability is unchanged, and the arithmetic is simply made to reflect what can actually occur.**

**The typical reduction schedule:**

| Number of floors carried by the member | Reduction in total imposed load |
|---|---|
| **1 (the roof or topmost floor)** | **NO reduction** ← |
| **2** | **10 %** |
| **3** | **20 %** |
| **4** | **30 %** |
| **5 to 10** | **40 %** |
| **Over 10** | **50 % — the maximum permitted** ← |

> **THE CAP AT 50 PER CENT IN THE LAST ROW IS IMPORTANT AND IS THERE FOR A REASON: the probabilistic argument would allow a larger reduction for a very tall building, but the code stops at half.**

> **The reduction rests on an assumption about independence between floors that becomes less reliable at the extremes, and half the imposed load is retained as a floor beneath which the argument is not pushed.**

**The important EXCLUSIONS, which are where marks and mistakes are made:**

| Exclusion | Why |
|---|---|
| **BEAMS and SLABS get NO reduction** ← | **They carry ONE floor, so there is no multi-floor improbability to exploit** ← |
| **Storage, warehouse and plant-room loads are NOT reduced, or are reduced less** ← | **These are permanent, not transient — a warehouse really is full on every floor at once** ← |
| **Loads exceeding 5 kN/m² generally not reduced** | **They indicate a storage or industrial use** ← |
| **The reduction applies to IMPOSED load only, never to dead load** ← | **Dead load is present on every floor all the time, with certainty** ← |

> **THE STORAGE EXCLUSION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE WITH REAL CONSEQUENCES, and it follows directly from the reasoning behind the rule:**

> **The reduction is justified only because imposed load is TRANSIENT and independent between floors. Stored goods are neither.**

> **A warehouse's floors are all loaded, all the time, and applying an office building's reduction to it removes real load that is genuinely there.**

> **This also means the reduction is invalidated by a CHANGE OF USE — an office block converted to filing storage or a light industrial use may have columns designed with a 40 per cent reduction that is no longer justified, and that is a serious and entirely invisible reduction in safety.**

> **Which is why change of use of an existing building requires a structural appraisal rather than merely a permit, and why the design assumptions ought to be recorded somewhere the next engineer will find them.**

**And a related idea worth noting alongside it:**

> **The same probabilistic reasoning underlies the reduced factor of 1.2 in the DL + LL + WL combination, and the fact that the imposed load factor in serviceability checks is 0.8 rather than 1.0 when combined with wind.**

> **In every case the code is saying the same thing: independent unfavourable events are unlikely to coincide at their extremes, and a design that assumes they do is not safer but merely more expensive.**

> **Recognising the common principle behind these scattered clauses makes them much easier to remember than treating each as a separate rule.**

examTip.trick: **Every floor reaching its full imposed load at once is improbable** — 10 % per floor up to a maximum of 50 %, applied only to columns, walls and foundations.
examTip.trap: **Beams and slabs get NO reduction** (they carry one floor), and STORAGE loads get none either — stored goods are permanent, not transient, so the independence argument fails.
examTip.mnemonic: **A CHANGE OF USE invalidates the reduction invisibly** — an office converted to filing storage has columns designed with 40 % of the live load missing. Hence a structural appraisal, not just a permit.

questions.stem: SEGREGATION in fresh concrete is:
options: The SEPARATION of the constituent materials of the mix
The upward movement of water to the surface of freshly placed concrete
The loss of workability with time after mixing
The formation of shrinkage cracks in hardened concrete
questions.solution:
**The SEPARATION of the mix's constituents**, so that the coarse aggregate parts company with the mortar and the concrete ceases to be uniform.

> **Option (b) is BLEEDING, option (c) is SLUMP LOSS and option (d) is shrinkage cracking — all real phenomena, none of them segregation.**

**The two forms it takes:**

| Form | Condition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **COARSE AGGREGATE separating from the mortar** ← | **A DRY, harsh mix with too little fine material** ← | **The stones roll away and collect in one place** ← |
| **PASTE (cement and water) separating from the aggregate** ← | **A WET, over-fluid mix** ← | **The heavy aggregate sinks and the paste rises** ← |

> **BOTH EXTREMES OF WORKABILITY THEREFORE SEGREGATE, WHICH IS THE POINT WORTH GRASPING: it is not simply that wet concrete segregates.**

> **A very dry mix segregates because the mortar is not cohesive enough to hold the stones; a very wet mix segregates because it is too fluid to hold them up.**

> **Between the two lies a range of cohesive, workable mixes, and finding that range is much of what mix design is for.**

**The causes:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **Dropping concrete from a HEIGHT** ← | **More than about 1.5 m — the aggregate separates in flight and on impact** ← |
| **Discharging against an obstruction, formwork or reinforcement** | **The stones bounce away from the paste** ← |
| **Over-VIBRATION** ← | **Continuing to vibrate after the air has escaped drives the aggregate down and brings paste up** ← |
| **Using vibrators to MOVE concrete horizontally** ← | **A common and damaging site practice — the mortar flows and the stones stay** ← |
| **A badly graded mix, deficient in fines** | ← |
| **Too high a water content** | ← |
| **Long transport over rough ground without agitation** | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST FREQUENT SITE CAUSE AND THE EASIEST TO STOP: a poker vibrator is for COMPACTING concrete where it lies, never for shifting it along the form.**

> **Used to move concrete, it liquefies the mortar, which runs ahead and leaves the coarse aggregate behind — producing a stone pocket at one end and a paste-rich, weak, shrinkage-prone zone at the other.**

> **Concrete should be DEPOSITED in position, in layers, and vibrated only to consolidate it.**

**The consequences, which persist for the life of the structure:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **HONEYCOMBING — voids where stones have collected with no mortar** ← | **Visible on striking the formwork, and often much worse than it looks** ← |
| **Weak, paste-rich, porous layers** | **Low strength, high shrinkage** ← |
| **Exposed reinforcement with no effective cover** ← | **A direct path to corrosion** ← |
| **Variable strength through the member** | ← |
| **Repairs are never as good as the original** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST SERIOUS, and it is why honeycombing at the bottom of a column or beside a congested reinforcement cage must never be simply plastered over: the concrete behind the patch is porous and the bars in it are unprotected.**

> **The correct repair is to cut out to sound concrete, expose the bars fully, clean them, and make good with a proper repair mortar — and to record it.**

**Prevention, which is almost entirely a matter of site practice:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Limit the free fall to about 1.5 m** ← | **Use a chute, a tremie, or a flexible trunk in deep pours** ← |
| **Place in horizontal LAYERS of 300 to 450 mm and vibrate each** | ← |
| **Never use the vibrator to move concrete sideways** | ← |
| **Vibrate just until the surface glistens and air stops rising** ← | **Then withdraw slowly — over-vibration is as bad as under-vibration** ← |
| **Use a cohesive, well-graded mix with adequate fines** | **A plasticiser gives workability without extra water** ← |
| **Design the reinforcement so concrete can actually pass through it** ← | **Congested cages force segregation however careful the placing** ← |

> **The last row is a DESIGN responsibility rather than a site one, and it is worth naming as such: a beam-column joint detailed with so much steel that a 20 mm aggregate cannot pass between the bars will be honeycombed, and no amount of care on site will prevent it.**

> **Buildability is part of design, and the drawing that cannot be built as drawn will be built as something else.**

The coarse aggregate parts from the mortar and the concrete is no longer uniform.

examTip.trick: **Segregation = separation of the constituents.** Option (b) is bleeding, (c) slump loss, (d) shrinkage cracking — all real, none of them this.
examTip.trap: **BOTH extremes segregate** — a dry harsh mix lets the stones roll away, a wet mix lets them sink. It is not simply that wet concrete segregates.
examTip.mnemonic: **A poker vibrator COMPACTS where the concrete lies; it never MOVES it along the form.** Used to shift concrete it leaves stones at one end and weak paste at the other. And a cage too congested to pass 20 mm aggregate is a DESIGN fault.

questions.stem: As per IS 456:2000, NOMINAL MIX concrete (proportioned by fixed volume or mass ratios such as 1:1.5:3) may be used only:
options: For any grade of concrete, at the designer's discretion
Up to grade M20, and only where design mix concrete cannot be used for reasons such as the small scale of the work
Only for grades above M25
Only for plain concrete containing no reinforcement
questions.solution:
**Up to grade M20 only**, and even then only where design mix concrete cannot reasonably be used — for instance because the work is small or no testing facility is available.

**The two approaches:**

| Aspect | NOMINAL MIX | DESIGN MIX |
|---|---|---|
| **Proportions** | **FIXED by the code — 1:3:6 (M10), 1:2:4 (M15), 1:1.5:3 (M20)** ← | **Determined by CALCULATION and TRIAL for the specific materials** ← |
| **Basis** | **Long experience with typical materials** ← | **The target mean strength, the actual aggregate grading, the cement's strength, the water demand** ← |
| **Grade limit** | **Up to M20 only** ← | **Any grade; MANDATORY above M20** ← |
| **Economy** | **Conservative — usually uses MORE cement than necessary** ← | **Optimised** ← |
| **Requires** | **Nothing but the ratio** | **Materials testing and trial mixes** ← |
| **Quality control** | **Limited** | **Full, with a specified standard deviation** ← |

> **Option (a) is the working assumption on many small sites and it is wrong; option (c) inverts the rule; option (d) confuses the mix method with the presence of reinforcement.**

**Why nominal mixes are LIMITED to M20, which is the substance of the answer:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **A fixed ratio takes NO account of the actual aggregate's grading, shape or absorption** ← | **The same 1:1.5:3 gives quite different strengths with rounded river gravel and with angular crushed stone** ← |
| **It takes no account of the WATER content, which is left to the mixer operator** ← | **And the water-cement ratio is what actually determines the strength** ← |
| **Nor of the cement's own strength class** | **43 grade and 53 grade OPC differ substantially** ← |
| **The resulting variability is large** | **Acceptable for M20; unacceptable for M25 and above, where the margin over the characteristic strength would have to be enormous** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE DECISIVE ONE AND WORTH STATING BLUNTLY: a nominal mix specifies the SOLIDS and says almost nothing about the WATER.**

> **Since Abrams' law makes strength a function of the water-cement ratio above all else, the one variable that matters most is the one the nominal mix leaves uncontrolled.**

> **In practice the mixer operator adds water until the concrete looks workable — and on a hot day, with dry aggregate, or when the labourers want it easier to place, that means a great deal of water and a much weaker concrete.**

> **The nominal mix compensates by being generous with cement, which is why it is uneconomical: it buys tolerance of poor water control with surplus cement.**

**Where each is appropriate:**

| Work | Mix |
|---|---|
| **A small house, a boundary wall, a rural culvert, blinding concrete** ← | **NOMINAL, up to M20 — no testing facility, small quantities, and the cost of mix design would exceed the saving** ← |
| **Any structural concrete of M25 or above** | **DESIGN mix, mandatory** ← |
| **Large volumes, where the cement saving is significant** | **DESIGN mix, on economic grounds alone** ← |
| **Anything with special requirements — durability, pumpability, low heat, exposure** ← | **DESIGN mix, since nominal mixes address strength only** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW POINTS AT A LIMITATION THAT IS EASILY MISSED: nominal mixes are specified for STRENGTH, and modern concrete specifications are increasingly about DURABILITY.**

> **Minimum cement content, maximum water-cement ratio and minimum grade for a given exposure condition are durability requirements, and they frequently govern over strength — a member in a severe exposure may need M30 for durability although M20 would carry the load easily.**

> **A nominal mix cannot address that at all, which is a further reason its use is confined to small works in benign conditions.**

> **And the durability requirement is the one most often ignored in practice, because unlike strength its absence produces no immediate consequence — the structure stands perfectly well for fifteen years and then begins to spall.**

examTip.trick: **Nominal mixes up to M20 only; design mix is MANDATORY for M25 and above.** 1:3:6 = M10, 1:2:4 = M15, 1:1.5:3 = M20.
examTip.trap: **A nominal mix specifies the SOLIDS and leaves the WATER to the operator** — and the water-cement ratio is what determines strength. It compensates with surplus cement, which is why it is uneconomical.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nominal mixes address STRENGTH only, never DURABILITY** — minimum cement content, maximum w/c and minimum grade for an exposure often govern over strength, and a nominal mix cannot deliver them.

questions.stem: A DOUBLY REINFORCED beam — one with compression steel as well as tension steel — is adopted principally when:
options: The beam is in a corrosive environment
The concrete grade is very high
The section's dimensions are RESTRICTED and it cannot develop the required moment as a singly reinforced section without exceeding its limiting moment of resistance
The beam carries only axial load
questions.solution:
**When the section's DIMENSIONS are restricted**, so that as a singly reinforced section it cannot develop the required moment without exceeding its limiting moment of resistance.

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A singly reinforced section has a LIMITING moment M_u,lim** ← | **Set by the maximum permitted neutral axis depth x_u,max — 0.48 d for Fe 415** ← |
| **That limit exists to ensure the section is UNDER-reinforced and therefore DUCTILE** ← | **The steel must yield before the concrete crushes** ← |
| **If the applied moment exceeds M_u,lim, the section must be enlarged** ← | **Which is the first and best answer** ← |
| **If the DEPTH cannot be increased — headroom, architecture, a fixed floor-to-floor height** ← | **Then compression steel is added instead** ← |
| **The compression steel carries the EXCESS moment above M_u,lim** | **With matching additional tension steel to balance it** ← |

> **SO A DOUBLY REINFORCED SECTION IS A SECOND-BEST SOLUTION ADOPTED UNDER CONSTRAINT, and it is worth saying so: making the beam deeper is cheaper and structurally better whenever it is possible.**

> **Depth is far more effective than steel — the moment capacity goes roughly as d², while adding compression steel gives a much smaller return per rupee.**

**The other reasons compression steel is used:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **To reduce LONG-TERM DEFLECTION** ← | **Compression steel restrains CREEP in the compression zone, and can halve the long-term deflection — a real and often decisive benefit** ← |
| **To increase DUCTILITY** | **It reduces the neutral axis depth, so the section can rotate further before the concrete crushes — which is why seismic codes REQUIRE compression steel** ← |
| **Where the moment REVERSES** ← | **Under earthquake or wind, the bottom of the beam goes into tension at the supports, so steel is needed on both faces anyway** ← |
| **To carry the hanger bars for the stirrups** | **Nominal top steel is present in every beam for this reason alone** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN WHY ALMOST EVERY BEAM IN A SEISMIC FRAME IS DOUBLY REINFORCED, whatever the moment calculation says:**

> **Under earthquake loading the moments at a beam's ends reverse direction as the building sways back and forth. Steel that is in compression in one half-cycle is in tension in the next.**

> **So continuous top and bottom reinforcement, properly anchored into the columns, is mandatory — and the codes go further, requiring the bottom steel at a support to be at least half the top steel.**

> **The ductility benefit compounds it: a heavily reinforced beam with no compression steel has a deep neutral axis, crushes early and fails in a brittle manner, which is precisely what seismic design exists to prevent.**

**The essential detailing requirement, which is where doubly reinforced beams go wrong:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Compression bars must be restrained by STIRRUPS against BUCKLING** ← | **A compression bar is a slender column; without lateral restraint it buckles outward and spalls the cover off** ← |
| **Stirrup spacing limited to 16 times the compression bar diameter** ← | **And not more than the least lateral dimension, or 300 mm** ← |
| **Every corner bar and alternate bars must be held by a stirrup corner** | ← |
| **Closer spacing in the plastic hinge zone near supports** | **Seismic detailing — typically d/4 over a length of 2d** ← |

> **THE BUCKLING POINT IN THE FIRST ROW IS NOT THEORETICAL: it is exactly what is seen in earthquake damage photographs of failed columns and beam ends — the cover spalled away and the longitudinal bars bowed outward between widely spaced ties.**

> **Once the cover spalls the bars are unrestrained over a greater length, they buckle further, the concrete core is unconfined and crushes, and the member loses its capacity entirely.**

> **Close, well-anchored stirrups with 135° hooks bent into the core prevent all of it — and they are the cheapest reinforcement in the structure. A 90° hook opens under load and does nothing, which is why the hook detail is specified so insistently and why it is the detail most worth checking on site.**

examTip.trick: **Used when the DEPTH is restricted and the moment exceeds M_u,lim.** Making the beam deeper is cheaper and better — capacity goes as d², so compression steel is a second-best under constraint.
examTip.trap: **Compression steel also halves LONG-TERM deflection by restraining creep, and raises DUCTILITY** — which is why seismic codes require it regardless of the moment calculation.
examTip.mnemonic: **A compression bar is a slender column and buckles without stirrups** — spacing ≤ 16 × bar diameter, and 135° hooks bent into the core. A 90° hook opens under load and does nothing.

questions.stem: As per IS 456:2000, the BASIC span-to-effective-depth ratios for controlling the deflection of beams are:
options: 10 for cantilevers, 15 for simply supported and 20 for continuous
5, 12 and 18 respectively
20, 26 and 32 respectively
7 for CANTILEVER, 20 for SIMPLY SUPPORTED and 26 for CONTINUOUS spans
questions.solution:
**7 for a CANTILEVER, 20 for SIMPLY SUPPORTED and 26 for CONTINUOUS spans.**

**The basic values and the modification factors:**

| Support condition | Basic span/depth |
|---|---|
| **CANTILEVER** | **7** ← |
| **SIMPLY SUPPORTED** | **20** ← |
| **CONTINUOUS** | **26** ← |

| Modification factor | Depends on | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **For TENSION reinforcement** ← | **The percentage and the service stress f_s = 0.58 f_y × (A_st required / A_st provided)** ← | **More steel, or lower stress, INCREASES the permitted ratio** ← |
| **For COMPRESSION reinforcement** | **Its percentage** | **INCREASES the ratio — up to about 1.5** ← |
| **For FLANGED beams** | **The web-to-flange width ratio** | **REDUCES it** ← |
| **For spans over 10 m** | **Multiply by 10/span** ← | **Reduces it, except for cantilevers, where a proper calculation is required** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION 7, 20, 26 HAS A CLEAR LOGIC: the greater the end restraint, the smaller the deflection for a given span, so the deeper permitted span-to-depth ratio.**

> **A cantilever has restraint at one end only and its free end deflects most, so it needs to be much deeper — the ratio of 7 against 20 means a cantilever must be nearly THREE TIMES as deep as a simply supported beam of the same span.**

> **That is the single most useful thing to carry from this table, because cantilever depth is consistently underestimated at the preliminary design stage.**

**Why a span/depth check is used instead of calculating the deflection:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Deflection calculation for cracked reinforced concrete is genuinely difficult** ← | **It needs the cracked and uncracked moments of inertia, the extent of cracking, the tension stiffening, and creep and shrinkage over time** ← |
| **Creep can DOUBLE or TREBLE the immediate deflection over years** ← | **And it depends on the humidity, the age at loading and the sustained load fraction** ← |
| **The span/depth rule embodies all of that empirically** | **It is calibrated so that a section satisfying it will normally satisfy the deflection limits** ← |
| **Only where the rule is not satisfied need a full calculation be done** | ← |

> **THE CREEP FACTOR IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE REASON THE SUBJECT IS DIFFICULT AND THE REASON THE EMPIRICAL RULE IS TRUSTED: the deflection a beam shows on striking the formwork is perhaps a third of what it will show in ten years.**

> **A beam that looks perfectly flat at handover can develop a visible sag, crack the partitions beneath it, and jam the doors — none of which is a strength failure and all of which is a real defect.**

**The deflection limits the rule is calibrated against:**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Total deflection, including creep and shrinkage** | **span / 250** ← |
| **Deflection occurring AFTER construction of partitions and finishes** ← | **span / 350, or 20 mm, whichever is LESS** ← |

> **THE SECOND LIMIT IS THE STRICTER AND THE MORE IMPORTANT, and the reason is in its wording: what damages a partition is not the beam's total deflection but the movement that occurs AFTER the partition was built.**

> **A beam that had already sagged 15 mm before the blockwork went up carries that sag harmlessly — the wall was built to the deflected line. A further 15 mm afterwards cracks it.**

> **So the sequence of construction matters to the serviceability outcome, and a practical measure is to delay building rigid partitions and brittle finishes until the structure has taken up most of its early creep — which costs nothing and is regularly ignored because it does not suit the programme.**

> **The 20 mm absolute cap is there because a long span would otherwise be permitted a large movement: span/350 on a 12 m beam is 34 mm, which would crack anything built beneath it regardless of the ratio.**

examTip.trick: **7 cantilever, 20 simply supported, 26 continuous.** More end restraint means less deflection, hence a larger permitted ratio.
examTip.trap: **A cantilever must be nearly THREE times as deep as a simply supported beam of the same span** — consistently underestimated at preliminary design.
examTip.mnemonic: **Limits are span/250 total, and span/350 or 20 mm for movement AFTER partitions are built** — the second is what cracks walls. Delay brittle finishes until early creep has occurred.

questions.stem: PRE-TENSIONING differs from POST-TENSIONING in that in pre-tensioning:
options: The tendons are stressed BEFORE the concrete is cast, and the force is transferred to the hardened concrete by BOND when the tendons are released
The tendons are stressed after the concrete has hardened, against the member itself
No tendons are used at all
The concrete is precompressed by external jacks left permanently in place
questions.solution:
**The tendons are stressed BEFORE the concrete is cast**, and the prestress is transferred to the hardened concrete by BOND when the tendons are released from their abutments.

**The two systems compared:**

| Aspect | PRE-TENSIONING | POST-TENSIONING |
|---|---|---|
| **Sequence** | **Stress tendons → cast concrete → cure → RELEASE tendons** ← | **Cast concrete with DUCTS → cure → thread and stress tendons → anchor → GROUT** ← |
| **Force transferred by** | **BOND along a transmission length** ← | **END ANCHORAGES bearing on the concrete** ← (option b describes it) |
| **Where done** | **In a FACTORY, on a long stressing bed** ← | **On SITE, or in a factory** ← |
| **Tendon profile** | **Usually STRAIGHT (deflecting is possible but awkward)** ← | **CURVED to follow the bending moment diagram — a major advantage** ← |
| **Suits** | **Mass production of identical units: railway sleepers, poles, piles, hollow-core slabs, small bridge beams** ← | **Large, one-off members: long-span bridge girders, flat slabs, tanks, silos, nuclear containments** ← |
| **Anchorage** | **None permanent — bond does the work** | **Permanent anchorages, which must be protected against corrosion** ← |
| **Losses unique to it** | **Elastic shortening is fully effective** | **FRICTION and wobble in the duct; ANCHORAGE slip** ← |

> **THE TENDON PROFILE ROW IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL DIFFERENCE AND IS WORTH EXPANDING, because it explains why long spans are post-tensioned:**

> **The ideal prestressing force follows the bending moment diagram — low at the supports, where the moment is small, and deep at midspan, where it is large.**

> **A post-tensioned duct can be laid to exactly that parabolic profile, so the prestress provides an upward load that directly opposes the applied load along the whole span.**

> **A pre-tensioned tendon is straight between the abutments, so at the ENDS of the member, where there is no moment to balance, the eccentric prestress produces TENSION in the top fibre — which must be dealt with by debonding some strands near the ends or by deflecting them.**

> **That end-zone problem is why pre-tensioned members are usually short, and why post-tensioning takes over as spans grow.**

**The LOAD BALANCING idea, which is the most elegant way to see prestressing:**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **A curved tendon under tension pushes UPWARD on the concrete along its length** ← | **A parabolic tendon of force P and drape h produces an equivalent upward UDL of 8 P h / L²** ← |
| **Choose P and h so that this balances the dead load** ← | **The beam then carries NO net transverse load under that condition** ← |
| **Consequently it has no bending and NO DEFLECTION at all** ← | **It is under pure axial compression** ← |

> **THAT IS A REMARKABLE RESULT AND IT IS THE REAL POINT OF PRESTRESSING: a prestressed beam is not merely a stronger reinforced beam.**

> **It is a beam in which the designer has chosen to cancel a selected part of the loading, leaving the member in a state of uniform compression under that condition — which is exactly the state concrete is good at.**

> **Hence the characteristic advantages: no cracking under service load, so the full section is effective and durability is much better; smaller sections and longer spans; and little or no deflection under sustained load.**

**And the reason prestressing demands high-strength materials:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **HIGH-STRENGTH steel is essential, not merely economical** ← | **Creep and shrinkage of the concrete shorten the member by a strain of perhaps 0.0006 — which would wipe out most of the prestress in mild steel and only a small fraction of it in a 1,860 MPa strand** ← |
| **HIGH-STRENGTH concrete (M40 and above)** | **To resist the high bearing stress at anchorages and the large compressive prestress** ← |
| **Low relaxation strand** | **To limit the steel's own long-term loss** ← |

> **The first row is the fundamental reason prestressing had to wait for high-strength steel, and it is why the nineteenth-century attempts failed: the concept was understood, but with the steel then available the prestress simply vanished within a few years as the concrete crept.**

> **Freyssinet's insight was that the loss is a fixed STRAIN, so the way to survive it is to start from a much higher stress — and that made the whole technology possible.**

examTip.trick: **Pre-tensioning: stress FIRST, cast, release — force transferred by BOND, in a factory, straight tendons. Post-tensioning: cast with ducts, stress AFTER — force transferred by END ANCHORAGES, curved profile.**
examTip.trap: **The curved profile is post-tensioning's big advantage** — it follows the moment diagram. A straight pre-tensioned tendon produces TOP TENSION at the ends, which is why such members stay short.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load balancing: a parabolic tendon gives an upward UDL of 8Ph/L²** — cancel the dead load and the beam has no bending and no deflection. And high-strength steel is essential because creep loss is a fixed STRAIN.

questions.stem: A reinforced concrete column classified as SLENDER must be designed for:
options: The axial load alone, with no moment
The primary moments PLUS ADDITIONAL MOMENTS arising from the lateral deflection of the column under load (the P-delta effect)
A reduced axial load only
The same moments as a short column, with a larger cover
questions.solution:
**For the primary moments PLUS ADDITIONAL moments** caused by the column's own lateral deflection under load — the P-delta effect.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **The column carries an axial load P** | ← |
| **It deflects laterally by an amount Δ** ← | **From the primary moments, from initial crookedness, or from sway of the frame** ← |
| **The axial load, now acting at an eccentricity Δ, produces an ADDITIONAL moment P × Δ** ← | ← |
| **That extra moment increases the deflection further** ← | **Which increases the moment again** ← |
| **The process CONVERGES for a stable column, and DIVERGES at the buckling load** ← | **Which is what buckling is** ← |

> **THE FEEDBACK IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WHAT MAKES SLENDERNESS DANGEROUS: the effect is SELF-AMPLIFYING, so it is not a small correction that grows linearly but one that accelerates as the load rises.**

> **A column at 50 per cent of its buckling load has its moments magnified by roughly a factor of two; at 80 per cent, by a factor of five.**

**The classification:**

| Criterion | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHORT column** | **Both slenderness ratios l_ex/D and l_ey/b are LESS than 12** ← |
| **SLENDER column** | **Either ratio is 12 or more** ← |
| **Absolute limit** | **The unsupported length must not exceed 60 times the least lateral dimension** ← |
| **For a column free at one end** | **The limit is 100 b²/D** ← |

> **Note that BOTH directions must be checked, and a column can be short about one axis and slender about the other — which is common in a frame braced in one direction only.**

**How the additional moment is computed:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **M_ax = P D (l_ex/D)² / 2000** ← | **The IS 456 expression for the additional moment about the major axis** ← |
| **It depends on the SQUARE of the slenderness ratio** ← | **So a modest increase in slenderness produces a large increase in the additional moment** ← |
| **A reduction factor k may be applied** | **Where the axial load is well below the balanced value, the effect is less severe** ← |
| **The additional moment is ADDED to the primary moment** | **And the column is designed for the combination** ← |

> **THE SQUARE-LAW IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRACTICAL WARNING: doubling the effective length QUADRUPLES the additional moment.**

> **So the cheapest way to deal with slenderness is almost never to strengthen the column — it is to REDUCE ITS EFFECTIVE LENGTH by bracing it, tying it into a floor, or introducing a shear wall.**

**The BRACED and UNBRACED distinction, which is fundamental and often missed:**

| Frame | Note |
|---|---|
| **BRACED** | **Lateral stability is provided by shear walls, cores or bracing — the frame does not SWAY** ← |
| **UNBRACED (sway) frame** | **The columns themselves must resist lateral load, and the whole storey moves sideways** ← |
| **Effective length** | **BRACED: between 0.5 L and 1.0 L. UNBRACED: from 1.2 L to 2.0 L and beyond** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE IN EFFECTIVE LENGTH BETWEEN THE TWO CASES IS A FACTOR OF TWO OR MORE, AND THEREFORE A FACTOR OF FOUR IN THE ADDITIONAL MOMENT — which is why the single most valuable decision in the layout of a tall building is to provide a shear wall or a core.**

> **A braced frame's columns are short, carry axial load efficiently, and can be slim. An unbraced frame's columns must be large enough to provide the building's entire lateral stability by frame action alone, which is expensive and gets rapidly worse with height.**

> **In a seismic region the case is stronger still: an unbraced frame relies entirely on its beam-column joints, and those joints are the hardest part of the structure to detail, to construct correctly and to inspect.**

> **The soft-storey failures seen repeatedly in earthquakes — including in Nepal in 2015 — are the extreme expression of this: a ground floor left open for shops or parking, with infill walls above, concentrates the entire sway demand into one storey's columns, and they fail by exactly the P-delta mechanism described here.**

examTip.trick: **Slender when either l_e/D or l_e/b ≥ 12.** Design for primary moments PLUS the additional moment M_ax = P D (l_ex/D)²/2000.
examTip.trap: **The effect is SELF-AMPLIFYING and goes as the SQUARE of slenderness** — doubling the effective length quadruples the additional moment. So brace the column rather than strengthen it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Braced l_e = 0.5-1.0 L; unbraced 1.2-2.0 L** — a factor of 4 in additional moment. A shear wall or core is the single most valuable layout decision, and its absence is what produces SOFT-STOREY failures.

questions.stem: In the plastic analysis of steel structures, a PLASTIC HINGE is:
options: A real pin connection provided at a joint
A hinge that forms only under seismic loading
A section at which the ENTIRE cross-section has YIELDED
A point of contraflexure in a beam
questions.solution:
**A section at which the WHOLE cross-section has yielded**, so it rotates freely at a CONSTANT moment equal to the plastic moment M_p — while continuing to transmit that moment.

**How it forms:**

| Stage | State of the section |
|---|---|
| **Elastic** | **Stress varies linearly; maximum at the extreme fibre** ← |
| **First YIELD, at M_y = f_y × Z (elastic section modulus)** ← | **The extreme fibre reaches yield; the rest is still elastic** ← |
| **Partial plasticity** | **Yielding spreads inward from both faces; an elastic core remains** ← |
| **FULLY PLASTIC, at M_p = f_y × Z_p (plastic section modulus)** ← | **The whole section has yielded — compression over half the area, tension over the other half** ← |
| **Beyond that** | **The section rotates at constant moment — a PLASTIC HINGE** ← |

> **THE CRUCIAL DISTINCTION FROM A REAL HINGE IS IN THE LAST ROW AND IT IS WHAT OPTION (A) TESTS: a real pin transmits NO moment at all.**

> **A plastic hinge transmits its FULL plastic moment M_p, and goes on transmitting it while it rotates.**

> **It is a hinge in the kinematic sense — it permits rotation — and not at all in the static sense.**

**The SHAPE FACTOR, which measures the reserve beyond first yield:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Shape factor S = M_p / M_y = Z_p / Z** ← | **The ratio of full plastic to first yield moment** ← |

| Section | Shape factor |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **1.5** ← |
| **Solid circle** | **1.70** |
| **I-section, bending about the major axis** | **1.10 to 1.20** ← |
| **Diamond (square about a diagonal)** | **2.0** ← |

> **THE I-SECTION'S LOW SHAPE FACTOR HAS A SATISFYING EXPLANATION: an I-section already concentrates its material at the extreme fibres, so when the outer fibres yield, most of the section yields almost at once.**

> **There is little material near the neutral axis left to contribute extra capacity — hence only 10 to 20 per cent reserve.**

> **A rectangle, by contrast, has half its material within the middle half of the depth doing very little elastically, and that material provides the extra 50 per cent.**

> **So the shape factor is inversely related to how efficiently the section was already using its material — an efficient elastic section has little plastic reserve, which is a fair trade rather than a defect.**

**What plastic analysis achieves:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A statically indeterminate structure does not collapse when the FIRST hinge forms** ← | **It merely becomes less indeterminate, and the load redistributes** ← |
| **Collapse occurs only when enough hinges form to create a MECHANISM** ← | **Requiring (degree of static indeterminacy + 1) hinges** ← |
| **The collapse load is therefore substantially HIGHER than the first-yield load** ← | **Often 15 to 40 per cent, and more in a highly redundant frame** ← |
| **Plastic design uses that reserve** | **Giving lighter, more economical structures** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW GIVES THE COUNTING RULE THAT SOLVES MOST EXAMINATION PROBLEMS: a propped cantilever is once indeterminate, so it needs 2 hinges; a fixed beam is twice indeterminate and needs 3.**

**And the essential precondition, which limits where plastic design may be used:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The section must be able to ROTATE at M_p without failing** ← | **Which requires the material to be ductile and the section to be COMPACT (plastic class)** ← |
| **A SLENDER section buckles locally before it can develop M_p** ← | **The flange or web folds, the moment drops, and no hinge forms at all** ← |
| **Hence the width-to-thickness limits that classify sections as plastic, compact, semi-compact or slender** ← | **Only PLASTIC sections may be used in plastic design** ← |
| **Lateral torsional buckling must also be prevented** | **The member must be restrained** ← |

> **The whole method depends on the hinge being able to rotate through a substantial angle at constant moment, and a section that buckles locally cannot do that.**

> **This is the same requirement, in a different material, as the ductility demanded of reinforced concrete sections through the x_u,max limit and the stirrup detailing: plastic redistribution is only available to a structure whose members can deform without losing strength, and securing that is the price of using the reserve.**

It rotates at a constant moment equal to the plastic moment M_p, while still transmitting that moment.

examTip.trick: **A plastic hinge transmits its FULL plastic moment M_p while rotating** — a real pin transmits none. Kinematically a hinge, statically not at all.
examTip.trap: **Shape factor: rectangle 1.5, I-section only 1.10-1.20** — an I-section already has its material at the extremes, so little reserve remains once the outer fibres yield.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hinges needed for collapse = static indeterminacy + 1** — propped cantilever 2, fixed beam 3. And only COMPACT (plastic-class) sections qualify: a slender one buckles locally before M_p is reached.

questions.stem: In load-bearing masonry buildings in a seismic region, HORIZONTAL SEISMIC BANDS (plinth, lintel, sill and roof bands) are provided principally to:
options: Improve the appearance of the elevation
Support the floor slab directly
Reduce the quantity of masonry required
TIE the walls together into a BOX
questions.solution:
**To TIE the walls together into a BOX**, so that the building acts as a single unit and the walls do not separate at the corners and collapse outward.

**Why unreinforced masonry fails in earthquakes:**

| Failure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **OUT-OF-PLANE collapse of a wall** ← | **A wall shaken PERPENDICULAR to its own plane has almost no bending strength and topples outward** ← |
| **Separation at CORNERS** ← | **The two walls meeting at a corner pull apart, and each is then unsupported at that edge** ← |
| **Delamination of a thick wall** | **The inner and outer wythes separate** |
| **Gable-end collapse** | **A triangular gable with no restraint at the top** ← |
| **Diagonal shear cracking of in-plane walls** | ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS ARE THE DOMINANT KILLERS AND THEY ARE CONNECTED: a masonry wall is strong in its OWN plane and very weak out of plane.**

> **In any earthquake, some walls are shaken in plane and others out of plane, and the out-of-plane walls collapse first.**

> **But if the walls are TIED to one another, the weak out-of-plane wall is held at its top and its ends by the strong in-plane walls, which can carry the load easily.**

> **The whole building then behaves as a BOX rather than as four separate panels, and its resistance is transformed — at a cost of a few per cent of the construction budget.**

**The bands and their positions:**

| Band | Position | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **PLINTH band** | **At plinth level, above the foundation** ← | **Ties the walls at the base; important on soft or uneven ground** ← |
| **SILL band** | **At window sill level** | **Reduces the effective height of the pier between openings** ← |
| **LINTEL band** | **At the top of door and window openings, CONTINUOUS all round** ← | **The most important single band — it ties the walls at the level where openings weaken them most** ← |
