| **ROOF/EAVES band** | **At the top of the walls, beneath the roof** ← | **Ties the wall tops and connects them to the roof; essential where there is no rigid slab** ← |
| **GABLE band** | **Following the slope of a gable end** | **Restrains the gable triangle, which otherwise has no support at the top** ← |

> **THE WORD "CONTINUOUS" IN THE LINTEL BAND ROW IS THE ENTIRE POINT AND THE THING MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG ON SITE: a band that stops at a corner, or is interrupted at a doorway, or is not lapped properly, does nothing.**

> **The band works only as a closed loop right around the building. A gap of half a metre at one corner defeats the whole system, because the tension it was meant to carry has nowhere to go.**

> **This is why the corner reinforcement detail — the L-bend lap of the longitudinal bars around the corner, with adequate lap length — is the single most important detail to check in a band, and why prefabricating and inspecting it before casting is worth the trouble.**

**The other elements of seismic masonry construction:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **VERTICAL reinforcement at CORNERS and at jambs of openings** ← | **Bars from the foundation up through the wall, tied into every band — resisting the vertical bending and holding the corners** ← |
| **THROUGH-STONES (bond stones) in stone masonry** ← | **Stones running the full thickness of the wall, at about 1.2 m spacing horizontally and 600 mm vertically — preventing the wall delaminating into two skins** ← |
| **Limits on the SIZE and POSITION of openings** | **Openings kept away from corners, and their total width limited to a fraction of the wall length** ← |
| **A RIGID diaphragm at floor and roof level** | **An RCC slab acts as one; a flexible timber or CGI roof does not, which is why the eaves band matters so much there** ← |
| **Good mortar and proper wall-to-wall bonding at junctions** | ← |

> **THE THROUGH-STONE REQUIREMENT IN THE SECOND ROW IS SPECIFIC TO NEPAL'S TRADITIONAL STONE-IN-MUD CONSTRUCTION AND IT SAVED AND COST MANY LIVES IN 2015: a random rubble stone wall built as two outer skins with rubble packed between behaves as two thin, unconnected walls.**

> **Shaken out of plane, the outer skin peels away and the wall collapses. Through-stones convert the two skins into one thick wall.**

> **They cost nothing but the mason's care in selecting and placing long stones, and their presence or absence was one of the clearest distinctions between buildings that survived the 2015 earthquake and those that did not.**

> **That is the encouraging lesson from all of this: the measures that matter most in masonry are cheap, low-technology and buildable by the same masons using the same materials — bands, vertical bars at corners, through-stones, and restraint on openings. The obstacle has never been cost or technology, only knowing and insisting.**

They act as a single unit and the walls do not separate at the corners and fall outward.

examTip.trick: **Bands tie the walls into a BOX** — plinth, sill, lintel, eaves/roof and gable. Masonry is strong in its own plane and very weak out of plane; tying lets the strong walls hold the weak ones.
examTip.trap: **A band must be CONTINUOUS right around the building** — a gap at one corner defeats the whole system, so the corner lap detail is the critical thing to inspect before casting.
examTip.mnemonic: **THROUGH-STONES at ~1.2 m horizontally and 600 mm vertically stop a rubble wall delaminating into two skins** — they cost nothing but the mason's care, and in 2015 their presence or absence distinguished the buildings that stood.

questions.stem: In water supply engineering, the DESIGN PERIOD adopted for a component is generally SHORTER for pumping machinery than for a trunk main because:
options: Pumps are more expensive per unit of capacity
Pumps have a shorter WORKING LIFE and are EASILY replaced or added to later
Pipelines wear out faster
Pumping demand does not grow with population
questions.solution:
**Because pumps have a shorter working life and can easily be replaced or supplemented later**, whereas replacing a buried trunk main means digging up the whole route.

**Typical design periods:**

| Component | Design period | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Storage dams and large reservoirs** | **50 years** ← | **Very long life; enormously costly and disruptive to enlarge** ← |
| **Water TREATMENT plant units** | **15 years** ← | **Can be extended in modules on the same site** ← |
| **TRUNK mains and conveyance pipelines** | **30 years** ← | **Buried, long-lived, and very disruptive to replace or duplicate** ← |
| **Distribution network (small pipes)** | **30 years** ← | **Extended as the town grows** |
| **PUMPS and pumping machinery** | **10 years** ← | **Short mechanical life; easily replaced or an extra unit added** ← |
| **Service reservoirs** | **15 to 25 years** | **Additional cells can be built** |

> **THE PRINCIPLE BEHIND EVERY ONE OF THESE FIGURES IS THE SAME, and it is the real answer to the question: the design period should match how DIFFICULT and DISRUPTIVE the component is to enlarge later.**

> **Something easily added to is designed for a short period, and the addition made when it is needed. Something almost impossible to add to is designed for a long period, and the spare capacity paid for at the outset.**

**The economic trade-off behind the choice:**

| Longer design period | Shorter design period |
|---|---|
| **Higher capital cost NOW** ← | **Lower capital cost now** ← |
| **Capacity stands idle for years, earning nothing** ← | **Capacity matched to demand throughout** ← |
| **Interest is paid on money invested well before it is used** ← | **Investment deferred, so its present cost is lower** ← |
| **But no future disruption or repeated mobilisation** ← | **Repeated construction, each with its own mobilisation and disturbance** ← |
| **Economies of scale captured once** | **Lost — a 600 mm pipe costs far less than twice a 300 mm one** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHY PIPES ARE DESIGNED FOR LONG PERIODS AND IS WORTH QUANTIFYING: the cost of laying a pipeline is dominated by EXCAVATION, bedding, backfill, reinstatement and traffic management — not by the pipe itself.**

> **Those costs are almost the same for a 300 mm pipe as for a 600 mm one, and they are incurred all over again if a second pipe is laid later.**

> **So doubling the diameter at the outset may add only 20 or 30 per cent to the total cost while quadrupling the capacity, and laying a second pipe in twenty years costs nearly as much as the first.**

> **The arithmetic favours generosity in pipe sizing very strongly, and under-sized trunk mains are one of the most common and least reversible mistakes in urban water supply.**

**The other factors in fixing a design period:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **The reliability of the POPULATION FORECAST** ← | **Forecasts beyond 30 years are speculative, which caps the sensible design period whatever the economics say** ← |
| **The interest rate** | **A high rate discourages early investment and shortens the period** ← |
| **Availability of FUNDS now** | **Often the real determinant, whatever the analysis concludes** ← |
| **The rate of growth** | **A rapidly growing town outgrows a short period almost immediately** ← |
| **Ease of staging** | **Modular treatment units favour short periods; a dam does not** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IMPOSES A LIMIT THAT THE ECONOMICS CANNOT OVERRIDE, and it deserves emphasis: a component designed for 50 years is being sized on a population forecast 50 years ahead.**

> **Nobody can forecast a town's population that far with any confidence — a new road, an industry, a change in migration or an administrative reorganisation can double it or halt it entirely.**

> **So a very long design period buys certainty of capacity at the cost of designing against a number that is largely invented, and the honest response is to design the STRUCTURE for a long life while leaving its capacity STAGEABLE where the layout allows — a second pipe route reserved, a treatment plant site large enough to extend, foundations built for a taller reservoir.**

> **Reserving the SPACE costs almost nothing and preserves the option; building the capacity costs a great deal and forecloses it.**

Replacing a buried pipeline is disruptive and costly.

examTip.trick: **Match the design period to how DIFFICULT the component is to enlarge later.** Dams 50 yr, pipes 30 yr, treatment 15 yr, pumps 10 yr.
examTip.trap: **Pipeline cost is dominated by EXCAVATION and reinstatement, not the pipe** — so doubling the diameter may add 30 % of cost for 4× capacity, while laying a second pipe later costs nearly as much as the first.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 50-year design period sizes on a 50-year population forecast, which nobody can make.** Reserve the SPACE for expansion instead — it costs nothing and keeps the option open.

questions.stem: ARSENIC contamination of shallow tube well water in Nepal's Terai is a serious public health concern principally because arsenic:
options: Gives the water a strong bitter taste that consumers can detect
Causes water to become turbid on standing
Corrodes the tube well casing rapidly
Is COLOURLESS, ODOURLESS and TASTELESS
questions.solution:
**Because arsenic is colourless, odourless and tasteless** — the water looks and tastes perfectly good — while long-term ingestion causes skin lesions, and cancers of the skin, bladder and lung.

**Why it is such a difficult problem:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **UNDETECTABLE without a chemical test** ← | **No colour, no smell, no taste — the water is often clear and pleasant** ← |
| **The health effects are CHRONIC, appearing after years of exposure** ← | **Not an acute poisoning, so no immediate warning links the illness to the water** ← |
| **It varies enormously between neighbouring wells** ← | **One tube well may be safe and the next, fifty metres away, badly contaminated — so a village cannot be cleared by testing a sample of wells** ← |
| **It is NATURAL in origin** | **Released from the aquifer's own sediments; it is not a pollution incident that can be stopped at source** ← |
| **The affected wells were installed to ESCAPE bacterial disease** ← | **A public health success created a public health problem** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE BITTER IRONY OF THE WHOLE EPISODE ACROSS THE GANGES BASIN, and it deserves to be stated:**

> **Millions of shallow tube wells were installed from the 1970s onward precisely to move people off contaminated surface water, and they achieved an enormous reduction in diarrhoeal disease and infant mortality.**

> **Nobody tested for arsenic, because there was no reason to expect it and the test was not routine.**

> **The consequence is one of the largest mass poisonings in history, and it stands as a permanent argument for testing water sources for the FULL range of parameters rather than only for the hazard one is currently thinking about.**

**The limits and the scale:**

| Standard | Limit |
|---|---|
| **WHO guideline value** | **0.01 mg/L (10 ppb)** ← |
| **Nepal's National Drinking Water Quality Standard** | **0.05 mg/L (50 ppb) — an INTERIM value, relaxed on grounds of feasibility** ← |
| **India's standard** | **0.01 mg/L, with 0.05 permitted where no alternative source exists** ← |

> **The gap between 10 and 50 ppb is a policy judgement about what is achievable rather than a scientific disagreement, and it means that water compliant with the national standard may still carry five times the WHO guideline exposure.**

**The health effects, in order of appearance:**

| Stage | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Early** | **MELANOSIS — dark patches on the skin** ← |
| **Then** | **KERATOSIS — hard, rough patches on the palms and soles** ← |
| **Later** | **Skin cancer; cancers of the BLADDER and LUNG** ← |
| **Also** | **Peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, and developmental effects in children** ← |
| **Together termed** | **ARSENICOSIS** ← |

**The responses available, with their honest limitations:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **TEST every well and paint it RED or GREEN** ← | **The essential first step — cheap field kits exist, and it lets people switch to a safe neighbouring well** ← |
| **Switch to a DEEPER aquifer** | **Deep wells are usually arsenic-free, but cost more and risk drawing contamination down if badly sealed** ← |
| **Switch to a treated SURFACE source** | **Solves arsenic; reintroduces the need for full treatment and reliable operation** ← |
| **Household or community REMOVAL units** | **Iron-based adsorption, coagulation-filtration; effective but need maintenance and spent-media disposal** ← |
| **RAINWATER harvesting; dug wells** | **Viable supplements** ← |

> **THE WELL-PAINTING PROGRAMME IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST EFFECTIVE SINGLE MEASURE AND THE CHEAPEST, and it is worth appreciating why: because contamination varies so sharply between adjacent wells, most affected households have a SAFE well within a few minutes' walk.**

> **They simply do not know which one it is. Testing every well and marking it visibly converts an invisible hazard into a visible one, and people respond to it.**

> **It is a rare case where the intervention with the highest health return is information rather than infrastructure — and it also shows why blanket assumptions about "the groundwater in this area" are useless: the resolution of the problem is one well, not one district.**

Contaminated water appears perfectly safe, while long-term ingestion causes skin lesions and cancers.

examTip.trick: **Colourless, odourless, tasteless — the water seems perfectly good** — and the effects are CHRONIC, appearing after years, so nothing links the illness to the source.
examTip.trap: **WHO guideline 0.01 mg/L; Nepal's interim standard 0.05 mg/L** — the gap is a feasibility judgement, so compliant water can still carry five times the WHO exposure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Contamination varies well by well, so most affected households have a safe well nearby and do not know it** — testing and painting wells red/green is the cheapest, highest-return measure there is.

questions.stem: NON-REVENUE WATER (NRW) in an urban water supply system is:
options: The difference between the water put into the distribution SYSTEM and the water BILLED to consumers
The water used for firefighting only
The water lost by evaporation from service reservoirs
The proportion of water that fails the quality standard
questions.solution:
**The difference between the water put INTO the distribution system and the water BILLED** — made up of physical leakage, unbilled authorised consumption, and commercial (apparent) losses.

**Its three components:**

| Component | Contents |
|---|---|
| **PHYSICAL (real) LOSSES** ← | **Leakage from mains, service connections and reservoirs; overflows** ← |
| **COMMERCIAL (apparent) LOSSES** ← | **Meter under-registration, illegal connections, data handling and billing errors, unauthorised use** ← |
| **UNBILLED AUTHORISED consumption** | **Firefighting, mains flushing, public standposts, water for the utility's own use** ← (option b is only part of this) |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO IS THE MOST IMPORTANT ONE OPERATIONALLY, and the reason is that they call for completely different responses:**

> **A PHYSICAL loss means water was produced, treated, pumped — and never reached anybody. The cost is the cost of producing it, and the remedy is engineering: leak detection, pressure management, pipe replacement.**

> **A COMMERCIAL loss means the water WAS delivered and consumed, and simply was not paid for. It costs the utility revenue but not production, and the remedy is administrative: metering, meter replacement, billing reform, and dealing with illegal connections.**

> **Spending an engineering budget on a commercial-loss problem achieves nothing, and vice versa — which is why the two are separated before any programme is designed.**

**Typical figures, which show the scale of the problem:**

| System | NRW |
|---|---|
| **A well-run utility** | **Below 15 %** ← |
| **Acceptable in a developing-country context** | **20 to 25 %** |
| **Kathmandu and many South Asian cities** | **Commonly 30 to 40 %, and higher in places** ← |

> **A system losing 35 per cent is producing, treating and pumping roughly one and a half litres for every litre it sells — so a third of its treatment plant, its pumping energy and its source abstraction exists purely to feed the leaks.**

**Why leakage is so hard to reduce, stated honestly:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **The leaks are BURIED and mostly invisible** ← | **Only a small fraction ever surfaces; most seeps away unseen** ← |
| **INTERMITTENT supply makes detection almost impossible** ← | **Acoustic leak detection needs a pressurised, continuously flowing system** ← |
| **Old pipes, poor jointing and unrecorded connections** | **Many networks have no accurate map of what is buried where** ← |
| **Repairing a leak raises the pressure and bursts the next weakest point** | **A real and demoralising effect in a fragile network** ← |
| **It competes for funds with new connections, which are politically visible** ← | **A leak repaired serves nobody who notices** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS A VICIOUS CIRCLE WORTH SPELLING OUT, because it is the central difficulty of South Asian urban water supply:**

> **Supply is intermittent because there is not enough water. There is not enough water partly because so much leaks away. The leakage cannot be found and fixed efficiently because the supply is intermittent.**

> **Intermittent operation also actively damages the network: pipes fill and empty daily, so they are cycled in pressure and are alternately full and empty, which accelerates joint failure — and when empty and at negative pressure they draw in contaminated groundwater through the very leaks that lose the water.**

> **So intermittency causes leakage, wastes water, and contaminates the supply, all at once.**

> **Breaking the circle requires moving to CONTINUOUS pressurised supply in one district at a time — the district metered area approach — rather than trying to improve the whole city simultaneously, and that is now the standard strategy precisely because the incremental approach does not work.**

**And PRESSURE MANAGEMENT deserves a note, because it is the cheapest measure:**

> **Leakage from a given hole rises with pressure — roughly with the square root for a fixed orifice, and considerably faster for the flexible cracks that predominate in real networks.**

> **So reducing excess night-time pressure with a pressure-reducing valve can cut leakage substantially, immediately, and with no excavation at all.**

> **It also reduces the rate at which new bursts occur, which is a compounding benefit — and it is usually the first intervention worth making, before any leak is looked for.**

Comprising physical leakage, unbilled authorised consumption, and commercial losses such as meter under-registration and illegal connections.

examTip.trick: **Water into the system minus water BILLED** — physical leakage, commercial losses (meters, illegal connections, billing) and unbilled authorised use. Option (b) is only part of the third component.
examTip.trap: **Physical losses need ENGINEERING (leak detection, pipe replacement); commercial losses need ADMINISTRATION (metering, billing).** Spending one budget on the other problem achieves nothing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Intermittency causes leakage, wastes water and contaminates supply all at once** — and prevents the acoustic detection that would fix it. Break the circle district by district; and manage PRESSURE first, since it needs no excavation.

questions.stem: The OPERATING POINT of a centrifugal pump installed in a pipeline is found at:
options: The point of maximum efficiency on the pump curve, always
The shut-off head of the pump
The INTERSECTION of the PUMP's head-discharge characteristic curve with the SYSTEM curve of the pipeline
The point at which the pump's power input is minimum
questions.solution:
**At the INTERSECTION of the PUMP's head-discharge curve with the SYSTEM curve.**

**The two curves:**

| Curve | What it represents | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| **PUMP characteristic (H-Q) curve** ← | **The head the pump CAN generate at each discharge — a property of the machine** ← | **FALLS as discharge increases** ← |
| **SYSTEM curve** ← | **The head the pipeline REQUIRES at each discharge — static lift plus friction and minor losses** ← | **RISES as discharge increases, roughly as Q²** ← |

> **THE PUMP CAN ONLY DELIVER WHAT THE SYSTEM WILL ACCEPT, AND THE SYSTEM CAN ONLY RECEIVE WHAT THE PUMP WILL GIVE — so the flow settles at the single discharge where the two agree.**

> **That is the operating point, and it is a property of the PAIR, not of the pump alone.**

> **Option (a) is the commonest misconception and the one worth correcting explicitly: the pump will operate at its best-efficiency point ONLY if the system curve happens to pass through it. The designer's job is to SELECT a pump whose best-efficiency point sits at, or close to, the intersection — the efficiency does not migrate to meet the duty.**

**The system curve, written out:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **STATIC head** | **The vertical lift from the suction water level to the delivery level — independent of discharge, so a horizontal line** ← |
| **FRICTION and minor losses** | **Proportional to roughly Q² — a rising parabola added to the static head** ← |
| **H_system = H_static + K Q²** | **The system curve** ← |

> **THE RELATIVE SIZE OF THE TWO TERMS DETERMINES HOW THE INSTALLATION BEHAVES, and this is worth knowing:**

| System type | Curve | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Mostly STATIC lift, short pipe** | **Nearly FLAT** ← | **Discharge is very sensitive to the pump's head; throttling is ineffective** ← |
| **Mostly FRICTION, long pipeline** | **STEEP** ← | **Discharge is insensitive to the pump curve; a small head change moves the flow little** ← |

**What happens when conditions change:**

| Change | Effect on the operating point |
|---|---|
| **A valve is THROTTLED** | **The system curve steepens; the point moves LEFT — less flow at more head, with the extra head simply wasted across the valve** ← |
| **The pipe becomes ROUGHER with age** ← | **The system curve steepens; discharge FALLS over the years, sometimes markedly** ← |
| **The static lift changes as a reservoir empties** | **The whole system curve shifts up or down** ← |
| **Two identical pumps in PARALLEL** | **The combined pump curve doubles the discharge at each head — but the actual gain is LESS than double, because the system curve rises** ← |
| **Two in SERIES** | **Doubles the head at each discharge** ← |

> **THE PARALLEL PUMP ROW CONTAINS A RESULT THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND MATTERS IN DESIGN: adding a second identical pump in parallel does NOT double the flow.**

> **The two pumps together offer twice the discharge at any given head — but pushing more flow down the same pipe requires more head, so the new intersection sits higher up both curves.**

> **On a friction-dominated (steep) system the gain may be only 30 or 40 per cent for twice the pumps and roughly twice the energy. On a static-dominated (flat) system it approaches the full doubling.**

> **So whether parallel pumping is worthwhile depends entirely on the SHAPE OF THE SYSTEM CURVE, and installing a second pump without checking it is a well-known way to spend money for very little extra water.**

> **THE PIPE ROUGHENING ROW IS THE OTHER PRACTICAL WARNING: a pump selected to sit exactly at its best-efficiency point on a new pipeline will drift off it as the pipe ages and the system curve steepens.**

> **Sensible practice is to check the operating point against both the new and the aged pipe condition, and to select a pump that remains within its acceptable operating range across the whole of that span — rather than one that is perfect on the day of commissioning and increasingly wrong thereafter.**

examTip.trick: **Intersection of the pump's falling H-Q curve with the system's rising H_static + KQ² curve.** It is a property of the PAIR, not of the pump alone.
examTip.trap: **The pump runs at best efficiency only if the system curve happens to pass through that point** — efficiency does not migrate to meet the duty. Select the pump to suit the system.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two pumps in parallel do NOT double the flow** — pushing more down the same pipe needs more head. On a friction-dominated system the gain may be only 30-40 % for twice the energy.

questions.stem: In BREAKPOINT CHLORINATION, the "breakpoint" is the dose at which:
options: The chlorine gas cylinder is exhausted
All the ammonia and oxidisable matter have been destroyed
The taste of chlorine first becomes detectable
The water's pH falls below 7
questions.solution:
**The dose at which all the ammonia and oxidisable matter have been destroyed** — the combined residual has been driven down to a minimum, and any further chlorine added appears as FREE residual chlorine.

**The four stages of the breakpoint curve, as the dose is increased:**

| Stage | What happens | Residual |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Immediate demand** | **Chlorine is consumed by reducing agents — iron, manganese, hydrogen sulphide, nitrite, organic matter** ← | **NO residual at all** ← |
| **2. Chloramine formation** | **Chlorine reacts with AMMONIA to form monochloramine and dichloramine** ← | **COMBINED residual, RISING with dose** ← |
| **3. Chloramine DESTRUCTION** ← | **Further chlorine OXIDISES the chloramines already formed, releasing nitrogen gas** ← | **Combined residual FALLING — the counter-intuitive part** ← |
| **4. Beyond the BREAKPOINT** ← | **Nothing left to react with** | **FREE residual, rising linearly with dose** ← |

> **THE FALLING SECTION IN STAGE 3 IS WHAT MAKES THE CURVE MEMORABLE AND IS WHY THE PHENOMENON HAS A NAME: adding MORE chlorine REDUCES the measured residual.**

> **An operator who does not know this, seeing the residual fall as the dose is increased, will conclude that something is wrong and reduce the dose — moving back up the wrong side of the curve and making matters worse.**

> **The correct response is to push THROUGH the breakpoint, and the residual then rises reliably with dose thereafter.**

**Why free residual is wanted rather than combined:**

| Property | FREE chlorine (HOCl, OCl⁻) | COMBINED chlorine (chloramines) |
|---|---|---|
| **Disinfecting power** | **Much STRONGER — roughly 25 times** ← | **Weak** ← |
| **Speed of action** | **Fast — minutes** | **Slow — hours** ← |
| **Persistence in the network** | **Decays relatively quickly** | **PERSISTS much longer** ← |
| **Taste and odour** | **Less** | **MORE — chloramines cause the characteristic "swimming pool" smell** ← |
| **THM formation** | **Higher** | **Lower** ← |

> **THE TASTE ROW CORRECTS A WIDESPREAD MISCONCEPTION AND IS WORTH STATING: the strong chlorinous smell people complain about is usually caused by CHLORAMINES, that is by too LITTLE chlorine rather than too much.**

> **The water has been dosed into stage 2 of the curve and stopped there. Increasing the dose past the breakpoint destroys the chloramines and the smell disappears.**

> **So the intuitive remedy — reduce the dose — produces exactly the objectionable condition it is meant to cure, and the counter-intuitive one works.**

**The relative disinfecting power of the free forms, which depends on pH:**

| Species | Note |
|---|---|
| **HYPOCHLOROUS ACID, HOCl** | **The powerful form — dominant at LOW pH** ← |
| **HYPOCHLORITE ion, OCl⁻** | **Perhaps 80 times WEAKER — dominant at HIGH pH** ← |
| **The changeover is around pH 7.5** ← | **At pH 6 chlorination is highly effective; at pH 9 much less so** ← |

> **THIS IS WHY THE pH MATTERS AS MUCH AS THE DOSE, and why chlorinating water that has just been softened by lime — leaving it at pH 10 or above — is far less effective than the residual figure suggests.**

> **The measured residual counts both species, but only one of them is doing most of the work, so the same residual gives quite different disinfection at different pH.**

> **Recarbonation after softening, which brings the pH back down, therefore serves disinfection as well as corrosion control.**

**And the terminology, since it is examined:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chlorine DEMAND** | **Dose applied MINUS residual remaining after a stated contact time** ← |
| **PRE-chlorination** | **Applied before the main treatment — controls algae and aids coagulation** ← |
| **POST-chlorination** | **After filtration — the main disinfection step** ← |
| **SUPER-chlorination followed by DECHLORINATION** | **A very high dose for a short contact, then the excess removed with sulphur dioxide or activated carbon** ← |
| **Breakpoint chlorination** | **Dosing past the breakpoint to obtain a free residual — this question** ← |

The combined residual has fallen to a minimum, and any FURTHER chlorine added appears as FREE residual chlorine.

examTip.trick: **Four stages: demand consumed → chloramines form (combined residual rises) → chloramines DESTROYED (residual FALLS) → free residual rises.** The breakpoint is the minimum.
examTip.trap: **Adding more chlorine can REDUCE the residual** — an operator who then cuts the dose moves back up the wrong side of the curve. Push THROUGH the breakpoint.
examTip.mnemonic: **The "swimming pool" smell is CHLORAMINES — too LITTLE chlorine, not too much.** And HOCl dominates below pH 7.5 and is ~80× stronger than OCl⁻, so pH matters as much as dose.

questions.stem: In a SLOW SAND FILTER, the layer chiefly responsible for the removal of bacteria and fine suspended matter is:
options: The gravel underdrain layer
The layer of supernatant water above the sand
The lowest 100 mm of the sand bed
The SCHMUTZDECKE
questions.solution:
**The SCHMUTZDECKE** — the biologically active "dirty skin" that develops on the top surface of the sand bed.

**What it is and how it works:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A gelatinous mat 20 to 30 mm thick, forming over 1 to 3 weeks** ← | **The RIPENING period** ← |
| **Composed of algae, bacteria, protozoa, rotifers and trapped particles** | **A living community** ← |
| **Removes by BIOLOGICAL action, not merely by straining** ← | **Pathogens are consumed by the predatory organisms in the mat** ← |
| **Also removes fine particles far smaller than the sand's pores** | **By adsorption and by the mat's own fine structure** ← |
| **Achieves 99 to 99.9 % bacterial removal when mature** ← | **Comparable with a much more complex plant** ← |

> **THE BIOLOGICAL MECHANISM IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE KEY POINT AND IS WHAT DISTINGUISHES THE SLOW SAND FILTER FROM EVERY OTHER FILTER: it is not a strainer, it is an ECOSYSTEM.**

> **The sand grains are far too coarse to catch a bacterium mechanically. The bacteria are EATEN, by protozoa and other predators living in the mat.**

> **This has an immediate practical consequence: a slow sand filter must be kept CONTINUOUSLY in operation and never allowed to dry out or be dosed with chlorine, because doing so kills the organisms doing the work and the filter must be re-ripened over several weeks.**

**Slow against rapid sand filters:**

| Feature | SLOW sand filter | RAPID sand filter |
|---|---|---|
| **Filtration rate** | **0.1 to 0.4 m³/m²/h — very low** ← | **4 to 6 m³/m²/h, some 20 to 40 times faster** ← |
| **Area required** | **LARGE** ← | Small |
| **Sand size** | **Fine, 0.2 to 0.4 mm effective size** ← | **Coarse, 0.4 to 0.7 mm** |
| **Mechanism** | **BIOLOGICAL, at the surface** ← | **Physical straining and adsorption, through the DEPTH** ← |
| **Pre-treatment needed** | **NONE for reasonably clear water** ← | **Coagulation, flocculation and sedimentation are ESSENTIAL** ← |
| **Cleaning** | **SCRAPING off the top 20-25 mm by hand, every 1-3 months** ← | **BACKWASHING with water and air, every 24-48 hours** ← |
| **Bacterial removal** | **99 to 99.9 %** ← | **Poor — perhaps 80 %, so disinfection is essential** ← |
| **Operating skill and power** | **Minimal; no chemicals, no power** ← | **Skilled operation, chemicals, and power for backwashing** ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND EIGHTH ROWS TOGETHER MAKE THE CASE FOR SLOW SAND FILTRATION IN RURAL NEPAL, and it is a strong one:**

> **A slow sand filter needs no coagulant, no power, no dosing equipment and no skilled chemist. It is built of sand, gravel and masonry, operated by opening and closing two valves, and cleaned by a labourer with a shovel every couple of months.**

> **A rapid sand filter needs a reliable supply of alum, a functioning dosing pump, electricity for backwashing, and an operator who can run a jar test.**

> **In a village where all of those are uncertain, the slow filter produces better water indefinitely and the rapid one produces poor water as soon as the alum runs out or the power fails — which happens.**

> **The right technology is the one that will still be working in ten years, and that is a judgement about the operating environment rather than about the process.**

**The limitations, stated fairly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **LARGE land area** | **Twenty to forty times that of a rapid filter for the same output** ← |
| **Cannot handle high TURBIDITY** ← | **Above about 30 NTU the mat clogs within days; a roughing filter or plain sedimentation is needed first** ← |
| **The 1-3 week RIPENING period after each scraping** | **Which is why several beds are provided and cleaned in rotation** ← |
| **Cannot remove colour, dissolved substances or algae blooms** | ← |
| **Vulnerable to freezing, and to being dosed with chlorine by a well-meaning operator** ← | **Both kill the biology** ← |

> **The TURBIDITY limit is the binding constraint in Nepal, where monsoon river water may exceed a thousand NTU — which is exactly why the ROUGHING FILTER (a horizontal or vertical gravel filter placed before the slow sand filter) is such a common and successful pairing in hill water supply schemes.**

A biologically active mat of algae, bacteria and trapped particles that develops on the TOP surface of the sand.

examTip.trick: **The SCHMUTZDECKE on the TOP surface** — a living mat that removes bacteria BIOLOGICALLY (they are eaten), not by straining. Sand pores are far too coarse to catch a bacterium.
examTip.trap: **Never let it dry out or chlorinate it** — that kills the organisms and the filter must re-ripen over 1-3 weeks. Cleaning is by SCRAPING the top 20-25 mm, not backwashing.
examTip.mnemonic: **No power, no chemicals, no skilled operator, 99 %+ bacterial removal** — which is why slow sand plus a gravel ROUGHING filter suits rural Nepal, where a rapid filter fails the day the alum runs out.

questions.stem: CROWN CORROSION of a concrete sewer — the progressive destruction of the pipe's soffit above the water line — is caused by:
options: Hydrogen sulphide released from septic sewage being oxidised by bacteria on the moist crown to SULPHURIC ACID
Abrasion by grit carried in the flow
Freezing and thawing of the sewage
The weight of the soil above the pipe
questions.solution:
**Hydrogen sulphide released from septic sewage, oxidised by bacteria on the moist crown to SULPHURIC ACID**, which dissolves the cement paste of the concrete.

**The mechanism, step by step:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. The sewage becomes SEPTIC** ← | **Anaerobic, because it has stagnated, moved too slowly, or been held in a long rising main** ← |
| **2. Sulphate-reducing bacteria in the SLIME LAYER below the water line convert sulphate to SULPHIDE** ← | **Desulfovibrio and similar organisms, working in the anaerobic slime** ← |
| **3. Hydrogen sulphide gas is released into the sewer's AIR SPACE** ← | **Especially where there is turbulence — drops, junctions, the discharge of a rising main** ← |
| **4. The gas dissolves in the MOISTURE condensed on the crown** ← | **The coolest, wettest surface in the sewer** ← |
| **5. AEROBIC bacteria (Thiobacillus) there oxidise it to SULPHURIC ACID** ← | **This is the crucial biological step** ← |
| **6. The acid attacks the cement, converting it to gypsum and ettringite** | **Which are soft, expansive and have no strength** ← |
| **7. The crown is progressively eaten away and the sewer eventually COLLAPSES** ← | ← |

> **THE LOCATION IS THE DIAGNOSTIC FEATURE AND IT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM THE MECHANISM: the damage occurs ABOVE the water line, on the crown and upper walls, while the invert — permanently submerged — is often untouched.**

> **That is the reverse of what abrasion or ordinary wear would produce, and it is why the phenomenon is unmistakable once seen.**

> **The acid produced can bring the surface pH down to 1 or below, which no ordinary Portland cement concrete can withstand.**

**What promotes it:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **Low flow VELOCITY and long detention** ← | **Sewage goes septic — which is one more reason for the 0.6 m/s self-cleansing velocity** ← |
| **High TEMPERATURE** | **Biological activity roughly doubles for every 10 °C — so it is far worse in the Terai than in the hills** ← |
| **High SULPHATE in the sewage or the ground water** | **The raw material** ← |
| **TURBULENCE, which strips the gas out of solution** ← | **Drops, steep gradients, junctions, pumping station discharges** ← |
| **Poor VENTILATION of the sewer** ← | **Which lets the gas concentrate instead of being carried away** ← |
| **Flat gradients and long rising mains** | **Long anaerobic detention** ← |

> **THE VENTILATION ROW IS THE MOST DIRECTLY ACTIONABLE, and it is the reason sewers are ventilated at all: the perforated manhole cover and the ventilating column are not there for the comfort of passers-by but to keep the sewer's atmosphere moving and dilute.**

**Prevention:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Maintain the SELF-CLEANSING velocity so the sewage stays fresh** ← | **The single most effective measure** ← |
| **VENTILATE the sewer adequately** | ← |
| **Avoid unnecessary turbulence; design drop structures to contain it** | ← |
| **Use SULPHATE-RESISTING cement, or a richer, denser mix** | **Helpful, but it slows the attack rather than preventing it** ← |
| **LINE the crown — PVC, HDPE or epoxy liners; or use vitrified clay or HDPE pipe** ← | **The definitive answer where the risk is high** ← |
| **Dose the sewage with oxidant, nitrate or alkali in bad cases** | **Operationally expensive** |

> **THE FOURTH ROW CONTAINS A DISTINCTION WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT: sulphate-resisting cement resists SULPHATE attack, and crown corrosion is ACID attack.**

> **The acid dissolves the calcium in the cement paste regardless of which cement it is, so sulphate-resisting cement is only partially helpful — it slows the process without stopping it, and specifying it is not a solution to a serious sulphide problem.**

> **Where the conditions are genuinely aggressive, the concrete must be physically SEPARATED from the acid by a liner, or a non-cementitious pipe used.**

**And the SAFETY dimension, which is more important than the corrosion:**

> **Hydrogen sulphide is highly TOXIC. At low concentrations it smells strongly of rotten eggs; at higher concentrations it PARALYSES the sense of smell within minutes, so the warning disappears exactly when the danger becomes lethal.**

> **Above about 700 ppm it causes immediate collapse and death.**

> **Sewer and manhole entry has killed many workers — and characteristically kills several at once, because the first collapses, a colleague climbs down to help, and is overcome in turn.**

> **Confined space entry procedure — gas testing before and during entry, forced ventilation, harness and lifeline, a trained attendant who does NOT enter, and breathing apparatus — is not bureaucracy. It is the accumulated response to exactly that pattern of deaths, and the rule that the rescuer must never enter unprotected is the one written in the most blood.**

Which attacks the cement.

examTip.trick: **Sulphide from the anaerobic slime → H₂S gas → dissolves in crown moisture → Thiobacillus oxidises it to SULPHURIC ACID.** Damage is ABOVE the water line; the submerged invert is often untouched.
examTip.trap: **Sulphate-resisting cement resists SULPHATE attack, but this is ACID attack** — it slows the process without stopping it. Serious cases need a LINER or a non-cementitious pipe.
examTip.mnemonic: **H₂S paralyses the sense of smell exactly as it becomes lethal** — and it typically kills several workers at once, because the rescuer climbs down after the first. The attendant never enters.

questions.stem: Where a sewer changes to a LARGER diameter at a manhole, the two pipes are normally connected so that:
options: Their INVERT (bottom) levels coincide
Their centre lines coincide
Their SOFFIT (crown) levels coincide, so the larger pipe's invert is set LOWER
The larger pipe is set 300 mm higher throughout
questions.solution:
**Their SOFFIT (crown) levels are matched**, which sets the larger pipe's invert LOWER than the smaller one's.

**Why the soffits are matched and not the inverts:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A sewer is designed to flow PART FULL, and the depth of flow may approach the soffit at peak** ← | ← |
| **If the INVERTS were matched, the larger pipe's soffit would be HIGHER** ← | **Then when the smaller pipe runs full, the flow must RISE to enter the larger one — it cannot** ← |
| **The result would be BACKING UP and surcharging of the upstream sewer** ← | **A hydraulic step in the wrong direction** ← |
| **Matching SOFFITS means the water surface can pass through without rising** ← | **The larger pipe always has capacity available beneath the incoming flow line** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE IS SIMPLY THAT THE HYDRAULIC GRADE LINE MUST NEVER BE FORCED UPWARD as the flow moves downstream — matching soffits guarantees it, and matching inverts does not.**

> **A useful way to remember it: think about the WATER SURFACE, not the pipe bottom. The water surface must be able to continue at the same level or fall; matching the tops of the pipes ensures that, whatever the depth of flow.**

**The rules for levels at a manhole, gathered:**

| Situation | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Same diameter, straight through** | **Continue the gradient; a small drop of 20 to 30 mm is often given across the manhole to compensate for the energy lost** ← |
| **DIAMETER INCREASES** | **Match the SOFFITS** ← (this question) |
| **A branch sewer joins** | **The branch's soffit at or above the main sewer's soffit, so the branch cannot be drowned; and the junction made in the direction of flow** ← |
| **The invert drops more than about 600 mm** ← | **Provide a DROP MANHOLE, so the flow is brought down in a vertical pipe rather than cascading into the chamber** ← |
| **A change of direction** | **A smooth channel (benching) curved through the manhole; sharp angles avoided** ← |

> **THE BRANCH RULE IN THE THIRD ROW HAS THE SAME LOGIC AS THE SOFFIT RULE and it is worth linking them: a branch entering below the main sewer's water level is DROWNED, so its own flow is held back and the main sewer's contents can flow up it.**

> **Both rules exist to prevent one part of the system from backing up into another, and both are about the WATER LEVELS rather than the pipe geometry.**

**And the BENCHING, which the last row mentions and which is easily neglected:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A manhole is a chamber much larger than the pipe** | **So the flow would spread, slow down and deposit solids** ← |
| **BENCHING is a shaped channel formed in the manhole floor** ← | **Continuing the pipe's own profile through the chamber, with the sides raised** ← |
| **It keeps the velocity up and the solids moving** | **Without it, every manhole becomes a settling tank** ← |
| **It also gives a safe standing area for a worker** | **Sloped to drain back into the channel** ← |

> **A manhole with a flat floor and no benching is a common defect in poorly supervised work, and its effect is cumulative: on a long sewer with a manhole every 30 m, dozens of small settling basins are created, each one silting up and each one reducing the effective capacity.**

> **The sewer then requires constant desilting, and the cause is a detail that cost almost nothing to get right and is invisible once the cover is on — which is a fair description of a great deal of what determines whether a buried system works.**

> **It is also why sewers are inspected before backfilling and, increasingly, surveyed by CCTV on completion: the whole system is about to disappear underground for fifty years, and the last opportunity to see what was actually built is the day before it is covered.**

examTip.trick: **Match SOFFITS (crowns), not inverts** — matching inverts would put the larger pipe's soffit higher, so a full incoming pipe could not discharge and the upstream sewer would surcharge.
examTip.trap: **Think about the WATER SURFACE, not the pipe bottom** — it must be able to continue level or fall. The same logic gives the rule that a branch's soffit must not be below the main sewer's.
examTip.mnemonic: **Without BENCHING, every manhole is a settling tank** — a manhole every 30 m makes dozens of them. It costs nothing, is invisible once covered, and decides whether the sewer works.

questions.stem: In the operation of an activated sludge plant, the SLUDGE VOLUME INDEX (SVI) is used to assess:
options: The organic strength of the incoming sewage
The SETTLEABILITY of the mixed liquor sludge
The chlorine demand of the final effluent
The rate of oxygen transfer in the aeration tank
questions.solution:
**The SETTLEABILITY of the mixed liquor sludge** — a high SVI indicates a bulking sludge that will not settle properly in the secondary clarifier.

**The definition and the test:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A one-litre sample of mixed liquor is settled for 30 minutes** ← | **In a graduated cylinder** |
| **The settled sludge volume is read, in mL** | ← |
| **SVI = settled volume (mL/L) × 1,000 ÷ MLSS (mg/L)** ← | **Giving the volume in mL occupied by 1 gram of dry sludge solids after 30 minutes** ← |

| SVI | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Below 100** | **EXCELLENT settling — a dense, compact sludge** ← |
| **100 to 150** | **GOOD — the normal operating range** ← |
| **Above 150** | **BULKING — the sludge is light and fluffy and settles poorly** ← |
| **Above 200** | **Serious bulking; solids will be carried over into the effluent** ← |

> **The test takes half an hour, needs a measuring cylinder and a solids determination, and tells the operator more about the plant's condition than almost any other single measurement — which is why it is done daily.**

**Why settleability matters so much:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The whole process depends on SEPARATING the biomass from the treated water** ← | **Aeration grows the organisms; the clarifier must then get them out** ← |
| **And on RETURNING that biomass to the aeration tank** ← | **The returned activated sludge is what maintains the MLSS concentration** ← |
| **If the sludge does not settle, both fail at once** ← | **Solids escape in the effluent, AND the aeration tank loses its biomass** ← |
| **The plant can then fail completely within a day or two** | **A "washout" — the organisms are literally flushed out of the system** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY BULKING IS THE MOST FEARED OPERATIONAL PROBLEM IN AN ACTIVATED SLUDGE PLANT: it attacks the process from both ends simultaneously.**

> **The effluent deteriorates because solids are escaping, and the treatment capacity collapses because the biomass that was doing the treating is leaving with them.**

> **A plant that has washed out takes weeks to re-establish, and there is nothing to do in the meantime but discharge poorly treated sewage.**

**What causes bulking, and the corresponding remedy:**

| Cause | Note | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| **FILAMENTOUS organisms proliferating** ← | **Long thread-like bacteria that bridge between flocs and prevent them compacting — the dominant cause** ← | **Chlorinate the return sludge; adjust the conditions below** ← |
| **Low DISSOLVED OXYGEN in the aeration tank** ← | **Filaments outcompete floc-formers at low DO because of their high surface area** ← | **Increase aeration** ← |
| **Low F/M ratio (over-aeration, under-loading)** | ← | **Adjust sludge wasting** |
| **Nutrient deficiency — nitrogen or phosphorus** ← | **Common with industrial wastes low in N and P; the classic BOD:N:P ratio of 100:5:1 must be maintained** ← | **Dose nutrients** ← |
| **Septic or high-carbohydrate influent; low pH** | ← | Pre-aeration; pH control |
| **RISING sludge (denitrification in the clarifier)** ← | **Not true bulking — nitrogen bubbles lift settled sludge to the surface** ← | **Remove sludge from the clarifier faster** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DESCRIBES A DIFFERENT PROBLEM THAT LOOKS THE SAME AND IS TREATED DIFFERENTLY, which is worth distinguishing: in RISING sludge the sludge settles perfectly well and then floats back up.**

> **Nitrate in the settled sludge is denitrified by bacteria in the clarifier's anoxic depths, producing nitrogen gas bubbles that attach to the floc and buoy it up.**

> **The SVI is normal, and the operator who diagnoses bulking and chlorinates the return sludge is treating the wrong disease. The correct remedy is to reduce the sludge's residence time in the clarifier.**

> **THE NUTRIENT RATIO IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WORTH REMEMBERING AS A NUMBER: BOD : N : P = 100 : 5 : 1.**

> **Domestic sewage naturally satisfies it comfortably, which is why nobody thinks about it. An industrial effluent — from a sugar mill, a distillery, a brewery — may have enormous BOD and almost no nitrogen or phosphorus, and the biomass then cannot build cells however much air is supplied.**

> **Treating such a waste requires deliberate nutrient dosing, and its absence is a common reason an industrial treatment plant fails to perform while every other parameter looks correct.**

A high SVI indicating a bulking, poorly settling sludge.

examTip.trick: **SVI = settled volume (mL/L) × 1000 / MLSS (mg/L)** — the mL occupied by 1 g of dry solids after 30 minutes. Below 100 excellent, 100-150 good, above 150 bulking.
examTip.trap: **Bulking attacks from both ends at once** — solids escape in the effluent AND the aeration tank loses the biomass doing the treating. A washout takes weeks to recover from.
examTip.mnemonic: **RISING sludge is not bulking** — the SVI is normal, and nitrogen bubbles from denitrification float settled sludge back up. And keep BOD:N:P at 100:5:1, which industrial wastes rarely do on their own.

questions.stem: The MITIGATION HIERARCHY applied in environmental assessment requires that adverse impacts be addressed in the order:
options: Compensate, mitigate, minimise, avoid
Mitigate first, then avoid whatever remains
Compensate financially for all impacts, since prevention is impractical
AVOID, then MINIMISE, then MITIGATE (restore or repair), and only finally COMPENSATE or offset what remains
questions.solution:
**AVOID → MINIMISE → MITIGATE (restore) → COMPENSATE (offset)** — in that order, each step applied only to what the previous step could not deal with.

**The four steps:**

| Step | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1. AVOID** ← | **Do not cause the impact at all — change the location, the alignment, the technology or the timing** ← | **Route a road AROUND a forest or a landslide zone rather than through it; site a plant away from a settlement** ← |
| **2. MINIMISE** | **Reduce the impact's magnitude, extent or duration** ← | **Reduce the road's width in the sensitive reach; work outside the breeding season; control dust and noise** ← |
| **3. MITIGATE / RESTORE** | **Repair or rehabilitate what has been affected** ← | **Replant the disturbed slope; restore the borrow area; rebuild a diverted stream channel** ← |
| **4. COMPENSATE / OFFSET** ← | **Provide an equivalent benefit elsewhere for what cannot be avoided, reduced or repaired** ← | **Plant forest elsewhere; pay compensation; create replacement habitat** ← |

> **THE ORDER IS NOT A PREFERENCE BUT A REQUIREMENT, and the reason is that the steps are not equally effective:**

> **AVOIDANCE is certain. The impact does not happen, and no monitoring, maintenance or good faith is required afterwards.**

> **COMPENSATION is a promise about the future, made by an organisation that will have moved on, in a place other than the one that was damaged, and involving something — a rebuilt ecosystem, a relocated community — that is very hard to recreate.**

> **The measures therefore become progressively less reliable as one moves down the list, which is precisely why they are ranked.**

**Why avoidance is so often skipped, stated honestly:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Avoidance requires decisions at the PLANNING stage** ← | **Alignment, siting and technology — and by the time an EIA is commissioned these are usually settled** ← |
| **The EIA is frequently prepared to justify a chosen design, not to inform the choice** ← | **Which reduces it to steps 3 and 4** ← |
| **Avoidance may cost more in capital** | **A longer alignment; a more expensive site** ← |
| **Compensation is easier to write into a budget than a design change** ← | **It is a line item; avoidance is a different project** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE STRUCTURAL FAILURE OF EIA PRACTICE AND IT IS WORTH NAMING PLAINLY: an assessment carried out after the alignment is fixed cannot avoid anything.**

> **It can only describe the impacts and propose mitigation, which means the most powerful tool in the hierarchy has already been given up before the environmental specialist is appointed.**

> **The remedy is to bring the environmental input into the FEASIBILITY and ALTERNATIVES stage, where the corridor is chosen — which is the same influence-curve argument that governs cost and buildability, applied to environmental outcomes.**

**The ALTERNATIVES analysis, which is where avoidance actually happens:**

| Alternative to consider | Note |
|---|---|
| **The NO-PROJECT alternative** ← | **A required baseline — what happens if nothing is built? Sometimes the honest answer changes the case entirely** ← |
| **Alternative SITES or ALIGNMENTS** | **Where most avoidance opportunity lies** ← |
| **Alternative TECHNOLOGIES or designs** | **A tunnel instead of a cutting; a bridge instead of a causeway** ← |
| **Alternative SCALES** | **A smaller scheme with proportionately less impact** ← |
| **Alternative TIMING or phasing** | **Avoiding a breeding season, or a festival, or the monsoon** ← |

> **THE NO-PROJECT ALTERNATIVE IN THE FIRST ROW IS TREATED AS A FORMALITY AND SHOULD NOT BE: it is the only baseline against which the project's benefits and costs can honestly be compared.**

> **Including it seriously occasionally shows that the problem the project addresses is better solved another way — by managing demand rather than building supply, by maintaining what exists rather than building new — and a process that cannot reach that conclusion is not an assessment.**

**And the EMP, which is what makes any of this real:**

> **The Environmental Management Plan sets out, for each impact, the measure adopted, who is responsible, when it is done, what it costs, and how it will be monitored.**

> **The single most important thing about it is that its items must appear in the BILL OF QUANTITIES as measured, paid work.**

> **A mitigation measure listed in a report and absent from the contract will not be carried out, because nobody is paid to do it and no one can be held to it — which is the recurring conclusion of every honest review of EIA effectiveness, and the one recommendation that would change most.**

examTip.trick: **AVOID → MINIMISE → MITIGATE → COMPENSATE**, each applied only to what the previous step could not handle. The order reflects declining reliability, not preference.
examTip.trap: **Avoidance requires decisions at the PLANNING stage** — an EIA commissioned after the alignment is fixed can only mitigate and compensate, having surrendered the most powerful tool in the hierarchy.
examTip.mnemonic: **The NO-PROJECT alternative is the only honest baseline**, not a formality. And EMP items must appear in the BILL OF QUANTITIES as paid work — a measure in a report and not in the contract does not happen.

questions.stem: The NET IRRIGATION REQUIREMENT of a crop is obtained from its consumptive use by:
options: DEDUCTING the EFFECTIVE RAINFALL and any contribution from the groundwater or from soil moisture already stored
Adding the conveyance losses in the canal system
Multiplying by the intensity of irrigation
Dividing by the base period in days
questions.solution:
**By DEDUCTING the effective rainfall** and any contribution from groundwater or from soil moisture already stored in the root zone.

**The chain of quantities, from the plant outward:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CONSUMPTIVE USE (evapotranspiration)** | **The total water transpired by the crop plus that evaporated from the soil surface** ← |
| **NET irrigation requirement (NIR)** | **Consumptive use − effective rainfall − groundwater contribution − stored soil moisture** ← |
| **FIELD irrigation requirement (FIR)** | **NIR ÷ field application efficiency — adding the losses in applying the water to the field** ← |
| **GROSS irrigation requirement (GIR)** | **FIR ÷ conveyance efficiency — adding the canal losses** ← (option b belongs at this step, not the previous one) |
| **Plus any LEACHING requirement** | **Extra depth deliberately applied to carry salts below the root zone** ← |

> **THE SEQUENCE MOVES OUTWARD FROM THE PLANT TO THE HEADWORKS, adding a loss at each stage — and the question asks about the FIRST step, where the natural contributions are subtracted before any losses are added.**

**EFFECTIVE RAINFALL, which is the subtle term:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Not all rainfall is useful to the crop** ← | **Which is the whole reason for the qualifier "effective"** ← |
| **Rain that RUNS OFF the field is lost** | **A heavy storm on a saturated or sloping field** ← |
| **Rain that PERCOLATES below the root zone is lost** ← | **The soil can only hold so much — anything beyond field capacity drains away** ← |
| **Rain falling when the crop needs nothing is largely lost** | **Out of season, or immediately after an irrigation** ← |
| **So effective rainfall may be only 60 to 80 per cent of the total** ← | **And in a monsoon climate with intense storms, considerably less** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND IT EXPLAINS A GENUINE PARADOX OF MONSOON AGRICULTURE: a region receiving 1,500 mm of rain can still need irrigation.**

> **The rain arrives in a few intense months, in storms that deliver more in a day than the soil can hold. Most of it runs off or percolates away within hours.**

> **The soil's storage is limited to the water it can retain between field capacity and wilting point over the root depth — perhaps 100 to 150 mm — and once that is full, further rain simply passes through.**

> **So Nepal's problem is not the QUANTITY of water but its TIMING, and the whole apparatus of storage, groundwater development and dry-season canals exists to move water from a season of destructive excess to a season of scarcity.**

**The LEACHING REQUIREMENT, mentioned in the table and worth its own note:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **All irrigation water contains dissolved SALTS** ← | **Even good quality water — and the crop takes up water and leaves the salt behind** ← |
| **So salts CONCENTRATE in the root zone over seasons** ← | **Inevitably, unless something removes them** ← |
| **The remedy is to apply MORE water than the crop needs** ← | **The excess percolates down, carrying salt below the root zone** ← |
| **And that excess must be able to DRAIN AWAY** ← | **Or it raises the water table and brings the salt straight back up by capillary action** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CONDITION THAT MAKES OR BREAKS THE WHOLE SCHEME, and it connects directly to the drainage question: leaching without drainage is worse than no leaching at all.**

> **Applying extra water to a field with no outfall simply raises the water table, and a rising water table brings the dissolved salts back to the surface where they evaporate and are deposited.**

> **So the leaching requirement is not an independent design item; it is inseparable from the provision of drainage, and specifying one without the other is a recipe for the salinisation that has ruined irrigated land throughout history.**

**And the practical measurement of consumptive use, for completeness:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **LYSIMETER** | **A tank of soil with the crop growing in it, weighed or with its drainage measured — the most direct method** ← |
| **Field water balance** | **Soil moisture measured before and after irrigation** |
| **BLANEY-CRIDDLE and similar empirical formulae** | **Consumptive use from temperature, daylight hours and a crop coefficient — used where data are scarce** ← |
| **PENMAN and Penman-Monteith** | **A physically based energy balance — the modern standard, needing more data** ← |
| **PAN evaporation × a pan coefficient** | **Simple and widely used** ← |

examTip.trick: **Consumptive use − effective rainfall − groundwater − stored moisture = NET requirement.** Conveyance losses (option b) come later, at the GROSS stage.
examTip.trap: **"Effective" rainfall excludes what runs off or percolates below the root zone** — often only 60-80 % of the total, and much less in intense monsoon storms.
examTip.mnemonic: **Leaching without DRAINAGE is worse than none** — the extra water raises the water table and capillary action brings the salt straight back to the surface. The two are inseparable.

questions.stem: An irrigation scheme has a culturable command area of 8,000 hectares with an intensity of irrigation of 40 per cent. Taking the duty at the canal head as 1,600 hectares per cumec, the required capacity of the canal is:
options: 1.28 cumec
1.60 cumec
2.00 cumec
5.00 cumec
questions.solution:
**2.00 cumec.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Area actually IRRIGATED** | **CCA × intensity = 8,000 × 0.40 = 3,200 hectares** ← |
| **Duty D = area ÷ discharge, so discharge Q = area ÷ D** | ← |
| **Substituting** | **Q = 3,200 / 1,600** |
| **Canal capacity** | **= 2.00 cumec** ← |

> **Option (d) 5.00 cumec is the answer with the INTENSITY forgotten — 8,000/1,600 — which sizes the canal for the whole command area being irrigated at once.**

> **That is the characteristic error in this calculation, and it produces a canal two and a half times too large.**

**The areas, which must be kept distinct:**

| Area | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS COMMAND AREA (GCA)** | **The TOTAL area bounded by the canal's irrigation boundary — including everything within it** ← |
| **CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA)** | **The part of the GCA that is CULTIVABLE — excluding villages, roads, ponds, rock outcrops, forests, barren land** ← |
| **INTENSITY of irrigation** | **The percentage of the CCA actually irrigated in a season** ← |
| **Area irrigated** | **CCA × intensity — the figure used in the calculation** ← |

> **WHY THE INTENSITY IS LESS THAN 100 PER CENT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN JUST APPLYING:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Not enough WATER to irrigate the whole area** ← | **The commonest reason — the supply is spread over as much land as it will serve** ← |
| **Crop ROTATION leaves land fallow** | **Deliberately, to restore fertility** ← |
| **Farmers choose not to irrigate some plots** | ← |
| **Different crops in different seasons** | **Which is why intensity is quoted separately for kharif and rabi** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW REFLECTS A DELIBERATE POLICY CHOICE THAT IS WORTH APPRECIATING, because it is not obvious:**

> **A given quantity of water can either irrigate a small area intensively or a large area thinly.**

> **Irrigating a large area at low intensity spreads the benefit over many more households and gives each of them a partial crop, which greatly reduces the risk of famine in a bad year.**

> **Irrigating a small area fully maximises the yield per hectare and the total production.**

> **Indian and Nepali canal systems have historically chosen the FIRST — protective irrigation, spread wide and thin — precisely because their purpose was famine protection rather than maximum output, and that choice is why intensities of 40 to 70 per cent are normal rather than being a sign of failure.**

**And the FULL SUPPLY discharge, which is what the answer represents:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The computed 2.0 cumec is the canal's FULL SUPPLY DISCHARGE** ← | **The maximum it is designed to carry** ← |
| **It is fixed by the PEAK demand period, not by the average** ← | **Usually the KOR watering, when a crop's demand is at its most concentrated** ← |
| **The kor demand is computed from the kor depth and the kor period** | **Δ_kor over the kor period gives a much higher instantaneous demand than the seasonal average** ← |
| **The canal is then sized for the LARGEST of the seasonal peak demands** ← | **Kharif or rabi, whichever governs** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE REFINEMENT THAT A REAL DESIGN ADDS TO THIS CALCULATION: the duty used must be the duty at the PEAK demand period, not a seasonal average, or the canal will be too small exactly when the crop most needs water.**

> **A canal that runs at half capacity for most of the season and is 20 per cent short during the kor watering has failed, because the kor watering is the one that determines the yield.**

> **Which is why the design duty is quoted for the kor period, and why the kor depth and kor period appear in the standard tables alongside the delta.**

examTip.trick: **Area irrigated = CCA × intensity = 3,200 ha; Q = area / duty = 3,200/1,600 = 2.00 cumec.** Option (d) forgets the intensity and oversizes the canal 2.5×.
examTip.trap: **GCA includes villages, roads and barren land; CCA is the cultivable part; intensity is the fraction of CCA actually watered.** Three distinct areas, easily conflated.
examTip.mnemonic: **Low intensity is a POLICY choice, not a failure** — spreading water thin over many households protects against famine, which is what protective irrigation was for. And size the canal on the KOR peak, not the seasonal average.

questions.stem: Among the types of canal lining, a CEMENT CONCRETE lining is generally preferred to a brick or a compacted earth lining where:
options: High VELOCITIES are to be carried
The canal is very small and temporary
The soil is highly expansive and unstable
The water carries no sediment at all
questions.solution:
**Where high velocities are to be carried, the canal is large and important, and a long, maintenance-free life is wanted** — accepting the higher initial cost.

**The types of lining and where each belongs:**

| Lining | Character | Suited to |
|---|---|---|
| **CEMENT CONCRETE (cast in situ or precast)** | **Strong, durable, smooth (n ≈ 0.014), permits HIGH velocity; 40+ year life; highest cost** ← | **Large main canals; high velocity; important schemes** ← |
| **SHOTCRETE / guniting** | **Sprayed concrete; good for irregular or existing surfaces** | Repairs and rock cuts |
| **BRICK or tile lining** | **Cheaper; uses local materials and labour; moderate durability** ← | **Medium canals where bricks are available and labour is cheap** ← |
| **STONE / boulder lining** | **Where stone is abundant; rough surface, so lower velocity** | Hill areas |
| **Compacted EARTH or clay lining** | **Cheapest; reduces seepage but not friction; needs continual maintenance** ← | **Small canals; where seepage control is the only objective** ← |
| **Boulder / soil-cement** | Intermediate | ← |
| **PLASTIC membrane (LDPE/HDPE), buried under earth cover** ← | **Excellent seepage control at low cost; but MUST be covered, and is easily punctured** ← | **Where seepage is the sole concern and labour is scarce** ← |

> **THE MEMBRANE ROW DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD: a plastic membrane stops seepage extremely well and does NOTHING for the canal's hydraulic performance.**

> **It must be buried under a protective earth or concrete cover, because exposed plastic is destroyed by ultraviolet light within a year or two and punctured by any traffic, animal or tool.**

> **So it is a seepage barrier, not a lining in the hydraulic sense — and choosing it means accepting the unlined canal's roughness, section and velocity limits.**

**The benefits of lining, which determine whether any of it is worthwhile:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reduced SEEPAGE loss** | **Often the primary justification — 60-80 % of the loss eliminated** ← |
| **A SMALLER SECTION for the same discharge** ← | **Because a higher velocity is permitted and the roughness is lower — saving land and excavation** ← |
| **No WEED growth** | **Weeds in an unlined canal can halve its capacity, and clearing them is a continual cost** ← |
| **Prevention of WATERLOGGING and salinity in the command** ← | **Canal seepage is a principal cause of rising water tables** ← |
| **No scouring or silting of the bed** | **The section stays as designed** ← |
| **Lower maintenance** | ← |
| **A flatter GRADIENT can be used, extending the command** ← | **Since less head is lost to friction, the canal commands more land** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE BENEFIT MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND SOMETIMES THE LARGEST: a lined canal's lower roughness means less head is consumed by friction over its length.**

> **The water therefore arrives at the tail at a higher elevation, and land that could not previously be commanded comes within reach.**

> **On a long canal that additional command can be thousands of hectares, and its value may exceed the water saved from seepage — yet it rarely appears in the economic comparison, which is usually confined to the seepage saving alone.**

**And the difficulties of lining, stated fairly:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **High initial cost** | **Often the reason it is deferred and then never done** ← |
| **UPLIFT pressure behind the lining when the canal is EMPTIED** ← | **A high external water table can lift and crack a concrete lining — hence the need for pressure relief holes and drainage behind it** ← |
| **Cracking from settlement, thermal movement and expansive soils** | **Option (c)'s expansive soil is a difficulty, not a reason to choose concrete** ← |
| **Difficult and disruptive to line an EXISTING canal in service** | **The canal must be emptied, which means a season's supply lost** ← |
| **Repairs to a cracked lining are only partially effective** | ← |

> **THE UPLIFT PROBLEM IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMONEST CAUSE OF LINING FAILURE AND IS ENTIRELY PREVENTABLE: while the canal is running, the water inside balances the groundwater outside.**

> **When the canal is emptied for maintenance — usually at the end of the season, when the water table is at its highest after the monsoon — that balance disappears, and the full external head acts upward on a thin concrete slab that has almost no weight and no tensile capacity.**

> **The slab lifts, cracks and is destroyed, and the damage is done during the maintenance shutdown rather than in service.**

> **The remedy is simple and cheap: pressure relief holes with inverted filters through the lining, and a drainage layer behind it — the same solution as the drainage holes in a gravity dam and the weep holes in a retaining wall, and for exactly the same reason.**

examTip.trick: **Concrete lining for large, important canals at high velocity with a long life** — the highest cost and the best performance. Brick and earth linings are the cheaper, lower-duty alternatives.
examTip.trap: **A plastic membrane is a SEEPAGE barrier, not a hydraulic lining** — it must be buried (UV destroys it) and it does nothing for roughness, section or velocity.
examTip.mnemonic: **A lining's flatter gradient EXTENDS THE COMMAND** — often worth more than the seepage saved, and usually left out of the economics. And put relief holes through it, or emptying the canal will lift it.

questions.stem: SEEPAGE loss from an unlined irrigation canal is conventionally expressed as:
options: A percentage of the canal's cross-sectional area
A discharge lost per unit of WETTED PERIMETER per unit LENGTH of canal
The depth of water in the canal divided by its width
A fixed quantity per kilometre, independent of the canal's size
questions.solution:
**As a discharge lost per unit of WETTED PERIMETER per unit length** — that is, per unit area of wetted surface, commonly expressed as cumecs per million square metres of wetted surface.

**Why the WETTED SURFACE is the right basis:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Seepage occurs through the bed and the SIDES that are in contact with water** ← | **Not through the cross-sectional area, and not through the free surface** ← |
| **So the loss is proportional to the AREA of that contact** ← | **Wetted perimeter × length** ← |
| **A wide shallow canal has a larger wetted perimeter than a deep narrow one of the same area** ← | **And loses correspondingly more** ← |
| **Option (d) is wrong for the same reason** | **A large canal loses far more per kilometre than a small one** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW GIVES A DESIGN CONSEQUENCE WORTH NOTING: the MOST ECONOMICAL section — the one with the minimum wetted perimeter for a given area — is also the section with the LEAST SEEPAGE.**

> **So the hydraulically best section, chosen originally to minimise friction and excavation, happens to minimise seepage too.**

> **That is a pleasing coincidence rather than a designed one, and it is one more argument for the semicircular or half-hexagonal trapezoidal section that regime theory and economics both point toward.**

**Typical seepage losses:**

| Canal condition | Loss |
|---|---|
| **Unlined, in sandy soil** | **HIGH — 3 to 6 cumec per million m² of wetted surface** ← |
| **Unlined, in loam** | **1.5 to 3** |
| **Unlined, in clay** | **0.9 to 1.5** ← |
| **LINED with concrete** | **0.1 to 0.3 — a reduction of 80 to 95 per cent** ← |
| **As a fraction of the discharge, over a long main canal** | **Frequently 30 to 45 per cent of the water released is lost before it reaches the fields** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE FIGURE THAT MATTERS AND IT IS STARTLING WHEN FIRST MET: on many older unlined systems, more water is lost in transit than is delivered to the crop.**

> **A scheme abstracting 100 cumec may deliver 60 to the outlets, and of that perhaps 35 reaches the root zone.**

> **So roughly a third of the water abstracted from the river does any agricultural work at all, and the rest recharges the groundwater, waterlogs the command, or evaporates.**

**The two components of the loss, which are worth separating:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **PERCOLATION** | **Where the canal's water surface is well ABOVE the water table, so the seepage is FREE DRAINING and depends on the soil's permeability alone** ← |
| **ABSORPTION** | **Where the water table has RISEN to meet the canal, so the two are hydraulically connected and the loss falls sharply** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW DESCRIBES A SELF-LIMITING PROCESS THAT IS EASILY MISREAD: a canal in a dry area loses heavily at first, the losses recharge the groundwater, the water table rises toward the canal, and the seepage rate then FALLS.**

> **An engineer measuring the loss after some years may find it much lower than the design figure and conclude that the canal is performing well.**

> **In fact the reduced seepage is a SYMPTOM of the water table having risen to canal level — which is the beginning of waterlogging in the command, and a far worse problem than the seepage was.**

> **A falling seepage loss in an unlined canal is therefore something to investigate rather than to welcome, and it is a good example of how a favourable-looking measurement can indicate a deteriorating condition.**

**And the practical measurement, since the tables are only a guide:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **INFLOW-OUTFLOW method** | **Measure the discharge at two sections of a reach; the difference, corrected for any offtakes, is the loss** ← |
| **PONDING method** | **Isolate a reach with bulkheads, fill it, and measure the rate at which the level falls — the most accurate** ← |
| **SEEPAGE METER** | **A small device placed on the bed measuring the local rate** |
| **Analytical and flow net methods** | **From the soil's permeability and the canal geometry** ← |

> **The PONDING method is the most reliable because it eliminates the difficulty that makes the inflow-outflow method unsatisfactory: the loss may be only a few per cent of the flow, and measuring two large discharges to find a small difference between them compounds both measurements' errors into the answer.**

For example cumecs per million square metres of wetted surface.

examTip.trick: **Loss per unit of WETTED SURFACE** — the bed and sides in contact with water, not the cross-sectional area. So a wide shallow canal loses more than a deep narrow one of the same area.
examTip.trap: **A FALLING seepage rate is bad news, not good** — it usually means the water table has risen to canal level, which is waterlogging beginning in the command.
examTip.mnemonic: **On old unlined systems, 30-45 % is lost in transit** — abstract 100 cumec, deliver 60, and put 35 in the root zone. The most economical section also happens to have the least seepage.

questions.stem: At a point on the downstream floor of a weir, the residual uplift head is 3.0 m of water. Taking the specific gravity of the floor material as 2.4, the minimum floor THICKNESS needed to balance the uplift by its own submerged weight is:
questions.solution:
**About 2.14 m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Uplift pressure per unit area** | **h γ_w, with h = 3.0 m** ← |
| **Downward SUBMERGED weight of the floor per unit area** | **t (G − 1) γ_w — the floor is under water, so buoyancy reduces its weight** ← |
| **Equating for balance** | **h γ_w = t (G − 1) γ_w** |
| **Cancelling γ_w** | **t = h / (G − 1)** ← |
| **Substituting** | **t = 3.0 / (2.4 − 1) = 3.0 / 1.4** |
| **t** | **= 2.14 m** ← |

> **Option (a) 1.25 m divides by G instead of (G − 1) — that is, it forgets BUOYANCY, which is the error the question is built around.**

> **Option (d) 3.00 m takes the thickness equal to the head, which would be correct only if the floor had a specific gravity of 2.0.**

**Why (G − 1) and not G, which is the whole point:**

> **The floor is SUBMERGED. It displaces water, so it loses the weight of the water it displaces.**

> **A concrete slab of specific gravity 2.4 weighs 2.4 units in air and only 1.4 units under water.**

> **Since the uplift is being resisted by the slab's weight while that slab is submerged, it is the SUBMERGED weight that counts — and using the full weight overstates the resistance by 70 per cent, giving a floor far too thin.**

> **This is exactly the same buoyancy correction met in the critical hydraulic gradient, i_c = (G−1)/(1+e), and in the submerged unit weight of soil, and recognising the common form makes all three easier to recall.**

**What a real design adds to this:**

| Addition | Note |
|---|---|
| **A FACTOR OF SAFETY of about 4/3** ← | **Giving t = (4/3) × h/(G−1) = 2.86 m here — the value usually specified** ← |
| **The uplift head h is the RESIDUAL head** ← | **Taken from Khosla's analysis at that point, after allowing for the creep length and the sheet piles** ← |
