| **The weight of water STANDING on the floor may be counted** | **Where a tailwater depth is assured — but never where the floor might be dry** ← |
| **The thickness is greatest just DOWNSTREAM of the hydraulic jump** ← | **Where the uplift is still substantial and the tailwater depth is least reliable** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS A TRAP WORTH NAMING: the water standing on the floor does help hold it down, and it is tempting to count it.**

> **But the critical condition is precisely when that water is ABSENT — during a maintenance drawdown, or when the gates are closed and the downstream apron drains while the groundwater beneath is still at full head.**

> **So the design case is the floor DRY above and fully loaded below, and counting the tailwater in that case is the sort of optimistic assumption that produces a floor which lifts during the first shutdown.**

**And the alternative to thickening the floor, which is usually better:**

| Approach | Note |
|---|---|
| **THICKEN the floor** | **Direct, and expensive — concrete in a large apron is a substantial quantity** ← |
| **REDUCE the uplift instead** ← | **By lengthening the creep path — deeper cut-offs, a longer upstream apron, an upstream impervious blanket** ← |
| **RELIEVE the uplift** ← | **Pressure relief holes with an inverted filter through the downstream floor, letting the water out without pressure** ← |
| **Combine all three** | **The usual real solution** |

> **REDUCING THE CAUSE IS ALMOST ALWAYS CHEAPER THAN RESISTING THE EFFECT, and this is a clear case: an extra metre of sheet pile at the upstream end costs far less than an extra half metre of concrete over the whole apron area, and it reduces the uplift everywhere downstream rather than at one point.**

> **The relief holes are cheaper still, and they carry the same caution as everywhere else they appear — they must have a properly graded inverted filter beneath them, or they become a piping path rather than a relief, and the remedy becomes the failure.**

examTip.trick: **t = h/(G−1) = 3.0/1.4 = 2.14 m.** Option (a) divides by G and forgets BUOYANCY — the slab weighs 2.4 in air but only 1.4 submerged.
examTip.trap: **Design adds a 4/3 factor of safety** (giving 2.86 m here), and the critical case is the floor DRY above with full uplift below — never count on tailwater that a shutdown will remove.
examTip.mnemonic: **Same (G−1) buoyancy correction as i_c = (G−1)/(1+e) and submerged soil unit weight.** And reducing the uplift with a deeper cut-off beats thickening the whole apron.

questions.stem: A SLOPING GLACIS type of weir, as distinct from a vertical drop weir, is characterised by:
options: A vertical downstream face with a cistern at its toe
A crest formed to the shape of the lower nappe of a free-falling sheet of water
A rockfill body with no impervious floor
A gently SLOPING downstream apron on which a HYDRAULIC JUMP is deliberately formed to dissipate the energy
questions.solution:
**A gently sloping downstream apron on which a HYDRAULIC JUMP is deliberately formed** to dissipate the flow's energy.

**The three principal weir types:**

| Type | Form | Energy dissipation | Suited to |
|---|---|---|---|
| **VERTICAL DROP weir** | **A masonry or concrete body with a VERTICAL downstream face and a cistern (a depressed floor) at its toe** ← (option a) | **By the IMPACT of the falling sheet into the cistern's water cushion** ← | **Low heads; firm foundations; small rivers** ← |
| **SLOPING GLACIS weir** | **A gentle downstream slope, typically 3:1 to 5:1** ← | **By a HYDRAULIC JUMP formed on the glacis** ← | **PERMEABLE (alluvial sand) foundations; medium and high heads — the standard modern type** ← |
| **OGEE weir** | **The crest shaped to the profile of the lower nappe of a free overfall** ← (option b) | **By a stilling basin or bucket below** | **Spillways of concrete dams; where discharge efficiency matters most** ← |
| **Rockfill / Parabolic weir** | **A rockfill body with a sloping downstream face** ← (option c) | Through the rockfill | **Where stone is plentiful and the head is low** |

> **THE HYDRAULIC JUMP IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE FEATURE THAT DEFINES THE GLACIS TYPE AND MAKES IT SUPERIOR ON ALLUVIAL FOUNDATIONS, and the reasoning is worth following:**

> **A weir converts a large amount of potential energy into kinetic energy. That energy must be destroyed before the water reaches the erodible river bed, or the bed will scour and the structure will be undermined.**

> **A vertical drop dissipates it by IMPACT, which is violent, concentrated and hard on the structure.**

> **A sloping glacis dissipates it by a HYDRAULIC JUMP, which is a controlled, well-understood phenomenon whose position and length can be CALCULATED — so the apron can be made exactly long enough and no longer.**

> **Being able to predict WHERE the energy will be destroyed is the whole advantage: the designer can place the concrete where the turbulence will be and stop it where the flow has become tranquil.**

**Why the jump's POSITION is the design problem:**

| Condition | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Tailwater depth EXACTLY equals the jump's conjugate depth** ← | **The jump forms on the glacis, where it is wanted — the design condition** ← |
| **Tailwater TOO LOW** | **The jump is SWEPT DOWNSTREAM, off the protected apron and onto the erodible bed — the dangerous case** ← |
| **Tailwater TOO HIGH** | **The jump is DROWNED (submerged), which dissipates less energy and leaves a fast current along the bed** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE FAILURE MODE THAT DESTROYS WEIRS, and it is why the tailwater rating curve must be known accurately across the full range of discharges:**

> **A jump swept off the end of the apron takes its violent turbulence onto unprotected sand, scours a hole, and the scour works backward until it undermines the apron's toe.**

> **The remedy is to DEPRESS the floor — build the cistern below the river bed level — so that the available tailwater depth is always sufficient to hold the jump on the apron; or to provide baffle blocks and an end sill to force the jump to form.**

> **And because the tailwater depth and the discharge both vary through the season, the check must be made at SEVERAL discharges, not merely at the design flood. A weir can be perfectly safe at its design flood and fail at 40 per cent of it, where the tailwater has fallen faster than the energy to be dissipated.**

> **That non-obvious result — that an intermediate discharge is often more critical than the maximum — is one of the more valuable things to know about energy dissipation, and it applies equally to spillway stilling basins.**

**And the associated protective works, which complete the design:**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Upstream and downstream CUT-OFFS (sheet piles)** | **Control seepage and the exit gradient; and provide against scour undermining** ← |
| **INVERTED FILTER downstream of the impervious floor** ← | **Lets seepage escape without carrying the foundation sand with it** ← |
| **LAUNCHING APRON of loose stone beyond that** ← | **Launches down the face of the scour hole as it develops, armouring it automatically** ← |
| **Baffle blocks, friction blocks and an end sill on the glacis** | **Stabilise the jump and shorten the apron** ← |
| **Upstream impervious blanket** | **Lengthens the creep path** |

> **The LAUNCHING APRON is the most elegant of these because it is SELF-ADJUSTING: it is not designed to prevent the scour hole but to respond to it, sliding down and paving the hole's slope as it forms, so the protection appears exactly where it turns out to be needed.**

examTip.trick: **Glacis weir dissipates energy by a HYDRAULIC JUMP on a 3:1 to 5:1 slope** — the standard type on alluvial foundations. Options (a), (b) and (c) describe the vertical drop, ogee and rockfill weirs.
examTip.trap: **Too little tailwater sweeps the jump OFF the apron onto erodible bed** — which is what destroys weirs. Depress the cistern so the jump is always held on the protected floor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the jump at SEVERAL discharges, not just the design flood** — an intermediate flow is often more critical, because tailwater can fall faster than the energy to be dissipated.

questions.stem: In the study of a meandering river, the MEANDER BELT is:
options: The WIDTH of the strip of the valley within which the meanders swing — measured between the outer edges of successive bends
The distance along the channel between two successive bends of the same phase
The straight-line distance between the two ends of a full meander
The radius of the curve at the apex of a bend
questions.solution:
**The WIDTH of the strip of valley within which the meanders swing** — measured across, between the outer edges of the bends on either side.

**The meander terminology, which must be kept apart:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **MEANDER LENGTH (wavelength)** | **The straight-line distance ALONG the valley between two corresponding points of successive bends of the same phase** ← (option c is close to this) |
| **MEANDER BELT (width)** | **The WIDTH of the strip within which the river swings — measured ACROSS the valley** ← |
| **MEANDER RATIO** | **Meander belt ÷ meander length** ← |
| **SINUOSITY** | **Length ALONG the channel ÷ length along the valley — a river is classed as meandering above about 1.5** ← |
| **Radius of the bend** | **At the apex; typically 2 to 3 times the channel width** ← (option d) |
| **Tortuosity** | **Sometimes used as (channel length − valley length) ÷ valley length, expressed as a percentage** |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN LENGTH AND BELT IS SIMPLY DIRECTION: meander LENGTH is measured ALONG the valley and meander BELT ACROSS it.**

> **The two together define the rectangle within which the river wanders, and their ratio characterises how tightly it does so.**

**Why the meander belt matters in engineering:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **It defines the WIDTH of land the river may occupy over time** ← | **Anything built within the belt is at risk from bank erosion, whatever the present channel position** ← |
| **It governs the SPACING and LENGTH of GUIDE BANKS at a bridge or barrage** ← | **The guide bunds must confine the river against the belt's natural width** ← |
| **It determines the land to be acquired for river training** | ← |
| **It sets the minimum bridge length where the river is not to be constricted** | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL WARNING AND IT IS ROUTINELY IGNORED: the present channel position tells you where the river is today, not where it will be in twenty years.**

> **A meandering river migrates continuously — the outer bank erodes and the inner bank builds — so the channel sweeps steadily across its belt, and it may move by tens of metres a year.**

> **Building within the meander belt is therefore building on land the river will reclaim, and the fact that it has been dry ground for a generation is no protection at all.**

> **This is why floodplain zoning based on the MEANDER BELT, and not merely on the present flood level, is the correct basis for controlling development beside an alluvial river.**

**Why rivers meander at all, since it is worth understanding rather than accepting:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **Any small irregularity deflects the flow toward one bank** ← | **And once deflected it stays deflected** ← |
| **A SECONDARY (helical) current develops at the bend** ← | **Surface water moves OUTWARD, bottom water INWARD** ← |
| **The outer bank is attacked and ERODES; the inner bank receives the sediment and BUILDS** ← | **A point bar** ← |
| **So the bend GROWS, and the pattern propagates downstream** ← | **The process is self-reinforcing** ← |
| **Eventually the bend is so tight that the river CUTS THROUGH the neck** | **Leaving an OX-BOW LAKE, and the pattern begins again** ← |

> **THE SECONDARY CURRENT IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE MECHANISM BEHIND SEVERAL PRACTICAL RULES MET ELSEWHERE, and it is worth collecting them:**

> **Because the bottom current moves INWARD, the bed load migrates toward the INNER bank — which is why an intake should be sited on the OUTER bank of a bend, where the water is cleaner and deeper.**

> **The outer bank is also where the erosion is, which is where bank protection and spurs are needed.**

> **And the deepest point of the channel (the thalweg) crosses from one side to the other between bends, which is why a bridge pier sited at a crossing point may be founded in shallow bed today and in the deepest scour hole in ten years.**

> **One piece of fluid mechanics, explaining the intake siting, the erosion pattern and the scour risk together.**

examTip.trick: **Meander LENGTH is measured ALONG the valley; meander BELT is measured ACROSS it.** Their ratio is the meander ratio; sinuosity is channel length ÷ valley length.
examTip.trap: **The present channel position is not where the river will be** — it migrates across its whole belt, tens of metres a year. Floodplain zoning should use the BELT, not just the flood level.
examTip.mnemonic: **Secondary current: surface OUT, bottom IN — so bed load goes to the INNER bank.** Hence intakes on the OUTER bank, protection on the outer bank, and the thalweg crossing between bends.

questions.stem: The FLEXIBILITY of a canal outlet is defined as the ratio of:
options: The outlet's discharge to the distributary's discharge
The rate of change of the OUTLET's discharge to the rate of change of the DISTRIBUTARY's discharge
The outlet's width to its depth
The head lost at the outlet to the head available
questions.solution:
**The ratio of the PROPORTIONATE rate of change of the OUTLET's discharge to the proportionate rate of change of the DISTRIBUTARY's discharge.**

**Written out:**

> **F = (dq/q) ÷ (dQ/Q)**, where q is the outlet's discharge and Q the distributary's.

> **It measures how SENSITIVELY the outlet responds when the parent channel's supply changes.**

> **Option (a) defines the outlet's SETTING or its share, not its flexibility; option (d) is closer to the outlet's efficiency.**

**The three classes:**

| Flexibility | Name | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **F = 1** | **PROPORTIONAL outlet** ← | **The outlet's discharge changes in the SAME proportion as the distributary's — each offtake keeps its fair share whatever the supply** ← |
| **F > 1** | **HYPER-proportional** ← | **The outlet takes MORE than its share when the supply rises, and less when it falls — it exaggerates the change** ← |
| **F < 1** | **SUB-proportional** ← | **The outlet's discharge changes LESS than proportionately — it is relatively stable against supply changes** ← |

> **THE PROPORTIONAL OUTLET IS THE IDEAL FOR EQUITY, and that is the whole reason the concept exists:**

> **When the river supply falls, every cultivator along the distributary should suffer the same proportionate reduction. A proportional outlet guarantees that automatically, with no gates, no operator and no negotiation.**

> **Without it, the head-reach outlets take their full share and the tail-enders get nothing — which is the classic and chronic inequity of canal irrigation, and the source of most disputes on a distributary.**

**The related definitions:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **SETTING** | **The depth of the outlet's sill BELOW the distributary's full supply level** ← |
| **SENSITIVITY** | **The rate of change of the outlet's discharge with respect to the change in the distributary's WATER LEVEL** ← |
| **EFFICIENCY** | **The head recovered ÷ the head put in — how much of the head is not wasted** ← |
| **DROWNING RATIO** | **For a submerged outlet, the ratio of the downstream to the upstream head** |
| **MINIMUM MODULUS** | **The minimum head at which a modular outlet still works properly** ← |

> **THE SETTING IN THE FIRST ROW IS WHAT THE DESIGNER ACTUALLY CONTROLS, and it is how proportionality is achieved: for a given type of outlet there is one setting at which F = 1, and the outlet is built to that setting.**

> **A shallower setting makes the outlet hyper-proportional; a deeper one sub-proportional. So flexibility is not an inherent property of the outlet type alone but of the type AND its setting together.**

**The three classes of outlet by their behaviour:**

| Class | Discharge depends on | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **NON-MODULAR** | **BOTH the distributary's level and the watercourse's level** ← | **A simple pipe or open sluice** ← |
| **SEMI-MODULAR (flexible)** | **The DISTRIBUTARY's level only — independent of the watercourse** ← | **Open flume; Kennedy's gauge outlet; pipe outlet discharging freely** ← |
| **MODULAR (rigid)** | **NEITHER — a constant discharge over a range of both levels** ← | **Gibb's module; the various rigid modules** ← |

> **THE SEMI-MODULAR CLASS IS THE ONE ACTUALLY USED FOR MOST DISTRIBUTION, and the reason is a practical compromise worth appreciating:**

> **A NON-MODULAR outlet can be tampered with from the downstream side — a cultivator who lowers the water level in his watercourse increases the flow he receives, at his neighbours' expense.**

> **A fully MODULAR outlet cannot be tampered with at all, but it needs a substantial working head, is complicated, and silts up.**

> **A SEMI-MODULAR outlet is immune to downstream interference, needs only a modest head, and is simple enough to be built and maintained in quantity — so it delivers most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.**

> **The design objective throughout is worth stating plainly: an outlet should deliver a FAIR share, AUTOMATICALLY, and be impossible to tamper with — and the ranking of outlet types is essentially a ranking by how well they achieve those three things for the head and the money available.**

Both expressed as fractions of their own values.

examTip.trick: **F = (dq/q) ÷ (dQ/Q).** F = 1 proportional, F > 1 hyper-proportional, F < 1 sub-proportional. Option (a) is the outlet's share, not its flexibility.
examTip.trap: **Flexibility depends on the outlet TYPE and its SETTING together** — the setting (sill depth below FSL) is what the designer adjusts to make F = 1.
examTip.mnemonic: **A proportional outlet gives every cultivator the same proportionate cut when supply falls — automatically, with no operator.** Without it the head reach takes its fill and the tail-enders get nothing.

questions.stem: The principal cause of WATERLOGGING in an irrigated command is:
options: Excessive evaporation from the soil surface
Deep ploughing of the fields
SEEPAGE from unlined canals together with OVER-IRRIGATION
A fall in the regional water table
questions.solution:
**Seepage from unlined canals together with over-irrigation, with inadequate drainage** — so the water table rises steadily into the root zone.

**The causes, in order of importance:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **SEEPAGE from unlined canals and distributaries** ← | **Usually the largest single source — a canal is a continuous line source of recharge across the command** ← |
| **OVER-IRRIGATION by cultivators** ← | **Applying more water than the crop needs, which is common where water is cheap or free and supply is uncertain** ← |
| **INADEQUATE DRAINAGE** ← | **The natural drainage lines blocked by roads, railway embankments and the canal itself** ← |
| **Flat topography and impervious subsoil** | **Nothing carries the water away** ← |
| **Heavy rainfall added to irrigation** | ← |
| **Obstruction of natural drainage by the project's own works** ← | **A canal crossing a valley on an embankment dams the natural drainage unless cross-drainage works are provided** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND SIXTH ROWS TOGETHER CONTAIN THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH ABOUT WATERLOGGING: it is very largely caused by the irrigation project itself.**

> **The project adds water to the command — that is its purpose — and simultaneously obstructs the natural drainage with its embankments and canals.**

> **Adding water while impeding its escape has only one possible outcome, and it is entirely predictable from the day the scheme is designed.**

**Why over-irrigation is so persistent, since blaming the cultivator explains nothing:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water is charged by AREA, not by VOLUME** ← | **So using more costs the cultivator nothing** ← |
| **The supply is UNRELIABLE** ← | **So when water arrives, the rational response is to take as much as possible — nobody knows when the next turn will come** ← |
| **Insurance against a missed turn** | **Over-watering now protects against a shortage later** ← |
| **Little knowledge of crop water requirements** | ← |
| **Head-reach farmers face no shortage at all** | **And therefore have no reason to economise** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE MOST OFTEN MISSED: over-irrigation is a RATIONAL response to an unreliable supply, not ignorance or greed.**

> **A farmer who cannot rely on receiving water next week will apply as much as the field will take this week, and would be foolish to do otherwise.**

> **So the remedy is not exhortation but RELIABILITY: a supply that arrives when promised removes the incentive to hoard, and volumetric charging removes the incentive to waste.**

> **Both are institutional reforms rather than engineering ones, which is why waterlogging has proved so much harder to solve than to diagnose.**

**The consequences, which compound:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The root zone becomes SATURATED and the soil ANAEROBIC** ← | **Roots need air; without it they cannot respire and the plant dies** ← |
| **Yields fall sharply, then the land goes out of cultivation** | ← |
| **SALINITY follows** ← | **Capillary rise brings dissolved salts to the surface, where evaporation deposits them** ← |
| **Field operations become impossible** | **Machinery and animals cannot work saturated ground** ← |
| **Public health effects** | **Mosquito breeding, and damp housing** ← |

> **THE SALINITY LINK IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST DESTRUCTIVE PART AND IT IS WORTH BEING PRECISE ABOUT: waterlogging by itself is bad; waterlogging in a hot, dry climate causes SALINISATION, which is far worse.**

> **When the water table rises to within the capillary fringe of the surface — perhaps 1.5 to 2 m in a fine soil — water moves upward continuously and evaporates at the surface, leaving behind every dissolved salt it carried.**

> **The process is one-way and cumulative: the salts arrive and nothing removes them.**

> **The land turns white, and reclaiming it demands leaching, drainage and amendment at a cost far greater than the drainage that would have prevented it.**

> **This is the mechanism that destroyed the irrigated lands of Mesopotamia and has damaged millions of hectares in the Indus and Ganges basins, and it remains the single strongest argument in irrigation engineering: **provide the drainage from the start**.**

In the absence of adequate DRAINAGE, causing the water table to rise into the root zone.

examTip.trick: **Canal seepage + over-irrigation + inadequate drainage → the water table rises into the root zone.** The project adds the water and obstructs its escape simultaneously.
examTip.trap: **Over-irrigation is a RATIONAL response to unreliable supply**, not ignorance — take all you can now, because the next turn is uncertain. The remedy is reliability and volumetric charging, not exhortation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterlogging in a hot climate becomes SALINISATION** — capillary rise brings salt up, evaporation leaves it there, and nothing removes it. One-way and cumulative. Provide the drainage from the start.

questions.stem: SURFACE drainage differs from SUBSURFACE drainage of agricultural land in that surface drainage:
options: Uses buried perforated pipes laid below the root zone
Lowers the water table by pumping from tube wells
Is applicable only to sandy soils
Removes EXCESS WATER STANDING ON or running over the ground by means of graded open field drains and channels
questions.solution:
**It removes excess water standing ON or running over the ground, using graded open drains** — as distinct from subsurface drainage, which lowers the WATER TABLE.

**The two systems:**

| Aspect | SURFACE drainage | SUBSURFACE drainage |
|---|---|---|
| **Removes** | **PONDED and overland water from the surface** ← | **GROUND water, lowering the water table** ← |
| **Means** | **Graded open field drains, collector drains, land shaping and grading** ← | **Buried perforated TILE or PVC drains; mole drains; deep open drains; tube wells** ← (option a) |
| **Depth** | **Shallow — at the surface** | **1.0 to 2.0 m below ground** ← |
| **Deals with** | **Heavy rainfall, flooding, low-lying ponded areas** ← | **A high water table, waterlogging, salinity** ← |
| **Cost** | **LOW; buildable by the farmer** ← | **HIGH; needs machinery, materials and design** ← |
| **Land occupied** | **Open drains take land out of cultivation and obstruct machinery** ← | **NONE — buried and invisible; the field is farmed over it** ← |
| **Suits** | **Flat land with a heavy, slowly permeable soil, subject to ponding** ← | **Land with a high water table and reasonably permeable soil** ← |

> **Option (b) describes VERTICAL drainage by tube wells, which is a form of subsurface drainage rather than surface drainage.**

> **THE ROW THAT MATTERS FOR CHOOSING BETWEEN THEM IS THE FOURTH: they solve two DIFFERENT problems, and neither substitutes for the other.**

> **A field that ponds after heavy rain needs surface drainage, and the deepest tile system will not help — water sitting on an impermeable clay surface will not reach a pipe two metres down.**

> **A field with a water table 300 mm below the surface needs subsurface drainage, and the finest surface grading will not lower it.**

> **Diagnosing which problem is present, before designing anything, is therefore the first task — and land that suffers from both needs both.**

**Surface drainage methods:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **LAND GRADING and smoothing** ← | **Eliminating the depressions where water stands — often the cheapest and most effective measure** ← |
| **RANDOM field drains** | **Following the natural low lines, connecting the depressions** ← |
| **PARALLEL field drains** | **Shallow, regularly spaced, on flat land** ← |
| **BEDDING (ridge and furrow)** | **The land formed into gently crowned beds with furrows between — very old and still effective** ← |
| **Interceptor drains** | **Catching runoff from higher ground before it reaches the field** ← |
| **Collector and outfall drains** | **Carrying it away to a natural watercourse** ← |

> **THE OUTFALL IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ITEM THAT DETERMINES WHETHER ANY OF IT WORKS, and it deserves the emphasis it seldom gets:**

> **A drainage system needs somewhere to DISCHARGE, at a level low enough to take the flow by gravity.**

> **In flat terrain — the Terai, for instance — an adequate outfall may simply not exist, or may be flooded by the river during the very monsoon when the drainage is most needed.**

> **The system then backs up and achieves nothing, and the only alternatives are a very long outfall drain to reach a lower point, or PUMPED drainage with all its operating cost and dependence on power.**

> **So the outfall is the first thing to establish and the last thing to be discovered missing, and a drainage design that begins anywhere but at its discharge point is being done backwards.**

**And the priority between the two, which is the practical conclusion:**

> **SURFACE drainage should generally be provided FIRST, and often it is sufficient on its own.**

> **It is far cheaper, needs no imported materials, can be built and maintained by the farmers themselves, and removes the ponded water that does the most immediate damage to the crop.**

> **Subsurface drainage is a major investment, requires design, machinery and materials, and is justified where the water table itself is the problem — typically where salinity has begun.**

> **Installing an expensive tile system on land whose real problem is surface ponding is a waste, and it happens — which is why the diagnosis in the fourth row of the comparison table is worth making carefully before anything is designed.**

Rather than lowering the WATER TABLE.

examTip.trick: **Surface drainage removes PONDED water with open graded drains; subsurface drainage lowers the WATER TABLE with buried pipes.** Option (b) is vertical (tube well) drainage — also subsurface.
examTip.trap: **They solve different problems and neither substitutes for the other** — a tile drain 2 m down cannot remove water standing on impermeable clay, and surface grading cannot lower a water table.
examTip.mnemonic: **No OUTFALL, no drainage** — in flat Terai land the outfall may not exist or may be flooded during the monsoon. Establish the discharge point first, or the design is being done backwards.

questions.stem: The principal DIFFICULTY in operating a MULTIPURPOSE reservoir serving power generation, irrigation and flood control together is that:
options: The dam must be built higher than for a single purpose
The RESERVOIR OPERATING RULE required by each purpose CONFLICTS with the others
Multipurpose reservoirs cannot be built on alluvial foundations
The turbines must be of two different types
questions.solution:
**Because each purpose demands a DIFFERENT reservoir level at the same moment** — flood control wants empty space available, while power and irrigation want water stored.

**The conflict, set out:**

| Purpose | Wants the reservoir | Because |
|---|---|---|
| **FLOOD CONTROL** | **As EMPTY as possible before a flood** ← | **Empty space is what absorbs the flood peak** ← |
| **HYDROPOWER** | **As FULL as possible** ← | **A high level gives a high head and hence more power per cubic metre** ← |
| **IRRIGATION** | **FULL at the end of the monsoon** ← | **So that water is available through the dry season** ← |
| **Water SUPPLY** | **Full, with a reliable reserve** | ← |
| **NAVIGATION** | **A steady level, neither rising nor falling** ← | **Which conflicts with everything else** |
| **RECREATION and fisheries** | **A steady, high level** | ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS ARE DIRECTLY OPPOSED AND CANNOT BOTH BE SATISFIED, and the conflict is at its sharpest exactly when it matters most — during the monsoon, when the floods arrive and the reservoir is filling for the dry season.**

> **Every day the operator holds water back for irrigation and power, the flood cushion shrinks. Every day space is kept empty for flood control, water that could have been stored runs to the sea.**

> **And the decision must be made without knowing whether a large flood is coming.**

**How the conflict is managed:**

| Device | Note |
|---|---|
| **A RULE CURVE** ← | **A prescribed reservoir level for each date of the year, worked out from long hydrological records — the level is drawn DOWN before the flood season and allowed to fill toward its end** ← |
| **Dedicated FLOOD CUSHION** | **A block of storage reserved between two levels, not available for other purposes** ← |
| **Priority ORDER written into the operating agreement** | **Stating whose need prevails when they conflict** ← |
| **INFLOW FORECASTING** ← | **Which converts a blind decision into an informed one — the single most valuable improvement available** ← |
| **Real-time operation rather than fixed rules** | **Where the forecasting and telemetry support it** ← |

> **THE RULE CURVE IS THE STANDARD ANSWER AND IT IS A COMPROMISE RATHER THAN A SOLUTION: it does not remove the conflict, it settles it in advance, by a formula, so that the operator is not making the trade-off under pressure with a flood approaching.**

> **That is itself valuable — a decision made calmly from statistics is better than one made in an emergency by someone who will be blamed either way — but the rule curve is derived from the historical record, and it performs poorly in a year that does not resemble the record.**

> **INFLOW FORECASTING in the fourth row is what genuinely improves matters, and its value is easy to see: a reservoir with three days' warning of a large inflow can pre-release, creating flood space that it would otherwise have to keep empty all season.**

> **So the same reservoir delivers more of every service, purely because the operator knows more — which makes hydrological telemetry and forecasting one of the highest-return investments in water resources, and one of the least glamorous.**

**Why multipurpose projects are built at all, despite this:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **The dam, the reservoir and the access are paid for ONCE and serve several purposes** ← | **Enormous economies compared with separate schemes** ← |
| **A dam site is a scarce resource** ← | **There are only so many places a reservoir can be built, and using one for a single purpose forecloses the others permanently** ← |
| **Revenue from power can subsidise irrigation and flood control, which generate little income** ← | **Often the only way the non-revenue purposes get funded at all** ← |
| **Downstream benefits accrue widely** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE POLITICAL ECONOMY THAT MAKES MULTIPURPOSE PROJECTS ATTRACTIVE TO GOVERNMENTS AND IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: flood control produces no revenue, irrigation produces very little, and power produces a lot.**

> **Bundling them lets the power revenue carry the whole project, which is how flood control and irrigation get built.**

> **The corresponding risk is that once the project is operating, the revenue-earning purpose tends to dominate the operating decisions — and the flood cushion quietly shrinks year by year, because nobody is billed for the space it occupies until the flood arrives.**

Flood control wants the reservoir EMPTY, while power and irrigation want it FULL.

examTip.trick: **Flood control wants the reservoir EMPTY; power and irrigation want it FULL** — and the conflict is sharpest during the monsoon, when the decision must be made without knowing what is coming.
examTip.trap: **A RULE CURVE does not remove the conflict, it settles it in advance** from the historical record — and performs poorly in a year that does not resemble that record.
examTip.mnemonic: **Inflow FORECASTING lets a reservoir pre-release and serve every purpose better** — the highest-return, least glamorous investment in water resources. And watch the flood cushion shrink: nobody is billed for empty space until the flood arrives.

questions.stem: In Nepal's classification of hydropower plants by INSTALLED CAPACITY, a plant of 500 kW would be described as:
options: A large hydropower plant
A pico hydropower plant
A medium hydropower plant
A MINI hydropower plant
questions.solution:
**A MINI hydropower plant.**

**The classification by installed capacity:**

| Class | Capacity | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PICO** | **Up to about 5 kW** ← | **A single household or a mill; often a pico-turbine on a stream** ← |
| **MICRO** | **5 to 100 kW** ← | **A village supply; the mainstay of Nepal's off-grid rural electrification** ← |
| **MINI** | **100 to 1,000 kW (1 MW)** ← | **This question — a small town, or a grid-connected private plant** ← |
| **SMALL** | **1 to 25 MW** ← | **Nepal's commonest grid-connected private scheme size** ← |
| **MEDIUM** | **25 to 300 MW** | ← |
| **LARGE** | **Above 300 MW** ← | **Only a handful in Nepal** |

> **The boundaries vary somewhat between countries and documents — some place the small/medium boundary at 10 MW — so the CLASS names matter more than defending an exact threshold, and 500 kW falls unambiguously in the mini range under any of the definitions in use.**

**Why the classification MATTERS, rather than being mere labelling:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The LICENSING regime differs** ← | **Very small plants may need only registration rather than a full generation license** ← |
| **The ENVIRONMENTAL study required differs** ← | **A small plant may need only a Brief Environmental Study or an IEE; a large one an EIA** ← |
| **The tariff and power purchase arrangements differ** | **Standard PPAs exist for small plants; large ones are negotiated individually** ← |
| **Subsidy and rural electrification support** ← | **Micro and pico plants attract subsidy under rural energy programmes** ← |
| **Design standards and the level of investigation expected** | **Proportionate to the scale and the consequence of failure** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS EXPLAIN WHY A DEVELOPER'S CHOICE OF CAPACITY IS SOMETIMES INFLUENCED BY THE THRESHOLDS THEMSELVES, and it is worth being alert to it: a scheme designed at 24 MW rather than 26 MW may avoid a more onerous approval regime.**

> **That is a legitimate response to a rule, and it also shows why thresholds should be set where the physical impacts actually change rather than at round numbers — otherwise the regulation shapes the engineering rather than the other way round.**

**The Nepali context, since it is the subject of the question:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **MICRO-hydro has been Nepal's most successful rural energy technology** ← | **Thousands of plants, largely community-owned, built with local materials and local manufacturing** ← |
| **Locally manufactured turbines** | **Cross-flow (Banki) turbines made in Nepali workshops — simple, repairable, and understood locally** ← |
| **Community ownership and management** | **Which has proved more durable than externally managed schemes** ← |
| **The challenge as the grid EXTENDS** ← | **Micro-hydro plants built for isolated villages are being reached by the national grid, and must either interconnect or be abandoned** ← |
| **Small (1-25 MW) run-of-river is the private sector's staple** | **Standard PPA, manageable finance, buildable in a few years** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES A REAL AND SOMEWHAT PAINFUL TRANSITION, and it is worth thinking about because it is a general lesson about infrastructure:**

> **A micro-hydro plant built to serve a village that had no other option becomes redundant when the grid arrives with cheaper, more reliable and unlimited power.**

> **The community's investment, and the donor's, appears wasted — but that is the wrong way to see it: the plant delivered twenty years of electricity that would not otherwise have existed, and its purpose was fulfilled.**

> **The constructive response is to design for INTERCONNECTION where the grid is likely to arrive — a plant that can sell into the grid keeps its value — and to accept that appropriate technology is appropriate to a time as well as to a place.**

> **The CROSS-FLOW turbine in the second row deserves a closing word, because it is the technical reason the programme worked: it is inefficient by modern standards, at perhaps 75 to 80 per cent, and it can be fabricated from sheet steel and pipe in a small workshop, repaired by the person who built it, and understood by the operator.**

> **A turbine at 90 per cent efficiency that must be sent abroad for repair delivers less energy over twenty years than one at 78 per cent that is running.**

examTip.trick: **Pico ≤ 5 kW, micro 5-100 kW, MINI 100-1,000 kW, small 1-25 MW, medium 25-300 MW, large above 300 MW.** 500 kW is mini under any definition in use.
examTip.trap: **The class determines the LICENSING and ENVIRONMENTAL regime** — which is why a scheme is sometimes sized at 24 MW rather than 26 to stay under a threshold.
examTip.mnemonic: **A locally made cross-flow turbine at 78 % that is running beats an imported one at 90 % that is awaiting repair.** Appropriate technology is appropriate to a time as well as a place — hence designing micro-hydro for eventual grid interconnection.

questions.stem: A FLOW DURATION CURVE for a river is obtained by:
options: Arranging the recorded discharges in DESCENDING order of magnitude and plotting each against the PERCENTAGE OF TIME it is equalled or exceeded
Plotting the discharge against the date on which it occurred
Plotting the cumulative volume of flow against time
Plotting the flood peaks against their return periods
questions.solution:
**By arranging the recorded discharges in DESCENDING order and plotting each against the percentage of time it is equalled or exceeded.**

**How it is constructed:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Take a long record of discharges — daily, ten-daily or monthly** ← | **The longer the record, the more reliable the curve** ← |
| **Rank them in DESCENDING order, largest first** ← | **The chronological order is DISCARDED** ← |
| **For each, compute the exceedance probability** | **P = m / (n + 1) × 100 %, with m the rank and n the number of values** ← |
| **Plot discharge against that percentage** | **Often on log or probability paper, since the range is large** ← |

> **Option (b) describes the HYDROGRAPH — the same data in chronological order; option (c) the MASS CURVE; option (d) a flood frequency plot.**

> **THE DISCARDING OF CHRONOLOGY IN THE SECOND ROW IS BOTH THE CURVE'S STRENGTH AND ITS LIMITATION, and understanding that is understanding the curve:**

> **It tells you HOW MUCH water is available and FOR WHAT PROPORTION of the time — which is exactly what a power plant's economics depend on.**

> **It does NOT tell you WHEN, or for how long CONSECUTIVELY. A curve showing that 5 m³/s is exceeded 80 per cent of the time cannot say whether the dry 20 per cent is one long dry season or scattered dry days.**

> **For a run-of-river plant that distinction hardly matters, since it generates whatever is available at the time. For a STORAGE plant it matters completely — the required reservoir size depends entirely on the LENGTH of the deficit period, which the flow duration curve cannot show.**

> **That is why reservoir sizing uses the MASS CURVE (Rippl diagram) instead, which preserves the chronology.**

**What is read from the curve:**

| Quantity | Note |
|---|---|
| **Q₄₀ — exceeded 40 % of the time** ← | **The conventional DESIGN DISCHARGE for a run-of-river plant in Nepal** ← |
| **Q₉₅ or Q₁₀₀** | **The FIRM (dependable) flow, from which firm power is computed** ← |
| **The AREA under the curve** ← | **The total volume of flow over the period — hence the total energy potential** ← |
| **The SHAPE of the curve** | **Which tells you a great deal about the catchment, as below** ← |

> **THE SHAPE IS THE MOST INFORMATIVE FEATURE AND IS WORTH LEARNING TO READ:**

| Curve shape | Catchment character |
|---|---|
| **STEEP curve** ← | **Highly variable flow — a small, steep, impermeable catchment with rapid runoff and little natural storage; large floods and very low dry-season flows** ← |
| **FLAT curve** ← | **Well-regulated flow — a large catchment, or one with substantial groundwater, lakes, forest or SNOW and GLACIER melt providing natural storage** ← |

> **A FLAT curve is far better for hydropower, and the reason is direct: the plant's installed capacity is limited by the low flows and its annual energy by the whole curve.**

> **A catchment with natural storage delivers more of its water at a usable, steady rate and less of it as unusable flood peaks — so it supports a higher plant factor and a better return from the same annual runoff.**

> **This is precisely why SNOW-FED and GLACIER-FED Himalayan rivers are so valuable for hydropower: the snowpack acts as a natural reservoir, releasing water through the spring and early summer when the monsoon has not yet arrived.**

> **A purely rain-fed river of the same annual volume would deliver almost all of it in three monsoon months and very little in the dry season, giving a much steeper curve and a much poorer plant.**

> **And it is why the long-term retreat of Himalayan glaciers is a hydropower planning issue and not only an environmental one — it changes the SHAPE of the curve on which every plant in the basin was designed, increasing flows for a period and then reducing dry-season flows permanently.**

examTip.trick: **Rank the discharges DESCENDING and plot against the percentage of time equalled or exceeded.** Option (b) is the hydrograph, (c) the mass curve, (d) a flood frequency plot.
examTip.trap: **It discards CHRONOLOGY** — it says how much and for what fraction of time, never when or for how long consecutively. Reservoir sizing therefore needs the MASS CURVE, not this.
examTip.mnemonic: **A FLAT curve means natural storage — snow, glacier, lakes, groundwater — and is far better for hydropower.** Which is why glacier retreat changes the curve every plant in the basin was designed on.

questions.stem: A power station generates 4,380,000 kWh of energy in a year, and the maximum demand on it during that year was 1,000 kW. Its annual LOAD FACTOR is:
questions.solution:
**0.50.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Hours in a year** | **8,760 h** ← |
| **AVERAGE load** | **Energy ÷ hours = 4,380,000 / 8,760 = 500 kW** ← |
| **Load factor** | **Average load ÷ MAXIMUM demand** ← |
| **= 500 / 1,000** | **= 0.50, or 50 per cent** ← |

> **A load factor of 0.5 means the station, over the year, produced half of what it would have produced had it run continuously at its peak demand.**

**What the load factor tells you:**

| Load factor | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **HIGH (approaching 1)** | **A steady, uniform load — the plant is well utilised and the cost per unit generated is LOW** ← |
| **LOW** | **A peaky load — expensive capacity stands idle most of the time, so the cost per unit is HIGH** ← |

> **THE COST CONNECTION IS THE WHOLE REASON THE FIGURE IS TRACKED, and it is worth setting out because it explains electricity tariffs:**

> **A power system's CAPITAL cost is fixed by the PEAK demand — enough plant must exist to meet the highest moment of the year, whether that moment lasts an hour or a month.**

> **Its REVENUE, however, comes from the ENERGY sold, which depends on the average load.**

> **So a system with a low load factor has bought a great deal of plant and sells relatively little energy from it, and the fixed cost must be recovered over fewer units.**

> **Improving the load factor — flattening the demand curve — therefore reduces the cost per unit for everybody without any new generation at all, which is one of the few genuinely free improvements available in a power system.**

**How the load factor is improved:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **TIME OF DAY tariffs** ← | **Charging more at peak and less off-peak, so consumers shift their use** ← |
| **Encouraging off-peak INDUSTRIAL load** | **Night-shift working, off-peak pumping and heating** ← |
| **A diverse MIX of consumer types** ← | **Domestic peaks in the evening, industry during the day, irrigation seasonally — their peaks do not coincide** ← |
| **INTERCONNECTION with other systems** | **Whose peaks occur at different times, or in different seasons** ← |
| **Storage — pumped storage, or batteries** ← | **Absorbing off-peak energy and returning it at peak, which flattens the load seen by the generators** ← |
| **Direct demand management of large loads** | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE BOTH APPLICATIONS OF DIVERSITY — in the type of consumer and in geography — and the fourth is particularly relevant to Nepal.**

> **Nepal's hydropower produces a large surplus in the monsoon and a deficit in the dry season; northern India's demand peaks in summer for cooling and its own hydro follows a similar seasonal pattern.**

> **Trading across the border allows each system to use the other's off-peak and off-season capacity, and both achieve a higher effective load factor than either could alone.**

> **That is the economic argument for regional power trade in one sentence, and it is a stronger argument than the political discussion around it usually reflects: diversity in time is worth real money, and it requires no new generation to realise.**

**And a caution about the figure itself:**

| Caution | Note |
|---|---|
| **The load factor says nothing about EFFICIENCY** ← | **A plant can have a high load factor and a poor thermal or hydraulic efficiency** ← |
| **It is a property of the DEMAND, not of the plant** ← | **Which is why a peaking plant's low load factor is not its fault, and not a criticism of it** ← |
| **The period must be stated** | **Daily, monthly and annual load factors differ substantially** ← |

> **The second row repeats the point made about the plant capacity factor and is worth reinforcing: these ratios describe how a plant is USED, not how well it is built — and judging a machine by a number that measures somebody else's behaviour is a common analytical error.**

examTip.trick: **Average load = energy ÷ 8,760 h = 500 kW; load factor = 500/1,000 = 0.50.**
examTip.trap: **Capital cost is set by the PEAK; revenue comes from the ENERGY.** A low load factor spreads a large fixed cost over few units, which is why flattening demand cuts the cost per unit for everybody.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal's monsoon surplus and India's summer peak are diverse in TIME** — trading lets both systems raise their effective load factor with no new generation at all.

questions.stem: In an EARTH DAM, the PHREATIC LINE is:
options: The line joining the crest to the toe of the downstream slope
The TOP FLOW LINE of the seepage through the dam body
The line of maximum shear stress in the embankment
The boundary between the core and the shell
questions.solution:
**The TOP FLOW LINE of the seepage through the dam** — the surface along which the pore water pressure equals atmospheric pressure, with saturated soil below it and unsaturated soil above.

**Its significance:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It divides the SATURATED zone below from the unsaturated zone above** ← | **Which is what determines the unit weight to use in the stability analysis** ← |
| **Its shape is approximately a BASE PARABOLA** ← | **Casagrande's construction, with corrections at the entry and exit** ← |
| **Below it, the soil is submerged and its effective weight and strength are reduced** ← | **Which is why its position governs the downstream slope's stability** ← |
| **Where it EMERGES on the downstream face, seepage exits** ← | **And this is where the danger lies** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CRITICAL ONE AND IT IS THE ENTIRE REASON FOR THE DRAINAGE ARRANGEMENTS IN AN EARTH DAM:**

> **If the phreatic line intersects the downstream FACE of the dam, water emerges on the slope. The emerging seepage exerts a force in the direction of flow — down the slope — precisely where the slope is least stable.**

> **It saturates the downstream shell, softens it, and can start progressive erosion at the point of emergence, which works backward into the embankment.**

> **This is PIPING, and it is the commonest cause of earth dam failure.**

**How the phreatic line is kept away from the downstream face:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **A HORIZONTAL DRAINAGE BLANKET at the base of the downstream shell** ← | **Draws the phreatic line DOWN into the foundation, well clear of the slope** ← |
| **A ROCK TOE (toe drain)** | **A permeable zone at the downstream toe, collecting the seepage safely** ← |
| **A CHIMNEY (vertical) DRAIN** ← | **A vertical filter behind the core, intercepting the seepage before it can travel through the shell at all — the most effective arrangement** ← |
| **An impervious CORE with pervious shells** | **Concentrating the head loss in the core** ← |
| **An UPSTREAM impervious blanket** | **Lengthening the seepage path** ← |

> **THE CHIMNEY DRAIN IS THE MODERN STANDARD AND ITS ADVANTAGE IS WORTH SPELLING OUT: a horizontal blanket only catches the seepage after it has passed through the whole width of the embankment.**

> **A vertical chimney drain catches it as soon as it leaves the core, so the entire downstream shell stays DRY and its full strength is available.**

> **It also intercepts any leakage through a crack in the core — and cracks are the real danger in an earth dam, arising from differential settlement, from seismic shaking, or from hydraulic fracture.**

> **A chimney drain converts a potentially catastrophic concentrated leak into a measurable flow arriving at the toe drain, which is the difference between a warning and a failure.**

**The FILTER criteria, which govern every one of these drains:**

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **RETENTION (piping) criterion** | **D₁₅ of the filter ≤ 4 to 5 × D₈₅ of the protected soil — fine enough that the soil cannot wash through** ← |
| **PERMEABILITY criterion** | **D₁₅ of the filter ≥ 4 to 5 × D₁₅ of the protected soil — coarse enough that water passes freely without building pressure** ← |
| **The filter must not be GAP-GRADED or segregate** | ← |
| **Several graded LAYERS may be needed** | **Where a fine core must be protected by coarse rock, no single filter can bridge the gap** ← |

> **THE TWO CRITERIA PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DESIGN PROBLEM: the filter must be fine enough to hold the soil and coarse enough to pass the water.**

> **A filter that fails the first criterion lets the soil through and becomes a piping path — the remedy becoming the failure, as with relief holes.**

> **A filter that fails the second becomes an impermeable barrier, builds up pressure behind it, and does the opposite of its job.**

> **Getting the grading right, and then ensuring on site that the material actually delivered matches the specified grading and is placed without segregation, is one of the most important quality control tasks in embankment dam construction — and it is entirely invisible once the dam is built.**

The surface on which the pore pressure equals ATMOSPHERIC pressure.

examTip.trick: **The top flow line of seepage — pore pressure equals atmospheric on it.** Saturated below, unsaturated above; approximately a base parabola by Casagrande's construction.
examTip.trap: **It must NEVER intersect the downstream face** — emerging seepage pushes down the slope where it is weakest and starts PIPING, the commonest cause of earth dam failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Filter criteria pull opposite ways: fine enough to RETAIN the soil (D₁₅f ≤ 4-5 D₈₅s), coarse enough to PASS the water (D₁₅f ≥ 4-5 D₁₅s).** Fail the first and the filter becomes the piping path.

questions.stem: The spillway of a large dam whose failure would cause loss of life is designed to pass the:
options: Mean annual flood
Flood with a 25-year return period
Flood recorded in the longest historical record available
PROBABLE MAXIMUM FLOOD (PMF), or a flood of very long return period
questions.solution:
**The PROBABLE MAXIMUM FLOOD, or a flood of very long return period** — because a spillway that cannot pass the flood leads to overtopping, and overtopping destroys an embankment dam.

**Why the spillway design flood is so much larger than for other structures:**

| Structure | Design return period | Consequence of exceedance |
|---|---|---|
| **Urban storm drain** | **2 to 10 years** ← | **Temporary local flooding — inconvenient** ← |
| **Road culvert or minor bridge** | **50 to 100 years** | **Road closed; possible washout** ← |
| **Major bridge** | **100 years, checked for more** | **Loss of the structure** ← |
| **Large dam spillway** | **PMF, or 1,000 to 10,000 years** ← | **FAILURE OF THE DAM and a catastrophic flood wave downstream** ← |

> **THE DESIGN STANDARD FOLLOWS THE CONSEQUENCE, NOT THE STRUCTURE'S COST, and that is the principle the question is testing.**

> **A drain that floods a street twice in a lifetime is an acceptable design. A dam that fails once is not, however unlikely — because the consequence is measured in lives rather than in inconvenience.**

> **So the acceptable probability of failure is driven down until it is very small, and that means designing for a flood far larger than anything in the record.**

**What the PMF is:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Derived from the PROBABLE MAXIMUM PRECIPITATION (PMP)** ← | **The greatest depth of rainfall meteorologically possible over the catchment for a given duration** ← |
| **PMP is estimated by MAXIMISING the moisture and efficiency of observed storms** ← | **Not by statistical extrapolation of the record** ← |
| **The PMF is the flood that PMP would generate on a saturated catchment** | **With the most unfavourable antecedent conditions and storm movement** ← |
| **It has no return period** ← | **It is a physical upper bound, not a statistical value — which is the essential distinction** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE POINT MOST OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD: the PMF is not "the 10,000-year flood".**

> **A statistical flood of any return period is obtained by fitting a distribution to a record of perhaps 40 years and extrapolating — which is a large extrapolation resting on the assumption that the distribution holds far beyond the data.**

> **The PMF instead asks a PHYSICAL question: how much water can the atmosphere possibly deliver to this catchment, and what flood would that produce?**

> **The two approaches are quite different in kind, and the PMF is preferred for the highest-consequence structures precisely because it does not depend on extrapolating a short record.**

**Gated against ungated spillways, which the design flood interacts with:**

| Aspect | UNGATED (free overflow) | GATED |
|---|---|---|
| **Operation** | **AUTOMATIC — no decision, no power, no operator** ← | **Requires gates to be opened correctly and in time** ← |
| **Reliability** | **Very high — nothing to fail** ← | **Gates jam, power fails, operators err** ← |
| **Storage** | **Cannot store above crest level** ← | **The gates allow storage up to their top, gaining useful capacity** ← |
| **Flood routing** | **Limited control** | **Pre-release possible with forecasting** ← |
| **Cost** | **Lower** | **Higher, plus permanent operation and maintenance** ← |

> **THE RELIABILITY ROW IS THE ARGUMENT FOR UNGATED SPILLWAYS AND IT IS A STRONG ONE, though it is often overridden by the storage benefit: a free overflow spillway works during a power failure, at night, during an earthquake, and when nobody is present.**

> **Several serious dam incidents have involved gates that could not be opened — jammed by debris, immobilised by a power failure, or not opened because the operator did not appreciate the size of the incoming flood.**

> **Where gates are used, the standard responses are independent backup power, manual operation capability, and a portion of the spillway left ungated as a fail-safe — so that even with every gate inoperative, some capacity exists.**

> **That last measure is a good example of designing for the failure of one's own safety system, which is the habit that distinguishes dam engineering from most other civil engineering: the consequence is severe enough that the failure of the protection must itself be provided for.**

The consequence of the spillway being overtopped is failure of the dam itself.

examTip.trick: **The design standard follows the CONSEQUENCE** — 2-10 years for a storm drain, 100 for a bridge, PMF for a large dam whose failure would kill people.
examTip.trap: **The PMF is not "the 10,000-year flood"** — it is a PHYSICAL upper bound derived from probable maximum precipitation, not a statistical extrapolation of a 40-year record.
examTip.mnemonic: **An ungated spillway works at night, in a power cut, with nobody present.** Where gates are used, leave part of the spillway ungated as a fail-safe — designing for the failure of your own safety system.

questions.stem: A SPILLING WEIR (side spillway) provided along the approach canal or headrace of a run-of-river hydropower scheme serves to:
options: Automatically SHED any EXCESS water admitted at the intake during a flood
Increase the discharge entering the canal
Trap the sediment carried by the flow
Measure the discharge entering the powerhouse
questions.solution:
**To automatically SHED excess water admitted during a flood**, returning it to the river before it can overtop or damage the conveyance.

**Why excess water is admitted in the first place:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **During a river FLOOD the head over the intake rises sharply** ← | **And an ungated or partly gated intake admits far more than the design discharge** ← |
| **The gates may not be closed in time** | **A flash flood in a Himalayan stream can rise within minutes, at night** ← |
| **The turbine may TRIP suddenly** ← | **The flow it was taking has nowhere to go, and the canal level rises** ← |
| **Operator error** | ← |

> **THE TURBINE TRIP IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE CASE THAT DESIGNERS SOMETIMES OVERLOOK AND IT IS THE MOST SUDDEN: the plant is running at full discharge, the generator trips, the guide vanes close, and the entire headrace flow is stopped at its downstream end within seconds.**

> **The water already in the canal has nowhere to go but up, and it arrives at the forebay as a surge.**

> **The spilling weir at the forebay handles exactly that: the level rises above the weir crest and the surplus pours over into a spillway channel, back to the river.**

**Where spilling weirs are provided:**

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Just downstream of the INTAKE** ← | **Sheds flood water admitted at the intake, immediately and close to the river, before it travels down the canal** ← |
| **At intervals along a long HEADRACE canal** | **Protects each reach; sheds any local inflow from side streams** ← |
| **At the FOREBAY** ← | **Handles the surge from a turbine trip, and any surplus reaching that point** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SITING POINT AND THE LOGIC IS THE SAME AS FOR A CANAL ESCAPE: shed the water as EARLY as possible, and as CLOSE to the river as possible.**

> **A spilling weir near the intake returns the surplus to the river over a few metres. One at the far end of a 3 km headrace has to discharge down a hillside to reach the river, with all the erosion and land acquisition that implies — and the excess has meanwhile travelled the whole length of a canal that was not designed to carry it.**

**Why it is a WEIR and not a gate — the same argument that recurs throughout:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A fixed crest set just above the normal full supply level** ← | **It spills the instant the level exceeds design, with no decision required** ← |
| **No power, no operator, no moving parts** ← | **Which is what makes it reliable at 3 a.m. during a flood** ← |
| **It cannot be forgotten, jam, or be operated too late** | ← |
| **Its length is designed so the maximum credible excess spills with an acceptable rise in level** ← | **Using the weir formula Q = C L H^1.5 — a long weir sheds a lot for a small rise** ← |

> **THE LENGTH RELATION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE DESIGN LEVER: because Q varies with H^1.5, doubling the head over the crest only increases the discharge by about 2.8 times, while doubling the LENGTH doubles it exactly.**

> **So where the permissible rise in water level is small — and it always is, since the canal's freeboard is limited — the answer is a LONG weir rather than a deeper overflow.**

> **This is why spilling weirs are often surprisingly long, running for tens of metres along the canal bank, and why side-channel and duckbill (labyrinth) shapes are used to fit more crest length into a given reach.**

**And the ELEMENTS of a run-of-river headworks that this completes:**

> **INTAKE (with trashrack) → GRAVEL TRAP → SPILLING WEIR and flushing → SETTLING BASIN → HEADRACE → FOREBAY (with its own spillway and trashrack) → PENSTOCK → POWERHOUSE → TAILRACE.**

> **Each has a protective function as well as a conveying one, and the sequence is not arbitrary: the gravel trap protects the settling basin from being filled with coarse material, the settling basin protects the turbine from abrasion, the spilling weirs protect the canal from overtopping, and the forebay protects the penstock from air entrainment and surge.**

> **As in a treatment train, each element largely exists to protect the next one — which is a useful way to remember the sequence, since it explains why each item is where it is rather than requiring the order to be memorised.**

examTip.trick: **A fixed crest just above full supply level that sheds surplus automatically** — from a flood at the intake, from side inflows, or from a turbine trip surge at the forebay.
examTip.trap: **Shed the water EARLY, close to the river** — a spilling weir at the end of a 3 km headrace must discharge down a hillside, and the excess has already travelled a canal not designed for it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Q = C L H^1.5, so LENGTH is the lever, not depth** — hence long, side-channel and labyrinth weirs where the permissible rise is small. And in the headworks train, each element protects the next.

questions.stem: In a Himalayan run-of-river scheme, a HEADRACE TUNNEL is often preferred to a surface canal for the water conveyance principally because a tunnel:
options: Is always cheaper to construct per metre
Requires no lining of any kind
Follows a SHORTER, more DIRECT route and is immune to LANDSLIDES, rockfall, erosion and land acquisition along an unstable hillside
Allows a much higher flow velocity than any canal
questions.solution:
**Because a tunnel follows a shorter, more direct route and is immune to landslides, rockfall, erosion and land acquisition** along an unstable hillside.

**The comparison:**

| Aspect | SURFACE CANAL | TUNNEL |
|---|---|---|
| **Route** | **Must follow the CONTOUR, so it is long and winding** ← | **Goes STRAIGHT through the ridge — often less than half the length** ← |
| **Exposure to landslides and rockfall** | **HIGH — it sits on the hillside, in the path of everything coming down** ← | **NONE once inside sound rock** ← |
| **Land acquisition** | **A continuous strip, often through cultivated terraces and settlements** ← | **Only the two portals** ← |
| **Maintenance** | **Continual — clearing slips, repairing washouts, desilting** ← | **Very low** ← |
| **Cost per metre** | **LOWER** ← | **HIGHER** ← (so option (a) is false) |
| **Total cost** | **May be higher despite the lower unit rate, because the route is so much longer** ← | **Often competitive, and increasingly the preferred choice** ← |
| **Construction risk** | **Predictable** | **GEOLOGICAL — the greatest uncertainty in the whole project** ← |
| **Head loss** | **Free surface, gentle gradient** | **Can be pressurised, which allows a different profile** ← |

> **ROWS FIVE AND SIX TOGETHER CONTAIN THE ECONOMIC POINT AND IT IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES THE QUESTION: a tunnel costs more per metre and may cost LESS in total, because it needs so many fewer metres.**

> **A canal contouring around a spur may run 4 km to cover a 1.5 km straight line. At three times the unit rate, the tunnel is still competitive — and it then has no landslide exposure, no land acquisition and almost no maintenance.**

> **Adding the whole-life cost of clearing slips from a hillside canal every monsoon for thirty years usually settles the comparison decisively.**

**Why the canal option is so vulnerable in Nepal specifically:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **Steep, young, tectonically active slopes** ← | **Landsliding is the normal state of the terrain, not an exceptional event** ← |
| **Intense monsoon rainfall** | **Triggering slides along the whole alignment at once** ← |
| **A canal CUT into a slope destabilises it** ← | **The cut removes toe support from the material above, and the spoil loads the slope below — so the canal creates the slides that then destroy it** ← |
| **Seepage from an unlined canal saturates the slope** ← | **Raising pore pressures and reducing effective stress, which is precisely how slopes fail** ← |
| **A single slide can cut off the whole plant's water** | **Stopping generation until it is cleared** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE A SELF-DESTRUCTIVE MECHANISM WORTH NAMING PLAINLY: a canal cut along an unstable hillside and leaking water into it is doing the two things most likely to cause a landslide.**

> **It removes support at the toe of the material above, and it raises the pore water pressure in the slope.**

> **So a hillside canal is not merely exposed to landslides — it substantially increases their likelihood, and the losses that follow are partly self-inflicted.**

> **This is why, where a canal is unavoidable, LINING it is a slope stability measure as much as a water conservation one, and why the drainage of the hillside above the canal matters as much as the canal itself.**

**The tunnel's own risk, which must be stated honestly:**

| Risk | Note |
|---|---|
| **GEOLOGICAL uncertainty is the dominant risk in Himalayan tunnelling** ← | **Weak, sheared, folded rock; fault zones; high in-situ stresses; squeezing ground** ← |
| **WATER inrush** | **A tunnel intercepting a water-bearing fault can flood, and can drain the springs the villages above depend on** ← |
| **Squeezing and rock burst at depth** | **Requiring heavy support and sometimes a redesign in progress** ← |
| **Cost and time OVERRUNS are common** | **And they are the principal cause of hydropower projects failing financially in Nepal** ← |
| **Investigation can reduce but never eliminate the uncertainty** ← | **You cannot drill the whole alignment** ← |

> **THE SPRING DRAINAGE MENTIONED IN THE SECOND ROW IS AN IMPACT THAT IS EASY TO MISS AND VERY SERIOUS FOR THE COMMUNITIES CONCERNED: a tunnel driven beneath a hillside can intercept the groundwater feeding the springs on which villages above depend, and those springs may dry up permanently.**

> **The tunnel is hundreds of metres below and out of sight, the connection is not obvious, and the affected households have no way to demonstrate it.**

> **So baseline monitoring of spring flows BEFORE construction is essential — not merely as good practice but because without it there is no way to establish what the tunnel did, and the community is left with a loss and no remedy.**

> **It is a good illustration of why baseline data collection, which produces nothing visible and is always a candidate for the budget cut, is one of the more important things an EIA actually delivers.**

examTip.trick: **A tunnel is shorter and immune to landslides, rockfall and land acquisition** — costlier per metre but often cheaper in total, since a contour canal may run three times as far.
examTip.trap: **A hillside canal CAUSES the landslides that destroy it** — the cut removes toe support and the seepage raises pore pressure. Lining is a slope stability measure, not just water conservation.
examTip.mnemonic: **A tunnel can permanently drain the SPRINGS the villages above depend on** — invisible, unprovable without baseline flow monitoring taken BEFORE construction.

questions.stem: An AIR VALVE (air inlet) is provided immediately DOWNSTREAM of the main inlet valve at the foot of a penstock principally to:
options: Release air trapped during filling only
Admit AIR into the penstock as it DRAINS after the valve is closed
Increase the pressure at the turbine inlet
Cool the main inlet valve
questions.solution:
**To ADMIT AIR as the penstock drains after the main inlet valve is closed**, preventing a vacuum forming and collapsing the pipe.

**The mechanism of the danger:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **The main inlet valve at the foot of the penstock is CLOSED** ← | **Isolating the pipe from the forebay** |
| **Water continues to drain from the pipe** ← | **Through a leaking turbine seal, a drain valve, or the valve's own bypass** ← |
| **The water level in the penstock FALLS** | **And the space above it cannot be filled from the top, because the upper end is closed too** ← |
| **A partial VACUUM forms inside** ← | ← |
| **Atmospheric pressure outside CRUSHES the pipe** ← | **Buckling it inward, permanently** ← |

> **THE DECISIVE POINT IS THAT A THIN CYLINDER IS ENORMOUSLY WEAKER AGAINST EXTERNAL PRESSURE THAN INTERNAL, and it is worth being precise about why:**

> **Against internal pressure the shell fails by YIELDING — it must be stressed to its full strength before it bursts, and the penstock is designed for many times atmospheric pressure.**

> **Against external pressure it fails by BUCKLING — an instability, which occurs at a stress far below yield and depends on the shell's thickness cubed and its diameter.**

> **A penstock designed for 2 MPa internal pressure may collapse under 0.05 MPa of external pressure differential — a mere half-atmosphere.**

> **So a large, expensive pipe can be destroyed by a small vacuum, and the device preventing it is a valve costing a tiny fraction of the pipe.**

**Where air valves are needed and what each type does:**

| Type | Function |
|---|---|
| **AIR RELEASE (small orifice) valve** | **Releases air that accumulates at high points during NORMAL operation, where it would otherwise reduce the flow area** ← |
| **AIR/VACUUM (large orifice) valve** ← | **Expels large volumes of air during FILLING, and admits large volumes during DRAINING — the function in this question** ← |
| **COMBINATION valve** | **Both functions in one body — the usual choice** ← |

| Location | Why |
|---|---|
| **At all HIGH POINTS of the pipeline** ← | **Where air collects, and where the vacuum is deepest on draining** ← |
| **Immediately downstream of a closing valve** ← | **This question's case** ← |
| **Upstream of a valve that may be closed rapidly** | ← |
| **At long descending or ascending runs** | **At intervals** ← |

> **THE HIGH POINT REQUIREMENT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST IN A PIPELINE OVER UNDULATING GROUND: air accumulates at every summit, and a pocket of trapped air reduces the effective flow area — sometimes drastically, and in a way that is very hard to diagnose from the ground.**

> **A pipeline delivering far less than its calculated capacity, with no visible leak and no obvious blockage, is frequently suffering from air locks at its high points, and the remedy is an air valve rather than a bigger pump.**

**And the other components of a penstock installation, to place the air valve:**

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **MAIN INLET VALVE (butterfly or spherical) at the turbine** ← | **Isolates the turbine for maintenance and shuts the water off in an emergency** ← |
| **AIR VALVE downstream of it** | **This question** ← |
| **ANCHOR BLOCKS** | **Resist the thrust at every bend and change of section; the pipe is fixed to them** ← |
| **SLIDE (support) BLOCKS between anchors** | **Carry the weight while allowing longitudinal movement** ← |
| **EXPANSION JOINTS** | **Between anchor blocks, absorbing thermal movement of an exposed pipe** ← |
| **Drain valve at the low point** | **For emptying** ← |
| **Manhole for inspection** | ← |

> **THE ANCHOR AND EXPANSION ARRANGEMENT IN ROWS THREE TO FIVE WORKS AS A SYSTEM AND IS WORTH SEEING AS ONE: the anchor blocks hold the pipe absolutely fixed at the bends, where the thrust is; the slide blocks between them carry the weight but let the pipe move along its length; and the expansion joint between each pair of anchors absorbs that movement.**

> **Omit the expansion joint and an exposed steel penstock heating in the sun generates enormous axial force against its anchors — enough to shift them.**

> **Fix the pipe to the slide blocks as well and the same happens between them.**

> **So each component's function depends on the others being correct, and a well-built penstock is one where the pipe is held exactly where it must not move and free everywhere else.**

examTip.trick: **It ADMITS air as the pipe drains, preventing a vacuum.** A penstock designed for 2 MPa internal can collapse under half an atmosphere external, because buckling is an instability, not yielding.
examTip.trap: **Air valves are needed at all HIGH POINTS**, not only at the valve — trapped air pockets cut the effective flow area and produce a pipeline that under-delivers with no visible cause.
examTip.mnemonic: **Anchor blocks fix the pipe at bends, slide blocks carry it in between, expansion joints absorb the movement.** Fix it everywhere and thermal force shifts the anchors; fix it nowhere and the thrust has nothing to react against.

questions.stem: In a grid-connected hydropower station, the generator is normally a SYNCHRONOUS machine rather than an induction machine because a synchronous generator:
options: Is cheaper and simpler to build
Requires no excitation system
Can run at any speed
Provides its own EXCITATION
questions.solution:
**Because a synchronous generator provides its own EXCITATION** — so it can control its terminal voltage and reactive power output, and can operate independently of a grid.

**The two machines compared:**

| Aspect | SYNCHRONOUS generator | INDUCTION generator |
|---|---|---|
| **Excitation (magnetic field)** | **Its OWN, from a DC field winding on the rotor** ← | **Drawn from the GRID as reactive power — it cannot make its own** ← |
| **Voltage control** | **YES, by adjusting the field current** ← | **NO — the grid fixes the voltage** ← |
| **Reactive power** | **Can SUPPLY or ABSORB it, as the system needs** ← | **Only ABSORBS it, worsening the system's power factor** ← |
| **Can it run ISOLATED (islanded)?** | **YES — it can start and supply a load with no grid present** ← | **NO — it needs a grid, or capacitors, to excite it** ← |
| **Speed** | **Exactly synchronous: N = 120 f / p** ← | **Slightly ABOVE synchronous — it runs at a small negative slip** ← |
| **Cost and complexity** | **Higher — needs excitation, an AVR and synchronising equipment** ← | **Lower, simpler, robust** ← (so option (a) is false of the synchronous machine) |
| **Used for** | **Almost all grid-connected plants of any size** ← | **Very small plants, and some wind turbines** ← |

> **THE REACTIVE POWER ROW IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES THE MATTER FOR A UTILITY, and it deserves explaining because reactive power is often treated as a mystery:**

> **A power system needs reactive power to magnetise its transformers, motors and lines. That reactive power has to come from somewhere.**

> **A synchronous generator can be OVER-EXCITED to supply it, or UNDER-EXCITED to absorb a surplus — so it actively helps the grid hold its voltage.**

> **An induction generator can only CONSUME reactive power, so every one connected makes the voltage regulation problem worse and must be compensated with capacitor banks.**

> **On a weak rural grid, which describes much of Nepal's network, voltage support is genuinely valuable, and a synchronous machine provides it as a by-product of generating.**

**The synchronous speed relation, which follows from the machine's construction:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **N = 120 f / p, with f the frequency in Hz and p the number of POLES** ← | **N in rpm** |
| **At 50 Hz: 2 poles gives 3,000 rpm; 4 poles 1,500; 20 poles 300; 40 poles 150** ← | ← |
| **The turbine's speed and the generator's must MATCH** ← | **Or a speed-increasing gearbox must be inserted, with its cost, losses and maintenance** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW EXPLAINS A VISIBLE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN PLANT TYPES AND IS WORTH NOTING: a low-head Kaplan turbine runs slowly, so its generator needs many poles and is therefore large in diameter — the characteristic wide, squat machine of a low-head station.**

> **A high-head Pelton turbine runs fast, needs few poles, and its generator is compact.**

> **So the generator's physical shape is dictated by the site's head, through the turbine's specific speed and the pole relation — which is a nice illustration of how a hydrological fact propagates all the way into the dimensions of an electrical machine.**

**And the associated control systems, since they define how the plant behaves:**

| System | Controls | By adjusting |
|---|---|---|
| **GOVERNOR** | **SPEED, and hence FREQUENCY; and the ACTIVE power output** ← | **The turbine's water flow — the guide vanes or the spear valve** ← |
