| **AUTOMATIC VOLTAGE REGULATOR (AVR)** | **Terminal VOLTAGE, and hence the REACTIVE power output** ← | **The field excitation current** ← |

> **THE PAIRING IS CLEAN AND WORTH MEMORISING AS A PAIR: the GOVERNOR controls the WATER and therefore the ACTIVE power and the frequency; the AVR controls the FIELD and therefore the REACTIVE power and the voltage.**

> **When the plant is connected to a large grid, the grid fixes both the frequency and the voltage, so the governor setting determines how much ACTIVE power the machine delivers and the AVR setting how much REACTIVE power.**

> **When the plant is running ISOLATED, the same two controls instead determine the frequency and voltage the consumers actually receive — which is why an isolated micro-hydro plant needs a working governor (or an electronic load controller doing the same job) or its frequency wanders with every change in load, and its consumers' equipment suffers for it.**

examTip.trick: **A synchronous machine makes its own excitation, so it controls voltage and reactive power and can run islanded.** An induction generator draws its excitation FROM the grid and cannot.
examTip.trap: **An induction generator only ABSORBS reactive power**, worsening the grid's power factor — a real drawback on a weak rural network, where a synchronous machine's voltage support is valuable.
examTip.mnemonic: **GOVERNOR controls the water → active power and frequency; AVR controls the field → reactive power and voltage.** And N = 120f/p means a slow Kaplan needs many poles, hence the wide squat generator of a low-head station.

questions.stem: In highway alignment, the LIMITING GRADIENT differs from the RULING GRADIENT in that the limiting gradient:
options: Is STEEPER than the ruling gradient and may be used over SHORT stretches where adopting the ruling gradient would greatly increase the cost
Is flatter than the ruling gradient and used on long straights
Applies only to hairpin bends
Is the gradient at which vehicles cannot climb at all
questions.solution:
**It is STEEPER than the ruling gradient**, and may be used over short stretches where holding to the ruling gradient would greatly increase the cost of the works.

**The family of gradients:**

| Gradient | Definition | Typical value (mountainous terrain) |
|---|---|---|
| **RULING (design) gradient** | **The gradient the designer normally adopts, and to which the alignment is fitted** ← | **5 % (1 in 20)** ← |
| **LIMITING gradient** | **STEEPER; used over SHORT lengths where the ruling gradient would be very costly** ← | **6 %** ← |
| **EXCEPTIONAL gradient** | **Steeper still; used only in unavoidable situations, over VERY short lengths — typically not more than 100 m at a stretch** ← | **7 %** ← |
| **MINIMUM gradient** | **The FLATTEST gradient that still DRAINS the side drains** ← | **1 in 200 in concrete drains; 1 in 100 in earth drains** ← |

> **The values differ by terrain — plain and rolling terrain uses about 3.3 %, 5 % and 6.7 % respectively, and steep terrain 6 %, 7 % and 8 % — but the RELATIONSHIP is always the same: ruling < limiting < exceptional.**

**Why several gradients rather than one limit:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Holding rigidly to one gradient everywhere would force enormous cut and fill** ← | **Where a short steep pitch avoids a deep cutting, it is worth taking** ← |
| **The occasional short steep length has little effect on journey time or fuel** ← | **A truck loses speed over 80 m and recovers; over 800 m it does not** ← |
| **But a long steep length is genuinely damaging** | **Slow trucks, overtaking demand, accidents, brake overheating on the descent** ← |
| **So the code permits steepness in inverse proportion to LENGTH** ← | **Which is exactly what the three grades express** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW STATES THE ORGANISING PRINCIPLE AND MAKES THE THREE VALUES EASY TO REMEMBER: the steeper the gradient, the shorter the length over which it may be used.**

> **This is why the exceptional gradient carries an explicit length limit while the ruling gradient does not, and why successive exceptional stretches must be separated by a reasonable length of gentler grade rather than strung together.**

**THE MINIMUM GRADIENT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN and it causes more trouble in practice than the maximum:**

> **A road on perfectly flat ground has no gradient at all, and its side drains therefore do not drain. Water stands in them, softens the subgrade beneath the shoulder, and the pavement edge fails.**

> **So a MINIMUM longitudinal gradient must be provided even where the ground is level — by raising the formation in a saw-tooth profile if necessary — purely so that the drains fall somewhere.**

> **In the Terai this is a live issue: the ground is flat, the water table is high, and roads built without an adequate longitudinal fall in their drains deteriorate from the edges inward within a few monsoons.**

**And the related concept of GRADE COMPENSATION, which interacts with all of these:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **On a horizontal CURVE, the curve resistance adds to the grade resistance** ← | **A vehicle must overcome both at once** ← |
| **So the gradient is REDUCED (compensated) through the curve** ← | **Grade compensation = (30 + R)/R per cent, subject to a maximum of 75/R** ← |
| **It is NOT applied where the gradient is flatter than 4 %** ← | **Because there is enough traction margin already** ← |

> **THE EXEMPTION IN THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS FREQUENTLY MISAPPLIED: grade compensation is a relief given where the combination of curve and grade would be too demanding.**

> **Below 4 per cent the combination is not demanding, so no relief is needed, and applying it there merely flattens the road pointlessly and lengthens the alignment.**

> **The principle behind it — that resistances ADD, so a curve and a gradient together are worse than either alone — is the same one that requires a hairpin bend's gradient to be flattened, and it is worth carrying as a general idea rather than as two separate rules.**

examTip.trick: **Ruling < limiting < exceptional** — 5 %, 6 %, 7 % in mountainous terrain. The steeper the gradient, the SHORTER the length over which it may be used.
examTip.trap: **The MINIMUM gradient (1 in 200 lined, 1 in 100 earth) exists so the SIDE DRAINS fall** — a road on flat Terai ground needs a saw-tooth formation or its drains hold water and the edges fail.
examTip.mnemonic: **Curve resistance and grade resistance ADD**, hence grade compensation (30+R)/R, capped at 75/R — and not applied below 4 %, where there is traction margin to spare.

questions.stem: In the alignment of a hill road, the RESISTING LENGTH of a route is:
options: The length of road that must be supported by retaining walls
The total length of the road measured along its centre line
The length that a vehicle must travel AGAINST the rise
The distance between two successive hairpin bends
questions.solution:
**The equivalent length a vehicle must travel against the rise** — obtained from the total rise of the route plus its ineffective rise and fall, expressed as an equivalent horizontal length.

**The idea:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A vehicle climbing a hill road does work against GRAVITY as well as against friction** ← | **And the gravity component dominates on a steep road** ← |
| **The RISING lengths cost fuel and time; the falling ones return very little** ← | **A descending vehicle recovers almost nothing, since it must brake** ← |
| **So two alignments of the same LENGTH may cost quite different amounts to operate** ← | **If one has more total rise than the other** ← |
| **Resisting length converts the rise into an EQUIVALENT length** ← | **So the alternatives can be compared on one number** ← |
| **The alignment with the LEAST resisting length is the most economical to operate** ← | ← |

> **THE PURPOSE IS COMPARISON, and that is the point of the concept: it reduces "this route is longer but flatter, that one shorter but steeper" to a single figure that can be judged.**

**INEFFECTIVE RISE AND FALL, which is the term that gives trouble:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A route may go UP over a spur and DOWN again, only to climb once more** ← | **That intermediate rise and fall gains no net height at all** ← |
| **The climb was pure waste — the height gained was thrown away in the descent** ← | **And it must be climbed again afterwards** ← |
| **Such rise is called INEFFECTIVE, and it is ADDED to the total rise when computing resisting length** ← | **It counts against the alignment** ← |
| **A well-chosen hill alignment has very little of it** ← | **It climbs steadily and does not undulate** ← |

> **THIS IS THE MOST USEFUL PRACTICAL LESSON IN HILL ROAD LOCATION AND IT IS EASILY STATED: on a hill road, HEIGHT GAINED SHOULD NEVER BE THROWN AWAY.**

> **Every metre climbed and then descended has cost fuel, time and construction, and delivered nothing. It must then be climbed again.**

> **An alignment that rises steadily from the valley to the pass, taking each metre of height once, is far better than one of the same length that undulates over every spur — even though on the map they look equally good, and the undulating one may even look shorter.**

> **The zero line (grade contour) technique exists precisely to find such an alignment: by tracing a line of constant grade across the hillside, it produces a route that climbs continuously and has no ineffective rise by construction.**

**How resisting length is computed:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Take the TOTAL RISE along the route, in metres** | **From the profile** |
| **Add the INEFFECTIVE RISE (and the fall associated with it)** | ← |
| **Convert to an equivalent length using the ruling gradient** ← | **Equivalent length = total rise ÷ ruling gradient** ← |
| **Add the horizontal length of the route** | ← |
| **Compare the alternatives on the total** | ← |

> **The conversion in the third row expresses the rise as "the length of road at the ruling gradient that would produce this much climb" — which puts height and distance into the same units so they can be added.**

**And the other economic considerations in hill road location, so this one is in proportion:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Resisting length — vehicle operating cost** | **This question** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION cost — cut, fill, retaining walls, cross-drainage** ← | **Often dominant, and it rises steeply with the difficulty of the ground** ← |
| **Geological STABILITY of the route** ← | **Which usually overrides all economic arguments — a cheap alignment through unstable ground is not cheap** ← |
| **Land acquisition and settlements served** | ← |
| **Maintenance cost over the life** | **Which is where an unstable alignment declares itself** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH REPEATING AS THE FINAL WORD: resisting length is a genuine and useful economic criterion, and it is subordinate to geology.**

> **An alignment with an excellent resisting length that crosses an active landslide will be closed for weeks every monsoon, and the vehicle operating cost saved will be dwarfed by the cost of the closures and the repairs.**

> **Economic optimisation is worth doing among alignments that are all geologically sound — and is worth nothing applied to one that is not.**

Computed from the total RISE plus the INEFFECTIVE RISE AND FALL, converted to an equivalent length.

examTip.trick: **Total rise plus INEFFECTIVE rise, converted to an equivalent length at the ruling gradient, plus the route's own length.** The alignment with the least resisting length is cheapest to operate.
examTip.trap: **Ineffective rise is height gained and then thrown away** going over a spur — it must be climbed twice and gains nothing. Two routes of equal length can differ greatly in it.
examTip.mnemonic: **On a hill road, never throw away height you have gained** — which is exactly what the ZERO LINE technique guarantees. And all of it is subordinate to GEOLOGY: a cheap alignment through unstable ground is not cheap.

questions.stem: The OVERTAKING SIGHT DISTANCE on a two-lane two-way highway is made up of:
options: d₁, the distance travelled during the driver's REACTION
The braking distance alone
The stopping sight distance multiplied by two
The distance between two successive vehicles in a stream
questions.solution:
**Three components: d₁ the reaction distance, d₂ the overtaking distance, and d₃ the distance covered by the ONCOMING vehicle during the manoeuvre.**

**The three parts:**

| Component | Represents | Expression |
|---|---|---|
| **d₁** | **The distance the overtaking vehicle travels while the driver DECIDES and pulls out** ← | **v_b × t, with t about 2 seconds and v_b the speed of the slow vehicle** ← |
| **d₂** | **The distance travelled while actually OVERTAKING** ← | **b + 2s, where b = v_b T and s is the spacing; T = √(4s/a)** ← |
| **d₃** | **The distance the ONCOMING vehicle travels toward you during that time** ← | **v × T, at the design speed** ← |
| **Total OSD** | **d₁ + d₂ + d₃ on a TWO-WAY road** ← | **On a ONE-WAY road or a divided carriageway, only d₁ + d₂ — there is no oncoming vehicle** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL DISTINCTION AND THE ONE MOST OFTEN ASKED: on a divided or one-way road, d₃ is omitted, and the required distance falls by roughly a third.**

**How OSD compares with the other sight distances:**

| Sight distance | At 80 km/h | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **STOPPING sight distance (SSD)** | **About 120 m** ← | **The ABSOLUTE MINIMUM available at every point of every road** ← |
| **Intermediate sight distance (ISD)** | **2 × SSD ≈ 240 m** ← | **A compromise where full OSD cannot be provided** ← |
| **OVERTAKING sight distance (OSD)** | **About 470 m** ← | **Nearly FOUR times the SSD** ← |

> **THE MAGNITUDE OF THE OSD IS THE POINT WORTH ABSORBING: nearly half a kilometre of clear visibility is needed for a safe overtaking manoeuvre at 80 km/h.**

> **That is a great deal, and on a winding or undulating road it is available only occasionally — which has a direct design consequence.**

**OVERTAKING ZONES, which follow from that:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Full OSD cannot be provided everywhere on a two-lane road** ← | **It would demand impossibly flat and straight alignment throughout** ← |
| **So OVERTAKING ZONES are provided at intervals** ← | **Stretches where the full OSD is available, and where overtaking is permitted** ← |
| **Minimum length of an overtaking zone: 3 × OSD; desirable 5 × OSD** ← | **A short zone is worse than none — a driver who commits and then runs out of zone is in the worst possible position** ← |
| **Signs mark the beginning and end of the zone** | **Placed one OSD in advance** ← |
| **Elsewhere, a continuous centre line PROHIBITS overtaking** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS A GENUINE SAFETY PRINCIPLE AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: an overtaking zone that is too short is actively dangerous.**

> **A driver entering it will begin a manoeuvre; if the zone ends mid-manoeuvre, the driver is committed on the wrong side of the road with a vehicle approaching and nowhere to go.**

> **Better to mark the whole stretch as no-overtaking, so that no one begins, than to offer 200 m of permission and withdraw it.**

> **This is the general form of a principle that recurs in road safety: PARTIAL provision of a facility can be worse than none, because it invites a behaviour it cannot support.**

> **The same argument applies to a footpath that stops halfway, a cycle lane that ends at a junction, and a climbing lane that merges on a bend.**

**And the practical difficulty in Nepal, worth stating:**

> **On a two-lane hill highway with heavy slow truck traffic and almost no stretches offering 470 m of visibility, overtaking demand vastly exceeds the safe opportunity — and drivers overtake anyway, on blind curves, because the alternative is following a truck at 20 km/h indefinitely.**

> **Enforcement alone does not resolve that, because the underlying pressure is real. The engineering answers are CLIMBING LANES on sustained gradients — an extra uphill lane that lets slow vehicles be passed safely — and periodic overtaking zones deliberately created by choosing an alignment that provides them.**

> **A climbing lane on a long grade removes the largest single source of overtaking demand, and it is far cheaper than widening the whole route.**

D₂, the distance travelled while OVERTAKING; and d₃, the distance travelled by the ONCOMING vehicle during the overtaking manoeuvre.

examTip.trick: **OSD = d₁ (reaction) + d₂ (the overtaking manoeuvre) + d₃ (the oncoming vehicle).** On a ONE-WAY or divided road, d₃ is omitted.
examTip.trap: **OSD at 80 km/h is about 470 m — nearly FOUR times the SSD.** It cannot be provided everywhere, hence discrete overtaking zones of at least 3 × OSD.
examTip.mnemonic: **A short overtaking zone is worse than none** — a driver commits and then runs out of room. Partial provision invites a behaviour it cannot support: the same for footpaths, cycle lanes and climbing lanes.

questions.stem: The length of a VALLEY (sag) vertical curve on a highway is governed by:
options: The stopping sight distance in daylight only
The greater of the HEADLIGHT sight distance requirement at night and the COMFORT (centrifugal acceleration) criterion
The overtaking sight distance
The maximum permissible superelevation
questions.solution:
**The GREATER of the HEADLIGHT sight distance requirement at night and the COMFORT criterion** based on the rate of change of centrifugal acceleration.

**Why a valley curve is governed differently from a summit curve:**

| Curve | Governing criterion | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **SUMMIT (crest)** | **SIGHT DISTANCE over the crest, by DAY** ← | **The road surface itself obstructs the view — the driver cannot see over the hump** ← |
| **VALLEY (sag)** | **HEADLIGHT sight distance by NIGHT, and COMFORT** ← | **By DAY the sight distance is unobstructed — you can see right through a sag. The problem arises only at NIGHT** ← |

> **THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION AND IT IS EASILY REMEMBERED ONCE SEEN: a summit curve is a DAYTIME visibility problem, and a valley curve is a NIGHT-TIME one.**

> **In a sag, the driver's line of sight during the day passes freely over the dip — nothing blocks it.**

> **At night the driver sees only what the HEADLIGHT BEAM illuminates, and in a sag the beam strikes the rising road surface a short distance ahead. The visible distance is limited by the beam's geometry, not by the road's.**

**The two criteria:**

| Criterion | Basis | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| **HEADLIGHT sight distance** | **The beam must illuminate at least the STOPPING sight distance ahead** ← | **Headlight height 0.75 m; upward beam divergence 1°** ← |
| **COMFORT (centrifugal acceleration)** | **The rate of change of centrifugal acceleration must not exceed a comfortable value** ← | **Commonly 0.6 m/s³** ← |

> **THE COMFORT CRITERION EXISTS BECAUSE OF A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO CURVE TYPES THAT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: in a sag, the centrifugal force acts DOWNWARD, ADDING to the vehicle's weight.**

> **On a summit it acts UPWARD, reducing the weight — which is uncomfortable in a different way but is limited by the sight distance requirement long before comfort becomes an issue.**

> **In a sag, the added load pushes the passengers into their seats and works the suspension, and if the transition is abrupt the sensation is unpleasant. So comfort has to be checked explicitly, and it frequently governs on high-speed roads with gentle grade changes where the headlight criterion is easily satisfied.**

**The other considerations in a sag, which are practical rather than geometric:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **DRAINAGE** ← | **A sag is the LOW POINT — water collects there, and if it cannot get away the road floods** ← |
| **The longitudinal gradient passes through ZERO at the lowest point** ← | **So the side drains have no fall exactly where the most water arrives** ← |
| **Under a structure, the OVERHEAD CLEARANCE at the sag must be checked** | **Where an overbridge crosses a sag, the sight distance may be cut by the structure** ← |
| **Street LIGHTING relaxes the headlight criterion** ← | **Where the road is lit, the driver is not dependent on the beam, and a shorter curve is acceptable** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS TOGETHER DESCRIBE THE COMMONEST PRACTICAL FAILURE AT A SAG, and it is worth being explicit about:**

> **All the water from both approach gradients runs down to the low point, so the sag receives the most water on the whole alignment.**

> **And the longitudinal gradient there is zero, so the side drains have no fall at precisely that point.**

> **Unless a cross-drain or a catchpit with a positive outfall is provided AT the low point, the water simply ponds on the carriageway — flooding it, softening the shoulders, and destroying the pavement edge.**

> **A sag curve is therefore a drainage design problem quite as much as a geometric one, and the drainage detail at the low point is the thing to check on any longitudinal section.**

> **THE STREET LIGHTING ROW IN THE LAST POSITION IS A USEFUL PRACTICAL RELAXATION: since the headlight criterion exists only because the driver is relying on a headlight beam, providing lighting removes its basis.**

> **On a lit urban road the comfort criterion, or a simple minimum length for appearance, governs instead — which allows much shorter valley curves in constrained urban situations where a rural-standard curve would be impossible.**

examTip.trick: **Summit curve = a DAYTIME sight distance problem (the road blocks the view). Valley curve = a NIGHT-TIME one (the headlight beam limits it), plus comfort.**
examTip.trap: **Headlight height 0.75 m, beam divergence 1°, illuminating at least the SSD.** And in a sag the centrifugal force ADDS to the weight, which is why comfort (0.6 m/s³) must be checked separately.
examTip.mnemonic: **A sag receives all the water from both grades and has ZERO longitudinal fall there** — provide a catchpit with a positive outfall, or the carriageway ponds. And street lighting removes the headlight criterion entirely.

questions.stem: A GAP-GRADED aggregate mixture is one in which:
options: All particles are of nearly the same size
Every sieve size from the largest to the smallest is represented in suitable proportion
Certain INTERMEDIATE sizes are absent or present in very small proportion, while both coarse and fine fractions are present
The aggregate contains no fines at all
questions.solution:
**Certain INTERMEDIATE sizes are absent or nearly so**, while both the coarse and the fine fractions are present.

**The three gradings:**

| Grading | Particle size distribution | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **WELL (dense) GRADED** | **A continuous range of sizes, each in suitable proportion — the smaller filling the voids between the larger** ← (option b) | **Low void content, high density, high stability, low permeability** ← |
| **UNIFORMLY (poorly) GRADED** | **Nearly all particles of ONE size** ← (option a) | **HIGH void content; free draining; poor stability under load** ← |
| **GAP graded** | **Intermediate sizes MISSING; coarse and fine present** ← | **A coarse skeleton with fine filler and a deliberate void structure** ← |
| **OPEN graded** | **Coarse aggregate with very few fines** ← (option d) | **Very permeable; used for drainage layers and porous surfacing** ← |

> **THE FOUR ARE OFTEN CONFLATED, AND THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN GAP-GRADED AND OPEN-GRADED IS THE ONE MOST WORTH KEEPING: a gap-graded mix HAS fines, it simply lacks the middle sizes; an open-graded mix lacks the FINES.**

**Where each grading is used:**

| Grading | Application |
|---|---|
| **WELL graded** | **Dense bituminous macadam, bituminous concrete, concrete aggregate, granular subbase — anywhere STRENGTH and DENSITY matter** ← |
| **UNIFORMLY graded** | **Filter media, single-size chippings for surface dressing** ← |
| **GAP graded** | **Stone Mastic Asphalt (SMA), and some surface courses where a coarse skeleton carrying the load is wanted** ← |
| **OPEN graded** | **Drainage layers, porous friction courses, filter blankets, no-fines concrete** ← |

> **STONE MASTIC ASPHALT IS THE BEST ILLUSTRATION OF WHY A GAP GRADING IS DELIBERATELY CHOSEN, and the reasoning is instructive:**

> **In a well-graded (dense) mix, the load is carried partly by the coarse aggregate and partly by the mortar of fines and binder. Under heavy, slow, hot loading the mortar can deform, and the mix RUTS.**

> **In SMA the intermediate sizes are removed so that the coarse stones touch one another directly, forming a STONE-ON-STONE SKELETON that carries the load through direct contact.**

> **The gaps between them are filled with a rich mortar of filler, fibre and a large quantity of binder — which does not carry the load, but seals the mix and holds it together.**

> **The result is a surfacing that is highly rut-resistant, durable and textured, and it is now standard for heavily trafficked roads in many countries.**

> **The FIBRE is essential and worth noting: without cellulose or mineral fibre, the very high binder content simply drains out of the mix during transport and laying.**

**The maximum aggregate SIZE, which is the other half of gradation design:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Not more than about ONE THIRD of the layer's thickness** ← | **Or the stones cannot arrange themselves within the layer and the surface tears during compaction** ← |
| **For concrete: not more than a quarter of the least dimension, nor more than the clear spacing between bars less 5 mm** ← | **So the concrete can actually pass through the reinforcement** ← |
| **Larger maximum size means LESS surface area, hence LESS binder or paste needed** ← | **Which is economical** ← |
| **But larger size means poorer workability and a harsher mix** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW EXPLAINS A COUNTER-INTUITIVE ECONOMY THAT APPLIES TO BOTH CONCRETE AND BITUMINOUS MIXES: using the largest practicable aggregate reduces the total surface area to be coated.**

> **Since binder and cement paste are the expensive constituents and are needed in proportion to surface area, a larger maximum size means less of them for the same volume.**

> **So the maximum aggregate size is pushed up to whatever the layer thickness, the reinforcement spacing and the workability will allow — and the limits in the first two rows are what stop it, not any material consideration.**

examTip.trick: **Gap-graded lacks the INTERMEDIATE sizes but HAS fines; open-graded lacks the FINES.** Option (a) is uniformly graded, (b) well graded, (d) open graded.
examTip.trap: **SMA is gap-graded on purpose** — removing the middle sizes lets the coarse stones touch, forming a stone-on-stone skeleton that resists rutting, with a rich fibre-stabilised mortar filling the gaps.
examTip.mnemonic: **Max size ≤ ⅓ of layer thickness; for concrete ≤ ¼ of least dimension and ≤ bar spacing − 5 mm.** Bigger aggregate means less surface area and so less binder — the economy that pushes the size up.

questions.stem: STRIPPING in a bituminous pavement is:
options: The removal of the surface course before an overlay
The separation of the bituminous surfacing from the shoulder
Loss of the surface texture under polishing by traffic
The DISPLACEMENT of the bitumen film from the AGGREGATE surface by WATER
questions.solution:
**The displacement of the bitumen film from the aggregate surface by WATER**, destroying the adhesion between them and leading to disintegration of the mix.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Water penetrates the mix — through voids, cracks, or from below** ← | ← |
| **Water has a GREATER AFFINITY for most mineral surfaces than bitumen has** ← | **This is the root of the whole problem** ← |
| **It creeps between the bitumen film and the stone, displacing it** | ← |
| **The bond fails; the aggregate is left uncoated** ← | ← |
| **Under traffic the mix ravels, pot-holes form, and the layer disintegrates** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL DIFFICULTY OF BITUMINOUS CONSTRUCTION AND IT IS WORTH STATING BLUNTLY: water and bitumen are competing for the surface of the stone, and in the absence of any help, WATER USUALLY WINS.**

> **Bitumen adheres to a dry stone very well and to a wet one hardly at all — and once water has reached the interface, it can displace bitumen that was already there.**

> **Everything done about stripping is an attempt to change the outcome of that competition.**

**What makes stripping worse:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **ACIDIC (siliceous) aggregates — granite, quartzite, gneiss** ← | **Electrically negative surfaces, which attract water strongly and bitumen weakly — and these are exactly the rocks available in the Himalaya** ← |
| **DUSTY or DIRTY aggregate** ← | **The bitumen bonds to the dust rather than to the stone, and the dust washes away** ← |
| **WET or damp aggregate at mixing** | **A film of water already present at the interface** ← |
| **Inadequate compaction, leaving high VOIDS** ← | **Allowing water to enter and to move within the layer** ← |
| **Poor drainage; standing water; a high water table** | ← |
| **Traffic loading, which PUMPS water within the layer under each wheel** ← | **Accelerating the process greatly** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST IN NEPAL AND IS UNAVOIDABLE: BASIC aggregates such as limestone and basalt are electrically positive and bond well with bitumen.**

> **ACIDIC aggregates — granite, quartzite, gneiss — are negatively charged, attract water, and are prone to stripping.**

> **The Himalaya is largely composed of exactly those acidic rocks, and hauling limestone across the country is not an option.**

> **So the aggregate cannot be changed and the problem must be solved by other means — which is precisely what anti-stripping agents are for.**

**The remedies:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **ANTI-STRIPPING AGENTS (adhesion promoters)** ← | **Surface-active amines added to the bitumen; they attach to the stone and present a bitumen-friendly surface** ← |
| **HYDRATED LIME or cement as filler** ← | **1 to 2 per cent — cheap, very effective, and it also stiffens the mastic** ← |
| **Ensure the aggregate is CLEAN and DRY** ← | **Correct drying in the plant is essential, and the commonest failure** ← |
| **Achieve full COMPACTION and low voids** | **Target 3 to 5 per cent air voids — impermeable to water** ← |
| **Drain the pavement properly** | **Cross-fall, side drains, and drainage of the granular layers** ← |
| **Use a harder binder or a modified bitumen** | ← |

> **THE HYDRATED LIME REMEDY IN THE SECOND ROW IS UNDERUSED AND DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS: adding 1 to 2 per cent hydrated lime as part of the filler is inexpensive, uses a locally available material, and substantially improves resistance to stripping.**

> **It works by depositing calcium on the aggregate surface, converting an acidic, water-loving surface into a basic, bitumen-friendly one — and it stiffens the mastic, improving rutting resistance at the same time.**

> **Two benefits for a very small cost, using a material available in any district, makes it a strong candidate for routine specification on Nepali roads with acidic aggregate.**

> **AND THE VOIDS TARGET IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ANSWER: stripping requires water INSIDE the layer, and a properly compacted dense mix at 3 to 5 per cent voids is essentially impermeable.**

> **Above about 8 per cent voids the mix becomes permeable and water circulates freely within it, so under-compaction converts a stripping-resistant mix into a vulnerable one regardless of what was added to it.**

> **Compaction is therefore not merely a strength requirement but a durability one — which is why the specification is written on DENSITY achieved rather than on the number of roller passes.**

Causing loss of adhesion and disintegration of the mix.

examTip.trick: **Water displaces the bitumen film from the stone** — water has a greater affinity for most mineral surfaces than bitumen does, so it wins unless something is done.
examTip.trap: **ACIDIC aggregates (granite, quartzite, gneiss) are negatively charged and strip badly** — and they are exactly what the Himalaya provides. The aggregate cannot be changed, so the binder must be helped.
examTip.mnemonic: **1-2 % HYDRATED LIME as filler is cheap, locally available, and fixes both stripping and rutting.** And keep air voids at 3-5 %: above 8 % the mix is permeable and no additive will save it.

questions.stem: The SATURATION FLOW at a signalised intersection approach is:
options: The MAXIMUM rate at which vehicles can cross the stop line
The total number of vehicles arriving at the approach in an hour
The flow at which the approach becomes flooded in the monsoon
The number of vehicles that can be stored in the approach lane
questions.solution:
**The MAXIMUM rate at which vehicles cross the stop line, per hour of EFFECTIVE GREEN**, when a continuous queue is discharging.

**What it means and how it behaves:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Measured only while a QUEUE is discharging** ← | **If the queue clears, the flow is limited by arrivals rather than by capacity, and the measurement is invalid** ← |
| **Expressed per hour of GREEN, not per hour of clock time** ← | **So a saturation flow of 1,800 with 30 % green gives an actual capacity of 540 vehicles per hour** ← |
| **Typical value** | **About 1,800 PCU per hour of green per lane, for an ideal 3.5 m lane** ← |
| **Reduced by** | **Narrow lanes, gradients, turning movements, parking, pedestrians, poor surface, heavy vehicles** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE DEFINITION'S MOST IMPORTANT FEATURE AND THE ONE THAT MAKES THE CONCEPT USEFUL: it separates the approach's INHERENT capacity from the SHARE OF TIME the signal gives it.**

> **Saturation flow is a property of the road — its width, gradient, turning movements and surface. The green time is a property of the signal setting.**

> **Capacity is the product of the two, so a congested approach can be improved either by raising its saturation flow (widening it, banning parking, separating turns) or by giving it more green — and knowing which is cheaper requires the two to be separated.**

**The startup and clearance effects, which define "effective" green:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **START-UP LOST TIME** ← | **The first few vehicles accelerate slowly; the full saturation flow is not achieved until about the fourth or fifth vehicle — typically 2 seconds lost** ← |
| **END GAIN (clearance)** | **Some vehicles cross during the amber period — typically 2 seconds gained** ← |
| **EFFECTIVE GREEN** | **Actual green + amber − lost time — often nearly equal to the actual green, since the two effects roughly cancel** ← |
| **Total LOST TIME per cycle** | **The start-up lost time plus the all-red intergreen, for every phase** ← |

> **THE TOTAL LOST TIME IN THE LAST ROW IS WHAT LIMITS HOW SHORT A CYCLE CAN USEFULLY BE, and it has a direct and important consequence:**

> **Every phase change costs a few seconds of lost time. A junction with four phases and 5 seconds lost per phase loses 20 seconds every cycle.**

> **With a 60-second cycle, a third of the time is wasted. With a 120-second cycle, only a sixth is.**

> **So LONGER cycles are more efficient in capacity terms — and they impose longer waits on everyone, particularly pedestrians, who then cross against the signal.**

> **Webster's optimum cycle time, C = (1.5 L + 5)/(1 − Y), with L the total lost time and Y the sum of the critical flow ratios, balances exactly this trade-off: it finds the cycle that minimises the total delay.**

> **And its form shows the two forces directly — the cycle lengthens as the lost time L grows, and lengthens sharply as Y approaches 1, that is as the junction approaches saturation.**

**The other point worth making about signals:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A signal does not create capacity; it ALLOCATES it** ← | **Between the competing approaches** ← |
| **Signalising an over-capacity junction does not relieve it** ← | **It merely determines who waits** ← |
| **More PHASES means more lost time and less capacity** ← | **So each additional protected turning phase is paid for in throughput** ← |
| **Signals improve SAFETY by separating conflicting movements in time** | **Which is often the real reason for installing them** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS CONTAIN THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO UNDERSTAND ABOUT TRAFFIC SIGNALS AND IT IS ROUTINELY MISSED BY THOSE DEMANDING THEM: a signal cannot pass more vehicles through a junction than the junction's geometry allows.**

> **If the arriving demand exceeds the physical capacity, signalising it changes the queues' distribution and not their total length — and adding phases to protect turning movements actually REDUCES the total throughput.**

> **Where demand genuinely exceeds capacity, the answers are geometric (widening, flaring the approaches, a grade separation) or strategic (managing the demand) — and installing signals in the hope of solving it is a common and expensive disappointment.**

Expressed in vehicles per hour of EFFECTIVE GREEN time, when a continuous queue is discharging.

examTip.trick: **Maximum discharge rate per hour of EFFECTIVE GREEN, measured while a queue is discharging** — about 1,800 PCU/h/lane ideal. Capacity = saturation flow × green fraction.
examTip.trap: **Start-up lost time (~2 s) and amber end-gain (~2 s) roughly cancel**, so effective green ≈ actual green. The lost time that matters is per PHASE, and it limits how short a cycle can usefully be.
examTip.mnemonic: **A signal ALLOCATES capacity, it does not create it** — and each extra protected phase costs throughput. Webster: C = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y).

questions.stem: In flexible pavement design, the VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR expresses the damaging effect of an axle load relative to the standard axle, and it is taken as proportional to:
options: The axle load itself
The FOURTH POWER of the ratio of the axle load to the standard axle load
The square root of the axle load
The number of wheels on the axle
questions.solution:
**The FOURTH POWER of the ratio of the axle load to the standard axle load** — VDF = (L / L_standard)⁴.

**The relation and what it implies:**

| Axle load | Ratio to the 8.16 t standard | VDF |
|---|---|---|
| **4 tonnes** | **0.49** | **0.058 — almost negligible** ← |
| **8.16 tonnes (standard)** | **1.00** | **1.00** ← |
| **10.2 tonnes** | **1.25** | **2.44** ← |
| **16 tonnes (an overloaded axle)** | **1.96** | **14.8** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE FIGURE THAT MATTERS AND IT IS STARTLING: an axle carrying TWICE the legal load does not do twice the damage — it does nearly SIXTEEN TIMES the damage.**

> **One doubly loaded truck axle inflicts as much pavement damage as fifteen legally loaded ones.**

**The consequences, which follow arithmetically:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **OVERLOADING is by far the largest single cause of premature pavement failure** ← | **A modest proportion of overloaded vehicles can consume most of a pavement's design life** ← |
| **CARS do essentially no structural damage at all** ← | **A car axle of 1 tonne has a VDF of about 0.0004 — a hundred thousand cars equal a few trucks** ← |
| **Pavement design is therefore about TRUCKS, and only about trucks** ← | **Which is why traffic for design is counted as commercial vehicles, not as total vehicles** ← |
| **Axle load SURVEYS are essential to design** | **The VDF must be measured for the actual traffic, not assumed** ← |
| **AXLE LOAD CONTROL (weighbridges) is the cheapest road maintenance there is** ← | **Preventing overload costs far less than repairing its effects** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW HAS AN IMPLICATION THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: private cars contribute essentially nothing to the structural deterioration of a road.**

> **A road carrying nothing but cars would last almost indefinitely in structural terms, failing only from weathering and ageing.**

> **All the structural damage is done by heavy vehicles, and most of it by the heaviest and most overloaded among them.**

> **This has a clear policy corollary: the cost of maintaining a road's structure is caused by trucks, and recovering it through a charge on all vehicles equally means cars subsidising trucks — which is why axle-load-based charging is advocated by transport economists, and resisted by hauliers.**

**MSA — the design traffic — which is where the VDF is used:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Count commercial vehicles and measure their AXLE LOADS** ← | **By axle load survey with portable weighpads** ← |
| **Compute the VDF for the traffic stream** | **The weighted average of the individual axles' fourth-power factors** ← |
| **Project the traffic over the design life at the assumed growth rate** | ← |
| **Multiply by the lane distribution factor** | **Since not all lanes carry the same share** ← |
| **Result: the cumulative number of STANDARD AXLES, in MILLIONS (MSA)** ← | **The single number the pavement is designed for** ← |

> **THE WEIGHTED AVERAGE IN THE SECOND STEP HAS A PROPERTY WORTH NOTING: because of the fourth power, the average VDF is dominated by the HEAVIEST axles in the distribution.**

> **A survey that misses the small number of grossly overloaded vehicles — because they travel at night, or avoid the survey point — will produce a VDF that badly understates the real damage.**

> **So axle load surveys must cover the full 24 hours and be sited where they cannot be bypassed, or the design is built on a number that is systematically too low.**

> **The general lesson from the fourth power law is one of the most useful in pavement engineering: when an effect goes as a high power of a variable, the AVERAGE of that variable tells you very little, and the TAIL of its distribution tells you almost everything.**

examTip.trick: **VDF = (L / 8.16)⁴.** A 16 t axle gives (1.96)⁴ ≈ 14.8 — twice the legal load does nearly SIXTEEN times the damage, not twice.
examTip.trap: **Cars do essentially no structural damage** (VDF ≈ 0.0004), so pavement design counts COMMERCIAL vehicles only. All the deterioration is caused by the heaviest axles.
examTip.mnemonic: **With a fourth power, the AVERAGE tells you little and the TAIL tells you everything** — a survey that misses the night-time overloaded trucks understates the design traffic badly.

questions.stem: The MODULUS OF SUBGRADE REACTION (k) used in rigid pavement design is obtained from a plate load test and is defined as:
options: The ratio of the wheel load to the pavement thickness
The CBR value multiplied by 100
The PRESSURE applied to a standard plate DIVIDED by the corresponding DEFLECTION
The maximum deflection permitted under a standard axle
questions.solution:
**The applied PRESSURE divided by the resulting DEFLECTION** — k = p / Δ, expressed in kg/cm² per cm, or MPa/m.

**The test:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A rigid circular plate, standard diameter 750 mm, is loaded on the prepared subgrade** ← | **Smaller plates (300, 450, 600 mm) may be used with a correction** ← |
| **The pressure is increased and the settlement measured** | ← |
| **k is the pressure corresponding to a settlement of 1.25 mm, divided by 1.25 mm** ← | **A conventional definition point, not a measured elastic constant** ← |
| **Units** | **kg/cm² per cm, or MPa/m; typical values 3 to 12 kg/cm³ for subgrades** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW MATTERS BECAUSE IT SHOWS WHAT k REALLY IS: a CONVENTIONAL parameter defined at a chosen deflection, not a fundamental material property.**

> **Soil is not linearly elastic, so the ratio of pressure to deflection changes with the load level and the plate size.**

> **Fixing both by convention — 750 mm plate, 1.25 mm settlement — makes the results comparable, and it means that a k value quoted without its plate size and settlement basis is not usable.**

**Why RIGID pavements use k while FLEXIBLE pavements use CBR:**

| Pavement | Parameter | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **RIGID (concrete)** | **Modulus of subgrade reaction k** ← | **The slab is stiff and spreads the load widely; it behaves as a plate on an ELASTIC FOUNDATION, and Westergaard's analysis needs a foundation SPRING STIFFNESS — which is exactly what k is** ← |
| **FLEXIBLE** | **CBR (or the resilient modulus)** ← | **The layers deform with the subgrade; what matters is the subgrade's SHEAR STRENGTH against punching, which the CBR indexes** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE IS NOT ARBITRARY BUT FOLLOWS FROM HOW THE TWO PAVEMENTS CARRY LOAD, and that is the point worth taking:**

> **A concrete slab acts as a BEAM or PLATE, carrying the wheel load in bending over a wide area and delivering a low pressure to the subgrade. What the designer needs to know is how much the subgrade will DEFLECT under that low pressure, because the slab's bending stresses depend on how much it is allowed to sag — hence a stiffness.**

> **A flexible pavement transmits the load down through its layers with the pressure spreading as it goes, so the subgrade receives a much higher pressure over a smaller area. What matters there is whether it will fail in shear — hence a strength index.**

> **Two parameters, two mechanisms, and neither substitutes for the other.**

**Two practical cautions about k:**

| Caution | Note |
|---|---|
| **k is relatively INSENSITIVE to the subgrade's quality** ← | **Doubling k reduces the required slab thickness only slightly — because the slab's own stiffness dominates** ← |
| **A subbase increases the EFFECTIVE k** ← | **A granular or lean-concrete subbase raises the composite k value used in design** ← |
| **The test is slow, heavy and expensive** | **Which is why correlations from CBR are often used instead, with all their inaccuracy** ← |
| **k measured on a dry subgrade OVERSTATES the design value** ← | **The test should be done at, or corrected to, the worst moisture condition expected in service** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW HAS AN IMPORTANT DESIGN CONSEQUENCE THAT IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD: improving the subgrade beneath a CONCRETE pavement buys very little slab thickness.**

> **The slab is doing the work; the subgrade merely supports it. So spending heavily on subgrade improvement under a rigid pavement is poor value in structural terms.**

> **The reverse is true of a FLEXIBLE pavement, where the subgrade's CBR strongly governs the total thickness required, and improving it — by stabilisation or replacement — pays directly.**

> **BUT the subbase under a rigid pavement is still essential, for reasons that have nothing to do with k: it prevents PUMPING of fines from beneath the slab at the joints, provides a uniform working platform, and protects against frost and moisture movement.**

> **So the subbase is specified for uniformity and pumping resistance rather than for load spreading — which is why its specification emphasises non-erodibility and drainage rather than strength, and why a lean concrete or cement-treated subbase is preferred under heavily trafficked concrete pavements.**

Expressed in units such as kg/cm² per cm or MPa/m.

examTip.trick: **k = p/Δ, from a 750 mm plate at 1.25 mm settlement.** A CONVENTIONAL parameter defined at a chosen deflection, not a fundamental elastic constant — quote the plate size with it.
examTip.trap: **Rigid pavements use k (a foundation STIFFNESS, for Westergaard's plate on elastic foundation); flexible pavements use CBR (a SHEAR strength index).** The mechanisms differ, so the parameters differ.
examTip.mnemonic: **Improving the subgrade buys little slab thickness** — the slab dominates. But the subbase is still essential under concrete, for PUMPING resistance and uniformity, not for load spreading.

questions.stem: RUTTING in a bituminous pavement — longitudinal depressions along the WHEEL PATHS — is most commonly caused by:
options: Loss of the surface texture through polishing
Water entering through cracks in the surface
Excessive camber on the carriageway
PERMANENT DEFORMATION accumulating in the bituminous layers or the underlying layers under repeated heavy
questions.solution:
**Permanent deformation accumulating under repeated heavy, slow-moving loads** — in the bituminous layers themselves, or in the granular layers and subgrade beneath — aggravated by high temperature and excess binder.

**The two kinds of rutting, which have different remedies:**

| Type | Where the deformation occurs | Appearance |
|---|---|---|
| **STRUCTURAL rutting** ← | **In the SUBGRADE or granular layers — the whole pavement is pushed down** ← | **A broad, shallow depression with little or no heaving at the edges** ← |
| **INSTABILITY rutting** ← | **Within the BITUMINOUS layers, which shove sideways** ← | **A narrower rut with distinct HEAVING (shoulders) on either side** ← |

> **THE PRESENCE OR ABSENCE OF HEAVING IS THE DIAGNOSTIC FEATURE AND IT DETERMINES THE CORRECT REPAIR, which is why it is worth looking for:**

> **Heaving means the material has FLOWED sideways — it is still there, redistributed. That is a MIX problem, and the remedy is to mill out the bituminous layers and replace them with a stable mix.**

> **No heaving means the material has been pushed DOWN into a weak foundation. That is a STRUCTURAL problem, and resurfacing it will produce a smooth road that ruts again within a year, because nothing has been done about the cause.**

> **Overlaying a structural rut is one of the most common wasted maintenance expenditures on any road network.**

**The causes of instability rutting, since it is the more preventable:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **Excess BINDER in the mix** ← | **The aggregate floats in bitumen instead of interlocking; the mix behaves as a viscous fluid** ← |
| **Too much fine aggregate or rounded natural sand** ← | **Poor interlock; angular crushed material resists shoving far better** ← |
| **Insufficient compaction at construction** | **The mix continues to densify under traffic, which appears as a rut** ← |
| **A binder too SOFT for the climate** ← | **Hence VG-40 rather than VG-30 at junctions and on climbing lanes** ← |
| **HIGH pavement temperature** | **Bitumen is viscous; at 60 °C it deforms far more readily** ← |
| **SLOW, heavy, channelised traffic** ← | **Approaches to junctions, bus stops, toll plazas, and uphill grades where trucks crawl** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW EXPLAINS THE CHARACTERISTIC LOCATIONS OF RUTTING AND IS THE MOST USEFUL PREDICTIVE FACT: rutting appears where vehicles are SLOW and HEAVY, not where they are fast.**

> **Bitumen is a visco-elastic material — its response depends on the duration of loading as well as its magnitude. A fast wheel applies a load for a few milliseconds and the mix recovers; a crawling truck applies it for a second, and the deformation is largely permanent.**

> **So a junction approach, a bus bay or a long climbing grade suffers rutting that the open highway does not, with identical materials and identical traffic.**

> **The design response is local and cheap: a stiffer binder, a gap-graded SMA or a modified bitumen over those few hundred metres — which is a much better investment than upgrading the whole route.**

**And rutting placed among the other distresses:**

| Distress | Appearance | Principal cause |
|---|---|---|
| **RUTTING** | **Longitudinal depression in the wheel path** ← | **Permanent deformation — this question** |
| **SHOVING** | **Localised bulging and rippling, usually at junctions and bends** ← | **Instability under braking and turning forces** ← |
| **CORRUGATION** | **Regular transverse ripples** | **An unstable mix plus vehicle bouncing** ← |
| **RAVELLING** | **Progressive loss of aggregate from the surface** | **Insufficient binder, ageing, stripping** ← |
| **ALLIGATOR (fatigue) CRACKING** ← | **Interconnected cracks in a pattern like crocodile skin, in the wheel path** ← | **Fatigue of the bituminous layer under repeated bending — a STRUCTURAL failure** ← |
| **BLEEDING** | **A shiny film of binder on the surface** | **Excess binder; low voids** ← |
| **POTHOLES** | **Bowl-shaped cavities** | **The end state of ravelling or cracking, plus water** ← |

> **THE ALLIGATOR CRACKING ROW IS THE DISTRESS TO TAKE MOST SERIOUSLY, because unlike the others it indicates that the pavement's STRUCTURE has reached the end of its fatigue life.**

> **A surface treatment will hide it for a season and it will reappear, because the layer beneath is cracked through.**

> **Rutting and ravelling are surface problems that a resurfacing genuinely cures; alligator cracking is a structural one that needs strengthening — and telling them apart on a visual inspection is the most valuable skill in pavement maintenance management.**

Slow-moving loads, often aggravated by high temperature and excess binder.

examTip.trick: **Permanent deformation under repeated slow heavy loads.** HEAVING at the rut edges means the bituminous mix shoved sideways; NO heaving means the foundation was pushed down.
examTip.trap: **Overlaying a STRUCTURAL rut is wasted money** — it will rut again within a year because the cause is beneath. The diagnosis determines the repair.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rutting appears where vehicles are SLOW and HEAVY** — junction approaches, bus bays, climbing lanes — because bitumen is visco-elastic and load DURATION matters. Use VG-40 or SMA over those few hundred metres.

questions.stem: The symbol of a TRUNCATED CONE placed in the title block of an engineering drawing declares:
options: The scale to which the drawing is prepared
Whether the drawing is in FIRST ANGLE or THIRD ANGLE projection
The material of which the object is made
The tolerance class applied to the dimensions
questions.solution:
**Whether the drawing is in FIRST ANGLE or THIRD ANGLE projection.**

**Why the symbol exists at all:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The two conventions place the views in OPPOSITE positions** ← | **The same object, drawn correctly in each, produces two completely different sheets** ← |
| **There is no way to tell from the drawing itself which was used** ← | **Except for the symbol** ← |
| **Misreading it produces a MIRRORED or wrongly assembled object** ← | **Which is not a small error** ← |
| **So the symbol is a mandatory element of the title block** | ← |

> **THE SYMBOL IS ITSELF A TWO-VIEW DRAWING OF A TRUNCATED CONE, drawn in the projection it declares — so it demonstrates the convention rather than merely naming it.**

> **In FIRST angle, the view showing the smaller circle appears on the LEFT of the view showing the cone's outline; in THIRD angle it appears on the RIGHT.**

> **Since the symbol is drawn in the convention it announces, it is self-explanatory to anyone who understands either convention — which is exactly what an international standard symbol should be.**

**The two conventions:**

| Aspect | FIRST ANGLE | THIRD ANGLE |
|---|---|---|
| **The object is placed** | **BETWEEN the observer and the plane of projection** ← | **BEHIND the plane — the plane is between the observer and the object** ← |
| **The view is** | **PROJECTED THROUGH the object onto the plane behind it** ← | **Projected onto a transparent plane in front of it** ← |
| **Plan (top view) placed** | **BELOW the front view** ← | **ABOVE the front view** ← |
| **View from the LEFT placed** | **On the RIGHT of the front view** ← | **On the LEFT** ← |
| **In short** | **Views appear on the OPPOSITE side from which they are seen** ← | **Views appear on the SAME side from which they are seen** ← |
| **Used in** | **India, Nepal, most of Europe — the ISO default in these regions** ← | **The United States, Canada, Japan, Australia** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MEMORY DEVICE THAT MAKES BOTH CONVENTIONS RECOVERABLE WITHOUT MEMORISING THE TABLE: in THIRD angle, the view is placed on the SAME side as the direction you looked from — look from the top, the view goes on top; look from the left, it goes on the left.**

> **FIRST angle is the opposite in every case.**

> **One rule, applied consistently, generates every entry in the table, and it is far more reliable than trying to remember six separate placements.**

**Why this matters in practice, beyond the examination:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **International projects mix drawings from both conventions** ← | **A design office in Europe, a fabricator in the United States, a site in Nepal** ← |
| **A component fabricated from a misread drawing may be a MIRROR IMAGE** ← | **Which fits nothing, and is discovered at assembly** ← |
| **The error is expensive and entirely avoidable** | **A symbol in the title block prevents it** ← |
| **Some drawings state the convention in WORDS as well** ← | **Belt and braces, and worth doing on an international project** ← |

> **A MIRRORED COMPONENT IS A PARTICULARLY UNPLEASANT ERROR because it often looks correct: the dimensions are all right, the features are all present, and it simply cannot be assembled.**

> **In symmetric components the mistake is invisible; in asymmetric ones it appears only when the parts meet.**

> **Which is why the projection symbol, the scale, the units and the revision number belong together in the title block: each of them is a piece of information without which the geometry on the sheet is ambiguous, and each has caused expensive errors when omitted.**

> **The general point is worth carrying: a drawing is not just a picture, it is a picture PLUS a set of conventions, and the conventions must be declared or the picture cannot be read reliably.**

examTip.trick: **The truncated-cone symbol declares FIRST or THIRD angle** — and it is itself drawn in the convention it announces, so it demonstrates rather than names it.
examTip.trap: **One rule generates the whole table: in THIRD angle a view goes on the SAME side you looked from; in FIRST angle the opposite.** Look from the top → top view above (third) or below (first).
examTip.mnemonic: **A misread projection gives a MIRRORED component** — all dimensions correct, all features present, and it fits nothing. Discovered at assembly. India and Nepal use FIRST angle; the USA THIRD.

questions.stem: AS-BUILT (record) drawings prepared at the completion of a construction project are:
options: The drawings issued for tendering
Preliminary sketches prepared before design
The contractor's temporary works drawings
Drawings REVISED to show the works EXACTLY AS CONSTRUCTED
questions.solution:
**Drawings revised to show the works EXACTLY AS CONSTRUCTED**, incorporating every variation, and handed over as a permanent record.

**Why they matter:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Nothing is built exactly as drawn** ← | **Variations, site adjustments, obstructions found in the ground, and design changes all alter the works** ← |
| **The construction drawings therefore become INACCURATE the moment building begins** ← | **And progressively more so** ← |
| **Whoever operates, maintains, extends or repairs the works needs to know what is ACTUALLY there** ← | **Not what was once intended** ← |
| **They are needed for decades, by people who were not involved** ← | **Long after everyone who knew has left** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE WHOLE JUSTIFICATION, and it is felt most sharply with BURIED and CONCEALED work:**

> **A drainage pipe, a cable duct, a water main, a foundation, reinforcement in a slab — none of it can be inspected once complete, and every future intervention depends on the record.**

> **An excavator operator who does not know where the buried services are will cut them, which is the commonest cause of utility damage in urban work and a real cause of death where the service is an electricity cable or a gas main.**

**What as-built drawings must record:**

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| **The actual DIMENSIONS and positions of everything built** | ← |
| **All BURIED services — with levels, and dimensioned from permanent surface features** ← | **Not from a temporary peg, and not from a building that may be demolished** ← |
| **Every VARIATION incorporated, with its reference** | ← |
| **Actual foundation levels and the ground conditions found** ← | **Invaluable when the structure is later extended or investigated** ← |
| **Materials and grades actually used** | **Where they differ from those specified** ← |
| **Equipment installed: make, model, rating, serial number** | **For maintenance and spare parts** ← |
| **The date and the surveyor or engineer certifying them** | ← |

> **THE DIMENSIONING RULE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES WHETHER A RECORD IS USABLE IN TWENTY YEARS: a buried pipe located "3.2 m from the site office wall" is lost as soon as the site office is demolished.**

> **The same pipe located by coordinates and levels tied to a permanent benchmark, or dimensioned from a permanent kerb line or building corner, can still be found.**

> **The extra effort at the time is negligible and the difference in later value is total.**

**Why they are so often poor, stated honestly:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **They are prepared at the END, when everyone is leaving** ← | **The site staff who know what happened have moved to the next project** ← |
| **They are compiled from memory and marked-up prints rather than from records** ← | **If the records were not kept as the work proceeded, they cannot be reconstructed** ← |
| **Payment is often already largely released** | **So the commercial incentive to complete them properly is gone** ← |
| **Nobody uses them for years, so their poor quality is not discovered until it matters** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS POINT TO THE ONLY EFFECTIVE REMEDY, and it is worth stating as a rule: as-built information must be recorded AS THE WORK PROCEEDS, not assembled at the end.**

> **A buried pipeline must be surveyed BEFORE it is backfilled, because afterwards it cannot be. Reinforcement must be photographed and recorded before the pour. Foundation levels must be taken when the excavation is open.**

> **A drawing compiled at handover from recollection is not a record; it is a reconstruction, and it will be wrong in exactly the places that matter.**

> **THE COMMERCIAL REMEDY IN THE THIRD ROW IS EQUALLY IMPORTANT AND ENTIRELY WITHIN THE EMPLOYER'S CONTROL: make acceptance of complete, certified as-built drawings a CONDITION of the final certificate and of the release of retention.**

> **Where that is done, as-built drawings arrive complete and on time. Where it is not, they arrive late, incomplete, or not at all — which is a fair summary of how most contractual obligations behave when nothing depends on them.**

examTip.trick: **Revised to show the works exactly AS CONSTRUCTED**, incorporating every variation — the permanent record for whoever operates, maintains or extends the works decades later.
examTip.trap: **Dimension buried services from PERMANENT features or coordinates**, never from a site office or a temporary peg — a pipe located from a demolished building is a pipe that is lost.
examTip.mnemonic: **Record as the work PROCEEDS, not at the end** — a pipeline must be surveyed before backfilling. And tie the final certificate and retention release to accepting them, or they never arrive.

questions.stem: A machine costing Rs 1,00,000 is to be paid for by five equal annual instalments, the first payable one year from now, at an interest rate of 10 per cent per annum. Each instalment is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About Rs 26,380.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **The CAPITAL RECOVERY factor** | **A/P = i (1+i)ⁿ / [(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** ← |
| **(1 + 0.10)⁵** | **= 1.61051** ← |
| **Numerator** | **0.10 × 1.61051 = 0.161051** |
| **Denominator** | **1.61051 − 1 = 0.61051** |
| **Capital recovery factor** | **0.161051 / 0.61051 = 0.26380** ← |
| **Annual instalment** | **1,00,000 × 0.26380 = Rs 26,380** ← |

> **Option (a) Rs 20,000 is simply P/n, ignoring interest altogether — which would repay the principal and nothing else.**

> **Option (d) Rs 32,210 compounds the whole sum for five years and then divides by five, which charges interest on money already repaid.**

**A sanity check worth doing on any such answer:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **The instalment MUST exceed P/n = Rs 20,000** ← | **Because interest has to be paid as well as the principal** ← |
| **It must be LESS than P(1+i)ⁿ/n = Rs 32,210** ← | **Because the early instalments repay principal, so interest is not charged on the full sum throughout** ← |
| **So the answer lies between 20,000 and 32,210** ← | **Which immediately eliminates options (a) and (d)** ← |

> **THAT TWO-SIDED BRACKET IS AVAILABLE IN EVERY ANNUITY PROBLEM AND TAKES TEN SECONDS, and it will catch most of the errors that arise in this topic.**

**The six standard compound interest factors, since they are all variations of the same idea:**

| Factor | Symbol | Expression | Finds |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Single payment COMPOUND AMOUNT** | **F/P** | **(1+i)ⁿ** | **A future sum from a present one** ← |
| **Single payment PRESENT WORTH** | **P/F** | **1/(1+i)ⁿ** | **A present sum from a future one** ← |
| **Uniform series COMPOUND AMOUNT** | **F/A** | **[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]/i** | **The future value of a series** ← |
| **SINKING FUND** | **A/F** | **i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** | **The annual deposit to accumulate a future sum** ← |
| **Series PRESENT WORTH** | **P/A** | **[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]/[i(1+i)ⁿ]** | **The present value of a series** ← |
| **CAPITAL RECOVERY** | **A/P** | **i(1+i)ⁿ/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** | **The annual payment equivalent to a present sum** ← (this question) |

> **THE SIX FALL INTO THREE RECIPROCAL PAIRS, which is the way to remember them rather than as six formulae: F/P and P/F; F/A and A/F; P/A and A/P.**

> **Each pair is the same expression inverted, so learning three gives all six.**

> **And note the relation between the last two rows: A/P = A/F + i, which is worth checking here — the sinking fund factor is 0.10/0.61051 = 0.16380, and adding i = 0.10 gives 0.26380 exactly.**

> **The reason is intuitive: capital recovery = paying the interest each year (i) PLUS setting aside enough to replace the principal (the sinking fund factor). Which is exactly what a loan repayment is.**

**Where the capital recovery factor is used in engineering practice:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Converting a CAPITAL cost into an EQUIVALENT ANNUAL cost** ← | **So that it can be added to the annual operating cost and the alternatives compared on one figure** ← |
| **Comparing alternatives with DIFFERENT LIVES** ← | **The annual-worth method handles unequal lives directly, without needing the least common multiple** ← |
| **Loan and lease payment calculation** | ← |
| **Setting a tariff that recovers a plant's capital over its concession period** | **Exactly what a hydropower PPA tariff must do** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRACTICAL REASON ENGINEERS PREFER THE ANNUAL WORTH METHOD: comparing a pump with a 10-year life against a pipeline with a 40-year life by present worth requires a 40-year study period and three replacements of the pump.**

> **Converting each to an equivalent annual cost sidesteps that entirely, and the comparison is a single subtraction.**

examTip.trap: **Bracket the answer in ten seconds: it must exceed P/n = 20,000 and be less than P(1+i)ⁿ/n = 32,210** — which eliminates two options immediately.
examTip.mnemonic: **Six factors are three RECIPROCAL PAIRS: F/P–P/F, F/A–A/F, P/A–A/P.** And A/P = A/F + i — capital recovery is the interest plus a sinking fund for the principal, which is what a loan repayment is.

questions.stem: In economic appraisal, the REAL interest rate differs from the NOMINAL (market) interest rate in that the real rate:
options: Has the effect of INFLATION removed
Is always higher than the nominal rate
Applies only to government projects
Includes the lender's profit margin
questions.solution:
**The real rate has INFLATION removed** — it measures the increase in purchasing power rather than in money terms.

**The relation:**

| Form | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Exact** | **(1 + i_nominal) = (1 + i_real)(1 + f), with f the inflation rate** ← |
| **Rearranged** | **i_real = (1 + i_nominal)/(1 + f) − 1** ← |
| **Approximate, for small rates** | **i_real ≈ i_nominal − f** ← |

| Example | Working |
|---|---|
| **Nominal 12 %, inflation 8 %** | **i_real = 1.12/1.08 − 1 = 0.0370 = 3.70 %** ← |
| **The approximation gives** | **12 − 8 = 4 % — close, and slightly high** ← |

> **THE APPROXIMATION IS ADEQUATE FOR MODERATE RATES AND BREAKS DOWN AT HIGH ONES, which is worth knowing: at 40 per cent inflation and a 50 per cent nominal rate, the approximation gives 10 per cent and the exact formula gives 7.1 per cent.**

> **Since option (b) claims the real rate is always higher, it is worth being explicit: the real rate is LOWER than the nominal whenever inflation is positive, and it can be NEGATIVE — which happens whenever inflation exceeds the interest rate, and means a depositor is losing purchasing power despite earning interest.**

**THE GOLDEN RULE OF THE TOPIC, which is what examinations actually test:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Discount REAL (constant-price) cash flows at the REAL rate** ← | **Consistent** ← |
| **Discount NOMINAL (current-price, inflated) cash flows at the NOMINAL rate** ← | **Also consistent** ← |
| **NEVER mix them** ← | **Discounting real cash flows at the nominal rate deflates them twice and grossly understates the project's worth** ← |

> **THE ERROR IN THE THIRD ROW IS COMMON AND ITS DIRECTION IS ALWAYS THE SAME: it makes long-term projects look far worse than they are, because the double deflation compounds over the years.**

> **A 30-year infrastructure project appraised that way can show a negative net present value when its true worth is strongly positive — and long-lived infrastructure is exactly the kind of investment most damaged by the mistake.**

> **In practice the REAL approach is usually preferred for public infrastructure appraisal, because forecasting inflation over 30 years is guesswork and expressing everything in today's prices removes the need to try.**

**Where the distinction genuinely bites:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A LOAN at a fixed nominal rate during inflation** ← | **The borrower gains — the debt is repaid in money worth less than it was borrowed** ← |
| **A fixed-price CONTRACT over several years** ← | **The contractor bears the inflation risk, and prices for it — hence PRICE ADJUSTMENT (escalation) clauses in long contracts** ← |
| **A concession tariff fixed in nominal terms for 30 years** ← | **Its real value erodes steadily, which can make a project unviable late in its life** ← |
| **Comparing costs from different years** | **They must be brought to a common price base before any comparison** ← |

> **THE PRICE ADJUSTMENT CLAUSE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRACTICAL RESPONSE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING AS RISK ALLOCATION rather than as a concession to the contractor.**

> **A contractor asked to hold prices firm for four years must include a contingency for inflation — and being unable to predict it, must include a generous one.**

> **The employer pays that contingency whether inflation occurs or not.**

> **A price adjustment formula tied to published indices instead lets the contractor price the WORK and leaves the inflation risk with the employer, who is better placed to bear it and who pays only what actually occurs.**

> **The result is usually cheaper for the employer, which is the general principle of good risk allocation: a risk should be borne by the party best able to CONTROL or ABSORB it, and neither party can control inflation while the employer can absorb it more cheaply.**

examTip.trick: **(1 + i_nom) = (1 + i_real)(1 + f); approximately i_real ≈ i_nom − f.** The real rate is LOWER than nominal whenever inflation is positive, and can be negative.
examTip.trap: **Real cash flows at the REAL rate; nominal cash flows at the NOMINAL rate — never mix.** Discounting real flows at the nominal rate deflates twice and makes long-lived infrastructure look worthless.
examTip.mnemonic: **A PRICE ADJUSTMENT clause is risk allocation, not generosity** — without it the contractor prices a contingency the employer pays whether inflation happens or not. Risk goes to whoever can control or absorb it.

questions.stem: In a project network, the CRITICAL PATH is:
options: The path containing the most expensive activities
The LONGEST path through the network from start to finish
The path with the greatest number of activities
The shortest route through the network
questions.solution:
**The LONGEST path through the network**, along which every activity has ZERO total float, so that any delay to any of them delays the whole project.

**Its defining properties:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the LONGEST path in DURATION from start to finish** ← | **Not in cost, and not in the number of activities** ← |
| **Its length equals the PROJECT DURATION** ← | **The project cannot finish sooner, because that chain of work must be done in sequence** ← |
| **Every activity on it has ZERO total float** ← | **There is no slack anywhere along it** ← |
| **Delaying any critical activity delays the PROJECT, day for day** ← | ← |
| **SHORTENING the project requires shortening the critical path** ← | **Crashing anything else achieves nothing at all** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL MANAGEMENT CONSEQUENCE AND IS ROUTINELY IGNORED IN PRACTICE: accelerating a non-critical activity does not bring the project forward by a single day.**

> **It merely increases that activity's float, and it costs money.**

> **A manager under pressure who pushes every trade to work faster is largely wasting the effort — the correct response is to identify the critical path and apply the resources there, and to leave the non-critical work alone.**

**Three properties that are frequently got wrong:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **There may be MORE THAN ONE critical path** ← | **Two or more paths of equal length, all critical simultaneously — and then all of them must be shortened to gain a day** ← |
| **The critical path CHANGES as the project proceeds** ← | **Delay a non-critical chain enough and it becomes critical; crash the critical path enough and another takes over** ← |
| **"Critical" means schedule-critical, not IMPORTANT** ← | **A trivial administrative approval can sit on the critical path while a major structural element has weeks of float** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE REASON A NETWORK MUST BE UPDATED RATHER THAN DRAWN ONCE: a schedule prepared at the start and never revised describes a project that no longer exists.**

> **Once activities have started late, finished early, or been resequenced, the critical path is somewhere else — and managing to the original path means concentrating effort on work that no longer governs.**

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH DWELLING ON BECAUSE IT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND HAS REAL CONSEQUENCES: the word "critical" in this context is a purely technical term about float, and carries no implication of importance, value or difficulty.**

> **Waiting for a permit, a client decision, a customs clearance or a single specialist's visit can sit squarely on the critical path, while the main structure — expensive, difficult and visible — has ten days of float.**

> **Effort naturally gravitates to the impressive work, and the schedule is governed by the paperwork. Recognising that is much of what project scheduling contributes.**

**And crashing, which is what one does about it:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Identify the critical path** | ← |
| **Find the critical activity with the LOWEST cost slope** ← | **Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) ÷ (normal duration − crash duration), in rupees per day saved** ← |
| **Crash that activity by one increment** | ← |
| **RE-COMPUTE the critical path** ← | **Because it may have shifted to another chain — the step most often omitted** ← |
| **Repeat until the target is met, or until crashing costs more than the delay** ← | ← |
| **Remember the INDIRECT costs** | **Overheads, supervision and plant hire fall as the project shortens, which partly offsets the crashing cost** ← |

> **THE RE-COMPUTATION IN THE FOURTH STEP IS ESSENTIAL AND IS THE COMMONEST ERROR IN EXAMINATION PROBLEMS: crashing the critical path shortens it, and at some point another path becomes equally long.**

> **From then on, BOTH must be crashed together to gain another day, and the effective cost slope becomes the sum of the two.**

> **Missing that step produces an answer that shortens one path far below the length of another — which is impossible, since the project cannot finish before its longest path is complete.**

examTip.trick: **Longest path in DURATION, zero total float, and its length IS the project duration.** Not the most expensive path and not the one with most activities.
examTip.trap: **There may be several critical paths, and the critical path MOVES as the project proceeds** — so when crashing, RE-COMPUTE after every step or you will shorten one path below another.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Critical" means schedule-critical, not important** — a customs clearance can govern the project while the main structure has ten days of float. Effort goes to the impressive work; the paperwork sets the date.

questions.stem: In an ACTIVITY-ON-ARROW network, a DUMMY activity is:
options: An activity whose duration has not yet been estimated
An activity performed by a subcontractor
A activity that consumes resources but no time
An activity of ZERO duration consuming NO resources
questions.solution:
**An activity of ZERO duration consuming no resources**, introduced solely to express a logical dependency correctly, or to give two concurrent activities distinct start and end events.

**Its two purposes:**

| Purpose | Situation | Why the dummy is needed |
|---|---|---|
| **LOGICAL (dependency) dummy** ← | **Activity C depends on both A and B, while activity D depends on A ONLY** ← | **Without a dummy the network would wrongly make D depend on B as well** ← |
| **IDENTITY (grammatical) dummy** ← | **Two activities run between the SAME two events** ← | **In activity-on-arrow notation each activity is identified by its (i, j) event numbers, so two activities cannot share both — a dummy separates them** ← |

> **THE SECOND PURPOSE IS PURELY A CONSEQUENCE OF THE NOTATION AND HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH THE PROJECT, which is worth being clear about:**

> **If activities "pour slab" and "erect scaffold" both run from event 5 to event 6, they would both be called "activity 5-6", and the computer could not tell them apart.**

> **A dummy gives one of them its own end event, and the ambiguity disappears.**

> **The project has not changed at all — only its representation has.**

**Its properties:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Zero DURATION** | **It takes no time** ← |
| **Zero RESOURCES** ← | **Which is why option (c) is wrong — a dummy consumes nothing at all** ← |
| **Drawn as a DASHED arrow** | **To distinguish it visually** ← |
| **It CAN lie on the critical path** ← | **Adding nothing to the duration, but forming part of the governing chain of logic** ← |
| **It has a direction, which matters** | **Reversing a dummy changes the logic entirely** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS WORTH CONFIRMING: a dummy of zero duration can indeed be critical.**

> **Criticality is about whether an activity lies on the longest chain of DEPENDENCY, not about whether it takes time. A dummy that carries the logic from one chain to another can be an essential link in the governing path.**

**Why the whole issue disappears in ACTIVITY-ON-NODE notation:**
