| Aspect | ACTIVITY-ON-ARROW (AOA) | ACTIVITY-ON-NODE (AON / precedence) |
|---|---|---|
| **Activities shown as** | **ARROWS between event circles** ← | **BOXES (nodes), joined by dependency arrows** ← |
| **Dummies** | **REQUIRED, for both reasons above** ← | **NOT NEEDED AT ALL — dependencies are drawn directly** ← |
| **Identification** | **By the pair of event numbers (i, j)** | **By the activity's own identifier** ← |
| **Relationships expressible** | **Finish-to-start only** ← | **Finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish, start-to-finish, with LEADS and LAGS** ← |
| **Used by** | **Older texts and examinations** ← | **All modern project management software** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DECISIVE ADVANTAGE OF AON AND THE REASON IT HAS COMPLETELY DISPLACED AOA IN PRACTICE, and it is worth appreciating:**

> **Real construction sequences are rarely pure finish-to-start. Excavation for a trench does not have to FINISH before pipelaying starts — pipelaying can begin once excavation is a few days ahead, and the two proceed together.**

> **That is a START-TO-START relationship with a LAG, and AOA cannot express it without artificially chopping both activities into segments.**

> **AON states it directly, which produces a network that resembles how the work is actually done rather than an idealised sequence — and a schedule that resembles reality is far more likely to be followed.**

> **AOA nevertheless remains on examination syllabuses, partly because the dummy activity is a genuinely instructive exercise in expressing logic precisely, and partly because understanding events and their numbering makes the forward and backward pass calculations very transparent.**

Introduced only to show a logical DEPENDENCY correctly or to give two concurrent activities distinct start and end events.

examTip.trick: **Zero duration, zero resources, dashed arrow** — for a LOGICAL dependency, or to give two parallel activities distinct (i, j) event numbers.
examTip.trap: **A dummy CAN lie on the critical path** — criticality is about the chain of dependency, not about consuming time.
examTip.mnemonic: **AON needs no dummies at all and handles start-to-start with LAGS** — which is how trenching and pipelaying actually proceed. That is why all modern software uses it.

questions.stem: On a project, the earned value is Rs 9,00,000 and the planned value for the same date is Rs 12,00,000. The SCHEDULE PERFORMANCE INDEX (SPI) is 0.75, which means the project is:
options: BEHIND SCHEDULE
Ahead of schedule by 25 per cent
Over budget by 25 per cent
Exactly on schedule but over budget
questions.solution:
**BEHIND SCHEDULE** — only 75 per cent of the planned work has actually been accomplished by this date.

**The computation and its reading:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **SPI = Earned Value ÷ Planned Value** | **= 9,00,000 / 12,00,000 = 0.75** ← |
| **SPI < 1** | **BEHIND schedule** ← |
| **SPI = 1** | **On schedule** |
| **SPI > 1** | **Ahead of schedule** ← |
| **Schedule variance SV = EV − PV** | **= 9,00,000 − 12,00,000 = −Rs 3,00,000 — negative, confirming the delay** ← |

> **Option (c) confuses the SCHEDULE index with the COST index — a different ratio entirely, using ACTUAL COST rather than planned value.**

**The four earned value quantities:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PLANNED VALUE (PV / BCWS)** | **The budgeted cost of the work SCHEDULED to be done by this date** ← |
| **EARNED VALUE (EV / BCWP)** | **The budgeted cost of the work ACTUALLY DONE by this date** ← |
| **ACTUAL COST (AC / ACWP)** | **What has actually been SPENT to do it** ← |
| **Budget at Completion (BAC)** | **The total budget for the whole project** |

| Index | Formula | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| **SPI** | **EV / PV** ← | **SCHEDULE performance — am I where I should be?** ← |
| **CPI** | **EV / AC** ← | **COST performance — am I getting value for what I spend?** ← |
| **SV** | **EV − PV** | Schedule variance, in money |
| **CV** | **EV − AC** | Cost variance, in money |

> **THE EARNED VALUE IS THE COMMON TERM IN BOTH INDICES AND THAT IS THE INSIGHT THAT MAKES THE WHOLE METHOD WORK:**

> **Comparing what has been SPENT with what was BUDGETED tells you nothing on its own — a project may have spent half its budget because it is halfway through, or because it has done a quarter of the work at twice the cost.**

> **Earned value introduces a third, independent measurement: the budgeted value of the work actually COMPLETED.**

> **With that, spending can be compared against ACHIEVEMENT rather than against time, and the two questions — am I late? and am I overspending? — can finally be separated.**

> **Before earned value, they could not be, and that is the whole contribution of the technique.**

**The four situations, which are worth being able to read instantly:**

| SPI | CPI | Situation |
|---|---|---|
| **> 1** | **> 1** | **Ahead of schedule AND under budget — rare and excellent** ← |
| **< 1** | **> 1** | **BEHIND schedule but cost-efficient — often means under-resourcing: too few people, working efficiently** ← |
| **> 1** | **< 1** | **AHEAD of schedule but overspending — often overtime and acceleration** ← |
| **< 1** | **< 1** | **Behind AND over — the position that needs intervention** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS ARE THE INFORMATIVE ONES BECAUSE THEY POINT TO A CAUSE RATHER THAN JUST A SYMPTOM, and that is where earned value earns its keep:**

> **A project behind schedule with a good CPI is usually under-resourced — the work being done is being done efficiently, there is simply not enough of it happening. The remedy is more resources, and it will probably work.**

> **A project ahead of schedule with a poor CPI is buying time with money — overtime, extra shifts, acceleration. That may be a deliberate and correct decision, or it may be uncontrolled, and the difference matters.**

> **A single number can rarely diagnose anything; two numbers moving in opposite directions frequently can.**

**And the caution that must accompany all of it:**

| Caution | Note |
|---|---|
| **SPI is measured in MONEY, not in time** ← | **An SPI of 0.75 does not mean the project is 25 per cent late in days** ← |
| **SPI always converges to 1.0 at completion** ← | **Because at the end, EV = PV = BAC by definition — even for a project finishing a year late** ← |
| **It says nothing about the CRITICAL PATH** ← | **A project can have SPI = 1.0 with every critical activity late and every non-critical one early** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS ARE SERIOUS LIMITATIONS AND ARE THE REASON EARNED VALUE MUST BE READ ALONGSIDE THE NETWORK, never instead of it: SPI measures the VOLUME of work done, and the schedule is governed by WHICH work is done.**

> **A team that completes plenty of easy, non-critical work while the critical path stalls will show a healthy SPI and a project that is not moving at all.**

It has accomplished only 75 per cent of the work that was planned to be done by this date.

examTip.trick: **SPI = EV/PV = 9/12 = 0.75, so behind schedule.** CPI uses ACTUAL COST instead — option (c) confuses the two.
examTip.trap: **Earned value's contribution is separating the two questions** — comparing spend against budget alone cannot tell overspending from being ahead. The EV term is what makes both indices meaningful.
examTip.mnemonic: **SPI always returns to 1.0 at completion, even a year late, and ignores the CRITICAL PATH entirely** — plenty of easy non-critical work gives a healthy SPI on a stalled project. Read it with the network.

questions.stem: In project risk management, the four standard responses to an identified NEGATIVE risk (a threat) are:
options: Ignore, delay, escalate and record
Insure, insure again, inspect and audit
AVOID, TRANSFER, MITIGATE (reduce) and ACCEPT
Plan, do, check and act
questions.solution:
**AVOID, TRANSFER, MITIGATE (reduce), and ACCEPT.**

**The four responses:**

| Response | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **AVOID** ← | **Eliminate the risk entirely by changing the plan** ← | **Change the alignment to miss the unstable slope; choose a proven technology instead of a novel one; remove the scope that carries the risk** ← |
| **TRANSFER** ← | **Move the risk to a party better able to bear it — the risk still exists** ← | **INSURANCE; a fixed-price contract; a performance bond; a warranty** ← |
| **MITIGATE (reduce)** | **Reduce the PROBABILITY, the IMPACT, or both** ← | **Extra site investigation; a prototype; redundancy; early procurement of a long-lead item** ← |
| **ACCEPT** ← | **Take no action, but be conscious of it — with a CONTINGENCY (active) or without (passive)** ← | **Small risks, and risks too expensive to treat** ← |

> **Option (d) is the Deming quality cycle — a real and useful framework for something else entirely.**

> **THE ORDER MIRRORS THE ENVIRONMENTAL MITIGATION HIERARCHY, and the parallel is exact and worth noticing: avoid, reduce, pass on, accept what remains.**

> **In both cases the earlier options are more effective and less available, and the later ones are always available and less effective.**

**Two points about TRANSFER that are frequently misunderstood:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Transfer does not make a risk DISAPPEAR** ← | **It moves who pays for it — and the party accepting it charges for doing so** ← |
| **The party accepting it prices it, generously if it cannot assess it** ← | **So transferring a risk to someone who cannot evaluate or control it is EXPENSIVE and often ineffective** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE FOUNDATION OF SENSIBLE CONTRACT RISK ALLOCATION AND IT IS WORTH STATING AS A PRINCIPLE: a risk should be borne by the party best able to CONTROL it, or failing that, best able to ABSORB it.**

> **GROUND CONDITIONS are the classic illustration in civil engineering. A contractor asked to bear unforeseen ground risk cannot control it, has usually not commissioned the investigation, and has had a few weeks to price it.**

> **The rational response is to add a large contingency, which the employer pays whether the bad ground materialises or not — and if it does materialise and exceeds the contingency, the contractor claims anyway or goes under.**

> **The employer, who commissioned the investigation, owns the site and has the whole programme's context, is far better placed to carry that risk — which is why most standard forms give the contractor relief for genuinely unforeseeable physical conditions, and why the reference to a geotechnical baseline report has become standard practice.**

**The RISK MATRIX, which is how risks are prioritised for treatment:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Each risk is scored for PROBABILITY and for IMPACT** ← | **Typically on a 1-to-5 scale each** ← |
| **The product gives a risk SCORE, plotted on a matrix** | **Probability on one axis, impact on the other** ← |
| **HIGH probability and HIGH impact — treat urgently** ← | **Avoid or mitigate** ← |
| **LOW probability but CATASTROPHIC impact** ← | **The most difficult category — a low score, and a consequence that could end the project or kill people** ← |
| **High probability, low impact** | **Mitigate cheaply, or accept with contingency** ← |
| **Low and low** | **Accept and record** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHERE SIMPLE RISK SCORING FAILS AND THE FAILURE IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: multiplying probability by impact treats a 1-in-1,000 chance of 100 deaths as equivalent to a near-certainty of a minor delay.**

> **They are not equivalent, and no organisation actually treats them as such.**

> **Catastrophic risks must be handled separately from the matrix — by absolute limits, by design codes, by regulatory requirement — precisely because their expected value understates how seriously they must be taken.**

> **That is why dam spillways are designed for the PMF rather than for an economically optimal flood, why structural safety is governed by codes rather than by cost-benefit analysis, and why "the risk score was low" is never an acceptable explanation after a fatality.**

> **A risk register is a management tool for the ordinary risks of a project. It is not, and must never be allowed to become, the mechanism by which safety decisions are made.**

examTip.trick: **AVOID, TRANSFER, MITIGATE, ACCEPT** — the same hierarchy as environmental mitigation: earlier options are more effective and less available.
examTip.trap: **Transfer does not remove a risk, it moves who pays** — and a party who cannot assess or control it prices it generously, which the employer pays whether it occurs or not.
examTip.mnemonic: **Probability × impact fails for LOW-probability CATASTROPHIC risks** — which is why spillways use the PMF and structures use codes, not cost-benefit. "The risk score was low" is never an answer after a fatality.

questions.stem: An engineer, while working for a client under a confidentiality agreement, discovers a defect in the client's completed building that poses a serious danger to its occupants. The client instructs the engineer to say nothing. The engineer should:
options: Comply, since the confidentiality agreement is a binding contract
Inform the client in writing of the danger and of the engineer's duty
Resign quietly and say nothing to anyone
Discuss it publicly on social media to force the client to act
questions.solution:
**Inform the client in writing, urge them to act, and if they refuse, report the matter to the appropriate authority** — because the duty to protect public safety overrides the duty of confidentiality.

**The principle:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Every engineering code of ethics places the SAFETY, HEALTH AND WELFARE OF THE PUBLIC as the engineer's PARAMOUNT duty** ← | **The word "paramount" is used deliberately — it means it ranks above every other obligation** ← |
| **Confidentiality is a genuine and important duty** ← | **Owed to the client, and normally to be honoured strictly** ← |
| **But it is SUBORDINATE to public safety** ← | **When the two conflict, safety prevails** ← |
| **A confidentiality agreement cannot lawfully require the concealment of a danger to life** ← | **Which disposes of option (a)** ← |

> **OPTION (C) IS THE MOST TEMPTING WRONG ANSWER AND DESERVES A DIRECT REJECTION: resigning quietly protects the engineer and leaves the occupants in exactly the danger they were in.**

> **It is the choice that feels honourable and achieves nothing. The duty is to the people at risk, not to one's own conscience, and walking away discharges neither.**

> **OPTION (D) IS ALSO WRONG, and for a reason worth being clear about: going public immediately skips the steps that might resolve the matter properly, may cause disproportionate harm, and may be defamatory if the engineer's assessment turns out to be mistaken.**

> **A public accusation cannot be withdrawn. The proper channel exists for good reasons, and it should be used.**

**The correct SEQUENCE, which matters as much as the conclusion:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Be SURE of the technical facts** ← | **Verify the defect; obtain a second opinion if there is any doubt. An escalation based on an error is itself a serious harm** ← |
| **2. Inform the CLIENT, in WRITING, clearly** ← | **Stating the danger, the recommended action, and the engineer's professional obligation if it is not taken** ← |
| **3. Give the client a REASONABLE opportunity to act** | **Most clients do act once the position is put plainly and in writing** ← |
| **4. Escalate WITHIN the organisation if there is one** | **A superior, a director, a board** ← |
| **5. If the danger persists, REPORT to the appropriate authority** ← | **The building authority, the regulator, or the Engineering Council — the body with power to act** ← |
| **6. DOCUMENT every step contemporaneously** ← | **Dates, letters, meetings, and what was said** ← |

> **THE WRITTEN NOTICE IN STEP 2 IS THE MOST EFFECTIVE SINGLE ACTION AND IT IS OFTEN THE END OF THE MATTER: a client who has been told verbally may dismiss the concern; a client holding a signed letter setting out a danger to life understands their own exposure immediately.**

> **Most such situations resolve at that point, and the escalation is never needed.**

> **THE DOCUMENTATION IN STEP 6 PROTECTS EVERYONE, and it should be understood as more than self-protection: it establishes what was known, when, and what was done about it — which is what any subsequent investigation must determine, and which memory cannot supply.**

**What confidentiality DOES protect, so the exception is kept in proportion:**

| Protected | Note |
|---|---|
| **Commercial information, prices, tender strategy** ← | **Properly confidential, and disclosing it is a serious breach** ← |
| **Proprietary designs and methods** | ← |
| **The client's private business affairs** | ← |
| **NOT protected: information about a danger to life or health** ← | **Nor evidence of illegality** ← |

> **The exception is narrow and specific, and that is important: an engineer who treated confidentiality lightly, disclosing whenever they disagreed with a client, would be unemployable and rightly so.**

> **The duty is real and the exception is for danger — not for disagreement, not for a suspicion of poor value, and not for a difference of professional opinion about quality.**

> **Judging correctly which situation one is in is the substance of professional judgement here, and it is why the first step is to be certain of the facts. The rule is easy to state and the hard part is always the diagnosis, not the decision that follows it.**

Urge them to act, and if they still refuse, REPORT the matter to the appropriate authority.

examTip.trick: **Public safety is PARAMOUNT — it outranks confidentiality.** A confidentiality agreement cannot lawfully require concealment of a danger to life.
examTip.trap: **Resigning quietly (option c) feels honourable and achieves nothing** — the occupants remain in danger. And going straight to the public skips the channel that would probably have worked.
examTip.mnemonic: **A written letter to the client setting out the danger usually ends the matter** — a verbal warning is dismissed, a signed letter is not. Then document everything contemporaneously.

questions.stem: Under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, the Council may REMOVE an engineer's name from the register:
options: Only if the engineer ceases to pay the annual fee
At the request of any member of the public who is dissatisfied
Whenever the engineer changes employer
On being satisfied
questions.solution:
**On being satisfied, after due process, that the engineer has breached the code of ethics or professional conduct** — removal from the register being the Council's ultimate sanction.

**The graduated sanctions available:**

| Sanction | Note |
|---|---|
| **A WARNING or reprimand** | **For a minor or first breach** ← |
| **A direction to undertake further training or supervised practice** | **Remedial rather than punitive** ← |
| **SUSPENSION of registration for a period** ← | **The engineer may not practise during it** ← |
| **REMOVAL (striking off) from the register** ← | **The ultimate sanction — the person may no longer practise as an engineer at all** ← |
| **Referral to the police or the courts** | **Where a criminal offence may have been committed — the Council's jurisdiction is professional, not criminal** ← |

> **THE GRADATION IS DELIBERATE AND IMPORTANT: not every breach warrants ending a career, and a disciplinary system with only one penalty tends not to be used at all.**

> **A body that can only strike off will hesitate to act on a moderate breach, and the breach goes unaddressed — which is why the intermediate sanctions matter as much as the ultimate one.**

**DUE PROCESS, which is what makes the power legitimate:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The engineer must be INFORMED of the specific allegation** ← | **Not a vague complaint — the case must be stated** ← |
| **They must be given a fair OPPORTUNITY TO BE HEARD and to defend themselves** ← | **The fundamental principle of natural justice** ← |
| **The matter must be INVESTIGATED by a body competent to judge it** | **Usually a disciplinary committee including engineers** ← |
| **The decision must be REASONED and recorded** | ← |
| **There must be a right of APPEAL** ← | **To the full Council, or to a court** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SAFEGUARD AND IT PROTECTS THE PROFESSION AS WELL AS THE INDIVIDUAL: a disciplinary power exercised without a hearing would be a means of settling grievances rather than a means of maintaining standards.**

> **Option (b) is wrong precisely because of this — a member of the public may COMPLAIN, and the complaint triggers an investigation; it does not by itself remove anyone from anything.**

> **Options (a) and (c) confuse discipline with administration: non-payment of a fee is an administrative lapse dealt with by lapse or renewal, and changing employer has nothing to do with registration at all.**

**Typical grounds for disciplinary action:**

| Ground | Note |
|---|---|
| **Practising outside one's area of COMPETENCE** ← | ← |
| **CERTIFYING work not actually inspected, or known to be non-compliant** ← | **A serious and unfortunately common breach** ← |
| **Lending one's registration or SEAL to unqualified persons** ← | **Signing drawings prepared by someone unregistered — which defeats the entire purpose of registration** ← |
| **Undisclosed CONFLICT of interest** | ← |
| **Accepting or offering improper payments** | ← |
| **Gross negligence causing danger or loss** | ← |
| **Obtaining registration by false information** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESERVES PARTICULAR EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS SO WIDESPREAD AND SO OFTEN REGARDED AS TRIVIAL: an engineer who signs drawings or certificates prepared by an unregistered person, without genuinely reviewing and taking responsibility for them, has defeated the whole purpose of a professional register.**

> **The public's protection consists precisely in the fact that a competent, accountable person has taken responsibility for the work. A signature applied without that review is a false assurance, and it is worse than no signature at all — because it induces reliance where none is warranted.**

> **It also devalues every other engineer's signature, which is why the profession as a whole has an interest in it being taken seriously rather than tolerated as a convenience.**

> **AND THAT IS THE PROPER NOTE ON WHICH TO END THIS PAPER: registration, examination, licensing and discipline all exist for a single purpose, which is that when a member of the public relies on an engineer's judgement, that reliance should be justified.**

> **Everything in this syllabus — the mechanics, the materials, the hydraulics, the design codes and the ethics alike — serves that one end.**

Which is the Council's ultimate DISCIPLINARY sanction.

DUE PROCESS, that the engineer has acted contrary to the CODE OF ETHICS or professional conduct.

examTip.trick: **Removal is the ULTIMATE sanction, after due process, for a breach of the code of conduct** — with warning, retraining and suspension available below it.
examTip.trap: **A public complaint TRIGGERS an investigation; it does not remove anyone.** And non-payment of a fee or a change of employer are administrative matters, not disciplinary ones.
examTip.mnemonic: **Signing work you did not review defeats the whole purpose of a register** — the public's protection is that an accountable person took responsibility. A signature without review is worse than none: it induces reliance.
